bodyText: If you apportion utilities in a shared-metered building, Minnesota requires that you stay the bill payer and customer of record for the building; you may not apportion or bill tenants for electricity (it may only be submetered as the law allows); any administrative billing charge may not exceed $8 per billing period; a late charge on utilities billed separately from rent may not exceed $5 a month and may not compound; you must give tenants copies of the underlying bills on request; and you may not disconnect or cause disconnection of a tenant's service for nonpayment of utility charges (Minn. Stat. 504B.216). The required disclosure attachment is covered in "Required Utility Disclosure Attachment for Apportioned Billing".

title: Your Basic Habitability Duties
bodyText: Minnesota requires you to keep the property and common areas fit for the use the parties intended and in reasonable repair, including the services and conditions listed in Minn. Stat. 504B.381, subd. 1 (among them running water, hot water, heat, electricity, sanitary facilities and a refrigerator you provide; see "No Duty to Supply a Stove - But a Refrigerator Is on Minnesota's Emergency List"), heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit in all places meant for habitation, kitchens and bathrooms included, from October 1 through April 30 (unless a utility company requires it lowered), and extermination of insects, rodents, vermin and other pests (Minn. Stat. 504B.161). These duties don't apply to disrepair caused by the tenant's own willful, malicious or irresponsible conduct, or that of someone under the tenant's direction. You must also keep the property in compliance with health and safety laws, including any local rental-licensing ordinance, and make it reasonably energy efficient where that is cost-effective.

title: Tell Prospective Tenants About a Pending Foreclosure
bodyText: If you've received notice of a contract-for-deed cancellation or a mortgage foreclosure sale affecting the property, you must tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing the lease and before accepting rent or a deposit, including the date the cancellation period or redemption period ends (Minn. Stat. 504B.151). Until the contract is reinstated or paid, the default is cured, the mortgage is satisfied, the property is redeemed or a receiver is appointed, you may also only sign a periodic lease of no more than two months (or the time left in the cancellation or redemption period, if shorter) or a fixed-term lease that ends by the end of that period, unless the statute's exception for a longer lease applies. Breaking these rules makes you liable to the tenant for a $500 civil penalty, on top of the tenant's other remedies. Manufactured home parks are excluded (Minn. Stat. 504B.151, subd. 1). The lease's optional clause records that you gave the notice; the duty itself is owed before signing.

title: Minnesota Is Not a Just-Cause State, but Six Situations Still Block an Eviction
bodyText: Minnesota has no just-cause or good-cause eviction law for a tenancy under chapter 504B. A manufactured home park lot is different: Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.09, subd. 1 requires cause, and this lease is not for park lots (see the farm and park scope row). The end of the term is itself a ground: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.285 subd. 1(a)(2) lets you recover possession when a person holds over after the time for which the property was leased, and subd. 1(a)(3) covers a tenancy at will after a notice to quit. So a lease that says possession ends when the term ends is accurate here, unlike in a just-cause state. What Minnesota has instead is a set of situations where a particular eviction is blocked or delayed, and each one is worth knowing: you may not evict a tenant solely because they were the victim of the acts listed in Sec. 504B.206, or evict a tenant who terminated under that section, and doing so makes you liable for their attorney fees and expungement costs (Sec. 504B.285 subd. 1(b)); after a foreclosure the new owner (the immediate successor in interest) must give a tenant whose lease began after the mortgage at least 90 days' written notice to vacate, and must let a bona fide lease running more than 90 days past the redemption period run to its end unless the new owner or a later purchaser will live there, in each case while the tenant pays rent and keeps the lease (subd. 1a); after a contract for deed is cancelled, a tenant gets at least two months' written notice to vacate (subd. 1b); if you convert the building to a condominium or other common interest community, an occupant gets at least 120 days' notice and a right to buy (Sec. 515B.4-111; see "Converting a Rental Building to a Condominium or Other Common Interest Community"); retaliation is a defence, and if your notice to quit came within 90 days of the tenant's protected act the burden is on you (subd. 2); a rent increase or service cut used as a penalty is a defence to a nonpayment eviction if the tenant tenders the original rent (subd. 3); if the tenant has a Public Utilities Commission complaint pending about shared-metered gas or electricity, the court must stay a utility-nonpayment eviction and may not make the tenant post any money (subd. 4(b)); in a shared-metered building you may not bring a utility-nonpayment claim without first offering a payment plan, and may not file one for gas or electric charges from October 1 to April 30, for electric charges in a heat emergency, or during a certified medical emergency (Sec. 504B.216, subd. 12(d); see the utility-nonpayment eviction row); and retaliation for organising, or contacting law enforcement about a tenant's immigration status, carries up to $1,000 per occurrence plus fees (Sec. 504B.212 subd. 2). There is also a long-stop: no eviction may be brought against an occupant whose lease ended more than three years ago who has been in quiet possession for three consecutive years (Sec. 504B.311).

title: When the Tenant Causes the Damage: What Minnesota Gives You, and What It Doesn't
bodyText:
If a tenant, an occupant or a guest damages the home badly enough to make it uninhabitable, Minnesota helps you in three narrow ways and leaves the rest to your lease.

First, the tenant's own right to walk away does not apply: under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.131 a tenant may vacate and surrender a destroyed or uninhabitable building only if that happened 'through no fault or neglect of the tenant or occupant', so a tenant at fault stays on the lease and the rent keeps running. Second, your repair duty is excused for the damage itself -- Sec. 504B.161 subd. 1(a)(2) and (4) lift the repair and code-compliance covenants for disrepair caused by the tenant's willful, malicious or irresponsible conduct. Read that narrowly: the fitness covenant, the energy-efficiency duty and the 68-degree heat duty have no fault exception, so you still owe heat even where the tenant broke it. Third, Sec. 504B.165 gives you a damages action, with costs and attorney fees -- but only for 'willful and malicious' destruction.

The gap is negligence. A carelessly frozen pipe is neither willful nor malicious, so there is no statutory action, and because 'irresponsible' is not the same word, you may still owe the repair. That is why the library offers a tenant-caused-damage clause: it is the only place rent during repairs and lost rent after an early ending come from. Document the cause and keep your re-rental efforts, because Sec. 504B.154 makes mitigation a duty.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession, but a Three-Year Eviction Long-Stop
bodyText: Minnesota writes no covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession into residential leases. The covenants Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161 imposes are fitness for the intended use, reasonable repair including pest extermination, energy efficiency, compliance with health and safety law, and the 68-degree heat minimum -- quiet enjoyment is not among them, and is a matter of common law and of whatever your lease says. One related provision is worth knowing because it runs against you: under Sec. 504B.311 no eviction action may be brought against an occupant whose lease, or whose predecessor's lease, was terminated more than three years before the action, where that occupant or their predecessor was in quiet possession for the three consecutive years immediately before the filing. In other words a terminated tenancy you never acted on can harden into possession you cannot evict. Act on a termination; do not let three years pass.

title: Minnesota Supplies Five Pieces of Text You Must Reproduce
bodyText: Minnesota is a state where the statute writes the words for you in several places, and getting them wrong has consequences. The 14-day pre-eviction notice for nonpayment must contain three statements in the statute's own words -- about the right to legal help, about applying for financial help, and about the landlord's ability to file after 14 days (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.321 subd. 1a(a)(4) to (6)); a missing or defective notice means the court dismisses your case and expunges the file. A tenant terminating for violence may verify it with a Statement by Qualified Third Party on the form reproduced verbatim in Sec. 504B.206 subd. 6(3), and a police report is not on the closed list of five acceptable documents. If you apportion gas or water in a shared-metered building, Sec. 504B.216 subd. 10 requires a close-to-verbatim disclosure attached to the lease. And Sec. 504B.275 requires the Attorney General's statement of tenant rights and responsibilities to be available on request, with notice of that posted on the property. In an eviction from HUD Section 9 public housing alleging a breach of lease, Sec. 504B.268, subd. 1 requires the complaint's first page to carry, in bold 12-point type: 'If financially unable to obtain counsel, the defendant has the right to a court-appointed attorney.' Use the statutory wording rather than your own paraphrase in all five.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Law in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute restricting the use of algorithmic or software-assisted rent-setting, and no disclosure duty if you use one. Several states have begun legislating here, so treat this as a live watch item rather than a settled answer, and remember that using a shared pricing service with competitors can raise antitrust questions that have nothing to do with landlord-tenant law.

title: Minnesota Does Not Let You Redefine Fees as Rent
bodyText: No Minnesota statute lets a lease designate fees as rent, and you should not assume the label carries. Two things push the other way. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.177 says a late fee 'is not considered to be either interest or liquidated damages'. And Sec. 504B.172 is the one place the statutes recognise fees recovered 'directly, or through additional rent' -- and it uses that phrase to trigger attorney-fee reciprocity for the tenant, so dressing a fee up as rent there works against you rather than for you. Minnesota's pre-eviction notice reaches 'nonpayment of rent or other unpaid financial obligation in violation of the lease' (Sec. 504B.321 subd. 1a), so you can give notice for unpaid fees -- but the library's default clause still provides that failing to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the rent itself, does not by itself support termination or eviction.

title: No Right to Cure the Tenant's Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Minnesota has no provision like the uniform act's self-help repair rule, so you have no statutory right to perform a tenant's obligation, bill the cost, and collect it as rent. Minnesota is not a uniform-act state: its landlord duties sit in Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161 and its tenant obligations are narrow and conduct-specific rather than a general duty list. If you want the ability to do the work and charge for it, it has to come from your lease as a contract term, and the charge is a contract debt, not rent -- which matters, because an unpaid fee is not a nonpayment-of-rent ground on its own.

title: No Statutory Rule Against Blank Spaces in a Minnesota Lease
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute requiring every blank space in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, and no minimum type size for a lease. There is such a rule in Minnesota law, but it does not reach you: the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act requires all blank spaces filled before execution and a minimum eight-point type (Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.87), and that Act governs rent-to-own agreements for personal property -- Sec. 325F.84 defines 'personal property' as property that is not real property. Leaving blanks is still a bad idea, because the Plain Language Contract Act requires a clear and coherent lease and Sec. 504B.115 gives the tenant a defence if you never gave them a copy. Fill the blanks and hand over a copy.

title: No Statute on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute giving a tenant the right to install a security camera or video doorbell, and none letting you prohibit one. It is a matter for your lease, read alongside the alterations clause, and for the general criminal privacy law at Minn. Stat. Sec. 609.746, which makes surreptitious observation or recording in a place where a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy an offence regardless of who installed the device. If you permit a camera, be clear in writing about where it may point and who may see the recordings.

title: You May Not Keep a Political Candidate Out of a Multi-Unit Building
bodyText: If you own or manage an apartment house or any other multiple-unit residence, Minn. Stat. Sec. 211B.20 makes it unlawful to deny access to a candidate who has organised a campaign committee, filed a financial report, or filed an affidavit of candidacy -- and the candidate may bring campaign volunteers. The candidate must be seeking the office that represents the building's district, and must be there only to campaign or register voters. Once in, they must be allowed to knock on individual doors and leave materials at them. Where there are several buildings they may visit more than one in a single visit, one at a time. A violation is a petty misdemeanour. What you may still do: refuse entry to a particular unit, require reasonable identification, require an appointment, limit visits to a reasonable number of people and reasonable hours provided 9:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. is allowed at a minimum, and deny or remove someone for good cause. Check your no-solicitation rule against this, because a blanket ban on canvassers would violate it.

title: No Penalty for Knowingly Using a Prohibited Lease Term
bodyText: Minnesota does not punish you for including a prohibited term in a lease. There is no provision making the knowing use of a void clause an offence or a source of statutory damages, which is a meaningful difference from states that do. What happens instead is that the term is simply void: Chapter 504B contains more than thirty separate non-waiver sentences, worded in several ways ('contrary to public policy and void', 'void and unenforceable', 'may not be waived or modified'), so the clause fails and the rest of the lease stands. That is why a saving sentence is worth having here. Two exposures are not about the term but about what you do: bad-faith retention of a deposit, bad-faith interference with tenant organising, ouster, and mishandling a tenant's property each carry their own damages, and a Plain Language Contract Act violation can be enforced under Minn. Stat. Sec. 8.31.

title: Minnesota Has No Accessory Dwelling Unit Law, Only a Funding Incentive
bodyText:
Minnesota has not done what West Virginia and Massachusetts did. No Minnesota statute makes one accessory dwelling unit permitted by right, stops a city restricting one, bars an owner-occupancy requirement, or protects the rental of one. Whether you may build or rent an accessory dwelling unit is decided by the zoning ordinance of the city or county the property sits in.

What the legislature did instead is pay cities to allow them, and it is worth knowing because it tells you which way Minnesota policy is moving. Laws 2025, ch. 32, sec. 13, headed LOCAL ACTIONS TO SUPPORT HOUSING, directs the commissioner of the Housing Finance Agency, where practicable, to award an additional point or points, not to exceed five percent of the total available points in a given competitive development program, to proposals in competitive capital development programs located in a jurisdiction that meets any of eight listed criteria. The second criterion is that 'the jurisdiction allows for duplexes, accessory dwelling units, or townhomes within 50 percent of the area within the jurisdiction zoned for single-family housing, excluding areas covered by state or local shoreland regulations'. Others on the list include no parking mandate above one stall per unit, no mandated lot size larger than one-eighth of an acre for new single-family construction, no aesthetic mandates on new single-family construction, a density bonus for affordable housing, and an adopted inclusionary zoning policy.

Read its limits carefully before you rely on it. It binds the agency's scoring, not any city. It creates no right to build or rent an accessory dwelling unit anywhere. It reaches developers competing for agency capital, not an ordinary landlord. It is effective the day following final enactment and applies to selection criteria and scoring systems developed on or after that day. And it expires on December 31, 2029.

Two Minnesota rules do bite on an accessory dwelling unit you already rent out. First, you cannot push the upkeep of the shared parts of the lot onto the tenant: Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subd. 1(a) covenants that the premises 'and all common areas' are fit for the use intended and in reasonable repair, subd. 1(b) says the parties may not waive or modify those covenants, and subd. 2 says no tenant-maintenance agreement may relieve you of the duty to maintain common areas. Second, watch the meter. If the accessory dwelling unit and the primary residence are separate dwelling units in the same building and one meter serves both, you may be running a shared-metered residential building under Minn. Stat. section 504B.216, which brings a billing, disclosure and apportionment regime with its own non-waivable provisions. Get the metering right before you write a utilities clause.

title: No Agreed Notice Method - the Statute's Method Wins, and One Flexibility Runs the Tenant's Way
bodyText: Minnesota has no rule letting the lease add a method of giving notice -- no provision saying the parties may agree that a text message, an email or a tenant portal counts where the law requires notice. Minnesota works the other way round: each statute names its own method, and where a statute names one, that method is what you have to use. A lease clause designating email or a portal does not satisfy a statute that names something else, and a lease cannot downgrade a statutory written notice to a verbal one. Two rows in this library carry the detail and are where to go next: the notice-delivery-methods row sets out, notice by notice, which method each Minnesota statute requires, and the written-notice row covers the form question. There is one place Minnesota is flexible, and it runs the tenant's way, not yours. A tenant ending the lease because they fear imminent violence may deliver the required written notice by mail, in person, or by a form of written communication the tenant regularly uses to communicate with you -- which does include email or text if that is how you two normally deal. Notice what that tells you: the legislature wrote an express permission when it wanted one, and wrote none for the landlord. Two more cautions. Where a statute names certified mail, first class is not a substitute: the automatic-renewal notice and the abandoned-property sale notice both require more than ordinary post. And several of these notices carry hard consequences for getting delivery wrong, including dismissal and expungement of an eviction for a defective 14-day notice. Practical rule: build your lease's notice section around the statute's method, keep a record of how and when you sent each notice, and never let a convenient electronic channel replace a method a statute names. If you want the tenant's agreement to deal electronically for everything the law does NOT prescribe a method for, get it as a separate signed agreement and expect it to bind only so far as the electronic-transactions law allows.

title: The Tenant Owes You No Notice - but You Owe One Before You Sign
bodyText:
Minnesota puts no duty on a tenant to tell you about a proceeding against your property, so if you want that you have to ask for it in the lease; the library offers an optional clause for it. Two Minnesota cautions on how to word it. Do not tell the tenant flatly to pay rent to nobody but you. After a foreclosure or a contract for deed cancellation a tenant can become the holder's tenant by operation of law, and owes rent to the holder once the holder mails written notice of succeeding to your interest. And if a court appoints an administrator in a tenant remedies action, your right to collect rent is void and unenforceable until the administration ends, from your tenants as well as from the petitioner.

The duties running the other way are real and are yours. Before you sign a lease and before you take any rent or deposit, if you have received notice of a contract for deed cancellation or a mortgage foreclosure sale, you must tell the prospective tenant in writing and give the date the cancellation or redemption period ends. Until the matter is cured you may also only grant a short lease. Breaking that costs a $500 civil penalty per tenant, on top of their other remedies, and manufactured home parks are excluded.

Note what that duty does not say: it is a pre-lease duty, so a foreclosure notice arriving during a sitting tenancy triggers no statutory duty to tell that tenant. Telling them anyway is the better course. After a foreclosure the buyer owes a sitting tenant at least 90 days' written notice to vacate, and a bona fide lease running more than 90 days past the redemption period generally gets to run out.

If you own a manufactured home park, you have separate and much heavier notice duties on a park closing or a sale.

title: No Alarm-Tampering Fee in Minnesota; Charge Your Actual Cost
bodyText:
No Minnesota statute authorises, sets or caps a fee for a tenant who removes or tampers with a smoke alarm or a carbon monoxide alarm, so the library does not offer a set tampering fee. Minnesota handles tampering through duties and public penalties instead. No person may remove the batteries from, or in any way render inoperable, a required carbon monoxide alarm; a first violation brings a safety warning and a later one is a petty misdemeanour. An occupant who willfully disables a smoke alarm, or causes it to be nonfunctioning, and so causes damage or injury is guilty of a misdemeanour. Those penalties are the state's, not yours.

What you may charge is your actual reasonable cost of repairing or replacing the alarm, which the optional clause in this library does. In a multifamily building the occupant must also replace any carbon monoxide alarm that is stolen, removed, missing or rendered inoperable during their own occupancy.

Keep the charge to real cost: the deposit may be held back only in amounts reasonably necessary to remedy a default in paying funds due under an agreement or to restore the premises to their move-in condition, and Minnesota sets no liquidated-damages figure for a lease breach.

Do not charge a tampering fee for a smoke alarm you were responsible for maintaining anyway, and remember that your tenant's failure to report a nonfunctioning smoke alarm within 24 hours does not increase their liability for damages. A city may adopt stricter single-family smoke-alarm installation rules.

title: No Duty to Rehouse - Minnesota Abates the Rent or Redirects It Instead
bodyText: Minnesota does not make you rehouse a tenant or pay relocation costs when a unit becomes unusable. There is exactly one alternative-housing duty in the landlord-tenant act, and it is about a different situation: if new construction will not be ready by the lease's move-in date, you must notify every affected tenant within seven days and offer three options at the tenant's choice, one of which is alternative housing you provide that is reasonably equivalent in size, amenities and location (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.153). That duty, its reimbursement limb and its remedies are covered under the possession-delay topic and are not repeated here. Outside that, Minnesota's answer to an unusable unit is to let the tenant leave and to put the money under the court's control, not to make you find a bed. A tenant or occupant of a building that is destroyed or becomes uninhabitable or unfit for occupancy through no fault or neglect of the tenant may vacate and surrender it (Sec. 504B.131). The tenant may expressly agree otherwise, but only so far as Sec. 504B.161 permits, and Sec. 504B.161's covenants cannot be waived. The pressure comes from three remedies. A tenant may deposit rent with the court administrator in a rent escrow action (Sec. 504B.385), and those rights may not be waived or modified. For an emergency - a serious infestation, or loss of running water, hot water, heat, electricity or sanitary facilities, among others - a tenant may petition for emergency relief (Sec. 504B.381). And in a tenant remedies action the court has wide discretion: it may order you to fix the violation, order the tenant to fix it and deduct the cost from rent, abate the rent to the extent the violation impairs the tenant's use and enjoyment, keep jurisdiction over the building for a year after administration ends, and award the tenant attorney fees of up to $500 (Sec. 504B.425). The sharpest consequence is the administrator. The court may appoint one and direct that rents be paid to the administrator instead of to you, to be spent on debt service, taxes, insurance and the services you were obliged to provide. Once that happens your right to collect rent is void and unenforceable until the administration ends. Watch the two different start dates: for the tenant who petitioned, from the day the court signs the order for judgment; for every other tenant in the building, only from the time the judgment is served (Sec. 504B.435). So the practical planning point is not a relocation budget. It is that an unrepaired habitability problem can end with the tenant lawfully gone, the rent abated, or the rent going to someone else entirely. Manufactured home parks are different: a park closing triggers a statutory compensation scheme funded by a relocation trust fund, and this lease is the wrong instrument for a park lot.

title: No Right to Enter for a Tenant's Animal - and Three Animal Rules That Do Bind You
bodyText:
Minnesota gives you no animal-care entry right. There is no provision letting you go in to feed or water an animal, none letting you take custody of one, and none making a tenant's absent animal an emergency by itself. What you have is Minn. Stat. section 504B.211 and whatever the tenant agreed to in the lease.

Work the entry section honestly. Subd. 3's list of reasonable business purposes is open - it 'includes, but is not limited to' the nine named - so attending to an animal left without care can be a reasonable business purpose. But the purpose is not the notice. Unless subd. 4 applies you still owe a good faith effort at not less than 24 hours' notice, with a stated time or window, between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. Subd. 4 is the only no-notice route: you may enter if you reasonably suspect that immediate entry is necessary to prevent injury to persons or property because of conditions relating to maintenance, building security or law enforcement, or to determine a residential tenant's safety, or to comply with local ordinances about unlawful activity. A dog shut in an empty unit for days, barking and without water, is a plausible subd. 4 case on both the injury and the welfare-check limbs - but it is your judgement and it has to be reasonable, and if you enter when the tenant is not present without prior notice, subd. 5 requires you to leave a written disclosure of the entry in a conspicuous place. The safer route in a real case is the one anyone else would take: call an animal control officer, who is the officer Minnesota's own definition names for the job.

Three animal rules do bind you and all three are easy to trip over. First, service and support animals are not pets. Minn. Stat. section 504B.113 lets you ask for documentation from a licensed professional only where the disability or the need is not readily apparent, bars you from asking for medical records, and prohibits any additional fee, charge or deposit for the animal; subd. 3(b) makes a disclosure of that prohibition mandatory in the lease whenever you charge any pet fee, charge or deposit, and subd. 3(c) lets the tenant sue to recover pet fees paid if you left the disclosure out. Second, you may not require declawing or devocalization. Minn. Stat. section 504B.114, subd. 2 reaches advertising, refusing occupancy and requiring the procedure, and says 'Any requirement or lease provision that violates this subdivision is void and unenforceable', with civil penalties up to $1,000 per advertisement or per animal enforceable by a city, county or the attorney general. Its 'application for occupancy' covers all phases of applying, so a screening question is caught as surely as a lease term. Third, in a multiunit residential building a tenant of a disability accessible unit whose rent responsibility is reduced or eliminated by a subsidy must be allowed two birds, or one spayed or neutered dog, or one spayed or neutered cat, under Minn. Stat. section 504B.261. You may require a reasonable additional animal damage deposit, refundable to the extent it exceeds the damage the animal actually caused, and the tenant may not keep or have visits from an animal that threatens the health or safety of others or causes a noise nuisance - but a blanket no-pets rule does not reach that tenant.

Practical version: ask for a named animal caretaker in the lease and use it, treat a genuine welfare emergency as a subd. 4 entry and document why, and call animal control rather than handling the animal yourself.

title: You Need Not Supply an Appliance, But You Cannot Disclaim One You Do
bodyText:
Minnesota does not make you supply any appliance, so an exclusion clause is lawful here. It is also narrower than it looks, for one reason: your habitability covenants cannot be waived or modified by either party, and they reach more than most landlords expect. The covenant is to keep the premises and all common areas fit for the use the parties intended and in reasonable repair, including the services and conditions listed in Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.381, subd. 1 (Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1).

That incorporated list is where the hard limits live. It covers running water, hot water, heat, electricity, sanitary facilities, a serious infestation and a nonfunctioning refrigerator, and it closes with any condition, service or facility posing a serious and negative impact on health or safety, and other essential services or facilities. You cannot exclude any of that, however the clause is worded, and you must also furnish heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit from October 1 through April 30.

So the exclusion you can actually rely on is a small one. Use it for an appliance a prior occupant left behind, or one the tenant brings, and not for anything you hand over. An appliance you actually supply is inside the covenant whatever the lease says. The cleanest course for an item you do not want to maintain is to take it out before the tenancy starts rather than leave it with a disclaimer attached.

Three practical points. Do not charge for an excluded item: if you did, it would be a fee for something you do not supply, and every nonoptional fee has to be disclosed in the lease and counted in the first-page Total Monthly Payment (Sec. 504B.120). Record each excluded item at move-in, with photographs, because the argument later is about what you supplied. And Minnesota does have one narrow way to move repair work to the tenant: an agreement that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance, but only if it is supported by adequate consideration and set out in a conspicuous writing, and it can neither waive your covenants nor relieve you of maintaining common areas (Sec. 504B.161, subd. 2). That is a different instrument from an exclusion clause, and the library does not offer it.

title: Asbestos in Minnesota Rentals: A Ban and a Licence, No Disclosure
bodyText: Minnesota has asbestos law, but none of it makes you disclose asbestos to a tenant, test for it, or give notice before work that disturbs it. There is no Minnesota counterpart to the federal lead-paint disclosure. Two layers do apply to you. FIRST, A FLAT BAN. Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.01, subd. 1 bars any person, corporation, partnership, joint venture, firm or association from using, selling, delivering or receiving, or contracting to use, sell, deliver or receive, powdered asbestos 'whether in its powdered form or mixed with any other substance, and to be applied with a pressure sprayer, or in its molded form if asbestos dust will emanate from it due to handling, mixing or cutting, for purposes of constructing, remodeling or improving any building structure in this state.' A violation is a misdemeanor (subd. 2). SECOND, ASBESTOS WORK IS A LICENSED TRADE. Minnesota's asbestos licensing and project-permit rules sit in chapter 326; the 2025 act that amended them shows the shape of the duty. As amended, 'Any person performing any asbestos-related work within the state must be licensed by the commissioner, whether directly performing asbestos work or causing it to be performed through subcontracting or similar delegation,' and the only exemption is 'a domiciled owner of a single-family residence' doing the work in the residence they live in. A landlord is not that owner, so asbestos-related work in your rental must go to a licensed person, and a project permit fee is due five calendar days before the work begins. WHAT TO DO. Before any renovation, repair or demolition in an older building, have suspect materials (old floor tile, pipe and boiler insulation, cement sheeting, textured ceiling) assessed, and use a licensed asbestos contractor. Do not conceal damaged asbestos you know about: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) makes you covenant that the premises are fit for the use intended, that you will keep them in reasonable repair, and that you will maintain them in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state and of local government including rental licensing ordinances. Those covenants cannot be waived or modified by the parties (subd. 1(b)). And if an asbestos problem becomes a housing-inspection citation or a condemnation order, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195 makes you hand a copy to a person before they sign a lease or pay rent or a deposit, a duty a lease cannot waive.

title: No Minnesota Duty to Disclose Association Obligations, but Attach the Rules Anyway
bodyText:
Minnesota does not make you disclose an association's obligations, declaration, bylaws or rules to your tenant, and does not require any association statement in the lease. There is nothing of that kind in Minn. Stat. ch. 504B. So Minnesota has no analogue to Maryland's Montgomery County lease disclosure or to Puerto Rico's requirement that a condominium lease carry the owner's statement that it knows the condominium law and bylaws with a copy to the board.

THAT SAID, DISCLOSE THEM ANYWAY, as a matter of drafting rather than compliance. If your tenant is bound in practice by an association's parking, pet, noise, appearance or short-term-letting rules, those rules are terms the tenant needs before signing, and they are yours to pass on because the association is not a party to your lease. Attach them as an addendum and say in the lease that they are attached -- see addendum-precedence.

One Minnesota rule to watch while you do it: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.120 subd. 1 requires all nonoptional fees to be disclosed in the lease and the sum of rent and nonoptional fees to appear on the first page as the Total Monthly Payment, with treble damages under subd. 2 if you get it wrong -- so any association charge your tenant must pay belongs in that disclosure, not buried in an attached rule book.

Minnesota's common interest community laws are Minn. Stat. ch. 515B, and the older condominium acts in ch. 515 and ch. 515A that still govern parts of older condominiums. None makes a landlord disclose association documents to a tenant. Their tenant rules bind or protect the tenant directly. Minn. Stat. Sec. 515B.3-102(a)(1) lets an association adopt rules regulating the 'conduct of unit occupants'. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 515.28, tenants of an older condominium's owners 'shall be subject to' that act and to the association's declaration and bylaws. From January 1, 2027, Minn. Stat. Sec. 515B.3-107(f) limits an association's power over a tenant's parking on a public street and lets a resident park in the space designed for the unit's parking.

The disclosure duties chapter 515B does impose run from a unit owner to a PURCHASER, not to a tenant: Minn. Stat. Sec. 515B.4-107, as amended by Laws 2026, ch. 82, sec. 12, makes a unit owner reselling a unit furnish a resale disclosure certificate before any purchase agreement is signed, and the statutory form the act prints begins with the association's statement that there is no right of first refusal or other restraint on the free alienability of the unit except as stated. Your own declaration or the association's rules may still require you to give the tenant the rules or register the lease; that comes from those documents, not from state law, so read them.

title: Two Renewal Rules: a Certified-Mail Notice Window, and No Asking More Than Six Months Early
bodyText:
Minnesota lets a lease renew automatically, but puts two separate limits on renewals and you can lose the clause entirely by missing one of them.

The first limit is about enforcing an automatic-renewal clause. If the lease had an original term of two months or more, and renews for two months or more unless the tenant gives notice of an intention to quit, you cannot enforce that renewal unless you give the tenant a separate written notice drawing their attention to the renewal provision. The notice has to be served personally or sent by CERTIFIED mail -- first class is not enough -- and it has to land in a window: at least 15 days, and not more than 30 days, before the day the tenant's notice of an intention to quit is due.

Note that both ends matter. A notice sent two months ahead is as useless as one sent a week ahead, and the window is measured from the tenant's notice deadline, not from the end of the term. Miss it and the renewal clause simply cannot be enforced against the tenant; the term ends when it says it ends.

The second limit is about asking too early. On a lease running longer than ten months, you may not require the tenant to renew sooner than six months before the current lease expires, and any lease provision waiving that is contrary to public policy and void. Nothing stops you waiting until closer to expiry and simply asking. Keep the tenant's notice-of-intention-to-quit deadline comfortably inside six months of the end date, or a long deadline on a twelve-month lease starts to look like requiring an early renewal.

One more rule ties the two together: a notice of nonrenewal counts as a notice to quit, and your notice can never be shorter than the notice your lease asks the tenant to give you.

title: No Minnesota Balcony or Deck Inspection Statute
bodyText: Minnesota has no balcony inspection law. There is no periodic inspection interval, no engineer or architect certification, no filing with a state agency and no tenant notice tied to balconies, decks, landings, stairs or elevated walkways. If you were expecting something like California's exterior elevated element inspections, Minnesota does not have it. WHAT DOES APPLY, AND IT IS NOT NOTHING. Your balcony is caught by three general duties. First, the habitability covenant. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) covenants that "the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended by the parties" and that you will "keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair during the term of the lease or license" and "maintain the premises and all common areas in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state, and of the local units of government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing". Subd. 1(b) says the parties "may not waive or modify" those covenants, and subd. 3 says the section is liberally construed and that the chance to inspect before signing does not defeat the covenants. A balcony in a shared building is normally a common area, and subd. 2's final sentence is explicit that no tenant maintenance agreement may "relieve the landlord or licensor of the duty to maintain common areas of the premises". So you cannot hand balcony upkeep to a tenant. Second, the construction and fire codes. Structural and guard requirements for balconies and decks live in the State Building Code and the State Fire Code, which are rules and not statutes; they are where the actual railing height, load and guard specifications sit. Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.011, subd. 4 makes the State Fire Code applicable throughout the state and lets a local unit adopt requirements "equal to, in addition to, or more stringent than" it. Third, enforcement comes to you through code inspection, not through a scheduled balcony inspection. A failing balcony is a "violation" within Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.001, subd. 14(1) -- a violation of any state, county or city health, safety, housing, building, fire prevention or housing maintenance code applicable to the building -- which opens the inspection route in Sec. 504B.185, rent escrow in Sec. 504B.385 and the tenant remedies action in Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471. A collapsing balcony would also sit inside Sec. 504B.381, subd. 1(2)(x), "any conditions, services, or facilities that pose a serious and negative impact on health or safety", which is the 24-hour emergency route. WHERE THE REAL REQUIREMENT WILL BE: your city's property maintenance or housing code. Minneapolis, Saint Paul and many other Minnesota cities run rental licensing and periodic inspection programmes whose checklists cover porches, decks, stairs and guards. Read your own city's code, and in the meantime inspect and document elevated structures yourself on a schedule you set, because the habitability covenant will be measured against what a reasonable owner would have found. ONE 2026 CHANGE THAT IS NOT YOURS: Laws 2026, ch. 127 added family child care programme standards requiring that decks, balconies or lofts used by children more than 30 inches above the ground or floor be surrounded by a protective guardrail built to the State Building Code. That is a licensing duty on the child care provider. If your tenant runs a licensed family child care programme in your unit, it binds the tenant, not you -- but it may require work on your building, so it is worth knowing before a provider asks.

title: Pests Are Your Problem in Minnesota, and the Escape Hatch Is Narrow
bodyText:
Extermination is a Minnesota landlord's duty by statute, in every residential lease, whether or not the lease says so. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(2) covenants that you will keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair "including services and conditions listed in section 504B.381, subdivision 1, and extermination of insects, rodents, vermin, or other pests on the premises". The covenant applies to every lease or licence concluded or renewed on or after June 15, 1971, so it catches every live tenancy. You cannot contract out: subd. 1(b) says "[t]he parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section", subd. 3 says the section is liberally construed and that the chance to inspect before signing does not defeat the covenants, and subd. 4 says the covenants are in addition to anything imposed by law, ordinance or the lease itself.

THE EXCEPTION IS NARROWER THAN LANDLORDS EXPECT. The covenant does not apply where the disrepair "has been caused by the willful, malicious, or irresponsible conduct of the tenant or licensee or a person under the direction or control of the tenant or licensee". Three words, and none of them is "negligent". A tenant who unknowingly brought bed bugs home in a suitcase has not been willful, malicious or irresponsible, so the bill is yours. Do not borrow the test from a neighbouring section: Sec. 504B.415(2) says "willful, malicious, negligent, or irresponsible" and Sec. 504B.381, subd. 6 says "deliberate or negligent", but neither governs this covenant. If you want to charge a tenant, you are proving irresponsibility at least -- hoarding that defeats treatment, repeated refusal to prepare the unit, repeated refusal of entry. Document it.

YOU CAN AGREE THAT A TENANT DOES SOME WORK, BUT ONLY ON TERMS. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 2 permits an agreement that the tenant performs specified repairs or maintenance "but only if the agreement is supported by adequate consideration and set forth in a conspicuous writing", and "[n]o such agreement, however, may waive the provisions of subdivision 1 or relieve the landlord or licensor of the duty to maintain common areas of the premises". So you may not hand a tenant responsibility for extermination, and you certainly may not hand over the common areas -- which in an infestation is the whole point, because bed bugs and roaches move between units.

WHAT HAPPENS IF YOU DO NOT TREAT. A serious infestation is an express emergency. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.381, subd. 1(2)(i) lists "a serious infestation" first among the emergency conditions, so a tenant can petition the district court on 24 hours' attempted notice -- or with no notice at all if the court finds reasonable efforts to notify you failed -- and the court "shall order that the landlord immediately begin to remedy the violation" and may order any relief available under Sec. 504B.425, including appointing an administrator to collect the rents and do the work.

Your defence is in subd. 6: the section does not extend to emergencies resulting from "the deliberate or negligent act or omission of a residential tenant or anyone acting under the direction or control of the residential tenant" -- note that this test IS wider than the repair covenant's and does include negligence. Short of an emergency, a tenant can require a code inspection under Sec. 504B.185, escrow rent under Sec. 504B.385, or bring the tenant remedies action under Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471; and once a court order to remedy is in place, willful failure to comply carries the escalating fines and gross misdemeanour in "Fines and a Gross Misdemeanour for Ignoring a Repair Order".

DO NOT PENALISE THE COMPLAINT. Sec. 504B.441 says a tenant may not be evicted, nor the tenant's lease obligations increased or services decreased, as a penalty for complaining of a violation, and if that happens within 90 days of the complaint the burden of proving otherwise is on you. Raising a pest-treatment charge right after a complaint is exactly the shape of that problem.

NO DISCLOSURE, NO NOTICE PERIOD, NO TIMELINE. Minnesota sets no bed bug disclosure duty, no treatment deadline and no pre-treatment notice to tenants -- see "No Bed Bug Disclosure Statute in Minnesota" and "No Minnesota Pre-Treatment Pesticide Notice for Rentals". What it sets is an unwaivable duty with a fast court route attached, which in practice is stricter than a disclosure form.

title: No Arbitration Provision Anywhere in the Landlord-Tenant Act
bodyText:
Nothing in Minnesota's landlord-tenant act mentions arbitration. Chapter 504B contains no arbitration provision at all — no authorisation for a lease arbitration clause, no carve-out keeping possession actions in court, no preservation of the right to counsel, and no prohibition.

Arbitration does appear in Minnesota law, but nowhere that reaches a residential lease.

Minn. Stat. § 484.73 lets a majority of the judges of a judicial district establish "a system of mandatory, nonbinding arbitration within the district", and provides that "The Uniform Arbitration Act shall not be construed to apply to arbitration under this section except as otherwise provided in the rules of the judicial district." Minn. Stat. § 484.76 requires rules for alternative dispute resolution in civil cases, and says the methods "must be nonbinding unless otherwise agreed to in a valid agreement between the parties". Both are court-annexed programmes a judge runs, not something a lease can invoke.

Minn. Stat. § 327C.095, subd. 6 appoints a "qualified neutral third party" to act "as a paymaster and arbitrator" over contributions to and disbursements from the manufactured home relocation trust fund when a park closes. That is a park-closing mechanism, not a lease clause, and it is manufactured-home-park law.

Minn. Stat. § 325F.665 is the motor-vehicle lemon law's informal dispute settlement mechanism, whose decision "is nonbinding on the parties involved, unless otherwise agreed". Minn. Stat. § 325F.987 concerns private label goods, Minn. Stat. § 523.24 is the statutory short-form power of attorney, and Minn. Stat. § 363A.28, subd. 3(b) suspends the Human Rights Act limitation period while the parties are in a dispute resolution process. None is a lease rule.

One thing worth knowing, from the Human Rights Act. Minn. Stat. § 363A.31, subd. 1 voids a prospective waiver of a Human Rights Act right in "a lease, contract, or other agreement or instrument" — and the Revisor prints a note under the section recording that subdivision 1 "was found preempted by federal law with regard to arbitration agreements". So Minnesota's one statutory bar on waiving a discrimination claim has already met the Federal Arbitration Act and lost on that ground. Read that as a warning about how an arbitration question is likely to be analysed here, not as authority.

The general arbitration act. Whether an arbitration clause in a Minnesota residential lease is enforceable is governed by Minnesota's arbitration act, Minn. Stat. ch. 572B, and by the Federal Arbitration Act. Chapter 572B was read whole. It has no exclusion for leases, consumers, or personal injury or tort claims, and it says nothing about eviction actions. Under Minn. Stat. § 572B.06(a), an agreement in a record to arbitrate a later controversy is "valid, enforceable, and irrevocable except upon a ground that exists at law or in equity for the revocation of contract." Before a dispute arises, Minn. Stat. § 572B.04(b)(4) bars waiving a party's right to be represented by a lawyer. Whether such a clause can displace the summary eviction procedure, or would fail as unconscionable in a residential lease, only case law could settle.

Where that leaves you. Minnesota neither blesses nor bans a lease arbitration clause in its landlord-tenant act, and its general arbitration act would treat a written clause like any other contract term, subject to the open questions above. Do not add an arbitration clause to a Minnesota lease on the strength of this entry. If you want one, it needs the Federal Arbitration Act and Minnesota case law looked at properly by a lawyer. The cautious course is to keep possession actions in court — and note that an eviction is a summary proceeding under Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.281 to 504B.371 with its own expedited timetable, which an arbitration clause may well not be able to displace. The library now offers an optional clause, "Binding Arbitration of Money Claims" clause, built on these limits: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury and emergency claims kept in court, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

title: No Minnesota Carpet-Cleaning Rule, and What the Deposit May Cover
bodyText:
Minnesota has no statute about carpet cleaning: nothing requires it, nothing permits a cleaning fee, and there is no condition-and-age test for carpet or paint deductions of the kind some states use. The deposit statute does the work instead, and its list is closed. You may hold back only amounts reasonably necessary either to remedy the tenant's default in paying rent or other funds due to you under an agreement, or to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, with ordinary wear and tear excepted. In any dispute you carry the burden of proving why you withheld, and the statute cannot be waived, so a lease term committing the tenant to a flat cleaning charge whatever the condition does not survive it.

The practical consequence: charge the cost you actually paid, keep the invoice, and treat normal soiling from ordinary living as wear and tear.

If you want the tenant to have the carpets professionally cleaned at the end, the library offers an optional clause, usable only where the carpets were professionally cleaned immediately before the tenancy began, so that cleaning them restores the move-in condition rather than improving on it. Two Minnesota points go with it. An agreement that the tenant performs specified repairs or maintenance is good only if it is supported by adequate consideration and set out in a conspicuous writing, and it can never shift your own covenants, so give something for the promise and print it clearly. And you must tell the tenant in writing about the option of a move-out inspection, whose whole purpose is to let the tenant fix what you identify before you deduct anything; skipping that notice is itself a deposit violation.

A flat carpet-cleaning fee charged regardless of condition is a different thing altogether: it is a nonoptional fee, so it would have to be disclosed in the lease and included in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, with treble damages for failure, and it would still have to survive the deposit statute. This covers Minnesota's statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws.

title: Casualty You May Vary, Mitigation You May Not - and the Variation Stops at Habitability
bodyText: The two halves of this question have opposite answers in Minnesota, and that is the whole point. The casualty rule CAN be varied by the lease. The mitigation rule CANNOT be, at all. Casualty first. Minn. Stat. 504B.131 is two sentences. A tenant or occupant of a building that is destroyed or becomes uninhabitable or unfit for occupancy through no fault or neglect of the tenant or occupant may vacate and surrender it. And a tenant or occupant may expressly agree otherwise, except as section 504B.161 prohibits. So a Minnesota lease can take away the tenant's right to walk out after a fire. But the carve-out does real work, and it is where landlords go wrong. Section 504B.161 imposes five covenants in every residential lease -- that the premises and common areas are fit for the use intended, that you keep them in reasonable repair, that you make them reasonably energy efficient, that you keep them compliant with health and safety law, and that you furnish heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit everywhere intended for habitation, kitchens and bathrooms included, from October 1 through April 30 -- and the parties may not waive or modify any of them. A casualty waiver can therefore remove the tenant's EXIT. It cannot make the tenant accept a building you are still bound to keep fit, repaired and heated. Notice also which covenants have a tenant-fault escape and which do not: only the reasonable-repair covenant and the health-and-safety-compliance covenant are excused where the problem was caused by the tenant's willful, malicious or irresponsible conduct. Fitness, energy efficiency and heat have no such escape, so tenant fault never excuses the heat duty. Mitigation second, and this one is absolute. Minn. Stat. 504B.154 says any waiver of the rights it provides is void and unenforceable, so a lease cannot touch it. It also does more than require you to try to re-rent. If a tenant abandons during the term and you either fail to use reasonable efforts to re-rent at fair rental value or accept the abandonment as a surrender, the rental agreement is terminated on the date you had notice of the abandonment and the tenant owes no rent after that. For a periodic tenancy or a tenancy at will there is a ceiling regardless: the most the tenant can owe is the rent for the notice period required to end the lease, counted from that date. Practical summary: a Minnesota lease may vary the casualty rule but not the mitigation rule, and the casualty variation stops at the habitability covenants. This library does not offer the casualty-waiver clause; see the fire and casualty row for why and for what to do if you want one.

title: No Minnesota Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure, But Three Related Duties Bite Hard
bodyText: Minnesota has no state certificate of occupancy for rental housing and no duty to give a tenant a copy of one, attach it to the lease, or state in the lease that one exists. There is no state rule making a tenancy void or rent uncollectable because no certificate was issued. Neither of these statutory uses of "certificate of occupancy" is a landlord disclosure duty: Minn. Stat. Sec. 471.9995, which is about what a city-issued document must contain, and Sec. 144.4961, subd. 11, which excludes newly constructed homes from the radon licensing section "prior to the issuance of a certificate of occupancy". Certificates of occupancy in Minnesota are issued by cities under the State Building Code. WHAT STATE LAW DOES SAY ABOUT A CITY-ISSUED DOCUMENT. Minn. Stat. Sec. 471.9995 is the one state rule on the point, and it is a duty on the issuer rather than on you: "[a]ny license or registration or certificate of occupancy or a similar document that is issued by a home rule charter or statutory city or by a town and that is required to be posted in a building containing multiple rental dwelling units shall contain a statement that tenants of the dwelling units may contact the attorney general for information regarding the rights and obligations of owners and tenants under state law", and "[t]he statement shall include the telephone number and address of the attorney general." Your part is to post what the city issues, where the city requires it posted. Two useful consequences follow. First, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.181, subd. 2(a) says your own posting duty "is complied with if notices posted in compliance with other statutes or ordinances contain the information required by this section" -- so a posted city document carrying the manager's and landlord's name and address can satisfy it. Second, subd. 2(b) requires the separate attorney general notice only "[u]nless the landlord is required to post a notice by section 471.9995". And subd. 4 confirms that failing to post a Sec. 471.9995 notice "shall not prevent any action to recover rent or possession of the premises" -- unlike the main disclosure, which does block the action. THE DISCLOSURE DUTY MINNESOTA DOES HAVE IS ABOUT ORDERS, NOT CERTIFICATES, and it is the one to get right. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195 makes you provide copies of all outstanding inspection orders for which a citation has been issued that the housing inspector identifies as threatening the health or safety of the tenant, and all outstanding condemnation orders and declarations that the premises are unfit for human habitation -- to a tenant within 72 hours of the citation, to a person BEFORE signing a lease or paying rent or a security deposit, and to a person before taking new ownership. For an order that does not threaten health or safety you post a summary conspicuously in each affected building with notice that the order is available for review on request, and you must actually provide it when asked. Any lease provision waiving that section "is contrary to public policy and void". See "You Must Hand Over Outstanding Inspection and Condemnation Orders". AND THE RENT BAR, which is the real exposure. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.204 you may not accept rent or a security deposit once the premises have been condemned or declared unfit for human habitation, ordered to be vacated for violating a housing, health or fire code or rental licensing ordinance, or ordered vacated under a government taking. Do it anyway and you owe actual damages plus three times all money collected after the date of the order, plus costs and attorney fees, and the violation also breaches Sec. 504B.161. See "Never Accept Rent or a Deposit After a Condemnation or Vacate Order". PRACTICAL ADVICE. Minnesota gives you no certificate to disclose, so do not invent a lease statement about one. Instead: find out whether your city issues and requires posting of a licence, registration or certificate of occupancy; post whatever it issues; and build a habit of checking for outstanding inspection and condemnation orders before every new letting, because that is the disclosure Minnesota actually enforces and it must happen before the tenant signs or pays.

title: A Family That Grows During the Tenancy Gets a Year Plus Six Months Notice
bodyText:
Minnesota has a landlord-tenant rule on this that sits outside the Human Rights Act and is easy to miss. Minn. Stat. section 504B.315 says no residential tenant of residential premises may be evicted, denied a continuing tenancy, or denied a renewal of a lease on the basis of familial status commenced during the tenancy unless two things have both happened: one year has elapsed from the commencement of the familial status, and you have given the tenant six months prior notice in writing. The section lists its own exceptions - nonpayment of rent, damage to the premises, disturbance of other tenants, or other breach of the lease - so an ordinary lease-breach case is unaffected.

Read the trigger carefully. 'Familial status' takes its meaning from Minn. Stat. section 363A.03, subd. 18, and it is wider than having a baby. It covers one or more minors having legal status or custody with a parent, a legal guardian, or the guardian's written designee. It also covers residing with and caring for one or more individuals who lack the ability to meet essential requirements for physical health, safety, or self-care. And it covers being pregnant, and being in the process of securing legal custody of a person under the age of majority. A tenant who takes in a grandchild, becomes a foster or kinship caregiver, or begins caring for a parent who can no longer receive and evaluate information or make and communicate decisions has commenced familial status during the tenancy, and the clock starts then.

The section is not waivable. Any provision of any lease or other agreement by which any provision of it is waived by a tenant is contrary to public policy and void. That means you cannot answer this rule with an occupancy clause, an addendum, or a signed acknowledgment, and a term that purports to do so is simply ineffective. The practical effect is that a non-renewal or a notice to quit aimed at a household that has just grown is a dated decision: unless you have one of the listed breach grounds, the earliest lawful end of the tenancy is a year after the familial status began plus the six months of written notice, and that notice must be in writing.

title: Minnesota Sets No Occupancy Cap and Requires No Lease Text About Children
bodyText:
Two absences are worth knowing, because landlords often assume the opposite.

First, no Minnesota statute requires your lease to address occupancy by children, or to state a maximum number of occupants. Minnesota's lease-content rules say what they say and no more: Minn. Stat. section 504B.146 requires the lease start and end dates, and the amount of the prorated rent where the lease requires move-in or move-out on a date other than the first or last of the month. Children are not on that list. If you want the household written down, that is your own choice of term, not a disclosure the state requires.

Second, Minnesota does not itself set a persons-per-bedroom or persons-per-unit limit. What the Human Rights Act does is step out of the way: Minn. Stat. section 363A.21, subd. 2(a) says the familial-status prohibition 'shall not be construed to defeat the applicability of any local, state, or federal restrictions regarding the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling unit'. The limit therefore comes from somewhere else - the State Building Code and Minnesota Rules, and the local housing maintenance code of the city the property sits in. Find the number for your own city before you write one into a lease, and state it as that code's number rather than as a figure of your own.

Two familial-status exemptions in the same subdivision are broader than landlords expect, and are worth checking against your own portfolio. Minn. Stat. section 363A.21, subd. 2(a) takes the familial-status prohibition off any owner-occupied building containing four or fewer dwelling units, and off housing for elderly persons, which subd. 2(b) defines three ways - including housing intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person aged 55 or older per unit, where at least 80 percent of the units are so occupied and the owner publishes and adheres to policies showing that intent. Minn. Stat. section 363A.09, subd. 1(3) adds that the advertising ban does not stop you advertising a unit as adults-only if you reasonably believe the familial-status prohibition does not apply to it. None of this touches Minn. Stat. section 504B.315, which sits in the landlord-tenant act, carries no such exemption, and cannot be waived. The federal Fair Housing Act also applies in Minnesota.

title: In a Manufactured Home Park You Cannot Charge by the Head
bodyText:
If any part of your portfolio is a manufactured home park, a separate chapter applies to the lot rental and it bans occupancy-based charging outright. Minn. Stat. section 327C.03, subd. 3 says no park owner shall charge a resident any fee, whether as part of or in addition to the periodic rental payment, which is based on any of six things. Three of them are about who lives in or visits the home: the number of persons residing or staying in the resident's home, the number or age of children residing or staying in the home, and the number of guests staying in the home. The other three are the size of the home, the fact that the home is temporarily vacant, and the type of personal property used or located in the home.

Two things make this stricter than it first looks. The ban covers a fee charged 'as part of' the rent, so folding a per-person or per-child amount into the lot rent does not avoid it. And the same subdivision opens by requiring that all periodic rental payments be uniform throughout the park, with only three permitted reasons for a higher rent to one resident: the larger size or location of the lot, or the special services or facilities furnished by the park. The number of people in the home is not one of them. The subdivision does let you abate all or part of the rent of a particular resident with special needs, and it lets you charge a reasonable delinquent-rent fee if the rental agreement provides for one.

Scope matters here. This is chapter 327C, which governs manufactured home park lots, and it does not reach an ordinary apartment or single-family rental. For a conventional Minnesota tenancy there is no equivalent per-person or per-child fee ban, so a head-count charge there is governed instead by the fee-disclosure rules and by the familial-status rules, which is a different analysis and a different answer.

title: Charging a Tenant for Collection Costs
bodyText: No Minnesota landlord-tenant statute authorises a collection fee on past-due rent, and none bars one, so any such charge rests on your lease. Five things limit it. First, the charge has to be in the lease: the deposit may be held back only for amounts reasonably necessary to remedy a default in paying rent or other funds due to you under an agreement, or to restore the premises, so a collection cost with no lease term behind it is not deductible. Second, a fee the tenant cannot avoid must be disclosed in the lease and inside the first-page Total Monthly Payment, and a disclosure failure carries treble damages and possible attorney fees. Third, in a nonpayment eviction the tenant can redeem by paying the rent in arrears with interest, the costs of the action, and an attorney's fee of no more than $5, so you cannot make collection costs the price of keeping the tenancy. Fourth, if your lease lets you recover attorney fees, directly or through additional rent, the tenant becomes entitled to attorney fees on winning the same kind of action. Fifth, a late fee is capped at 8% of the overdue rent payment and is expressly neither interest nor liquidated damages, so a collection charge stacked on late rent should not be a second late fee by another name. Minnesota's collection agency law governs agencies collecting for others, not you collecting your own rent (Minn. Stat. § 332.31, subd. 3). If you refer a tenant debt to an agency, Minn. Stat. § 332.37(a)(20) bars it from collecting any interest, fee, charge or expense unless the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes it or the law otherwise permits it. So an agency fee your lease does not expressly allow cannot be passed on. The library offers no Minnesota collection-fee clause, because a fee wrongly disclosed carries treble damages. Charging through a lease term is not forbidden by these statutes: if you want it, write your own, keep it to the actual reasonable cost, do not charge it on a disputed amount, and get advice first.

title: No Minnesota Lighting Standard, But You Cannot Bill a Tenant for Common-Area Power
bodyText: Minnesota sets no lighting level for common areas. There is no statute requiring a minimum illumination in hallways, stairwells, entries, laundry rooms or parking areas, no foot-candle figure, and no requirement that common-area lights be on at particular hours. The Clean Indoor Air Act's definition of "smoking" as carrying a "lighted" product in, among other places, "common areas of rental apartment buildings" is a smoking rule, not a lighting rule. WHAT STILL REQUIRES YOU TO LIGHT THEM. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) covenants that "the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended by the parties", that you will "keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair", and that you will "maintain the premises and all common areas in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state, and of the local units of government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing". An unlit stairwell is not fit for its intended use. Those covenants cannot be waived or modified (subd. 1(b)), the section is liberally construed (subd. 3), and subd. 2's last sentence is explicit that no tenant maintenance agreement may "relieve the landlord or licensor of the duty to maintain common areas of the premises". So common-area lighting is your job and you cannot contract out of it. A total loss of lighting is also an emergency route: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.381, subd. 1(2)(v) lists "the loss of electricity" and subd. 1(2)(x) "any conditions, services, or facilities that pose a serious and negative impact on health or safety", either of which supports a petition on 24 hours' attempted notice. THE BILLING QUESTION, WHICH IS WHERE MINNESOTA IS EMPHATIC. Some states let a lease put common-area lights on a tenant's own electric service in a small building. Minnesota does not, where the building is shared-metered and you bill separately. Minn. Stat. Sec. 216B.023, subd. 2(b)(1) says a landlord who submeters electricity must "charge only for the electricity used in the tenant's unit", and then states it directly: "A landlord must not charge a tenant for electricity consumed in common areas or in spaces used exclusively or primarily by the landlord." Subd. 2(a) adds that a landlord who bills a tenant separately from rent for electricity "must not apportion the service" -- so you cannot divide a single electricity bill by square footage or by heads the way gas and water may be apportioned. The same bar appears in the apportionment rules for the other utilities: a landlord "must not charge any tenant for natural gas consumed in common areas, spaces used exclusively or primarily by the landlord, or any vacant unit" (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.216, subd. 6(c)), and must not charge for water and sewer usage "in common areas; in spaces used exclusively or primarily by the landlord; in vacant units; for maintenance of the property; or for shared amenities, including but not limited to laundry facilities and pools" (subd. 7(c)). And in a shared-metered residential building you, not the tenant, must be "the bill payer responsible" and "the customer of record contracting with a utility provider", a requirement that "may not be waived by contract or otherwise" (Sec. 504B.216, subd. 2). WHERE THE ACTUAL LIGHTING REQUIREMENT WILL BE. Two places. The State Building Code and the State Fire Code, which carry means-of-egress and emergency lighting requirements and are rules rather than statutes. And your city's housing or property maintenance code, which is where a Minnesota minimum light level for a habitable room, hallway or stairway is most likely to be written; Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.011, subd. 4 expressly lets a local unit impose requirements "equal to, in addition to, or more stringent than" the State Fire Code. Read your own city's code. In the meantime, light the common areas, keep the fixtures working, and never put them on a tenant's meter.

title: No Government Approval Needed for a Minnesota Lease
bodyText: Minnesota has nothing like the territorial communal-land schemes. No Minnesota statute requires a lease of communal, tribal or native-owned land to be approved by a government officer before it is valid, and there is no statutory consequence for rent or possession collected before such an approval. The word communal does not appear anywhere in Minnesota statutes. More broadly, no Minnesota statute conditions the validity of a residential lease on any government approval, registration or recording. A Minnesota residential lease is effective between the parties on its own terms. The only Minnesota recording rule that touches leases runs the other way: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.251 makes the county recorder record a landlord notice of cancellation or termination where the lease itself has already been recorded. That is a step after the fact, not a precondition to validity. Land held in trust for a tribe or its members is a different matter, governed by federal law and by tribal law rather than by the Minnesota statutes, and it is outside both this lease and this library. If you are letting land in that category, do not use this instrument.

title: Habitability Rules Other States Have That Minnesota Does Not
bodyText: Minnesota's habitability law is short, strict and non-waivable, so its gaps are not places to relax. They are places where you set the standard, or where a tenant protection you might expect simply is not there. Twelve features other states have and Minnesota does not. On the standard itself: no materiality threshold, so a small defect is still a violation and seriousness decides the abatement rather than liability; no presumption that you breached or that you took too long, and no statutory repair deadline running from a tenant's request; no requirement that the lease state the unit will be delivered or kept fit to live in, and no prescribed habitability wording. On changing the standard: no rule letting a tenant accept named defects in return for a stated rent reduction; no separate-document rule for a lower heat level; and no exception letting the lease waive the running water or hot water duty where the property has no well and no utility connection. Minnesota Statutes, section 504B.161, subdivision 1(b) is flat -- the parties may not waive or modify the covenants. On moving the work: no requirement that a tenant repair agreement be a separate signed document, no limit to single-family homes or small buildings, no good-faith recital and no precondition you must meet first. Minnesota's one route is subdivision 2, and it needs adequate consideration and a conspicuous writing. On remedies: no self-help repair-and-deduct and no right to withhold rent -- a deduction happens only on a court order; no repair-cost threshold letting either side end the lease; no small-landlord or owner-occupier exemption from rent escrow and so no exemption notice to give; no statutory designated-repairer rule, no statutory response time and no tenant right to hire a repairer at your cost; no rule about the form or timing of your promise to repair, and none letting the lease designate verbal notice or make your actual knowledge a substitute for the statutory written notice. What Minnesota has instead is concentrated and strong. Five covenants implied into every residential lease or licence, unwaivable, with a tenant-fault exception on only two of them -- reasonable repair and health and safety compliance -- and none on fitness, energy efficiency or the 68 degree winter heat duty. Four tenant routes: a municipal inspection, rent escrow, a tenant remedies action that a neighbourhood organisation or a code authority can also bring, and emergency relief on 24 hours' attempted notice. A fine schedule rising from $250 if you willfully ignore a repair order, and a gross misdemeanour on the third willful failure in three years. And an anti-penalty rule that puts the burden on you for 90 days after a complaint. Three habitability-adjacent absences the library records elsewhere are worth knowing together with these: Minnesota has no mould disclosure duty, no bed bug disclosure duty and no radon disclosure duty for rentals, no fire sprinkler duty and no duty to rekey or change locks between tenancies. It does have smoke alarm and carbon monoxide alarm duties, which many of its gaps might lead you to doubt. Practical course: document everything, answer repair requests in days rather than weeks, and never write a habitability limit into the lease. The one thing you can lawfully build is a conspicuous, consideration-backed agreement that the tenant performs named tasks.

title: Other Rules Minnesota Does Not Have
bodyText:
Minnesota legislates residential tenancies heavily, which makes its gaps easy to mistake for things you have not found yet. Three are worth knowing because in each one your lease, not a statute, decides the outcome.

(1) NO SUBLETTING OR ASSIGNMENT STATUTE. Nothing in Minnesota law gives a residential tenant a right to sublet or to assign the lease, nothing requires you to be reasonable about refusing, and nothing puts a clock on your answer. Chapter 504B mentions subletting exactly once, and it cuts your way rather than the tenant's: under Minn. Stat.
