Sec. 504B.181, subd. 5, a tenant 'who moves from or subleases the premises without giving the landlord at least 30 days written notice shall void any provision of this section as to that tenant' -- so a tenant who sublets without that notice loses the landlord-disclosure protection the section otherwise gives them. The only other place a sublessee appears is the Human Rights Act, which names a 'sublessee' among the people who may not discriminate (Sec. 363A.09, subd. 1). That is a duty on your subtenant, not a right for your tenant. Practical effect: write a clear term requiring your written consent before any sublet, assignment or additional occupant, say what happens if the tenant does it anyway, and say in the same place that consent does not release the original tenant. The library's no-subletting clause already covers Minnesota.

(2) NO DUTY TO GIVE THE LEASE IN THE TENANT'S LANGUAGE, OR TO TRANSLATE IT -- WITH ONE NARROW EXCEPTION THAT IS NOT ABOUT THE LEASE. No Minnesota statute requires a residential lease, an addendum or a notice to be provided in any language other than the one you wrote it in, even where the whole negotiation happened in another language. The one translation duty that exists is in the manufactured home park chapter, and it attaches to a single notice. A park owner must give residents 45 days' notice before selling the park. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.095, subd. 1, that notice 'must be sent by first class mail to a resident of each manufactured home in the park and made available in alternative formats or translations if requested by a resident and the request is a reasonable accommodation due to a disability of an adult resident or because there is not an adult resident who is able to speak the language the notice is provided in'. Note what that is: on request, for one notice, in a park. It is not a lease translation duty and it does not generalise. The absence is not a free pass either. Chapter 363A reaches discrimination in 'the terms, conditions or privileges' of a rental, and a lease the tenant could not read is the kind of fact that gets argued about. If the dealing was in another language, give a translation anyway and keep a record that you did.

(3) NO EXECUTION FORMALITY FOR A LEASE. A Minnesota residential lease does not have to be notarised, witnessed, sealed, attested or acknowledged before anyone. The nearest thing in chapter 504B is Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.235, which lists the forms of 'proper identification' a tenant screening service may require. Signatures are what Minnesota asks for. Two optional pieces of paper go with them, and both are evidence rather than formality. The first is a signed and dated receipt that the tenant got a copy of the lease; it 'is prima facie evidence that the tenant has received a copy' and may sit inside the lease itself (Sec. 504B.115, subd. 1). The second, where the tenant agrees, is your written acknowledgment of photos or videos in place of a move-in or move-out inspection (Sec. 504B.182, subd. 1(b)). Take both. The separate rule that a building of twelve or more units must have a written lease identifying the unit before signing (Sec. 504B.111) is about having a writing, not about executing it formally, and a failure there is a petty misdemeanour. The one place a lease needs an affidavit is recording: where a lease has been recorded, a notice of cancellation presented to the county recorder must come with proof of service and an affidavit that the tenant has not complied (Sec. 504B.251).

title: Squatters and Other Questions Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText:
(1) A squatter or unauthorised-occupant fast track: Minnesota has none. There is no sheriff removal on an owner's affidavit, no police removal of a transient occupant, no ex parte order against someone who was never a tenant and no expedited squatter track. The answer is the ordinary eviction action, whoever the person is, and the detail is in the unauthorised-occupant rows. (2) A duty to give a receipt for rent paid in cash: Minnesota HAS one, and it is easy to miss because it sits in a section whose name is about to change. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.118 requires a landlord 'receiving rent or other payments from a tenant in cash' to give a written receipt 'immediately upon receipt if the payment is made in person, or within three business days if payment in cash is not made in person'. On August 1, 2026 that section is retitled PAYMENT OF RENT and the cash-receipt duty becomes its subdivision 2 -- the words do not change, only the number and the headnote. If your procedures cite the old headnote, update the citation and keep doing the thing. The cash-receipt rows cover it. (3) Landlord registration as a precondition to a possession judgment: Minnesota has no state landlord registry and no state rental licence, so there is no registration to produce. But do not conclude that nothing blocks a possession judgment. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.181, subd. 4 says 'no action to recover rent or possession of the premises shall be maintained unless the information required by this section has been disclosed to the tenant' -- the landlord and manager name and address -- 'or unless the information required by this section is known by or has been disclosed to the tenant at least 30 days prior to the initiation of such action'. That is Minnesota's version of the rule, and it attaches to a disclosure rather than to a licence. Two business-registration statutes outside chapter 504B can also stop an eviction. If you rent under an assumed name without filing the certificate the assumed-name statute requires, the tenant may plead that failure in abatement of an action to recover possession, the case is stayed until you file, and you lose $250 in costs (Minn. Stat. Secs. 333.01 and 333.06). And an out-of-state limited liability company that owns income-producing real property here may not maintain an action until it has a certificate of authority, and an out-of-state corporation transacting business here faces the same bar (Minn. Stat. Secs. 322C.0803, subd. 2, 322C.0808, subd. 1, and 303.20; see "Minnesota Asks Every Landlord for an Agent, Not Just Out-of-State Ones"). Neither failure voids the lease. Municipal rental licensing is real and is a local matter.

If your situation involves a condominium or townhouse association, a foreclosure, an arbitration clause, a tenant portal, an offender-registry question, a collection fee, interest on an unpaid balance, a pool, or a case already in court, get Minnesota advice. Minnesota Rules and municipal ordinances may also apply; Minneapolis and Saint Paul in particular regulate rental housing heavily.

title: The Tenant-Improvement Lien Clause Is Lawful Here, but It Is Not a Lien Defence
bodyText:
Minnesota's construction-lien law is Minn. Stat. ch. 514, Secs. 514.01 to 514.17. FIRST, THE LEASE: nothing in Chapter 504B -- the landlord-tenant act -- says anything about construction liens, tenant improvements, or a landlord's exposure for work a tenant orders. Nothing in it voids a lease term allocating that work and its cost to the tenant, and nothing in the chapter's non-waivable provisions touches the subject. So the optional No Liens for Tenant Work clause is a lawful lease term in Minnesota, and it does what its own words do: it makes the tenant pay the people the tenant hires, makes the tenant clear any lien the tenant's work produces, denies that the tenant is your agent, requires the tenant to tell contractors and suppliers who is paying, and stops your consent to an alteration being read as an agreement to pay for it.

SECOND, THE LIEN ITSELF: that clause does not keep your interest in the land free of a lien; Minn. Stat. Sec. 514.06 governs that. When one person improves another's land, everyone interested in it 'shall be deemed to have authorized such improvements', so far as to subject their interests to liens. You protect your interest by notice. Within five days after you learn of the work, serve written notice on those doing it that the improvement 'is not being made at' your instance. Serve it personally or by certified mail, or post it and keep it posted in a conspicuous place on the premises. The same section adds: 'As against a lessor no lien is given for repairs made by or at the instance of the lessee.'

Where a repair ends and an improvement begins, and whether a lease that permits the tenant's work counts as your authorizing it, only case law could settle. So take the cautious course. TREAT THE CLAUSE AS AN ALLOCATION BETWEEN YOU AND YOUR TENANT, NOT AS A LIEN DEFENCE. When you learn a tenant is having real construction done -- not hanging a shelf, but work a contractor would file a lien for -- serve or post the Sec. 514.06 notice within five days. Get Minnesota construction-lien advice before you consent to such work in writing, because a written consent may mean the work is made at your instance and the notice no longer fits.

Two Minnesota points that ARE settled and worth keeping separate from this: Minnesota gives you no lien on a tenant's goods for rent (see "No Lien for Rent in Minnesota, but One Real Lien for Storage Costs After a Writ"), and Secs. 514.18 and 514.22 are a storage-and-care lien on personal property and its sale procedure, borrowed by Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.365 for post-eviction storage costs. They have nothing to do with construction.

title: The Consumer Fraud Act's Reach to a Lease Is Still Unsettled, but the Act Got Stronger
bodyText:
Minnesota's consumer fraud statute may or may not reach a residential lease. That is the honest answer, it has not moved, and the library already records it at "Minnesota Has No Landlord-Tenant Unconscionability Statute". What has changed is that the statute is now a good deal stronger if it does reach, and the exposure is worth understanding even while the threshold question is open.

The threshold question, in the statute's own words. Minn. Stat. § 325F.69, subd. 1 makes "any fraud, unfair or unconscionable practice, false pretense, false promise, misrepresentation, misleading statement or deceptive practice, with the intent that others rely thereon in connection with the sale of any merchandise" enjoinable. Minn. Stat. § 325F.68, subd. 2 defines "merchandise" as "any objects, wares, goods, commodities, intangibles, real estate, loans, or services" — real estate is in. But subdivision 4 defines "sale" as "any sale, offer for sale, or attempt to sell any merchandise for any consideration", which is selling and not leasing. And the very next subdivision of § 325F.69 shows the legislature writing both words when it means both: subdivision 2 says "any sale or lease" and speaks throughout of "lessor" and "lessee". That is a real argument that subdivision 1's "sale" does not reach a lease. No Minnesota case deciding it was available here. Treat it as unsettled.

What is new, and it matters. Minn. Stat. § 325F.69, subd. 8, added in 2023, now defines the standard the word "unconscionable" imports: "an unfair method of competition or an unfair or unconscionable act or practice is any method of competition, act, or practice that: (1) offends public policy as established by the statutes, rules, or common law of Minnesota; (2) is unethical, oppressive, or unscrupulous; or (3) is substantially injurious to consumers." Three disjunctive limbs, and the first one points straight at the rest of the statute book — a lease term that offends public policy as established by Minnesota's statutes is squarely inside limb (1), and Chapter 504B says of 14 separate non-waiver sentences that a waiver is "contrary to public policy". Anyone arguing the Act reaches leases now has a defined standard to argue under, where before there was only the bare adjective.

There are now two routes to a private claim, not one. Minn. Stat. § 325F.70, subd. 3, also added in 2023, provides directly: "a consumer injured by a violation of sections 325F.68 to 325F.70, in connection with a sale of merchandise for personal, family, household, or agricultural purposes, may bring a civil action and recover damages, together with costs and disbursements, including costs of investigation and reasonable attorney fees, and receive other equitable relief as determined by the court. An action brought under this section benefits the public." "Consumer" means a natural person or family farmer. That last sentence removes a hurdle: the claimant no longer has to establish a public benefit. The older route, Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 3a, also remains available, because § 8.31, subd. 1 expressly lists "the Prevention of Consumer Fraud Act (sections 325F.68 to 325F.70)".

The advertising section is a separate and wider door. Minn. Stat. § 325F.67 makes it a misdemeanour, and a public nuisance that may be enjoined, to place before the public an advertisement containing "any material assertion, representation, or statement of fact which is untrue, deceptive, or misleading", where done with intent to sell or dispose of "merchandise, securities, service, or anything offered" — or "to induce the public in any manner to enter into any obligation relating thereto, or to acquire title thereto, or any interest therein". Note what that last phrase does: it does not require a sale. Inducing the public to enter into an obligation, or to acquire an interest, covers a rental advertisement far more comfortably than subdivision 1's "sale of merchandise" does. Section 325F.67 is also named in Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 1, so it carries the subdivision 3a private action with attorney fees. Of everything in this family, this is the provision most likely to reach your advertising.

Two things the Act does not do. It contains no enumerated list of unlawful practices for leases — no "blank spaces filled in after signing" practice and no "no copy at signing" practice. Subdivision 1 is a general standard and subdivisions 2 to 8 cover referral and chain-referral selling, excluded advertising media, invoices for goods not ordered, going-out-of-business sales, deceptive use of a financial institution's name, conversion therapy, and the unconscionability standard. Both of those lease questions are answered inside the landlord-tenant act instead: the copy-at-signing duty is at Minn. Stat. § 504B.115 and the library answers the blank-spaces point at "No Statutory Rule Against Blank Spaces in a Minnesota Lease".

What to do about it. Do not treat the open threshold question as a safe harbour. Make sure your advertising is accurate, because Minn. Stat. § 325F.67 is the part of this family with the clearest path to a rental transaction. Keep fee disclosure right, since an undisclosed mandatory charge is the classic shape of a claim under all of these provisions. And do not rely on the absence of a Chapter 504B unconscionability section as permission for a one-sided term, because subdivision 8's limb (1) turns Minnesota's own statutes into the measure of what offends public policy.

title: The Deceptive Trade Practices Act Needs No Sale, and the Library Has Not Recorded It
bodyText:
Minnesota has a second consumer statute the library has not recorded, and it is in some ways a better fit for a landlord than the consumer fraud act. Chapter 325D's Deceptive Trade Practices Act, Minn. Stat. §§ 325D.43 to 325D.48, was read in full for this entry.

Minn. Stat. § 325D.44, subd. 1 provides that "A person engages in a deceptive trade practice when, in the course of business, vocation, or occupation, the person" does any of fourteen listed things. Note the trigger: in the course of business, vocation or occupation. There is no requirement of a sale, and no requirement of merchandise. A landlord renting residential property is acting in the course of a business. That is a materially easier threshold than Minn. Stat. § 325F.69, subd. 1's "in connection with the sale of any merchandise", which is the clause whose reach to a lease is unsettled.

Most of the fourteen clauses are about goods and services and will not touch you. Two are worth knowing.

Clause (13) was added in 2023 and reads simply that a person engages in a deceptive trade practice when they engage "in (i) unfair methods of competition, or (ii) unfair or unconscionable acts or practices". It carries no goods-or-services limitation of its own, and Minn. Stat. § 325D.44, subd. 2(b) ties it to the same test as the consumer fraud act: "For purposes of subdivision 1, clause (13), the standard of proof provided under section 325F.69, subdivision 8, applies."

Subdivision 1a, on advertised prices, is the one to check your advertising against. A person engages in a deceptive trade practice when they advertise, display or offer "a price for goods or services that does not include all mandatory fees or surcharges", and a mandatory fee "includes but is not limited to" one that must be paid to purchase what is advertised, is not reasonably avoidable by the consumer, or that a reasonable person would expect to be included. Whether rent is "goods or services" is arguable, but the overlap with Minn. Stat. § 504B.120 — which already requires every nonoptional fee to be disclosed in the lease and in any advertisement, on pain of treble damages — means the safe course is the same under both: advertise the all-in figure.

The exemptions do not help you. Minn. Stat. § 325D.46, subd. 1 excludes only conduct in compliance with the orders or rules of, or a statute administered by, a government agency, and actions pending on July 1, 1973. There is no real-estate exclusion and no lease exclusion. Minn. Stat. § 325D.44, subd. 3 adds that the section "does not affect unfair, deceptive, or misleading trade practices otherwise actionable at common law or under other statutes of this state", and Minn. Stat. § 325D.47 directs that the Act be construed to make the law uniform among the states that enact it.

The remedy is narrower, and that is the trade-off. Minn. Stat. § 325D.45, subd. 1 gives injunctive relief, with no need to prove monetary damage, loss of profits or intent to deceive — but it gives no damages. Subdivision 2 allows costs to the prevailing party and attorney fees only in two situations: where the complainant brought a groundless action knowing it to be groundless, or where the party charged "has willfully engaged in the trade practice knowing it to be deceptive". Subdivision 3 makes the relief cumulative. And unlike the consumer fraud act, Minn. Stat. §§ 325D.43 to 325D.48 are not among the laws listed in Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 1, so § 8.31, subd. 3a's private damages action does not attach to a Deceptive Trade Practices Act claim.

So the shape of the risk is: an easier threshold than the consumer fraud act, the same unconscionability standard, but injunction rather than damages, and fees only on a finding of wilfulness. Treat it as a reason to get advertising and fee disclosure right, which is the same conclusion every provision in this area points to.

title: Closing or Converting a Manufactured Home Park: 12 Months, Fixed 14-Point Words, and a Resident Chance to Buy
bodyText: Minnesota has one conversion-notice regime and it is for manufactured home parks: Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.095, PARK CLOSINGS. It is substantial, it carries two notices whose words and type size the statute fixes, it gives residents a chance to buy the park, and until now no row in this library mentioned it. It does not apply to this lease -- a park resident owns the home and rents the lot, which is Minn. Stat. ch. 327C, not ch. 504B (see "Farm Tenancies and Manufactured Home Parks Are Governed Elsewhere") -- but a landlord who buys or operates a park needs to know it exists. TWELVE MONTHS' NOTICE, FOUR RECIPIENTS, FIXED WORDS. Under subd. 1(a), at least 12 months before converting all or part of a park to another use, closing it, or ceasing to use the land as a park, the park owner must prepare a closure statement and give a copy to the commissioners of health and of the housing finance agency, to the local planning agency, and to a resident of each manufactured home whose residential use is being converted. The statement 'must include the following language in a font no smaller than 14 point: "YOU MAY BE ENTITLED TO COMPENSATION FROM THE MINNESOTA MANUFACTURED HOME RELOCATION TRUST FUND ADMINISTERED BY THE MINNESOTA HOUSING FINANCE AGENCY."' A statement issued more than 24 months before closure must carry a closure date, and must be reissued if the closure does not happen within 24 months and no date was given (subd. 1(b)). NOBODY HAS TO LEAVE QUICKLY. 'A resident may not be required to vacate until 90 days after the conclusion of the public hearing required under subdivision 4' -- so the 90 days runs from the hearing, not from the notice. And if a lot is available in a part of the park that will keep operating, the owner must let the resident move the home there unless its size or a local ordinance makes the lot incompatible. A public hearing follows within 90 days of the closure statement, with a neutral third party appointed to act as paymaster and arbitrator (subd. 4). RESIDENTS GET A CHANCE TO BUY. Under subd. 6, a purchaser who intends to close or convert the park within a year of the purchase agreement must tell the park owner in writing, and the owner must then give each manufactured home a 45-day written notice and may not sign a purchase agreement with anyone except a representative acting for the residents until the 45 days run out. During that window the residents' representative may match the cash price and the material terms and sign a purchase agreement to keep the park as a manufactured housing community, and the owner 'must in good faith negotiate' it. The representative puts up ten per cent as earnest money, and on a sale to the residents must certify to the commissioner of commerce that the park will be preserved as a park for ten years. Subd. 7 stops a purchaser who skipped the subd. 6 notice from giving a subd. 1 notice for twelve months after the purchase. REMEDIES ARE REAL, AND THEY COME TWICE. Subd. 9: if a park 'is finally sold or converted to another use in violation of subdivision 6 or 7, the residents have a right to any remedy provided in section 8.31'. Separately, Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.15 makes 'any violation of sections 327C.015 to 327C.14' a violation of a law referred to in Minn. Stat. Sec. 8.31 subd. 1 -- and Sec. 8.31 subd. 3a gives any person injured a civil action for damages, costs, investigation costs and reasonable attorney's fees, plus equitable relief. MONEY AND A SECOND FIXED NOTICE. Subds. 12 and 13 run the Minnesota manufactured home relocation trust fund: the park owner pays in on a change of use, with the amount capped by subd. 14 for smaller parks, and a home owner required to relocate claims actual relocation costs up to the statutory maxima, or may tender title instead where relocation has failed. Subd. 12(c) sets a $15 per licensed lot assessment and prescribes, 'in a font no smaller than 14-point', a notice for distribution to residents reading: 'THIS IS NOT AN OPTIONAL FEE. IF YOU OWN A MANUFACTURED HOME ON A LOT YOU RENT IN A MANUFACTURED HOME PARK, AND YOU RESIDE IN THAT HOME, YOU MUST PAY WHEN PROVIDED NOTICE.' A park owner assessed the $15 may recoup it as a lump sum or as a monthly fee of no more than $1.25 with lot rent. LOCAL ORDINANCES ARE PREEMPTED on relocation and buyout payments (subd. 15): a township, county or city 'must not adopt an ordinance requiring more compensation by the manufactured home park owners or its purchaser than what is provided for in this statute'. Two more park-sale notices sit alongside: Sec. 327C.096 requires concurrent written notice to each resident household when a park is offered to the public by newspaper advertising or a licensed broker, and Sec. 327C.097 requires notice to the Housing Finance Agency and each resident household of an unsolicited offer the owner intends to consider, with the price range and material terms.

title: Converting a Rental Building to a Condominium or Other Common Interest Community
bodyText: Minnesota's landlord-tenant act, Minn. Stat. ch. 504B, says nothing about converting a building. But converting a building to a condominium, cooperative or planned community gives its tenants real rights under the Minnesota Common Interest Ownership Act. They apply to 'conversion property': a building occupied for residential use or residential rental purposes at any time in the two years before the community is created (Minn. Stat. Sec. 515B.1-103(12)). Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 515B.4-111, for one year after the declaration is recorded, a unit owner may not make an occupant who lived in the unit at recording vacate without a conversion notice. The notice must be given at least 120 days before the occupant must leave. Hand deliver or mail it to the unit, addressed to the occupants, in an envelope boldly printed "Notice of Conversion." If the tenant gave you a different address, send it there too. It must set out the tenant's rights under the section and attach a purchase agreement offering the unit, with a statement of any significant declaration restrictions on use and occupancy. It must say the occupants may demand 60 more days if any of them, or anyone living with them, is 62 or older, has a disability, or is a minor child. That demand must be written, with reasonable proof, and given within 30 days. For 60 days the tenant has an option to buy on the attached terms. If the tenant does not sign, for the next 180 days you may not offer the unit to anyone at a better price or on better terms. During the notice period you may not change the terms of the tenancy, but the tenant may leave on one month's written notice. You may still require the tenant to leave sooner for nonpayment of rent, utilities or other money owed, violations of law, waste, or conduct that disturbs other occupants. No repair or remodeling may begin in occupied units or common areas during the notice period without reasonable precautions for the occupants' safety and security. The notice does not let you end a lease in violation of its terms. Failing to give it is a defense to an action for possession. A notice that also complies with chapter 504B and gives a move-out date doubles as the notice to vacate. A tenant has none of these rights if, less than two years before the community is created, the tenant got written notice of intent to convert before signing or renewing the lease or moving in. That notice must give the property's legal description and street address and the intended form of ownership. It must also say that tenants who sign leases after receiving it will not have these rights. Your city may also prohibit or condition conversions by ordinance under Minn. Stat. Sec. 515B.1-106(c), so check local law. Converting a building to another use, or demolishing it, carries no conversion notice in chapter 504B; the ordinary rules for ending a tenancy apply. If you are converting or closing a manufactured home park, the regime is Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.095 and it is set out in "Closing or Converting a Manufactured Home Park: 12 Months, Fixed 14-Point Words, and a Resident Chance to Buy".

title: Grounds for Eviction and the Absence of a Cure Period in Minnesota
bodyText:
Minnesota lists the grounds for eviction in Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subd. 1(a). A landlord may recover possession when a person holds over after a sale on execution or judgment, after the redemption period on a mortgage foreclosure or the termination of a contract to convey, or after the redemption period on a real estate tax judgment sale; when a person holds over after the lease term ends, holds over contrary to the conditions or covenants of the lease, or holds over after rent becomes due; or when a tenant at will holds over after a notice to quit. Subd. 4(a) preserves the landlord's right to terminate for a tenant's violation of a lawful, material provision of the lease.

Minnesota gives the tenant no statutory period to cure an ordinary breach of a lease covenant, and requires no warning notice before filing for one. The only pre-filing notice and correction period in the chapter is the 14-day written notice for nonpayment of rent or another unpaid financial obligation under Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 1a. Chapter 504B contains no equivalent for a non-rent breach. Minnesota's manufactured home park law is different and is not a guide here: Minn. Stat. section 327C.09 requires cause and gives a ten-day cure for overdue rent and 30 days to comply with a park rule.

Two limits still apply to a breach eviction. Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, subd. 2a bars a penalty or termination for conduct of the tenant, a household member or a guest off the premises and curtilage unless the conduct would be, or results in a conviction of, a crime of violence against another tenant, a tenant's guest, the landlord or the landlord's employees. And Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 3(3) requires the complaint to identify the lease clause breached, the conduct, the dates, and the clause granting the right to evict for that conduct, so the lease must actually contain an eviction-right clause before a breach can be pleaded.

title: Minnesota's 14-Day Written Notice Before a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText:
Before filing an eviction action for nonpayment of rent or another unpaid financial obligation under the lease, a Minnesota landlord must give the residential tenant written notice under Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 1a. The notice must state the total amount due; give a specific accounting of how much of the total is unpaid rent, late fees and other charges under the lease; give the name and address of the person authorised to receive rent and fees for the landlord; and carry three statements in the statute's own words - the legal-help statement naming Legal Aid and www.LawHelpMN.org, the financial-help statement naming the county or Tribal social services office, MNBenefits.mn.gov and 2-1-1 or 800-543-7709, and the statement that the landlord can file if the tenant does not pay or move out within 14 days, which must also say some local governments may have a longer eviction notice period.

The landlord or the landlord's agent must deliver the notice personally or by first class mail to the tenant at the leased premises. The landlord may file only if the tenant fails to correct the rent delinquency within 14 days of delivery or mailing, or within the longer period a local government requires, or fails to vacate. A copy of the notice must be attached to the complaint, and under subd. 1(d) the court must dismiss the action without prejudice and grant an expungement of the eviction case file if the notice was not given.

Two further points. Under subd. 1b the tenant's receipt of this notice is itself sufficient demonstration of an emergency for county assistance under Minn. Stat. section 256D.06, subd. 2, and the county must not ask the tenant for more verification of the emergency or more verification that the landlord will accept the funds. And a longer local notice period is a municipal matter: check the ordinance for the property's location before counting the 14 days.

title: No Defective-Drywall Rule in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota has no defective-drywall law and no duty to disclose defective drywall to a tenant. There is no Minnesota definition of defective or corrosive drywall, no disclosure rule and no termination remedy of the kind Virginia and Florida created after the imported-drywall problem. THREE THINGS DO REACH THE PROBLEM. First, your repair covenant. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) makes you covenant in every residential lease that the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended by the parties, that you will keep them in reasonable repair, and that you will maintain them in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state and of local government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing. Under subd. 1(b) the parties may not waive or modify those covenants, and under subd. 3 the section is liberally construed and the chance to inspect before signing does not defeat them. That covenant applies to every live Minnesota tenancy. Corroding wiring, failing air-conditioning coils and a sulfur smell are a fitness and repair problem whether or not Minnesota names the product. Second, hiding a known defect is risky. Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.69, subd. 1 makes fraud, an unfair or unconscionable practice, a false pretense, a misrepresentation, a misleading statement or a deceptive practice unlawful when used with the intent that others rely on it in connection with the sale of merchandise, and Sec. 325F.68, subd. 2 defines merchandise to include real estate and services. Sec. 8.31, subd. 3a gives any person injured by a violation a civil action for damages, costs of investigation and reasonable attorney fees. Whether a residential lease is a sale of merchandise for this purpose is a case-law question, so treat the risk as real rather than settled. Third, there is one statutory building-material notice. For urea-formaldehyde building materials Minnesota does prescribe a written IMPORTANT HEALTH NOTICE that a builder must give to a lessee of a new housing unit; see the prop65-rental-warning rows, where that duty is stated. WHAT TO DO. If you know or suspect corrosive drywall - a sulfur or rotten-egg smell, blackened copper wiring or pipes, repeated air-conditioning coil failures - have it assessed, fix it, and tell a prospective tenant in writing what you know. Do not rely on an as-is clause: it cannot reach the Sec. 504B.161 covenants. If the condition draws a housing-inspection citation or a condemnation order, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195, subd. 1 makes you give a copy to a person before they sign a lease or pay rent or a deposit, and subd. 5 makes any lease waiver of that section contrary to public policy and void.

title: A Price List Does Not Enlarge What You May Keep
bodyText:
No Minnesota statute lets a lease fix in advance what you will take from the deposit for cleaning, carpets, painting or repairs, and none requires a special notice for such a schedule. Minnesota regulates the ceiling instead of the list. You may withhold only amounts reasonably necessary to remedy a default in the payment of rent or of other funds due to you under an agreement, or to restore the property to its condition at the start of the tenancy with ordinary wear and tear excepted. And in any dispute the burden of proving the reason for withholding any part of the deposit, by a fair preponderance of the evidence, is on you.

So a price list cannot do the work landlords hope it will. A fixed charge higher than what the work actually cost is not reasonably necessary, and charging it leaves you arguing for an amount you cannot evidence, with the penalty, the interest and the bad-faith award of up to $500 behind it.

What does work is the narrower route the statute itself opens: the lease can make specific amounts due to you on a stated condition, which brings them inside other funds due under an agreement, and the optional Other Charges Payable from the Security Deposit clause does exactly that while keeping each charge tied to actual cost.

Two traps. If you make a charge payable whatever happens, it stops being a contingent charge and becomes a nonoptional fee, which must appear in the lease and inside the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, with treble damages and possibly the tenant's attorney fees for getting it wrong. And a schedule is no substitute for evidence: offer the initial inspection and the move-out inspection, keep dated photographs and keep the invoices, because that is what discharges your burden.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Instalments
bodyText: No Minnesota statute gives a tenant the right to pay the security deposit in instalments, and none requires you to offer one. You may ask for the whole deposit before occupancy. Minneapolis is the exception a Twin Cities landlord has to know about: by ordinance it requires instalments in one case, where prepaid rent is collected up front alongside the deposit. That is a municipal rule, and where a city rule applies it governs and is stricter than state law, so check the ordinance for the city the property is in. Nothing stops you offering instalments if you want to, and it is a reasonable thing to offer a good applicant who is short at move-in. If you do, say in the lease how much is due and on what dates, and keep two things in mind. The deposit is not rent, so an unpaid instalment is a default in other funds due to you under the lease rather than unpaid rent, which matters because the remedies are different. And interest runs from the first day of the month after the deposit is paid in full, so instalments delay the start of the interest clock rather than complicating it. Do not dress an instalment plan up as a fee: a nonoptional charge for paying the deposit over time would have to be disclosed in the lease and included in the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, and getting that wrong costs treble damages and possibly the tenant's attorney fees. The library does not offer an instalment clause, because no Minnesota rule turns on the lease having one; a landlord who wants one can add their own term and should take advice on it first.

title: In Minnesota the Deposit Clock Waits for the Tenant Address
bodyText:
Minnesota is one of the states where part of your deposit duty waits on the tenant. The duty to return the deposit with interest, or to send a written statement of the specific reasons for withholding it, arises within three weeks after the tenancy ends and after you receive the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions. The penalty for a late or missing statement is worded the same way. So ask for the address at move-out and write down when it arrived.

Do not treat this as a reason to sit on the money. The safest reading, and the one this library takes, is that you must act within three weeks of the tenancy ending, or promptly on receiving the address if that comes later; a landlord who had the address all along and waited longer has no defence. You get the benefit of the post: you comply with the time limit if the deposit or the statement goes into the United States mail as first class mail, postage prepaid, in an envelope with a proper return address, correctly addressed according to the address or delivery instructions the tenant gave you, within the time required.

What you cannot do is make the refund depend on anything else. Minnesota requires no move-out notice, no notice period, no forwarding address in a particular form and no return of keys as a condition of the deposit, and any attempted waiver of the deposit section is void, so a term making the deposit forfeit, or the clock pause, until the tenant gives notice or hands back keys does nothing but damage you in front of a judge. The optional Move-Out Address for the Deposit clause asks for the address without making it a condition, which is the lawful way to get the same result.

title: Who Does the Repairs: the Lease Decides, Within Limits
bodyText:
Minnesota says nothing about who does the repairs, so the lease is where this gets decided -- within limits. No statute requires you to name a repair contact or an approved repairer, none sets how fast you must respond to a repair request, and none lets a tenant hire a repairer and send you the bill. There is no self-help repair-and-deduct in Minnesota. A tenant deducts a repair cost from rent only when a court orders it, under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.425(c) in a tenant remedies action. The one self-help deduction chapter 504B does give a tenant is about utilities, not repairs: in a shared-metered building where you default on the utility bill and a tenant pays the utility to keep the service on, the tenant may deduct that payment from the next rent (Sec. 504B.216, subd. 13(i)). While a rent escrow case is pending the tenant must keep paying and "may not withhold rent to remedy a violation" (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 1(d)).

So a clause naming your repair contact and requiring your written approval before any repair at your expense is lawful and useful, and the library offers it as the optional Repair Contact and Approved Repairers section.

Four limits on it. First, it changes nothing about your own duties: the covenants in Sec. 504B.161 may not be waived or modified, and they do not depend on a tenant following your procedure.

Second, it cannot touch the court. A lease provision waiving Sec. 504B.381 or Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471 is contrary to public policy and void (Sec. 504B.465), so a court can still order the tenant to do the work and deduct the cost whatever your clause says.

Third, it cannot cut your entry notice. A tenant may not waive, and you may not require a tenant to waive, the right to prior notice of entry as a condition of entering into or maintaining the lease (Sec. 504B.211, subd. 2). Performing maintenance work is already a reasonable business purpose for entry, and you may already enter without notice where immediate entry is needed to prevent injury to persons or property because of conditions relating to maintenance -- so you do not need the lease to give you either.

Fourth, do not charge for reporting a defect. A call-out or inspection fee for a repair request would be a fee for performing your own covenant; every nonoptional fee must be disclosed in the lease and in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, with treble damages and attorney fees if it is not (Sec. 504B.120).

Access cuts the other way too, and in your favour. It is a sufficient defence to a rent escrow or tenant remedies complaint that a tenant of the building "has unreasonably refused entry to the landlord or the landlord's agent to a portion of the property for the purpose of correcting the violation, and that the effort to correct was made in good faith" (Sec. 504B.415(3)). Give proper notice, keep the record of the appointment, and that defence is available to you.

title: Minnesota Has Its Own Disability Accommodation and Modification Duties
bodyText:
Minnesota does not leave disability accommodation in housing to federal law. Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.10, subd. 1 spells out three things that count as discrimination under the housing section, Sec. 363A.09.

First, refusing to permit reasonable modifications of the premises, at the disabled person own expense, where the modification may be necessary for that person full enjoyment of the premises. You may, where it is reasonable, condition permission on the renter agreeing to restore the interior afterwards, excluding reasonable wear and tear.

Second, refusing to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services where that may be necessary to give a disabled person equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling - that limb is about your rules, not the building.

Third, for covered multifamily dwellings first occupied after 13 March 1991, failing to design and build them with accessible common and public-use areas, doors wide enough for a wheelchair, an accessible route into and through the dwelling, reachable light switches, outlets and environmental controls, bathroom-wall reinforcement for later grab bars, and kitchens and bathrooms a wheelchair user can manoeuvre in. Covered multifamily dwellings, per subd. 2, means a building of four or more units with one or more elevators, plus ground-floor units in other buildings of four or more units.

Two limits are yours to use. Subd. 4 says the section does not require you to make a dwelling available to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to the health or safety of other individuals, or would result in substantial physical damage to the property of others. Subd. 3 says the section does not cut down any state or local law requiring greater access, so a city accessibility code still bites.

Minnesota uses its own definition of disability, at Sec. 363A.03, subd. 12: a physical, sensory or mental impairment that materially limits one or more major life activities, a record of such an impairment, being regarded as having one, or an impairment that is episodic or in remission and would materially limit a major life activity when active. That last limb matters - an episodic or remitted condition counts.

Separately, Sec. 363A.09, subd. 5 makes it an unfair discriminatory practice to deny full and equal access to real property to a person who has a disability and who uses a service animal. You may not require extra compensation for the service animal, but the person is liable for damage the animal does to the premises.

Two exemptions sit alongside this, and one is commonly misread. Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.25 says nothing in the chapter prohibits any program, service, facility or privilege afforded to a person with a disability which is intended to habilitate, rehabilitate, or accommodate that person - so a disability-targeted set-aside or adapted-unit programme is protected rather than suspect. Its second sentence creates a serious-threat defence, but read it carefully: that defence is expressly available only to a complaint or action brought under the EMPLOYMENT provisions of the chapter. Your housing equivalent is not there; it is Sec. 363A.10, subd. 4, which is narrower and speaks of a direct threat to the health or safety of other individuals or substantial physical damage to the property of others.

One further scoping point before you rely on any of this: the statutory note printed under both Sec. 363A.09 and Sec. 363A.10 says the exemptions are at Secs. 363A.21, 363A.22 and 363A.26, and Sec. 363A.21, subd. 1(2) both exempts a resident owner-occupier renting a room in a one-family home from the disability ground and says no one selling, renting or leasing property is required to modify the property in any way, or to exercise a higher degree of care for a person having a disability. Read Sec. 363A.21 before applying Sec. 363A.10 to a room-renting owner-occupier. Nothing in Sec. 363A.10 requires any of this to be written into the lease, so it is background you work to rather than lease text you must carry.

title: New in 2026: Failing to Engage on an Accommodation Can Itself Be Discrimination
bodyText:
Laws 2026, ch. 99, sec. 1 added a new paragraph (c) to Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.02, subd. 1. It provides that failure to engage in the process to determine if a reasonable accommodation exists that would allow people with disabilities, as defined in Sec. 363A.03, subd. 12, to participate fully in - among other things - housing and real property may be an unfair discriminatory practice under the chapter.

This is an interactive-process duty, and it is new. Before it, your exposure turned on the outcome: did you refuse a reasonable accommodation or modification. Now the handling of the request is capable of being the violation in its own right, so ignoring a request, leaving it unanswered, or refusing to discuss alternatives is a risk even if a court would later have held the accommodation unreasonable. Note that the statute says may be, not is, so nothing is automatic - but it is enough to change how you should run the file.

Practically: log every accommodation and modification request when it arrives, respond in writing, say what information you need in order to decide, and record the alternatives you offered and why.

What the 2026 act did not do is widen the protected-class list. Paragraph (a), clauses (1) to (5) came through the amendment word for word unchanged, so the housing grounds are still race, color, creed, religion, national origin, sex, gender identity, marital status, disability, status with regard to public assistance, sexual orientation, and familial status.

title: No Minnesota Rule Suspends Your Guest Limit in a Disaster
bodyText:
Minnesota has no rule on this. Minnesota's landlord-tenant statutes contain nothing that lets a tenant house people displaced by a fire, flood, tornado or declared emergency over and above the lease's occupancy or guest terms, suspends a guest-stay limit during a state of emergency or peacetime emergency, bars you from treating a displaced relative as an unauthorised occupant, or gives you any special remedy if a tenant takes someone in. Your lease's occupancy and guest terms are what govern, exactly as they do on an ordinary day.

Two things sit close enough to be worth knowing. The first is that the Human Rights Act may reach the people most likely to arrive. 'Familial status', a protected class in Minnesota housing, is defined at Minn. Stat. section 363A.03, subd. 18 to include not only minors in a parent's or guardian's custody but 'residing with and caring for one or more individuals who lack the ability to meet essential requirements for physical health, safety, or self-care because the individual or individuals are unable to receive and evaluate information or make or communicate decisions'. A tenant who takes in a displaced parent who cannot manage alone may have commenced familial status, which engages Minn. Stat. section 504B.315's one-year and six-month protection against eviction, denied continuing tenancy or refused renewal. Enforce your occupancy terms on the facts, in writing, and do not reach for non-renewal.

The second is that the one Minnesota disaster-and-lease rule that does exist is a park rule and runs the other way. If you operate a manufactured home park, Minn. Stat. section 327C.025 requires you to give each resident a copy of the signed rental agreement 'with a copy of the evacuation or shelter plan attached', and the statutory notice that Minn. Stat. section 327C.02 puts in front of every park rental agreement tells the resident 'You must be given a copy of the shelter or evacuation plan for the park.' That is a disclosure duty about where residents shelter, not a permission to house anybody.

A practical note rather than a legal one. If a tenant asks to house someone displaced, the clean answer is a short written consent for a stated period, added under the lease's occupancy terms, rather than silence. Silence turns a guest into a regular occupant, and a regular occupant is a residential tenant under Minn. Stat. section 504B.001, subd. 12 whose removal takes a court.

title: The Shelter Plan Must Be Attached in a Park, and Nowhere Else in Minnesota
bodyText:
Minnesota has one evacuation-and-shelter rule for rental housing and it is for manufactured home parks. Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.025 is a single sentence: 'The park owner shall give a copy of the signed rental agreement to each resident with a copy of the evacuation or shelter plan attached.' So in a park the plan is not merely available -- it must physically travel with the signed agreement. The park owner also has to say so in advance: Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.02 subd. 5 requires a prospective resident, before being asked to sign, to be given a notice 'printed verbatim in boldface type of a minimum size of ten points', provided with the park residency application and posted in a conspicuous and public place in the park, which tells the resident among other things: 'You must be given a copy of the shelter or evacuation plan for the park. This document contains information on where to seek shelter in times of severe weather conditions. You should carefully review the plan and keep a copy.'

THE ENFORCEMENT IS REAL. Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.15 makes 'any violation of sections 327C.015 to 327C.14' a violation of a law referred to in Minn. Stat. Sec. 8.31 subd. 1, and Sec. 8.31 subd. 3a gives any person injured a civil action for damages, costs, investigation costs and reasonable attorney's fees, plus equitable relief. Sec. 327C.025 sits inside that range, so a park owner who hands over a signed agreement without the plan attached is exposed to a private action, not just to the attorney general.

FOR AN ORDINARY MINNESOTA RENTAL there is no equivalent. Minn. Stat. ch. 504B requires no evacuation plan, no shelter plan, no severe-weather notice and no disaster disclosure, and Minnesota has no statute ending a tenancy or abating rent after a declared disaster. What it has instead is Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.131: a tenant 'of a building that is destroyed or becomes uninhabitable or unfit for occupancy through no fault or neglect of the tenant or occupant may vacate and surrender such a building', and a tenant 'may expressly agree otherwise except as prohibited by section 504B.161'. That is the provision a storm, fire or flood actually runs through -- see "Destroyed or Uninhabitable Property" clause and "Fire or Casualty: The Tenant May Leave".

BECAUSE NOTHING IS REQUIRED, ANYTHING YOU DO IS YOUR OWN CHOICE AND IS LAWFUL. If your building has a basement, an interior corridor or a designated shelter area, saying where it is costs you nothing and the optional Severe Weather and Emergencies clause does it.

Two cautions. First, do not write the clause as though Minnesota required it, because it does not. Second, do not use it to disclaim your own duties: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161 subd. 1(b) says 'the parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section', which cover fitness for the intended use, reasonable repair and compliance with health and safety laws, so a sentence purporting to put emergency safety on the tenant would be void.

One boundary worth naming: Minnesota's emergency-management law is Minn. Stat. ch. 12 and its fire-code and building-code rules are in Minnesota Rules so if your building's occupancy class carries a posted evacuation-plan requirement, it will come from there, not from the landlord-tenant act. Check with your local fire marshal.

title: Why Minnesota Gets No Crime-Free Addendum: You Already Have the Covenant, and It Is Capped
bodyText: This library does NOT offer a crime-free or drug-free housing addendum for Minnesota, and the reason is not caution -- it is that Minnesota has already written the clause for you, and then capped how far it can reach. THREE STATUTORY REASONS. First, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.171 subd. 1 puts the covenant into EVERY residential lease or licence, 'whether in writing or parol'. Both you and the tenant covenant not to allow four things. Controlled substances in violation of any criminal provision of chapter 152. Prostitution or prostitution-related activity as defined in Sec. 617.80 subd. 4. The unlawful use or possession of a firearm in violation of Sec. 609.66 subd. 1a, Sec. 609.67 or Sec. 624.713. And stolen property or property obtained by robbery. Each limb reaches 'the premises or in the common area and curtilage of the premises', not just the unit. Subdivision 1(b) adds the tenant's own covenant not to commit an act listed in Sec. 504B.206 subd. 1(a) against another tenant, licensee or authorized occupant. So an addendum adds no covenant you do not already have. Note what subdivision 2 actually does on a breach: it voids the tenant's RIGHT TO POSSESSION, not the lease, and it says expressly that 'All other provisions of the lease or license, including but not limited to the obligation to pay rent, remain in effect until the lease is terminated by the terms of the lease or operation of law.' A breach is therefore a possession ground, not a release from rent. Second, subdivision 3 says 'The parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or MODIFY the covenant imposed by this section.' A clause drafted to reach further than the statute is a modification, and void to that extent -- so the extra reach you drafted is the part that does not survive. Third, and most important, subdivision 2a, headed 'Limitation on crime-free lease provisions', caps any such clause whatever it says. You may not impose a penalty on, or terminate the lease of, a tenant for the conduct of the tenant, a HOUSEHOLD MEMBER or a GUEST occurring OFF the premises or curtilage, unless one of two things is true. Either the conduct would constitute a crime of violence against another tenant, the tenant's guest, you, or your employees -- and that one applies 'regardless of whether a charge was brought or a conviction obtained' -- or the conduct results in a CONVICTION of a crime of violence against a person unrelated to the premises. HERE IS THE PART THAT DECIDES IT. 'Crime of violence' in subdivision 2a takes its meaning from Sec. 624.712 subd. 5, 'except that it does not include offenses under chapter 152'. Chapter 152 is the controlled-substances chapter, and Sec. 624.712 subd. 5 would otherwise have included it. Because chapter 152 offences are carved out, NEITHER exception can ever cover an off-premises drug offence. A drug-free addendum that lets you act on a tenant's, household member's or guest's drug conduct away from the property is unenforceable in Minnesota in every case, not merely in doubtful ones. WHAT TO DO INSTEAD. Rely on the statutory covenant, which you already have, and read the row on it in this library. Act on conduct on the premises, the common area or the curtilage. Document what you knew and when, because the covenant is only broken by a third party's conduct if you or the tenant 'knew or had reason to know' of it. And remember the covenant binds YOU too, so allowing the conduct is your own breach. If you still want an addendum -- for example because a lender or an insurer asks for one -- you may add your own clause, but have a Minnesota lawyer draft it against subdivisions 2a and 3 first, and expect the off-premises limb to be struck. One narrow exception exists. A sober housing program for people with substance use disorders may prohibit people in the program from possessing and using cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles and hemp-derived consumer products (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.1715). This library does not offer that clause, because a sober housing program is a specialised setting. If you run one, you may add your own clause, ideally drafted with advice.

title: After a Victims-of-Violence Termination the Tenant Gives Up the Deposit
bodyText: Minnesota sets no faster deposit deadline after a violence-related termination and has no rule pausing the clock until every occupant has handed over possession. It has something else, and it runs the other way from most states. A tenant who ends a lease under Minnesota's victims-of-violence section is responsible for the rent for the whole month in which the tenancy terminates, relinquishes all claims for the return of the security deposit, and is relieved of rent and any other charges for the rest of the term. Where there are several tenants and one of them terminates, the lease for the remaining tenants ends at the later of the end of that month or the end of the rent interval, all the tenants owe the rent for that full month, and on termination all of them relinquish their claims to the deposit; any of them may apply to take a new lease from you. Four cautions, because this is a provision that is easy to overreach. The relinquishment is confined to the deposit: it does not touch rent or other amounts the tenant already owed you before the termination, which you may still pursue, and it is not a licence to treat an ordinary move-out as this kind of termination. The section only operates where the tenant or another authorised occupant fears imminent violence after domestic abuse, criminal sexual conduct, sexual extortion or harassment, and has given you signed, dated advance written notice with a qualifying document. You must not disclose what the tenant gave you, the address the tenant has moved to, or the tenant's status as a victim; none of it may go into a shared database, and it may be used as evidence in a claim about the deposit only with the tenant's consent. A breach costs you $2,000 in statutory damages plus reasonable attorney fees and costs. And the tenant cannot waive the section and you may not require a waiver. Because the relinquishment happens by statute the moment the tenancy terminates this way, there is nothing for a lease clause to add, so the library does not offer one; a landlord who wants the words in the lease should take advice first, and should not state the rule more broadly than the statute does.

title: Victim Status Is a Shield Against Eviction, and Filing Anyway Costs You the Fees
bodyText:
Minnesota's eviction protection for victims sits in one paragraph, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.285, subd. 1(b), and it holds two separate bars. The first is a status shield: 'A landlord may not commence an eviction action against a tenant or authorized occupant solely on the basis that the tenant or authorized occupant has been the victim of any of the acts listed in section 504B.206, subdivision 1, paragraph (a).' Those acts are domestic abuse, criminal sexual conduct, sexual extortion and harassment. Two things about the shield are easy to miss. It covers an authorized occupant as well as the tenant. And it asks nothing of the tenant first -- no termination notice, no qualifying document, no court order. The second bar protects a tenant who has already ended the lease under Sec. 504B.206, and that one is covered in the qualifying-documents note rather than here.

The same paragraph writes in its own limits. Nothing in it 'should be construed to prohibit an eviction action based on a breach of the lease', and nothing in it protects a tenant who gave the Sec. 504B.206 notice 'but failed to vacate on or before the date provided in that notice'. The word 'solely' is doing work too: the bar is on making the victim status the basis of your case. So the practical question is always whether your ground is the abuse or something independent of it, and your file should show which.

Filing anyway costs you twice over. The paragraph makes a landlord who violates it 'liable to the tenant for reasonable attorney fees and costs incurred by the tenant for obtaining an expungement'. And Minn. Stat. Sec. 484.014, subd. 3(a)(6) makes that expungement mandatory on the tenant's motion once the court finds the case was filed in violation of subd. 1(b). You end up paying for the erasure of your own filing, and you keep no record of it.

Now the part that matters because other states are different. Minnesota has no lease bifurcation statute: there is no statutory route to evict a perpetrator cotenant while keeping the victim in place, and chapter 504B does not authorise one, so your only levers are the ordinary ones in the lease. This library does not offer a clause ending the lease as to one cotenant only. Any such clause must not collide with Sec. 504B.206, subd. 3(b), which ends the lease for all remaining tenants when a victim cotenant terminates. If you want one, have a Minnesota lawyer draft it. Minnesota has no application-stage rule either: no statute bars refusing to rent to a victim, and victim status is not among the protected classes listed in Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.09. And Minnesota sets no cap on a victim tenant's liability for damage the perpetrator caused -- several states write such a limit into their victim statutes and Minnesota does not. None of that is an invitation. It means the restraint on you here is Sec. 504B.285, subd. 1(b) and the retaliation defence in subd. 2, not a wider victim-status regime.

Two neighbouring Minnesota rules are covered under their own topics and are not restated here: Sec. 504B.205, subd. 2(a)(2) (you may not impose a penalty on a tenant for calling for police or emergency assistance) and Sec. 504B.206 subds. 2, 3 and 6 (the termination right, the confidentiality duty and the five qualifying documents).

title: No Lock-Change Right for a Victim of Violence - the Right Is to End the Lease
bodyText:
Minnesota gives a tenant who is a victim of violence a way out of the lease, not a new set of locks. There is no lock-change right in Minnesota law and no lock-change duty on the landlord, in either direction, and nothing voids a lease term on the subject because there is no rule to contract around.

What the tenant actually gets is in Minn. Stat. section 504B.206, headed RIGHT OF VICTIMS OF VIOLENCE TO TERMINATE LEASE. On the grounds listed in subd. 1(a) - domestic abuse under section 518B.01, subd. 2, criminal sexual conduct under sections 609.342 to 609.3451, sexual extortion under section 609.3458, or harassment under section 609.749 - a tenant who fears imminent violence may end the tenancy by giving signed and dated advance written notice with a qualifying document. The section carries its own non-waiver sentence in subd. 5: 'A residential tenant may not waive, and a landlord may not require the residential tenant to waive, the tenant's rights under this section.'

So if a tenant in this situation asks you to change the locks, you are not obliged to, you are not forbidden to, and the answer is a business decision rather than a legal one. Two things do bind you. First, you may not disclose the information the tenant gave you, the contents of the qualifying document, the tenant's new address, or the tenant's status as a victim, and subd. 2(d) makes a breach worth $2,000 in statutory damages plus reasonable attorney fees and costs - so do not explain a lock change to other tenants or to anyone else by naming the reason for it. Second, the lock you change has to stay a lock the tenant can use: Minn. Stat. section 504B.375 treats removing locks as constructive exclusion of the tenant, and a change that leaves the tenant without a working key is a lockout.

If you decide to change the locks as a courtesy, do it and give the tenant the new keys the same day. If you decide not to, say so plainly and in writing, and point the tenant at the termination right instead.

title: Minnesota's Protection-Order Citations Have Not Moved, and One of Them Is Yours
bodyText:
Nothing has moved. If your Minnesota forms carry protection-order citations, the numbers they should carry are the numbers they probably already carry, and that is worth knowing because several states have shifted theirs recently. Minnesota's order for protection has been Minn. Stat. Sec. 518B.01 since Laws 1979, ch. 214, sec. 1. The domestic abuse no contact order has been Minn. Stat. Sec. 629.75 since Laws 2010, ch. 299, secs. 13 and 14. The harassment restraining order has been Minn. Stat. Sec. 609.748 since Laws 1990, ch. 461, sec. 5. Harassment and stalking have been Minn. Stat. Sec. 609.749 since Laws 1993, ch. 326, art. 2, sec. 22. Each of those history lines was read in full and none of them records a renumbering.

The best practice is not to cite at all, because the statute does the citing for you. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.206, subd. 6(3) defines the five qualifying documents a tenant may give you, and two of them are orders: 'a valid order for protection issued under chapter 518B' and 'a no contact order currently in effect, issued under section 629.75 or chapter 609'. Notice how wide the second one is. It points at a whole chapter, not a section, so a harassment restraining order under Sec. 609.748 and a stalking no contact order under Sec. 609.749 both qualify without your form naming either. A form that lists sections will go stale; a form that repeats the statute's own words will not.

Two dead or new numbers to watch for, neither of them a renumbering. First, sexual extortion, Minn. Stat. Sec. 609.3458, is a new section, added by Laws 2021, First Special Session ch. 11, art. 4, sec. 22. It is one of the four grounds in Sec. 504B.206, subd. 1(a), so a form or policy written before 2021 is missing a ground rather than citing a wrong number. Second, Minn. Stat. Sec. 609.749, subds. 1 and 1a were repealed by Laws 2020, ch. 96, sec. 6. Anything that still cites Sec. 609.749, subd. 1 for the definition of stalking is citing a repealed subdivision; the current definitions are in subd. 2.

What an order for protection actually does to your building is the part landlords ask about, and three subdivisions answer it. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 518B.01, subd. 6(a)(2) the court may 'exclude the abusing party from the dwelling which the parties share or from the residence of the petitioner', and under subd. 9, on the petitioner's request, 'the court shall order the sheriff to accompany the petitioner and assist in placing the petitioner in possession of the dwelling or residence'. Then the one that catches people out: subd. 6(d) says an exclusion order 'is not voided by the admittance of the abusing party into the dwelling from which the abusing party is excluded'. The victim letting the excluded person back in does not cancel the order. But subd. 12 is equally short and pulls the other way: 'Nothing in this section shall affect the title to real estate.' An exclusion order moves a person out of a dwelling. It does not take anyone off your lease, and it does not decide who owes you rent.

One citation Minnesota gives you rather than the tenant, and no row in this library has carried it before. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.325 reads in full: 'A landlord or the landlord's agent may request expedited temporary relief by bringing an action under section 609.748 or filing a petition for a temporary restraining order, in conjunction with a complaint filed under section 504B.321.' So the harassment-restraining-order statute is a landlord's route as well as a tenant's, and it runs alongside the expedited eviction track rather than instead of it. The expedited track itself changed on August 1, 2026 and is covered in its own note.

title: Submetering Electricity Puts You Under the Public Utilities Commission
bodyText:
If you submeter electricity or natural gas in a shared-metered residential building, you do not become a public utility, but you do come under the Public Utilities Commission's authority. Minn. Stat. § 216B.022, subd. 2(a) says so directly, and § 504B.216, subd. 3 and § 216B.023, subd. 2(a) both make you subject to § 216B.024.

In practice that means a tenant who disputes a bill goes to you first. If you cannot agree, you must tell the tenant they may complain to the Commission's consumer affairs office and hand them its current phone number and email address. The Commission can then resolve the complaint, the tenant can appeal its resolution to the Commission itself, and from there seek judicial review.

Three hard limits are worth memorising. You may never apportion electricity — it may only be submetered (§ 504B.216, subd. 5(a)). Any submeter installed on or after January 1, 2025 must meet American National Standards Institute standards, and every submeter, however old, must measure accurately (§ 216B.022, subd. 2). And you may not charge tenants anything for installing, maintaining, repairing, replacing or reading a submeter. The only exception is an expense caused by the tenant's own willful, malicious or negligent conduct (§ 216B.022, subd. 5; § 504B.216, subd. 4(d)).

A pending Commission complaint also has teeth in court. If the tenant has a complaint about shared-metered gas or electricity before the Commission, a court must stay your utility-nonpayment eviction and may not make the tenant post money or a bond (§ 504B.285, subd. 4(b)). Separately, the attorney general may investigate and prosecute violations of § 504B.216 (§ 504B.216, subd. 17). A violation of subdivisions 2 to 12 of § 504B.216 is also a violation of § 504B.161, and of most of them a violation of § 504B.221 as well (§ 504B.216, subd. 16).

title: No Emergency-Contact Rule - What Minnesota Requires Instead
bodyText:
Minnesota has no emergency-contact rule in either direction. Nothing makes a tenant name an emergency contact, and nothing makes you publish an emergency telephone number, keep a 24-hour line or answer the phone outside business hours. The point is left to your lease.

What Minnesota does require is that the tenant always knows who you are and where to reach you. Minn. Stat. section 504B.181, subd. 1 requires disclosure to the tenant, either in the rental agreement or otherwise in writing before the tenancy begins, of the name and address of the person authorised to manage the premises and of the landlord or an agent authorised to accept service of process and receive notices and demands. Subd. 2 requires a printed or typewritten notice with that information in a conspicuous place on the premises. The teeth are in subd. 4: no action to recover rent or possession may be maintained unless that information was disclosed as the section requires, or was known to or disclosed to the tenant at least 30 days before the action started. And subd. 3 is the trap - if you have not complied, a caretaker, a manager or whoever collects the rent is deemed your agent for service of process and for notices, and must forward what they receive to you personally or by certified mail. That is already covered by the Disclosure of Landlord and Manager clause and its education row; the point here is that it, rather than an emergency number, is what the law guarantees the tenant.

Three related rules are worth knowing before you draft anything about emergencies. First, you may never penalise a tenant for calling for help: Minn. Stat. section 504B.205 protects a residential tenant's right to seek police and emergency assistance, and the tenant cannot waive it and you cannot require a waiver of it. Second, a medical emergency can stop an eviction: under Minn. Stat. section 504B.216, subd. 12, an eviction for unpaid natural gas or electric charges may not be filed, and one already filed must be stayed, where the tenant notifies you or the court of a household medical emergency, or where life-sustaining medical equipment requiring electricity is in use, with certification from a licensed medical health care professional within five days. Third, if you operate housing with services exempt from assisted living licensure, Minn. Stat. section 325F.722, subd. 4 gives you real emergency duties: a written emergency disaster plan covering evacuation, sheltering in place, temporary relocation sites and staff assignments, prominently posted; building emergency exit diagrams given to every resident on signing and posted on each floor; a written policy on missing residents; emergency and disaster training for all staff at orientation and annually; and a documented fire or other emergency drill at least once every six months.

If you ask for an emergency contact, ask for it as an optional lease term, use it only in a real emergency, and keep it to yourself. One Minnesota rule bites hard here: where a tenant has given you information under the victim-of-violence termination section, Minn. Stat. section 504B.206, subd. 2 bars you from disclosing it, from disclosing the address the tenant has relocated to, or from entering it into any shared database, says those duties override any release-of-information form the tenant signed earlier, and sets statutory damages of $2,000 plus attorney fees. A contact-details field in a property-management system is precisely where that goes wrong.

title: Minnesota Leaves Condemnation to the Lease, So the Optional Clause Is Doing Real Work
bodyText:
Nothing in Minnesota law, including its eminent domain chapter, Minn. Stat. ch. 117, ends a lease or abates rent when the property is taken, or divides the award between you and your tenant. That is why the Condemnation clause is offered as an optional lease term here: the point is left to the bargain, so the lease is where it has to be settled. Minn. Stat. Secs. 327C.095, 327C.096 and 327C.097 mention eminent domain only as an EXCLUSION, taking a manufactured home park bought or closed by eminent domain out of the park-closing notice, resident-offer and relocation-trust-fund duties.

Chapter 504B has no condemnation provision at all; its five uses of 'condemn' are all about a building condemned as unfit to live in by a housing inspector, which is a different thing entirely and is covered by "Never Accept Rent or a Deposit After a Condemnation or Vacate Order" and "You Must Hand Over Outstanding Inspection and Condemnation Orders".

THE NEAREST MINNESOTA DEFAULT, and the one to be careful about: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.131 says a tenant 'of a building that is destroyed or becomes uninhabitable or unfit for occupancy through no fault or neglect of the tenant or occupant may vacate and surrender such a building', and that a tenant 'may expressly agree otherwise except as prohibited by section 504B.161'. A partial taking that leaves the rest unfit can reach that description. The optional clause is consistent with it, because the clause also ends the lease rather than holding the tenant to it -- see "Destroyed or Uninhabitable Property" clause and "Fire or Casualty: The Tenant May Leave".

TWO LIMITS ON THE CLAUSE. First, it allocates the award as between you and your tenant; it cannot bind the condemning authority. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 117.025, subd. 3, an 'owner' in a taking includes tenants. Under Sec. 117.085 the commissioners make 'a separate assessment and award of the damages' to each owner, so your tenant may receive an award of its own. As between you and your tenant, the clause's assignment of the lease's value to you governs; whether a court will apply it when it apportions an award (Sec. 117.175) only case law could settle. So the clause keeps the tenant's own relocation payments, which the acquiring authority owes displaced persons under Sec. 117.52, and you should not try to claim them.

Second, the clause's deposit limb defers to the rest of the lease, which is right: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.178 applies in full to every live tenancy and 'any attempted waiver of this section by a landlord and tenant, by contract or otherwise, shall be void and unenforceable', so no condemnation term can shorten the deposit rules.

Before you rely on the award-allocation sentence in a real taking, get Minnesota condemnation advice.

title: Minnesota Does Not Make You Screen Staff -- It Regulates What You May Ask
bodyText: Minnesota does not require you to screen the people you employ at a rental property. There is no statute making a landlord run a background check on a caretaker, a manager, a maintenance worker or a contractor, and no statutory negligence shield for having run one. If you want employee screening, it is your policy, not a legal duty -- and the reason to have one is insurance and liability exposure, not compliance. WHAT MINNESOTA DOES REGULATE IS WHAT YOU MAY ASK. As an employer you are subject to the Minnesota Human Rights Act, and Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.08 subd. 4 makes it an unfair employment practice, except where there is a bona fide occupational qualification, to do any of the following before a person is employed. You may not require or request information pertaining to race, color, creed, religion, national origin, sex, gender identity, marital status, status with regard to public assistance, familial status, disability, sexual orientation or age. You may not require or request a physical examination, subject to Sec. 363A.20. You may not seek and obtain that same information from ANY SOURCE for the purpose of making a job decision -- which reaches your background vendor and your reference calls, not just your application form. And you may not publish a job advertisement that discloses a preference, limitation, specification or discrimination on any of those grounds. Anyone required to provide information prohibited by that subdivision is an aggrieved party and can bring a Human Rights Act claim. The practical consequence is that your screening vendor's standard report and questionnaire are your problem, not theirs: tell them in writing what you do not want returned. ONE EXEMPTION THAT MAY APPLY TO YOU. Minn. Stat.
