Sec. 363A.20 subd. 1 says the provisions of Sec. 363A.08 do not apply to the employment of an individual 'by the individual's parent, grandparent, spouse, child, or grandchild' or 'in the domestic service of any person'. So a small owner employing a family member at the property may be outside the section entirely. Do not stretch that: it is about who the employee is, not how small you are. CRIMINAL RECORDS: WAIT UNTIL THE INTERVIEW. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 364.021(a), a private employer may not ask about, consider or require disclosure of an applicant's criminal record until the applicant is selected for an interview. If there is no interview, wait until you make a conditional job offer. So keep the question off your application form. You may tell applicants that law or your policy disqualifies people with a particular criminal history from particular positions (Sec. 364.021(c)). The Commissioner of Human Rights enforces this against private employers by fines, up to $100 to $500 a violation depending on how many people you employ (Sec. 364.06, subd. 2). Federal law on background reports is also a separate regime not covered here.

title: Minnesota's Energy Benchmarking Law and Your Tenant's Usage Data
bodyText:
Minnesota has an energy benchmarking law, Minn. Stat. § 216C.331, and it reaches larger rental buildings. A 'covered property' has one or more buildings totalling 50,000 gross square feet or more. It must be served by an investor-owned utility in Anoka, Carver, Dakota, Hennepin, Ramsey, Scott or Washington County, or by a municipal or investor-owned utility in an outstate city of over 50,000 people. A residential property with fewer than five dwelling units is not covered (subd. 1(f)).

If your building is covered, you must benchmark it each year by June 1 in the federal Energy Star Portfolio Manager tool or an equivalent the commissioner approves (subds. 4 and 7). The commissioner may fine you $1,000 for failing to comply (subd. 16).

You get the data from the utility, not through a lease clause. On your request the utility must supply customer energy use data and aggregated whole-building data (subd. 8). An aggregated data set must combine at least four customers, and no one customer may exceed half the total. A smaller data set needs written consent: from every customer in it if there are three or fewer, or from any customer using more than half. Within 30 days of your request, a tenant of a covered property must give you any information about the energy use of the tenant's unit that you cannot otherwise get and need to comply (subd. 5(c)).

So the statute, not the lease, makes the tenant's data reach you. No Minnesota statute authorises a lease clause releasing it, and none voids a tenant's genuine written consent. Where you do need consent, for a building with three or fewer metered customers or one dominant one, get a specific, separate, revocable written consent when you need it rather than burying a data release in the lease. If you need a tenant's usage history outside benchmarking, ask the utility as the customer of record where you hold the account.

The other flow Minnesota regulates runs the other way: the landlord must give the tenant copies of the bills being apportioned, and must list that right in the lease or a written notice (Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 5(c) and (d)).

A city may impose stricter benchmarking by ordinance (§ 216C.331, subd. 11(b)). Minneapolis and St. Paul requirements are a municipal question, and § 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(4) already obliges you to comply with local health and safety laws including ordinances regulating rental licensing.

title: Can a Company Landlord Run Its Own Minnesota Eviction? Only Within Narrow Limits
bodyText:
If you own rental property through a corporation, an LLC or a partnership, do not assume an owner, a manager or an employee may file and argue the eviction. Settle it with a Minnesota lawyer before the hearing date, because the answer comes from the unauthorised-practice statute and the courts, not the landlord-tenant act, and it has limits.

What chapter 504B does say is worth knowing, and it cuts both ways. Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 1 requires only that "the person complaining" file the complaint, and Minn. Stat. section 504B.332, subd. 1 defines "plaintiff" for the service section as including "the plaintiff's attorney, employees of the plaintiff's attorney, or any other agent of the plaintiff" - so the statute contemplates non-lawyer agents doing at least the service work. Minn. Stat. section 504B.335(a) and (b) let the defendant answer at the appearance and either party demand a jury, and subd. (c) makes the proceedings the same as in other civil actions except as Minn. Stat. sections 504B.281 to 504B.371 provide. None of that tells you who may stand up for a company.

The rule that governs is Minn. Stat. section 481.02, the unauthorised-practice-of-law statute. Subdivision 2 bars a for-profit corporation from maintaining an action "by or through its officers or employees or any one else", except in its own behalf as a party. Subdivision 3 then lets some non-lawyers handle a residential eviction. Clause (12) lets an authorised management agent of a residential owner, including a business entity, bring and conduct an action to recover possession. Clause (13) lets any person conduct, for either side, an eviction under section 504B.285, subd. 1 or section 504B.301; only a nonprofit corporation may charge a separate fee for it. Clause (15) lets a corporation's sole shareholder appear for it. None of these lets a non-lawyer conduct a jury trial or handle an appeal. But the Revisor prints a note under the section: it "was deemed unconstitutional to the extent that it attempts to require courts to allow nonattorneys to appear in court on behalf of corporations." So whether a court must let your non-lawyer appear for your company only case law could settle, and the court may refuse. In Hennepin and Ramsey County Housing Court, General Rule of Practice 603 adds two requirements. The action must be brought in the owner's name, not the agent's. And no one but the principal or a lawyer may appear unless a Power of Authority is attached to the complaint when it is filed. The cautious course: have a lawyer appear for an entity landlord, and always for a jury trial or appeal. If a manager appears instead, name the entity as plaintiff and attach the Power of Authority to the complaint.

Three practical points that do not depend on the answer. Get the entity's exact legal name right on the complaint, because Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 5 requires the court to dismiss and expunge the record of any action where the person bringing it fails to comply with that section. Make sure the Minn. Stat. section 504B.181 landlord and manager disclosure names the entity and its agent correctly, since subd. 4 bars maintaining an action to recover rent or possession without it. And remember Minn. Stat. section 504B.172: if your lease lets you recover attorney fees, the tenant gets them on the same terms when the tenant wins, so running the case yourself to save fees does not remove your exposure to the tenant's.

title: No Landlord Environmental-Event Termination - and Condemnation Stops Your Rent Instead
bodyText: Minnesota gives a landlord no statutory right to end a lease because of an environmental event, a contamination, a hazard or a casualty. Every Minnesota provision in this area runs the other way. Minn. Stat. 504B.131 lets the TENANT vacate and surrender a building that is destroyed or becomes uninhabitable or unfit for occupancy through no fault or neglect of the tenant or occupant. Minn. Stat. 504B.195 makes you give a tenant, and a person about to sign, copies of outstanding inspection citations that threaten health or safety and of any condemnation order or declaration of unfitness. Minn. Stat. 504B.204 then bars you from accepting rent or a deposit at all once the premises have been condemned, declared unfit, ordered vacated for a code violation, or ordered vacated under a government taking. Breaking that costs actual damages plus three times everything collected, with costs and attorney fees, and counts as a breach of the habitability covenant. Neither section can be waived by the lease. So the condemnation case is not a termination right: it is a rent stop. You may still reserve an early-termination right by contract, because Minnesota is not a just-cause state and a holdover contrary to a lease condition is itself a ground for an eviction. The library does not offer that clause, for three reasons. Your fitness, repair, energy-efficiency, code-compliance and winter-heat covenants cannot be waived or modified, so a clause cannot convert your repair duty into an exit. The clause would sit on top of the tenant's own non-waivable rights. And the notice period you give can never be shorter than the notice your lease asks of the tenant. If you want such a clause, have a Minnesota lawyer draft it. Whatever it says, keep the three statutory duties above and recover possession only through the court.

title: A Charger Left Behind Is Abandoned Property, Not a Lease Question
bodyText:
Minnesota has no rule about electric vehicle charging equipment at the end of a tenancy. What it does have are two general rules that decide what happens to a charger the tenant leaves behind, and both of them beat whatever the lease says.

If the tenant abandons the premises, you may take possession of the property left there, but you must store and care for it. You may sell or dispose of it only 28 days after you get actual notice of the abandonment, or 28 days after it reasonably appears the tenant has abandoned the premises, whichever is later. Before a sale you must make reasonable efforts to notify the tenant at least 14 days ahead, by personal service or by first class and certified mail, and post notice on the premises for two weeks. You may apply a reasonable amount of the proceeds to removal, care and storage costs and to the claims security deposit law allows, and the rest goes to the tenant on written demand (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.271, subd. 1).

The sanction is real. If you hold the tenant's property and do not let the tenant retake it within 24 hours of written demand - 48 hours excluding weekends and holidays if you moved it off the premises - the tenant recovers punitive damages of up to twice actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus actual damages and attorney fees (Sec. 504B.271, subd. 2). None of this can be waived: a lease provision waiving any part of Sec. 504B.271 is contrary to public policy and void.

If instead you evict and the sheriff executes a writ, the rules are different. The tenant must pay the removal costs immediately, and if the tenant does not, you have a lien on all of the tenant's personal property for the reasonable costs of removing, caring for, storing and transporting it. You may hold the property until paid, and if nothing is paid for 60 days after the order to vacate is executed you may hold a public sale (Sec. 504B.365, subd. 3). That section may not be waived or modified by lease either.

So a lease may say a charger the tenant paid for stays the tenant's property, that the tenant may remove it or sell it to you at an agreed price, and that the tenant pays for removal damage. Minnesota contradicts none of that. But if the charger is still there after the tenant goes, you are in the abandoned-property procedure or the eviction-lien procedure, not in the lease. Agree removal in writing before move-out. One caution: a hard-wired charger may be a fixture, and whether it has become yours by attachment is a common-law question.

title: EV Charging in Minnesota: Installation Standards, and a Licence and Tax From 2027
bodyText:
Minnesota gives a tenant no right to install or demand electric vehicle charging, so whether a charger goes in is your decision. Three sets of Minnesota rules reach you once one does go in.

First, installation standards. Any electric vehicle infrastructure installed in this state must, without significant upgrading, allow use by any make, model or type of electric vehicle, meet the requirements of Minn. Stat. Sec. 326B.35 and the standards set by the Society of Automotive Engineers, and be capable of bidirectional charging once electric utilities can cost-effectively draw electricity from connected vehicles (Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.185). That duty is on whoever installs the equipment, which can be you or your tenant. Read section 326B.35 before you rely on it.

Second, selling the electricity. From July 1, 2027 nobody may act as a "public charging station operator" without a licence from the commissioner, and a tax of five cents per kilowatt-hour falls on every such operator (Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 296A.051 and 296A.075, added by Laws 2025, First Special Session ch. 8). A "public charging station" is a facility where a person conducts for-profit business using charging equipment and charges the customer for the electricity delivered. A landlord who bills tenants for charging should be measured against that definition before 2027. Three exemptions from the tax matter: charging at a private residence on power paid for by the owner or occupant and supplied by an electric utility; stations with a charging capacity under 50 kilowatts; and stations that do not require payment. Operating without the licence makes the tax immediately due, with a 25 percent penalty and interest, and operators must keep records for three and a half years.

Third, weights and measures. Minnesota now has a retail charging-equipment regime: an annual inspection, a $100 fee for each charging port payable by the equipment's owner, sale by the kilowatt-hour, a unit price displayed in whole cents or tenths of a cent, prescribed labelling, and the same price information on any sign or advertisement (Minn. Stat. Sec. 239.90, added by Laws 2025, First Special Session ch. 4). The section does not define "retail" equipment, so treat the edge of that regime as unsettled.

Billing a tenant for the electricity is the hardest part of all this, and in a shared-metered building it may not be possible at all. That is covered under the shared-area charging topic. Take advice before you resell charging electricity to a tenant.

title: Shared-Area EV Charging: No Rule on the Bay, Hard Rules on the Electricity
bodyText:
Minnesota has no statute about electric vehicle charging in a shared parking area, so a fee to reserve the bay where a charger is installed, and the allocation of damage to the equipment, are yours to set by lease. What Minnesota does regulate hard is the electricity, and that is where a shared-area charger runs into trouble.

If your building is shared-metered - more separate dwelling units than meters - and you bill tenants separately for electricity, three rules bite at once. Apportioning electricity to tenants is prohibited outright (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.216, subd. 5), and a landlord who bills separately for electricity must not apportion it (Sec. 216B.023, subd. 2). Electricity may only be submetered, and a submeter is defined as a meter that measures service consumed solely within an individual dwelling unit (Sec. 504B.216, subd. 1). A charger in a shared parking area is not inside anyone's unit. And you must not charge a tenant for electricity consumed in common areas or in spaces you use yourself (Sec. 216B.023, subd. 2).

On top of that, the only money you may add for utility service is one administrative billing charge of up to $8 per billing period and one late payment charge of up to $5 per month. The statute says no other fees or charges may be imposed on or collected from tenants for utility service (Sec. 504B.216, subds. 8 and 9).

Put together, a shared-metered Minnesota building has no clean statutory route to bill tenants for the electricity a shared-area charger uses. The practical answers are to absorb that electricity as a building cost, to put the charger on a bay served by the tenant's own directly metered utility service, or not to offer shared-area charging.

These rules do not apply to a manufactured home park, which the statute excludes, and they do not apply if every unit is directly metered by the utility - but then you are selling electricity you bought, which raises the licence and tax questions covered under EV charging requirements. Take advice before you bill for shared-area charging.

title: How Long Minnesota Courts May Delay an Eviction Writ
bodyText:
Minnesota has no hardship stay of an eviction. There is no provision letting a court postpone a writ because the tenant is ill, elderly, out of work, has young children, or cannot find another home, and there is no cold-weather or seasonal eviction moratorium. What Minnesota has instead is a set of short, fixed delays.

After judgment for the landlord, Minn. Stat. section 504B.345, subd. 1(d) requires the court to stay the writ of recovery of premises and order to vacate for a reasonable period, not to exceed seven days. That stay does not apply to an action brought under Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, or on the basis that the tenant engages in behaviour that seriously endangers the safety of other residents or intentionally and seriously damages the property of the landlord or a tenant, and it does not apply when the court has issued a default judgment.

Three other short delays can apply. Where the landlord combined a nonpayment allegation with a material lease violation and did not prove the violation, Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subd. 5(b) gives the tenant up to seven days of additional time to pay rent the court finds due. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1(b) a tenant who has paid the rent in arrears but cannot pay the interest, costs and attorney's fee may be allowed to pay those into court and be restored to possession within the same period for which the court stays the order to vacate. And if the tenant or the tenant's attorney tells the court the tenant intends to appeal, Minn. Stat. section 504B.371, subd. 1 requires a stay of the writ for at least 24 hours after judgment; once an appeal is taken, subds. 4 and 5 stay further proceedings and require the court to grant a stay of a writ already issued, with an appeal bond under subd. 3. Subd. 7 removes subds. 1, 4 and 5 where the landlord prevailed on a claim under section 504B.171, subd. 2 and gives a bond.

Minnesota's manufactured home park law is separate and more generous: Minn. Stat. section 327C.11, subd. 3 stays a writ for up to seven days to let the resident arrange to move the home, and subd. 4 allows a conditional writ leaving the home on the lot for 60 days for an in-park sale. Do not read those into a residential lease.

title: A Lease Cannot Shorten the Court's Stay or the Writ Procedure
bodyText:
Do not put a term in a Minnesota lease that waives, shortens or alters the stay of an eviction writ, the appeal stay, or how the writ is carried out. The stay under Minn. Stat. section 504B.345, subd. 1(d) is a duty the statute puts on the court, not a right of the tenant the tenant can give up, so a lease term cannot reach it. The appeal stays in Minn. Stat. section 504B.371 work the same way, and subd. 3 caps the appeal bond: the court may not require a bond including back rent, late fees, disputed charges or any other amount in excess of the regular rent as it accrues each month.

Execution of the writ is expressly non-waivable. Minn. Stat. section 504B.365, subd. 5 says of that section: "This section may not be waived or modified by lease or other agreement." That covers the officer's 24-hour demand, the removal and storage of the tenant's property, the inventory, the landlord's responsibility for the property, and the notice the landlord must send of the date and approximate time the officer is scheduled to remove the tenant. The same subdivision makes a landlord who enters and removes the tenant's property in violation of the section guilty of an unlawful ouster under Minn. Stat. section 504B.231 and subject to penalty under Minn. Stat. section 504B.225, unless the premises has been abandoned.

A term purporting to do any of this is unenforceable, and including it risks the chapter-wide enforcement power in Minn. Stat. section 504B.501, under which the attorney general may investigate and prosecute violations of chapter 504B using the authority in Minn. Stat. section 8.31.

title: Penalty and Fee Clauses Tied to an Eviction
bodyText: Minnesota has no rule like Colorado's voiding a lease clause that assigns a penalty arising from an eviction notice or an eviction action, and no rule authorising such a clause either. What Minnesota has instead is a set of limits that leave an eviction fee very little room. The court, not your lease, decides the money side of an eviction: if you win, the court taxes the costs against the tenant and issues execution for them. In a nonpayment case the tenant can redeem at any time before possession is delivered by paying the rent in arrears with interest, the costs of the action and an attorney's fee of no more than $5, which is the statutory ceiling on what you can require to be paid for the case itself. If your lease lets you recover attorney fees, directly or through additional rent, the tenant gets the same right by operation of law. The rules for executing the writ cannot be waived or changed by your lease, and they already give you a lien on the tenant's property for the reasonable costs of removing, caring for, storing and transporting it. Minnesota sets no liquidated-damages figure for a lease breach, and a late fee is expressly neither interest nor liquidated damages, so a flat sum charged because a notice went out or a case was filed looks like an unenforceable penalty rather than a measured charge. Minnesota does have one express penalty ban, and it is worth knowing: a tenant may not be evicted, and the tenant's obligations under the lease may not be increased nor services decreased, where that is intended as a penalty for the tenant's complaint of a violation, and for 90 days after the complaint you carry the burden of proving otherwise. That protection sits in the tenant remedies part of the chapter, and a lease provision waiving it is contrary to public policy and void. A separate rule bars penalising a tenant for calling for police or emergency assistance. On top of that, a fee the tenant cannot avoid has to be disclosed in the lease and in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, with treble damages for failure. So the library offers no eviction-penalty or eviction-fee clause for Minnesota. Nothing in the statutes bans one, so you may add your own, but take advice first and keep it to real, provable cost. Penalties in this area mostly run the other way: since August 1, 2026 you may not name a tenant's minor child as a defendant in an eviction complaint, that rule cannot be waived, and the tenant recovers actual damages or $300, whichever is greater. This covers Minnesota's statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. See the companion row "Charging a Tenant for Serving a Notice" for charges tied to serving a notice.

title: Four Ways a Minnesota Eviction Gets Dismissed and Expunged for Your Own Mistake
bodyText:
The library already explains Minn. Stat. section 484.014, the expungement statute, under the eviction-record-sealing topic. What that row does not cover is the set of provisions that make dismissal AND expungement the automatic consequence of a landlord's own procedural error. These are the ones that cost you the case, not just the record.

First, a missing 14-day notice. Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 1(d) requires the person filing to attach a copy of the subd. 1a written notice if applicable, and then: "The court shall dismiss an action without prejudice for failure to provide a notice as described in subdivision 1a and grant an expungement of the eviction case court file." Without prejudice means you may refile, but only after giving the notice and starting the 14 days again.

Second, any other failure to comply with the complaint-and-summons section. Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 5 is broader and blunter: "The court must dismiss and expunge the record of any action if the person bringing the action fails to comply with this section." That reaches the subd. 3 attachments - the lease and addenda, the itemised accounting, the identification of the clause breached and the clause granting the right to evict, the notice to vacate, and the housing-subsidy statement - as well as the summons requirements in subd. 4.

Third, losing. Minn. Stat. section 504B.345, subd. 1(c) requires the court, if the court or jury finds for the defendant, to enter judgment for the defendant, tax the costs against the landlord, issue execution in the defendant's favour, and expunge the records relating to the action under section 484.014 or the court's inherent authority, at the time judgment is entered or later on the defendant's motion.

Fourth, evicting a victim. Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subd. 1(b) bars commencing an eviction action against a tenant or authorised occupant solely because that person has been the victim of any of the acts listed in Minn. Stat. section 504B.206, subd. 1(a), and bars an action against a residential tenant who has terminated a lease under section 504B.206. A landlord violating that paragraph "is liable to the tenant for reasonable attorney fees and costs incurred by the tenant for obtaining an expungement as provided under section 484.014, subdivision 3" - so you pay for the expungement you caused. The paragraph preserves an eviction based on a breach of the lease, or where the tenant gave the section 504B.206 written notice but failed to vacate by the date in it.

The practical reading: in Minnesota the attachments are not administrative tidiness. Each one is a condition of keeping the case.

title: Which Eviction Papers the Court Writes and Which You Write
bodyText:
Minnesota splits eviction paperwork between the landlord and the court, and it is worth knowing which is which before you draft anything.

You write the complaint and its attachments under Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subds. 1 and 3, the affidavit supporting an expedited hearing under subd. 2, the 14-day nonpayment notice under subd. 1a, and any notice to quit or notice to vacate. If the case is a public housing breach-of-lease eviction, you must also put the court-appointed-counsel notice on the first page of the complaint in bold 12-point type under Minn. Stat. section 504B.268, subd. 1.

The court writes the rest. Minn. Stat. section 504B.361, subd. 1 requires the state court administrator to develop a uniform form for the summons and for the writ of recovery of premises and order to vacate, and sets two statements the writ must carry in the statute's own words - the legal-help statement naming Legal Aid and www.LawHelpMN.org, and the financial-help statement naming the county or Tribal social services office, MNBenefits.mn.gov and 2-1-1 or 800-543-7709. The summons itself must carry the six items in Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 4, including the same two statements. Minn. Stat. section 504B.355 sets out the form of the verdict or finding almost word for word.

One cross-reference in section 504B.361, subd. 1 was wrong and has been corrected. As compiled in 2025 it said the summons shall conform to the requirements in Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subdivision 3, which is the contents-of-complaint subdivision. Laws 2026, ch. 88, sec. 210 changes that to subdivision 4, which is the summons subdivision. Work from subd. 4 for the summons and subd. 3 for the complaint attachments.

Do not design your own summons or writ, and do not paraphrase the statutory statements. Where the statute writes the words, reproduce them.

title: How an Endangerment or Unlawful-Activities Case Keeps Priority to the End
bodyText:
The library already explains the expedited hearing itself under the expedited-criminal-eviction topic. What that row does not trace is what happens after the hearing: Minnesota gives the same narrow class of case priority at four further points, and a landlord should know the chain rather than assume speed stops at the hearing date.

The class is the one in Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 2(a) - an action under Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, or on the basis that the residential tenant engages in behaviour that seriously endangers the safety of other residents, or intentionally and seriously damages the property of the landlord or a tenant - and from August 1, 2026 a tenant who assaults the landlord or the landlord's employees or contractors.

First, scheduling. Minn. Stat. section 504B.335(d) requires the court to give priority in scheduling appearances and hearings to an eviction brought under section 504B.171, or on the endangerment or serious-damage basis.

Second, the writ. Minn. Stat. section 504B.345, subd. 1(b) requires the court to give priority in issuing the writ of recovery of premises and order to vacate for an action under section 504B.171 or on the basis that the tenant is causing a nuisance or seriously endangers the safety of other residents, their property or the landlord's property. Note the wording is not identical to subd. 2(a) of section 504B.321: it adds causing a nuisance and it reaches the safety of residents' property, not only their persons.

Third, the stay. Minn. Stat. section 504B.345, subd. 1(d) withholds the usual stay of up to seven days from an action brought under section 504B.171, or on the basis that the tenant engages in behaviour that seriously endangers the safety of other residents or intentionally and seriously damages property. So in this class the writ issues without the ordinary delay.

Fourth, marking and execution. Minn. Stat. section 504B.361, subd. 2 requires the court to identify such a writ and clearly note on the order to vacate that it is a priority order, in a manner obvious to the officer who must execute it. Minn. Stat. section 504B.365, subd. 2 then requires the officer to give priority to executing it.

Appeal is different again. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.371, subd. 7, where the landlord prevailed on a claim under Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, subd. 2, the ordinary appeal stays in subds. 1, 4 and 5 do not apply if the landlord gives a bond conditioned to pay all costs and damages if the judgment of restitution is reversed and a new trial ordered; the court then issues the writ notwithstanding the notice of appeal. That is a section 504B.171 claim only, not the whole expedited class.

title: The Course of a Minnesota Eviction Action
bodyText:
Possession in Minnesota is recovered only through a court eviction action. Minn. Stat. section 504B.281 says no person may occupy or take possession of real property except where allowed by law, and then only peaceably.

Filing. The landlord files a complaint under Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 1, stating the defendant's full name and date of birth unless not known, describing the premises, stating the facts authorising recovery and asking for possession. Missing the name or date of birth does not defeat jurisdiction or invalidate the complaint. Subd. 3 requires the landlord to attach the current or most recent written lease and any relevant addenda; an itemised accounting if nonpayment is alleged; the clause breached, the conduct, the dates and the clause granting the right to evict if a breach is alleged; the nature and dates of the conduct if a violation of Minn. Stat. section 504B.171 is alleged; any notice to vacate or notice to quit if a section 504B.285, subd. 1 ground is alleged; and a statement of whether the tenancy is affected by a federal or state housing subsidy programme, naming the administering agency. If the ground is nonpayment, the subd. 1a 14-day notice must also be attached, and under subd. 1(d) the court must dismiss without prejudice and expunge the file if it was not given. Under subd. 5 the court must dismiss and expunge the record of any action where the landlord fails to comply with section 504B.321 at all. Under subd. 6 the action is not accessible to the public until final judgment, though the parties and attorneys assisting a party may see the file.

Summons and appearance. The court issues a summons with the complaint attached, carrying the six items in subd. 4 including two statements in the statute's own words about legal help and financial help. The appearance is not less than seven nor more than 14 days from issuing the summons, except in the expedited procedure.

Service. Minn. Stat. section 504B.332 governs service and is the section to work from. The summons and complaint must be served at least seven days before the appearance. If the landlord regularly uses electronic written communication with the tenant, the landlord must also make a good faith attempt to tell the tenant the hearing is scheduled at least seven days before, with a time and date stamp and the date, time and place of the hearing. Personal or substitute service comes first; service by mail and posting is available only if personal or substitute service was unsuccessful, and for a residential eviction requires at least two personal service attempts on different days, one of them between 6:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. Affidavits must be filed at least three days before the appearance.

Trial and judgment. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.335 the defendant may answer at the appearance, either party may demand a jury, and the proceedings are the same as in other civil actions except as sections 504B.281 to 504B.371 provide. When setting a trial date the court must allow for a fair, thorough and timely adjudication of the merits, including the complexity of the matter, discovery, witnesses, the chance to seek counsel and raise affirmative defences, and the extenuating factors in section 504B.171. If the landlord wins, Minn. Stat. section 504B.345 requires immediate judgment for recovery of the premises, costs taxed against the defendant, and immediate issue of the writ, with a stay of up to seven days in most cases. If the defendant wins, the court enters judgment for the defendant, taxes costs against the landlord and expunges the records. The writ is executed under Minn. Stat. section 504B.365, which may not be waived or modified by lease or other agreement. Appeal is within 15 days under Minn. Stat. section 504B.371.

Two long-stops. A person may be evicted for unlawfully or forcibly occupying or taking possession, or for unlawfully detaining or retaining possession, under Minn. Stat. section 504B.301. But under Minn. Stat. section 504B.311 no eviction action may be brought where the occupant's lease was terminated more than three years before the action began and the occupant was in quiet possession for the three consecutive years immediately before filing.

title: Anyone in Possession Is Liable for the Rent
bodyText:
Minn. Stat. section 504B.125 gives a Minnesota landlord a claim against whoever is actually in possession, not only against the person who signed. Every person in possession of land out of which rent is due is liable for the amount or proportion of rent due from the land in possession, even if that is only part of the land originally leased. The rent may be recovered in a civil action, and the deed, lease or other instrument showing the lease terms may be used in evidence by either party to prove the amount due from the defendant.

Two things follow. The section reaches a person who never signed your lease but is in possession, which matters where an unauthorised occupant stays on, where a tenant has sublet, or where one of several tenants has left. And it closes with a preservation clause: "Nothing herein contained shall deprive landlords of any other legal remedy for the recovery of rent, whether secured to them by their leases or provided by law." Your lease remedies and this statutory claim sit side by side.

No lease clause is needed or offered. The liability is imposed by statute on a person in possession, so a lease cannot create it against a non-party and a clause restating it would add nothing. A landlord who wants a clause anyway may add their own and should take advice first. The useful drafting response is different: keep the written lease and any addenda, because the statute makes the lease instrument itself admissible to prove the amount due, and the complaint in a nonpayment eviction must in any event attach the lease and an itemised accounting under Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 3.

A money claim is not a possession claim. Recovering rent under this section is an ordinary civil action; recovering the premises still requires an eviction action under Minn. Stat. sections 504B.281 to 504B.371.

title: Public Housing Breach-of-Lease Evictions Carry a Right to Counsel
bodyText:
Minn. Stat. section 504B.268 gives a defendant a court-appointed attorney in a narrow but important class of case. A defendant in housing subsidised by the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development under Section 9 of the United States Housing Act of 1937, or the Consolidated and Further Continuing Appropriations Act of 2012, who faces an eviction action under Minn. Stat. sections 504B.281 to 504B.371 alleging breach of lease under Minn. Stat. section 504B.171 or 504B.285, and who is financially unable to obtain counsel, has the right to counsel appointed by the court.

This puts a drafting duty on the landlord, not only on the court. The statute says the complaint required by Minn. Stat. section 504B.321 "shall include the notice on the first page of the complaint in bold 12-point type: 'If financially unable to obtain counsel, the defendant has the right to a court-appointed attorney.'" Reproduce that sentence exactly, on the first page, in bold 12-point type. At the initial hearing the court must ask the defendant whether the defendant wants court-appointed counsel and explain what appointed counsel can accomplish.

Appointed counsel must have at least two years' experience handling public housing evictions, or training in handling them, or be supervised by an attorney who meets one of those. Compensation is set annually by the chief judge of the judicial district after consulting public housing attorneys, legal aid attorneys and the private bar, and may not exceed $5,000 per defendant exclusive of reasonable expenses unless the chief judge certifies that more is necessary for services of an unusual character or duration.

Two practical points. A Section 9 public housing landlord bringing a breach-of-lease eviction should expect the tenant to be represented and should plan the case accordingly. And this is a public housing rule: it does not reach a Section 8 voucher tenancy in privately owned housing, and it does not reach a nonpayment-only eviction, which is brought under Minn. Stat. section 504B.291 rather than as a breach of lease.

title: A Tenant Cannot Dispute Your Title in a Possession Action
bodyText:
Minn. Stat. section 504B.121 is short and favours the landlord: "A tenant in possession of real property under a lawful lease may not deny the landlord's title in an action brought by the landlord to recover possession of the property." A tenant sued for possession therefore cannot turn the eviction into a trial of who owns the property.

There is one carve-out, in the section's second sentence: the prohibition does not apply to a tenant who, before entering into the lease, possessed the property under a claim of title that was adverse or hostile to the landlord's. If you are leasing to someone who was already on the property claiming it as their own, that person keeps the ability to contest your title and the rule gives you nothing.

You do not need a lease clause for this. The rule applies by law to any tenant in possession under a lawful lease, so a lease term restating it would add nothing to your position, and a lease term trying to extend it to the adverse-claim tenant would be asking the lease to override the statute's own exception. This library does not offer a clause for it. A landlord who wants one anyway may add their own and should take advice first. What a lease can usefully do instead is be clear that it is a lease: the rule turns on the tenant being in possession "under a lawful lease", so a signed written lease identifying the parties and the premises is what makes the rule available to you.

title: A Minnesota Lease Cannot Name Someone to Accept Eviction Papers for the Tenant
bodyText:
Minnesota has no provision letting a lease name a person or address to accept a notice to quit or the eviction summons and complaint on the tenant's behalf. The one agency rule in the chapter runs the other way: Minn. Stat. section 504B.181, subd. 1(2) requires the landlord to disclose the landlord's own agent authorised to accept service of process and receive notices and demands, and subd. 3 deems a caretaker, manager or the person who receives the rent to be that agent if the landlord did not disclose one. Nothing mirrors it for the tenant.

So service on the tenant follows Minn. Stat. section 504B.332 and nothing else. Personal or substitute service comes first. If the defendant cannot be found in the county, a copy may be left at the defendant's last usual place of abode with a person of suitable age and discretion residing there, or, if the defendant had no place of abode, at the property described in the complaint with a person of suitable age and discretion occupying the premises. Service by mail and posting is available only if personal or substitute service was unsuccessful.

A lease clause purporting to appoint an agent for the tenant, or to agree that posting or email alone is good service, does not work and should not be used. It cannot shorten the seven-day service deadline, cannot replace the two personal-service attempts a residential eviction requires before mail and posting, and cannot excuse the affidavits that must be filed at least three days before the appearance. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 5 the court must dismiss and expunge the record of any action where the landlord fails to comply with that section, so getting service wrong costs the case, not just time.

Serve each adult tenant and each adult occupant in possession. Do not name a tenant's minor child as a defendant: Minn. Stat. section 504B.2136, effective August 1, 2026 for actions filed on or after that date, forbids it unless a minor is the only person renting the unit, cannot be waived or modified by the parties, and gives the tenant actual damages or $300, whichever is greater.

title: No Statute Bans an Exculpatory Clause, but the Habitability Covenants Cannot Be Modified
bodyText:
Minnesota has no statute prohibiting an exculpatory, indemnity or hold-harmless clause in a residential lease. The words do not appear. A search of the whole of the held Minnesota statutes returned no occurrence of "exculpatory" in any form and none of "hold harmless", and the only confession-of-judgment prohibition sits in a regime confined to property that is not real property. There is no Minnesota equivalent of the many states whose landlord-tenant acts void a clause limiting the landlord's liability.

That absence is narrower than it sounds, for three reasons, and all three cut against a broad exculpatory clause.

The habitability covenants cannot be waived or modified. Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 1(a) implies into every residential lease a covenant that the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended, a covenant to keep them in reasonable repair, an energy-efficiency covenant, a covenant to comply with applicable health and safety laws including rental licensing ordinances, and a covenant to furnish heat at a minimum of 68 degrees Fahrenheit from October 1 through April 30. Then subdivision 1(b): "The parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section." The word "modify" is doing real work. A clause that disclaims liability for the condition of the premises, or caps it, or makes the tenant carry it, modifies those covenants even though it never uses the word waiver. Subdivision 3 adds that the section "shall be liberally construed, and the opportunity to inspect the premises before concluding a lease or license shall not defeat the covenants".

The one shifting of repair duty Minnesota does allow is tightly conditioned. Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 2 lets you agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance, "but only if the agreement is supported by adequate consideration and set forth in a conspicuous writing" — and then: "No such agreement, however, may waive the provisions of subdivision 1 or relieve the landlord or licensor of the duty to maintain common areas of the premises." So the permitted agreement is specified repairs, in a conspicuous writing, paid for, and never the common areas. A general "tenant accepts the premises as is and assumes all risk" clause is not that agreement.

Third-party liability is expressly left alone. Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 5 provides: "Nothing in this section shall be construed to alter the liability of the landlord or licensor of residential premises for injury to third parties." The section neither creates nor removes that liability, so a clause purporting to shift it has nothing in Chapter 504B to lean on.

One clause type is squarely void, and it is the one a broad indemnity often tries to reach. Minn. Stat. § 363A.31, subd. 1 makes any provision "of a lease, contract, or other agreement or instrument which purports to be a waiver by an individual of any right or remedy provided in this chapter" — the Human Rights Act — "contrary to public policy and void", where it reaches claims arising after it was signed. An indemnity drafted widely enough to make the tenant bear a discrimination claim is caught by that.

Practical upshot. Minnesota does not ban an exculpatory clause by name, so a narrow one has no statute pointed at it. But anything that touches the condition of the premises, the common areas, or a Human Rights Act claim is reaching for ground the statutes have already taken. General contract doctrine, which is case law and not in scope here, is the other constraint. Take advice before relying on any liability-limiting clause in a Minnesota residential lease.

title: The Five-Day Deposit Clock After a Condemnation, and No Fee for an Early Refund
bodyText: Minnesota has two expedited deposit deadlines, and neither is one the tenant asks for. The first is for condemnation. If the tenant leaves the building or dwelling because it has been legally condemned, for reasons not due to the tenant's willful, malicious or irresponsible conduct, you have five days, not three weeks, to return the deposit with interest or to furnish the written statement of the specific reasons for withholding. Five days is five days: the ordinary three-week clock does not apply, and missing it triggers the same penalty as missing the three weeks, so the amount you withheld comes out of your pocket a second time, plus up to $500 per deposit if the retention was in bad faith. Two things make this manageable. You are entitled to the post, so the deposit or the statement mailed first class, properly addressed to the address or delivery instructions the tenant gave you, within the five days, is in time. And you will usually know a condemnation is coming, because you must already give a copy of every outstanding condemnation order and declaration that the premises are unfit for human habitation to a sitting tenant within 72 hours of the citation, and to anyone before they sign a lease or pay a deposit. The second deadline sits in the health chapter. If an assessing agency tells a tenant to vacate for lead hazard reduction and the tenant then ends the tenancy, you must return any deposit due within five days of the date the tenant vacates (Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9504, subd. 7(c)(2)). The statute applies notwithstanding any lease provision. What Minnesota has no trace of is the other kind of expedited disposition. There is no procedure by which a tenant asks you to settle the deposit early, no shorter deadline in exchange for giving up the itemised statement, and no authority to charge or deduct an administrative, processing, handling or expediting fee for dealing with the deposit sooner. Do not invent one: you may withhold only what is reasonably necessary to remedy a default in rent or other funds due to you under the lease, or to restore the property to its condition at the start of the tenancy with ordinary wear and tear excepted, and a processing fee is neither. Charging it separately is no better, because any nonoptional fee has to be disclosed in the lease and carried in the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, with treble damages and possible attorney fees for getting it wrong. The deadlines are outer limits, so you are always free to return the deposit sooner, and no fee is payable for doing so.

title: No Absence-Notice Duty, and No Right to Enter While the Tenant Is Away
bodyText:
Minnesota does not make a tenant tell you about a long absence, and it does not give you anything extra while the tenant is away. Both halves of that matter, because the standard URLTA package does both and most lease templates assume it.

There is no absence-notice statute. Nothing requires the tenant to notify you of an anticipated absence, nothing authorises the lease to require it with a statutory remedy behind it, and there is no 'willful failure, actual damages' provision. If you want the notice, it is a contract term and ordinary breach principles are all that back it. The optional clause under this topic does that.

There is also no absence entry right. In the URLTA states a landlord may enter at reasonably necessary times during an absence of more than seven or fourteen days. Minnesota has no such provision. Minn. Stat. section 504B.211 applies while the tenant is away exactly as it does while the tenant is home: a reasonable business purpose, a good faith effort at not less than 24 hours' notice, a stated time or window, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. An empty-looking unit is not an invitation. Two parts of the section do help. Subd. 4 lets you enter without prior notice if you reasonably suspect that immediate entry is necessary to prevent injury to persons or property because of conditions relating to maintenance, building security or law enforcement, or to determine a tenant's safety - a burst pipe or a welfare check qualifies, an idle look round does not. And subd. 5 requires that if you enter when the tenant is not present and prior notice has not been given, you put a written disclosure of the entry in a conspicuous place in the unit.

What Minnesota does have is a narrow cold-weather duty, and it is criminal. Minn. Stat. section 504B.155: except on termination of the tenancy, a tenant who between November 15 and April 15 removes from, abandons or vacates a building or any part of it containing plumbing, water, steam or other pipes liable to injury from freezing, without first giving the landlord three days' notice of intention to remove, is guilty of a misdemeanour. That is in the library as its own clause. Note what it does and does not cover: it is about leaving, not about a fortnight's holiday, and it gives you a criminal provision rather than a civil remedy. It does not authorise you to enter.

If a tenant really has gone, the question is abandonment, not absence, and it is answered elsewhere: Minn. Stat. section 504B.271 on the tenant's property left behind, with punitive damages up to twice actual damages or $1,000 if you get the retake-possession deadline wrong, and Minn. Stat. section 504B.154, under which abandonment ends the rent clock once you have notice of it unless you make reasonable efforts to re-let. Do not treat a long silence as abandonment: the cost of guessing wrong is the ouster and lockout exposure under Minn. Stat. sections 504B.225, 504B.231 and 504B.375.

Practical version: ask for the notice in the lease if you want it, use it to arrange checks the tenant has agreed to, and give the 24 hours' notice anyway for anything that is not a genuine emergency.

title: Two Minnesota Rules Change Your Property Once Child Care Starts
bodyText:
Minnesota does not make you allow licensed family child care, but it does have two rules that bite on the property once child care is happening in it. Neither is obvious from the landlord-tenant act.

The fire code treats the home as a home. Minn. Stat. section 299F.011, subd. 4a says that notwithstanding any contrary provision of that section, the fire marshal shall not adopt or enforce a rule regulating the means of egress from family or group family day care homes 'in addition to the egress rules that apply to the home as a single family dwelling', shall not confine day care home activities to the floor of exit discharge, and shall not establish staff ratios, age distribution requirements or limits on the number of children in care. 'Family or group family day care home' means, for that subdivision, 'a dwelling unit in which the day care provider provides the services referred to in section 142B.01, subdivision 18, to one or more persons'. The practical effect for you is reassuring: a tenant's licensed family child care does not trigger commercial egress requirements against your building through the fire code. The subdivision also preserves the children and families department's own authority over ratios and floor use, and lets that department ask the state or a local fire marshal to inspect day care homes for fire-code compliance, so inspections are still possible.

The smoking ban applies by statute, not by your lease. Minn. Stat. section 144.414, subd. 2 prohibits smoking in a family home or group family day care provider home licensed under Minnesota Rules, parts 9502.0300 to 9502.0445, during its hours of operation. If the proprietor permits smoking outside those hours, the subdivision requires disclosure to the parents or guardians of the children cared for on the premises, by posting a conspicuous written notice on the premises and by telling them orally. That duty is the provider's, not yours. But it means a unit you have allowed to be used for licensed child care is a non-smoking premises during operating hours whatever your lease says, which is worth knowing if your building otherwise permits smoking, and worth writing down if it does not.

title: Whether a Tenant May Run Licensed Child Care Is Your Call, With One Unread Caveat
bodyText:
Minnesota's landlord-tenant, human rights, consumer, fire, health, courts and manufactured-home-park statutes do not require you to let a tenant run a licensed family child care home in your rental, bar a lease from prohibiting one, or set lease conditions such as a liability waiver or an insurance floor if you allow one. There is no Minnesota equivalent of the Oregon provision. Because the library's lease limits the property to residential use, a tenant needs your written consent to run a child care business. If you consent, require proof of the licence and of liability insurance, and name yourself as an additional insured.

One caveat is real and you should not treat the absence as settled. Minnesota's family child care licensing law lives in chapters 142B, 142H and 142I and in Minnesota Rules, chapter 9502. Two signals suggest the licensing side does speak to rented premises. Minn. Stat. section 144.1222, subd. 2a and subd. 2b reach a 'family day care or group family day care home licensed under Minnesota Rules, chapter 9502' and, where the provider lets children in care use a swimming pool at the home, send the provider to the requirements of Minn. Stat. section 142B.41, subd. 9. And the family child care licensing provisions enacted as new chapter 142I by Laws 2026, ch. 127 carry a definition of 'owner or renter' - 'the individual, individuals, organization, or government entity listed in the property title, deed, lease, or equivalent legal document' - which is the vocabulary of a regime that contemplates a provider who rents. The provisions quoted above do not say whether any of it requires the landlord's permission, or conditions a licence on it.

What follows for you is practical. Before you refuse or permit, ask the applicant for the licence and read the licensing conditions it carries, because the licence may impose requirements on the property itself - pool fencing, water testing, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, capacity by room. Those requirements land on you through Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subd. 1(a), which makes you covenant that the premises are 'fit for the use intended by the parties' and that they comply with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state, and of the local units of government. If the lease permits child care, child care is the intended use, and those covenants may not be waived or modified by the parties. Zoning is a separate question again, under the municipal and county enabling acts and the city's own ordinance.

title: No Minnesota Rule on a Tenant Hunting or Fishing Rights
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute of the Arkansas kind that gives, or withholds, hunting or fishing rights to a tenant of rented land unless the owner grants them in writing. Nothing in the landlord-tenant code, the Human Rights Act, the trade-practice chapters, the health chapter, the court chapter or the manufactured home park chapter addresses a tenant right to hunt, fish or trap on leased land, and nothing in them makes the owner silence mean one thing rather than another. Two things follow. First, if you are leasing farmland or other land where hunting could arise, this lease is not the instrument - agricultural tenancies run on separate machinery, and the Minnesota Constitution adds its own trap, because Minn. Const. art. I, Sec. 15 voids leases and grants of agricultural lands for longer than 21 years reserving rent or service of any kind. Second, because no statute supplies a default, hunting and fishing on the premises is simply a matter for the lease. If it matters, say so expressly; silence buys you no statutory answer in either direction. Separately from who may hunt, the state game and licensing laws govern whether and how anyone may hunt at all, including on private land, and those are not landlord-tenant rules.

title: No Fee or Insurance Product Instead of a Deposit in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute authorising a nonrefundable fee in place of a security deposit, no insurance-backed deposit-replacement regime, no requirement that you offer such a product to every approved applicant, and no right for a tenant to switch out of one into a deposit. Nothing is pending either: no Minnesota statute directs an agency to write rules for deposit alternatives, so unlike Massachusetts there is no programme waiting on regulations. What Minnesota has instead is a definition that closes the door. The deposit section governs any deposit of money whose function is to secure performance of a residential rental agreement or any part of it, other than money that is exclusively an advance payment of rent. A monthly or one-off charge whose job is to stand in for a deposit has exactly that function, so it is a deposit in law however the paperwork reads: one percent simple noncompounded interest, return or a written statement within three weeks, withholding only what is reasonably necessary, the burden of proof on you, the penalty equal to the amount withheld plus interest, and the bad-faith award of up to $500 all attach, and any attempted waiver of them is void. Calling it a fee makes things worse rather than better, because a nonoptional fee has to be disclosed in the lease and carried in the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, and a landlord who gets that wrong is liable for treble damages and may be ordered to pay the tenant's attorney fees. Two things are genuinely open. A surety bond or deposit-replacement insurance the tenant buys from a third party is not regulated either way in Minnesota, and nothing stops you accepting one voluntarily - but you may not require it, you may not treat a payment the tenant makes to you as a nonrefundable substitute for a deposit, and you should take advice before building a programme on it. And money taken before a lease exists is its own regime: a prelease deposit needs a conspicuous written agreement and must be applied to the deposit or rent if the lease is signed.

title: Charging for a Service the Tenant Does Not Get
bodyText: Minnesota has no single landlord rule worded as a ban on charging a fee for a service you do not provide, but three sets of rules reach that result. Utility service is the strict one. If you bill any utility separately from rent, the only charges allowed are the utility service itself, one administrative billing charge of up to $8 a billing period and one late payment charge of up to $5 a month; no other fee or charge for utility service is permitted. You may not bill a tenant for utilities used in common areas, in spaces you use yourself, in vacant units, for maintenance of the property, or for shared amenities such as laundry rooms and pools, and you may not pass on the cost of installing, maintaining, repairing, replacing or reading a submeter. Second, your core duties are not billable extras: in every residential lease you covenant that the premises and all common areas are fit for the intended use, that you will keep them in reasonable repair, that you will exterminate pests, that you will maintain them in compliance with health and safety laws including rental licensing ordinances, and that you will furnish heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit from October 1 through April 30, and those covenants cannot be waived or modified. You may agree that the tenant performs specified repairs or maintenance, but only for adequate consideration and in a conspicuous writing, and never for the common areas. Third, Minnesota's consumer-fraud law makes it unlawful to solicit payment by statement or invoice for services not yet performed and not yet ordered, and separately reaches any unfair, unconscionable or deceptive practice in connection with the sale of merchandise, which is defined to include real estate and services; a person injured by a violation may recover damages, costs of investigation and attorney fees. That law's definition does not settle whether a residential lease is a sale of merchandise, so treat it as a real risk rather than a certainty. Practical course: charge only for a service you actually deliver, describe it in the lease, and stop or credit the fee when the service stops. Remember that a nonoptional fee has to be disclosed in the lease and inside the first-page Total Monthly Payment.

title: Minnesota's State Fire Code: Who Sets It, Who Enforces It, and How to Appeal
bodyText:
Minnesota has one State Fire Code and it reaches your rental wherever it is. Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.011, subd. 4 says the code "shall be applicable throughout the state and in all political subdivisions and municipalities therein". The commissioner of public safety adopts the rules needed to administer and enforce it, "specifically including but not limited to rules for inspection of buildings and other structures covered by the code" (subd. 3).

THE LOCAL LAYER IS REAL AND YOU MUST CHECK IT. The same subdivision lets a local unit of government otherwise authorised by law adopt or enforce an ordinance or regulation "which specifies requirements equal to, in addition to, or more stringent than the requirements of the State Fire Code". Such an ordinance must be directly related to safeguarding life and property from the hazards of fire, must be uniform for each class or kind of building covered, and may not exceed the applicable requirements of the State Building Code. So the state code is a floor, not a ceiling, and your city may sit above it. Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.391, subd. 3 carries the same rule for hospitals, nursing homes, schools, lodging houses and hotels. Check your own city's fire and property maintenance ordinance before you rely on the state code alone.

ONE SPECIFIC STATE RELAXATION worth knowing: "The State Fire Code shall not require stairways of existing multiple dwelling buildings of two stories or less to be enclosed" (Sec. 299F.011, subd. 4b), with "stories" taking its State Building Code meaning.

PENALTY AND THE NOTICE YOU ARE OWED. Violating the State Fire Code is a misdemeanour, but Sec. 299F.011, subd. 6 says "[n]o person shall be convicted for violating the State Fire Code unless the person shall have been given notice of the violation in writing and reasonable time to comply", and "[t]he notice must contain a statement explaining the right to appeal the orders". If you are handed an order without that statement, say so.

APPEALS AND VARIANCES, IN ORDER. Start locally: subd. 5 says no appeal to the state fire marshal for a variance from an order issued by a local fire official "shall be accepted until the applicant has first made application to the local governing body and the local unit has acted on the application". A local governing body may appoint a board of appeal to hear appeals from fire code orders, with a further appeal to the governing body, and if no board is appointed the appeal goes straight to the governing body (subd. 5a).

Then the state: on application the state fire marshal may grant a variance from the code's minimum requirements if there is substantial compliance with the code, the safety of the public and the occupants will not be jeopardised, and undue hardship will result unless the variance is granted; the fire marshal must consider the local body's decisions or recommendations, and anyone aggrieved may proceed before the fire marshal as a contested case under the Administrative Procedure Act.

AFFORDABLE HOUSING IS AN EXPRESS CONSIDERATION. Under subd. 5b, when considering appeals for variances the local appeal board or governing body, the state fire marshal, a state administrative law judge and a court "shall take into consideration the benefit to be obtained by complying with the fire marshal's orders and the effect on affordable housing, provided that the spirit of the code is complied with and public safety secured". That is a statutory argument available to a rental housing owner and it is rarely used.

The code's own rules are published as Minnesota Rules; a specific clearance, exit, extinguisher or alarm spec must be read in the rules themselves or taken from the inspector's order. Separately, smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms have their own statutes and their own duty split, covered by "Smoke Alarms" clause, "Carbon Monoxide Alarms" clause and "Minnesota Splits Smoke and CO Alarm Duties in Opposite Directions".

title: What a Minnesota Lease May Say About Firearms, and Where the Answer Runs Out
bodyText:
Minnesota is unusually quiet on firearms in rental housing, and the shape of that silence decides what your lease can say.

WHAT THE LAW ALREADY GIVES YOU. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.171 subd. 1(a)(1)(iii) puts into every Minnesota lease, oral or written, a covenant by both you and the tenant not to allow 'the unlawful use or possession of a firearm in violation of section 609.66, subdivision 1a, 609.67, or 624.713, on the premises or in the common area and curtilage of the premises'. That covers reckless or endangering discharge and unlawfully possessed suppressors (Sec. 609.66 subd. 1a), machine guns and short-barreled shotguns (Sec. 609.67), and possession by a person Minnesota makes ineligible -- for example a person under 18 outside the listed exceptions, or a person convicted of a crime of violence (Sec. 624.713 subd. 1). A breach voids the tenant's right to possession, though not the lease and not the rent obligation, and neither of you may waive or modify the covenant. Note one thing that follows from the covenant binding YOU: allowing unlawful firearm use or possession on the premises, the common area or the curtilage is your own breach as well as a ground against the tenant.

WHAT MINNESOTA DOES NOT DO. No Minnesota statute limits what a private landlord's lease may say about firearms. There is no provision barring a landlord from restricting lawful possession in the unit, no public-housing-authority carve-out of the kind some states have, and no parking-lot or locked-vehicle storage statute that would stop you making a rule about firearms in cars in your parking areas. The Minnesota Constitution contains no right-to-bear-arms provision at all.

SO WHAT MAY YOUR LEASE SAY? A term about DISCHARGE and about SAFE STORAGE is on solid ground, and that is the optional clause this library offers. A term banning lawful possession in the unit is not offered, and the reason is not that Minnesota forbids it -- as far as the Minnesota statutes and constitution go, it is not forbidden. It is that nothing in Minnesota law supports it either, and the three bodies of law that would decide it are the Second Amendment and federal law, Minnesota case law, and city ordinances. For federally subsidized or public housing there are also federal program rules.

If you want a possession restriction, you may add your own clause, but get Minnesota advice first and expect it to be contested. A narrower route usually gets you what you actually want: enforce the statutory covenant, require safe storage, and prohibit discharge.

title: No Flood Disclosure Duty in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota requires no flood disclosure to a residential tenant. There is no flood-zone notice, no flood-history statement, no signed flood rider and no tenant termination right tied to flooding - nothing like the Texas, New York, California or Oklahoma flood notices. FOUR THINGS STILL APPLY TO YOU. (1) Fitness and repair. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) makes you covenant that the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended by the parties and that you will keep them in reasonable repair; subd. 1(b) says the parties may not waive or modify those covenants, and subd. 3 says the chance to inspect before signing does not defeat them. A basement that floods is a repair problem you own. (2) The tenant can walk if the building is lost. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.131 says a tenant or occupant of a building that is destroyed or becomes uninhabitable or unfit for occupancy through no fault or neglect of the tenant may vacate and surrender it. The same section lets a tenant expressly agree otherwise, but only so far as Sec. 504B.161 allows; see the casualty-termination rows. (3) Code orders must be handed over. If flooding draws a housing inspection citation or a condemnation order, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195, subd. 1 makes you give a copy to a person before they sign a lease or pay rent or a security deposit, and subd. 5 makes any lease waiver of that section contrary to public policy and void. (4) Contents are not yours to insure. See the renters-insurance rows for what you may and may not require. WHAT TO DO. Minnesota does not stop you disclosing voluntarily, and a short factual statement of known flooding history costs nothing and heads off a dispute. Check the local floodplain ordinance: Minnesota floodplain management runs through Minn. Stat. ch. 103F and local ordinances, and a city or county may have its own notice or occupancy rule. Tell tenants plainly that your insurance does not cover their belongings.

title: After a Foreclosure the New Owner Owes the Tenant 90 Days, and a Good Lease Can Run Out
bodyText: When a mortgage on your rental property is foreclosed, Minnesota does not simply end your tenant's lease. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.285 subd. 1(a)(1) lists holding over after the redemption period, after an execution or judgment sale, or after a real estate tax judgment sale as grounds for eviction -- but subd. 1a puts a floor under a residential tenant first, and it is the successor owner, not you, who owes the notice. WHERE THE LEASE BEGAN AFTER THE MORTGAGE AND BEFORE THE REDEMPTION PERIOD RAN OUT (subd. 1a(a)): the 'immediate successor in interest' must give the tenant at least 90 days' written notice to vacate. The notice may be given no sooner than the day the redemption period expires and may take effect no sooner than 90 days after that day, so long as the tenant keeps paying rent and keeps to the lease. WHERE A BONA FIDE LEASE RUNS MORE THAN 90 DAYS PAST THE END OF REDEMPTION (subd. 1a(b)): the successor 'must allow the tenant to occupy the premises until the end of the remaining term of the lease', and the 90-day notice then takes effect no sooner than the day the lease expires. THERE IS ONE BIG EXCEPTION and it is easy to miss: if the successor, or an immediate subsequent bona fide purchaser, will occupy the unit as a primary residence, the lease does not get to run out -- 90 days' notice from the end of redemption is enough. A 'bona fide lease' is defined in the section: the tenant is not the mortgagor or the mortgagor's child, spouse or parent; the tenancy was an arm's-length transaction; and the rent is not substantially below fair market rent, unless it is reduced or subsidised by a federal, state or local subsidy. A Section 8 tenancy gets the same treatment under subd. 1a(c). ON A CONTRACT FOR DEED the numbers are different: subd. 1b requires only at least two months' written notice to vacate, either given no sooner than one month after the time for termination expires, or given no later than the expiry date with a statement that the sender will hold the tenant harmless for breaching the lease by vacating if the contract is reinstated. WHAT YOU OWE BEFORE ALL THIS: once you receive notice of a mortgage foreclosure sale or a contract for deed cancellation, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.151 limits how long a lease you may sign and requires a written notice to a prospective tenant before signing and before taking rent or a deposit -- see "Notice of Pending Foreclosure or Contract for Deed Cancellation" clause and "Tell Prospective Tenants About a Pending Foreclosure", which cover that section. One deposit point: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.178 subd. 8 bars a tenant from withholding the last month's rent on the footing that the deposit should cover it, and it extends that bar to the last month of a contract for deed cancellation period under Sec. 559.21 and of a mortgage foreclosure redemption period. Deposit handover on a change of ownership is covered by "Selling the Property Starts a 60-Day Deposit Clock". FOUR TENANT PROTECTIONS SURVIVE THE REDEMPTION PERIOD AND BIND THE NEW OWNER, which is easy to miss because they sit in the ouster and abandoned-property sections. Minn. Stat. Secs. 504B.225 (intentional ouster and interruption of utilities, a misdemeanour), 504B.231 (damages for ouster -- treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees), 504B.271 (the tenant's personal property remaining in the premises) and 504B.375 (unlawful exclusion or removal, actual or constructive) each say in terms that they 'also apply to occupants and owners of residential real property which is the subject of a mortgage foreclosure or contract for deed cancellation and as to which the period for redemption or reinstatement of the contract has expired'. Sec. 504B.375 subd. 6 goes further and applies the section to 'mortgagees and contract for deed vendors' as well. All four are non-waivable. So a buyer at a sheriff's sale who changes the locks or cuts the utilities on a holdover occupant is exposed exactly as a landlord would be.

title: Minnesota's Alien Land Law Reaches Only Agricultural Land, Leases Included
bodyText: Minnesota restricts who may acquire agricultural land, at Minn. Stat. Sec. 500.221, and the restriction reaches leases of it. 'Agricultural land' is land capable of use in producing crops, livestock, poultry, milk or dairy products, or fruit and other horticultural products. It does not include land a local government has zoned for a use other than, and nonconforming with, agricultural use (subd. 1). So an ordinary house or apartment on residentially zoned land is outside the section. Where it applies, 'interest in agricultural land' includes any leasehold interest (subd. 1). Under subd. 2, a natural person may not acquire any interest in agricultural land unless a U.S. citizen or a permanent resident alien as subd. 1 defines it. A business entity may not, unless citizens or permanent resident aliens hold at least 80 percent of each class of stock or of the ultimate beneficial interest. There are exemptions, among them rights secured by treaty and land acquired by inheritance or in collecting debts. The commissioner of agriculture enforces the section; a court that finds a violation orders the land divested within one year (subd. 3). The statute does not say whether a house lease on land zoned agricultural is itself an interest in agricultural land; only case law could settle that, so treat it as one. No 2025 or 2026 session law amended the section or added a foreign-adversary land restriction. Outside that section, nothing in the landlord-tenant code places any foreign-ownership condition on a residential tenancy. Chapter 504B does not restrict who may be a landlord or a tenant by nationality, citizenship or alienage, does not require a lease to state a nonresident alien name or address, and contains no provision voiding a leasehold on those grounds. The Human Rights Act does not list citizenship or alienage as a protected class, though national origin is an enumerated ground in Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.09, so a decision made on national origin is unlawful whatever the ownership rules say. The Minnesota Constitution contains no alien land provision. What to do. If the property is on land that is or could be farmed and is not zoned for another use, and either party is neither a citizen nor a permanent resident alien, or is an entity with foreign owners, take advice on Minn. Stat. Sec. 500.221 before signing.

title: What a Default Forfeits in Minnesota, and What It Does Not
bodyText:
A Minnesota lease default forfeits possession, not the lease. The clearest statement is Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, subd. 2, on the covenant against unlawful activities: a breach "voids the tenant's or licensee's right to possession of the residential premises. All other provisions of the lease or license, including but not limited to the obligation to pay rent, remain in effect until the lease is terminated by the terms of the lease or operation of law." So the tenant can lose the right to be there and still owe the rent.

A forfeiture or right-of-reentry clause buys a Minnesota landlord nothing. Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1(a) lets a landlord bring an eviction action for nonpayment "irrespective of whether the lease contains a right of reentry clause", and adds that such an action "is equivalent to a demand for the rent". The clause is neither needed nor sufficient: under Minn. Stat. section 504B.281 no person may take possession except where allowed by law, and then only peaceably, so forfeiture is worked by the court, never by the lease.

For nonpayment the tenant has a redemption right that undoes the forfeiture, set out in Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1. One strategic point belongs here: subd. 1(a) makes redemption available "unless the landlord has also sought to evict the tenant by alleging a material violation of the lease under section 504B.285, subdivision 5".
