A landlord who combines a nonpayment allegation with a material lease violation removes the redemption route, but Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subd. 5(b) then gives the tenant up to seven days of additional time to pay rent the court finds due if the landlord fails to prove the violation. Choose the grounds deliberately.

A long lease has its own regime. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 2, where the lease term is more than 20 years the landlord may not begin the action until serving written notice on the tenant and on all creditors with legal or equitable recorded liens on the property, stating that the lease will be cancelled unless the defaults are paid or performed within 30 days or a longer specified period, and that the landlord may then evict. If the lease requires more than 30 days' notice, the lease's period governs. Under subd. 2(c) the tenant or a lienholding creditor may be restored to possession under the original lease by paying the rent in arrears with interest and costs and performing the other defaults, at any time before six months after the landlord obtains possession by abandonment or surrender or prevails in the action.

Finally, record the result. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 3, on recovery of possession in the action a certified copy of the judgment is recorded with the county recorder or registrar of titles, and where the landlord recovered possession by the tenant's abandonment or surrender an affidavit of the landlord or the landlord's attorney is recorded in the same way. The recorded copy or affidavit is prima facie evidence of the facts stated about the recovery of possession.

title: Do Not Rely on a Forfeiture or Self-Help Clause in a Minnesota Lease
bodyText:
A clause saying the lease is forfeited, or that the landlord may re-enter and retake the premises, on a tenant's default is at best useless in Minnesota and at worst evidence against you. Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1(a) makes a nonpayment eviction available whether or not the lease has a right-of-reentry clause, so the clause adds nothing. And acting on it is unlawful.

If you act on a forfeiture clause instead of going to court, four provisions bite at once. Minn. Stat. section 504B.375 gives the tenant a summary action to recover possession for actual or constructive removal or exclusion, and subd. 4 says "A provision of an oral or written lease or other agreement in which a residential tenant waives this section is contrary to public policy and void." Minn. Stat. section 504B.231 gives treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees where the landlord unlawfully and in bad faith removes, excludes or forcibly keeps out a tenant. Minn. Stat. section 504B.225 makes an unlawful and intentional removal or exclusion a misdemeanour. And Minn. Stat. section 504B.365, subd. 5 says of the writ section: "This section may not be waived or modified by lease or other agreement."

Each of sections 504B.221, 504B.225 and 504B.231 also carries its own non-waiver sentence in the same words: any lease or other agreement provision by which the section is waived by a tenant "is contrary to public policy and void." Section 504B.375, subd. 4 uses a slightly different formula. Quote whichever section you are dealing with rather than assuming one house phrase covers all of them.

What a lease can properly say is that a default lets the landlord terminate and bring an eviction action, and that the tenant's other obligations, including rent, continue. That is the position Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, subd. 2 already takes.

title: Your Lease Cannot Pin Safety Standards to the Edition in Force at Signing
bodyText:
A lease cannot freeze Minnesota's safety standards at the edition in force when it was signed. Minnesota does not address the question with a rule about incorporation by reference — it addresses it by writing the covenant so that the question cannot arise.

Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(4) implies into every residential lease a covenant by the landlord "to maintain the premises and all common areas in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state, and of the local units of government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing, where the premises are located during the term of the lease or license". Read the tense: the obligation is compliance with the applicable laws during the term, not with the laws as they stood at signing. A standard that changes mid-tenancy changes what the covenant requires.

Two further provisions close the door on a clause trying to fix the standard at the signing date. Subdivision 1(b): "The parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section." A clause pinning the covenant to a superseded code edition modifies it, which is barred in terms. And subdivision 3: "This section shall be liberally construed, and the opportunity to inspect the premises before concluding a lease or license shall not defeat the covenants established in this section." The section is to be read in favour of the covenant, and the fact that the tenant could see the condition does not help you.

Nothing in Minnesota law goes the other way. There is no statute letting a lease specify a code edition, no grandfathering provision for an existing tenancy when a standard is amended, and no incorporation-by-reference rule for leases of any kind. One energy-efficiency measure is tied to a fixed calculation rather than a code edition: subdivision 1(a)(3) requires weatherstripping, caulking, storm windows and storm doors where the measure will produce energy procurement cost savings exceeding its cost, including interest, amortised over the following ten years — a test, not a published standard, so it has no edition to freeze.

Two things not to confuse with this. Where a Minnesota section does incorporate an outside standard, it generally does so in the moving form itself: Minn. Stat. § 504B.113, subd. 1(b) takes "service animal" from a federal regulation "as amended", and Minn. Stat. § 504B.285 and § 504B.161 both reference other law without fixing a date. And the June 15, 1971 date in Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 6 is not a frozen standard: it is the section's own commencement limit, and it catches every live tenancy. Subdivision 6 adds, for periodic tenancies, that "estates at will shall be deemed to be renewed at the commencement of each rental period".

What to do. Do not include a clause fixing the applicable code, standard or ordinance edition, and delete one if a form from another state carries it. If your lease recites a safety standard at all, recite it in moving terms — the standard as amended from time to time — so the lease says what the covenant already requires rather than contradicting it.

title: Renting Furnished in Minnesota: No Statute, Four Rules That Decide It
bodyText:
Minnesota has no furnished-rental statute. Nothing requires you to furnish a unit, nothing limits what you may furnish it with, and there is no separate furniture deposit or furniture-deposit cap - Minnesota has no statewide security deposit cap at all, though Minneapolis has one.

Four general rules shape a furnished letting here. First, the inventory is what protects you, and the deposit rule is why. You may withhold from the deposit only what is reasonably necessary to remedy defaults in payment or to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted, and in any dispute the burden of proving the reason for withholding is on you (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.178, subd. 3). A dated inventory listing each item and its condition is how that burden gets met.

Second, an inventory is not a substitute for the inspection notices. At the start of the tenancy, or within 14 days of the tenant moving in, you must notify the tenant of the option to request an initial inspection to identify existing deficiencies. Before the end of the term you must notify the tenant in writing of the option to request a move-out inspection and of the right to be present. If the tenant agrees, written acknowledgment of photos or videos can stand in for an inspection. None of this can be waived by the lease (Sec. 504B.182).

Third, furniture you provide is part of what the tenant bargained for. Your unwaivable covenants are that the premises are fit for the use intended by the parties and kept in reasonable repair (Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1). A furnished unit whose furniture is unusable is a weaker position than an unfurnished one.

Fourth, and this is the Minnesota trap worth knowing: putting an item in the lease can enlarge your obligations. The emergency tenant remedies list treats a nonfunctioning air conditioner and a non-working elevator as grounds for a court petition only "if included in the lease" (Sec. 504B.381, subd. 1). So listing a window air conditioner in the furniture inventory is the act that brings it inside that remedy. List what you supply, by all means, but know what listing does.

If you rent furnished, take dated photographs, use an inventory the tenant signs, give the two inspection notices on time, and do not take a separate furniture deposit: fold any security into the one deposit the lease already provides for.

title: No Good-Cause Notice for an Apartment - but Cause IS Required in a Manufactured Home Park
bodyText: For an ordinary apartment or house, Minnesota has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so there is nothing you have to disclose about one and no reason you have to state in a notice ending a tenancy. The end of the term is itself a ground, and a tenancy with no fixed end date is ended by notice without a reason. The library's for-cause eviction row sets out the whole picture, including the six situations where a particular eviction is blocked or delayed even though Minnesota is not a just-cause state; read that row rather than this one for the grounds. Three qualifications matter here. First, one Minnesota notice does have to state a cause. Before you bring an eviction for nonpayment of rent or another unpaid financial obligation, your written notice must specify the basis for the future eviction action, with the total due and a specific accounting of unpaid rent, late fees and other charges -- plus three statements the statute prescribes word for word. If that notice is missing or defective the court dismisses the case and expunges the file. Second, timing can shift the burden onto you. If your notice to quit lands within 90 days of the tenant's good-faith attempt to enforce a right, or their good-faith report of a code violation to a government authority, you have to prove the notice was not retaliatory. A notice that gives no reason is not safer here; contemporaneous records of why you decided are. Third, and this is the real exception: if you rent LOT space in a manufactured home park, cause IS required. A park owner may recover possession of a lot only for a reason the statute lists, each with its own notice period and content -- ten days for overdue rent or utilities, 30 days for a rule violation with the date, approximate time and nature of it specified, 30 days for endangerment or substantial annoyance with the same specificity, 90 days for park improvements with a statement of how they benefit residents' health and safety, and others. Park closings have their own rules again. If that is your situation, you need manufactured-home-park advice.

title: Passing a Government Fee to Your Tenant
bodyText:
Minnesota has no statewide rental registration or licensing fee and no statute saying whether you may pass a local government fee on to your tenant, so it is a matter for the lease, and the library offers an optional clause.

Three Minnesota rules decide how you may do it. First, disclosure. A fee the tenant cannot avoid must be disclosed in the lease and included in the sum labelled Total Monthly Payment on the first page, and a violation costs treble damages plus possible attorney fees. A pass-through that is not in the fee list is not collectable in practice and is a disclosure violation if you charge it anyway.

Second, your own compliance duty stays with you. You covenant in every residential lease to maintain the premises and common areas in compliance with health and safety laws, including ordinances regulating rental licensing, and that covenant cannot be waived or modified. Whether shifting the cost of a licence fee counts as waiving it has not been decided, so the clause we offer keeps the duty with you and excludes any fee or re-inspection charge that arises because you did not comply.

Third, fines are different from fees: a fine for a condition you are responsible for can never be passed on, and only a fine caused by the tenant can. Do not pass on property taxes or building permit and construction fees. Emergency response charges are their own case: state law preempts any local ordinance that lets a tenant's calls for police or emergency assistance be used to penalize you or charge you a fee, and you may not penalize the tenant for making such a call, a right the tenant cannot waive.

Because rental licensing in Minnesota is municipal, check your city's ordinance before you charge anything: state law itself expects the licence or registration document posted in a multiple-unit building to carry the attorney general's statement of owner and tenant rights, and a city may regulate what you can charge.

title: Passing a Government Fine to a Tenant
bodyText:
No Minnesota statute bars passing a government fine to a tenant, and none authorises it, so a reimbursement clause is a contract term and the library offers one as optional.

The line you cannot cross is set by the covenants Minnesota writes into every residential lease. You covenant to maintain the premises and all common areas in compliance with federal, state and local health and safety laws, including ordinances regulating rental licensing, except where the violation was caused by the willful, malicious or irresponsible conduct of the tenant or someone under the tenant's direction or control, and those covenants cannot be waived or modified.

So a clause that makes the tenant pay a fine for a condition you are responsible for is an attempted waiver, and a fine for a condition the tenant caused is fair game. Keep the clause to real amounts you actually paid, give the tenant a copy of the citation or order, and do not take it out of a rent payment.

One fine you can never pass on, and one a city cannot charge you in the first place: a landlord may not impose a penalty on a tenant for calling for police or emergency assistance in response to domestic abuse or any other conduct, including a mental health or health crisis, that right cannot be waived, and state law preempts any local ordinance providing that such calls may be used to penalize or charge a fee to a landlord. A tenant can recover $250 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees.

What is not preempted is a local ordinance that penalizes you for, or makes you abate, nuisance or disorderly conduct on the premises - so a nuisance fine can still reach you, and only the tenant-caused part of it can reach the tenant.

Two related points. A local health authority may order the owner or the occupant to remove or abate a public health nuisance within as little as ten days, so your tenant may receive an order directly. And if the premises are condemned or ordered vacated for housing, health, fire code or rental licensing violations, you may not accept rent or a security deposit at all, on pain of actual damages plus three times everything collected, plus costs and attorney fees, and that rule cannot be waived. City ordinances are where most rental fines come from.

title: No Minnesota Guarantor Statute - So the Guaranty's Own Words Decide
bodyText:
Minnesota has no statute about lease guarantors, cosigners or sureties. There is no rule that a guaranty must state a maximum, no rule that it ends with the original term, and no rule that it survives a renewal. The guaranty's own words decide, so write them carefully: state the maximum amount, and say expressly whether the guaranty covers a renewal, an extension or a month-to-month continuation, including a rent increase made under the lease. A guaranty silent about renewals leaves you arguing common law.

Two Minnesota points are worth knowing. First, money is money. Minnesota's security deposit statute is written by function, not by source: any deposit of money whose function is to secure performance of a residential rental agreement, or any part of it, other than a deposit that is exclusively advance rent, is governed by that statute (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.178, subd. 1). It is then held for the tenant who is party to the agreement, earns one percent simple interest and is subject to the three-week return and written-statement rules.

So a sum you take from a guarantor to secure the tenant's obligations is a security deposit and should be folded into the lease's one deposit, not treated as a separate pot. Minnesota sets no statewide deposit cap, but Minneapolis does, which is a municipal matter to check.

Second, do not confuse a guarantor with the statutory "guarantee" that appears in Minnesota's eviction law. In a nonpayment eviction the tenant may redeem on a written guarantee from a federal, state or local agency, or from a tax-exempt organisation administering a government rental assistance programme, that funds are available and will be provided to you (Sec. 504B.291). That is a payment guarantee from a programme, not a guarantor of the lease, and it gives you no claim against the agency beyond the guarantee's own terms.

A guaranty also cannot buy you anything the law does not allow. The guarantor's obligations can never be larger than the tenant's, and nothing in a guaranty can waive the habitability covenants, the deposit rules, the entry-notice right or any other provision Minnesota makes non-waivable. The safe course is the one the clause already takes: have the guarantor sign the lease itself and give them a copy.

title: You Cannot Penalise a Tenant for What a Guest Did Somewhere Else
bodyText:
Minnesota has one real guest rule, and it is a limit on you rather than a right the guest holds. Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, subd. 2a says a residential landlord may not impose a penalty on a residential tenant, or terminate the lease of a residential tenant, for the conduct of the residential tenant, a household member, or a guest occurring off of the premises or curtilage of the premises. Two things lift the bar. The first is conduct that would constitute a crime of violence against another tenant, that tenant's guest, you, or your employees - and the statute adds 'regardless of whether a charge was brought or a conviction obtained'. The second is conduct that results in a conviction of a crime of violence against a person unrelated to the premises. 'Crime of violence' takes its meaning from Minn. Stat. section 624.712, subd. 5, except that it does not include offences under the controlled-substances chapter.

The practical reading is narrow and worth getting right. Off-premises conduct by a guest is not a ground, unless it was violence aimed at your people or your other tenants, or it ended in a conviction. A drug offence off the premises is expressly outside both exceptions, because chapter 152 is carved out of the definition. And the subdivision does nothing to your position on conduct that happens on the premises or in the curtilage, where the covenant in subd. 1 and your own house rules still operate.

Check your crime-free or courtesy-officer addendum against this. A clause that lets you terminate for any arrest, any police contact, or any criminal conduct by a tenant, occupant or guest wherever it happens is wider than the statute allows, and the parties may not waive or modify the covenant that section 504B.171 imposes. Note also that the covenant in subd. 1(b) runs the other way for your benefit: every tenant covenants not to commit an act listed in Minn. Stat. section 504B.206, subd. 1(a) - domestic abuse, criminal sexual conduct, sexual extortion or harassment - against another tenant, a licensee, or any authorised occupant.

title: No Minnesota Statute Gives a Tenant a Right to Have Guests
bodyText:
The thing some states have, Minnesota does not. No Minnesota statute confers on a tenant a right to receive guests, visitors, suppliers or deliveries, caps how short a guest-stay limit a lease may set, makes any guest right non-waivable, or bars a guest fee in an ordinary tenancy. There is no three-or-more-household-building rule of the kind a few states carry. Your guest policy and your guest-stay day limit are therefore your own terms, and the library's standard guest clauses already apply in Minnesota.

Four real limits sit around them, and a guest policy that ignores them will fail even though no guest statute exists. First, Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, subd. 2a stops you penalising the tenant for a guest's off-premises conduct outside two narrow exceptions. Second, Minn. Stat. section 504B.205 says you may not bar or limit a residential tenant's right to call for police or emergency assistance, or impose a penalty for calling, and the tenant may not waive that right and you may not require the tenant to waive it - so a nuisance-call or excessive-call term reaching a guest's call is unlawful. Third, familial status is a protected class in Minnesota housing, so a guest rule applied differently to a household with children is a terms-and-conditions problem under the Human Rights Act. Fourth, if you charge anything for a guest, Minn. Stat. section 504B.120 requires every nonoptional fee to be in the lease and in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, with treble damages for getting it wrong.

If a guest stops being a guest, you are in different territory. Minnesota's definition of 'residential tenant' in Minn. Stat. section 504B.001, subd. 12 reaches 'all other regular occupants of that dwelling unit', so someone who settles in has chapter 504B's protections whether or not they ever signed. Removing that person is an eviction action, not a lockout. For manufactured home park lots a separate chapter applies, and there the law does speak to guests: Minn. Stat. section 327C.03, subd. 3 bans a fee based on the number of guests staying in the home, and Minn. Stat. section 327C.09, subd. 4 provides that loud noise created by residents, guests, or their equipment is a rule violation, with a 30-day written notice and a two-prior-incidents escalation.

title: Minnesota Has No "Material Defect" Threshold
bodyText: Minnesota sets no materiality threshold for habitability, and that cuts against you rather than for you. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161 states the five covenants without any qualifier about how bad a problem has to be, and the word "material" does not appear in the section at all. The remedies run on the defined word "violation", which Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.001, subd. 14 defines as any violation of a state, county or city health, safety, housing, building, fire prevention or housing maintenance code applicable to the building; any violation of chapter 504B; any violation of laws protecting tenants from discrimination; any violation of applicable tenant rights and landlord obligations for public and subsidised tenancies; or any violation of an oral or written agreement, lease or contract for the rental of a dwelling. There is no de minimis filter in that list. So do not assume a small defect is beneath the statute. What Minnesota has instead of a materiality test is a set of gradations that change the route or the amount, not whether a duty was broken. Four are worth knowing. First, speed: Sec. 504B.381 lets a tenant go to court for emergency relief, with only a 24-hour attempt at notice to you, for a revoked rental licence, a condemnation order or notice of intent to condemn, or for an emergency involving a serious infestation, loss of running water, hot water, heat, electricity or sanitary facilities, a nonfunctioning refrigerator, a nonfunctioning air conditioner or elevator if the lease includes it, any condition posing a serious and negative impact on health or safety, or other essential services or facilities. Everything else goes the ordinary route. Second, the amount: under Sec. 504B.425(e) a court may find "the extent to which any uncorrected violations impair the residential tenants' use and enjoyment of the property contracted for and order the rent abated accordingly", so seriousness sets the abatement, not liability. Third, your disclosure duty under Sec. 504B.195 is triggered by outstanding inspection orders the housing inspector identifies as requiring notice because the violations threaten the health or safety of the tenant -- the inspector's filter, not yours. Fourth, repeat refusal is what escalates: Sec. 504B.391 fines a landlord who willfully fails to comply with a court order to remedy a violation. Practical effect: fix what is reported and date your records. A condition you think is minor is still a violation, and its size will show up in how much rent a court abates, not in whether you lose.

title: What Minnesota Lets You Change About Habitability, and What It Does Not
bodyText: Minnesota fixes the habitability standard by statute and gives the lease no dial to turn it down. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(b) bars waiving "or modif[ying]" the covenants, so you cannot agree a lower heat level, a narrower idea of fitness, a softer repair standard or a longer response time. Several states let a lease drop one named duty; Minnesota lets you drop none. In particular there is no Minnesota equivalent of the rule some states have that lets the lease waive the running water or hot water duty where the property has no well and no direct utility connection. The water and hot water duties reach Minnesota through two routes that both stay with you: clause (2) of subd. 1(a) carries the services and conditions listed in Sec. 504B.381, subd. 1, which name the loss of running water and the loss of hot water as emergencies, and clause (4) carries the health and safety laws. What the statute does adjust, it adjusts itself. Only two of the five covenants bend for tenant fault: clause (2) reasonable repair and clause (4) health and safety compliance are excused where the problem was caused by the willful, malicious or irresponsible conduct of the tenant or licensee or a person under the tenant's direction or control. Clause (1) fitness, clause (3) energy efficiency and clause (5) heat have no such exception, so the heat duty survives even damage the tenant caused. Clause (3) has its own built-in limit, which is a cost test and not an agreement: weatherstripping, caulking, storm windows and storm doors are owed only where the measure saves more in energy procurement cost than it costs to install, with interest, over the ten years after the cost is incurred. Clause (5) has one built-in exception: heat may be reduced where a utility company requires and instructs it. The lease can move in one direction only. Subd. 4 says the covenants are in addition to any covenant or condition imposed by law, ordinance or the lease, so a lease term that promises more than the statute binds you to the higher promise, while a term promising less is simply not effective. The only lawful change to who does the work is Sec. 504B.161, subd. 2, and it moves performance of specified repairs, never the standard; see Changing Who Does the Repairs in Minnesota. A tenant's chance to look round before signing changes nothing (subd. 3), and nothing in the section alters your liability to third parties (subd. 5).

title: Nothing Is Presumed About Habitability in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota presumes nothing about habitability. No statute presumes that you broke a covenant, that you took too long, or that a code citation or a government notice proves a condition was serious. No statute sets a repair clock running from a tenant's request, so there is no deadline you are presumed to have missed. Some states presume a breach once a stated number of days passes after notice; Minnesota does not. In a rent escrow action or a tenant remedies action the tenant has to prove the violation. Minnesota does use presumptions, just not here, and it is worth knowing which ones exist so you do not confuse them. In a nonpayment eviction, rent is rebuttably presumed paid if the tenant produces money orders or original receipt stubs that total the rent, carry dates about when rent was due and, for copies of money orders, are payable to you; you rebut it with a business record showing nonpayment (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.291, subd. 1). If you interrupt electricity, heat, gas or water, intent to oust is presumed once the interruption is shown, and the burden to rebut is yours (Sec. 504B.225). Keeping a security deposit is presumed to be in bad faith if you missed the statutory deadlines and do not return it within two weeks of an action (Sec. 504B.178, subd. 7). And if you evict a tenant, increase their obligations or cut their services within 90 days after they complain about a violation, the burden of proving you were not penalising them is on you, unless the court finds the complaint was not made in good faith (Sec. 504B.441). That last one is the nearest thing to a habitability presumption in Minnesota law, and it is about your reaction to the complaint, not about the condition. One evidence rule does real work against you. In a rent escrow hearing a certified copy of an inspection report is admissible as an exception to the rule against hearsay and is treated as authenticated without a witness (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 6). That is not a presumption that the violation is serious; it means the report goes in without the inspector attending. Practical effect: keep dated records of every repair request, what you did and when. Nothing presumes against you, and nothing presumes for you either.

title: No Habitability Statement Required in a Minnesota Lease
bodyText: Minnesota does not make you write a habitability promise into the lease, because the promise is already there without you. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) puts the five covenants "[i]n every lease or license of residential premises", written or not, and subd. 1(b) stops either side waiving or modifying them. No Minnesota statute prescribes habitability wording, no statute requires a statement that the unit will be delivered fit for habitation, and no statute requires you to state the unit's agreed condition instead. Some states require one or the other; Minnesota requires neither. So adding your own habitability language gains you nothing, and a loosely worded version can only hurt. Under subd. 4 the covenants are in addition to anything the lease imposes, which means a lease sentence promising more than the statute holds you to the larger promise, while a sentence promising less is simply ineffective. Under subd. 3 the section is construed liberally and the chance to inspect before signing does not defeat the covenants, so a condition acknowledgment is a record of what the property was like, not a limit on what you owe. What Minnesota does require around the lease is different, and it is the part landlords miss. Before a person signs a lease or pays rent or a security deposit, you must give them a copy of every outstanding inspection order for which a citation has been issued that the housing inspector marked as threatening a tenant's health or safety, and every outstanding condemnation order and declaration that the premises are unfit for human habitation (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195, subd. 1). Where the citation does not threaten health or safety, you post a summary conspicuously in each affected building with a notice that the order is available on request. Miss that and the tenant gets the remedies in Minn. Stat. Sec. 8.31, subd. 3a plus equitable relief. That is the habitability-adjacent statement Minnesota actually asks for, and it is about orders, not promises. Two other lease-content rules worth noting while you are checking page one: a written residential lease must identify the lease start date and the lease end date, and must state the amount of any prorated rent (Sec. 504B.146); and rent plus all nonoptional fees must appear on the first page as the Total Monthly Payment (Sec. 504B.120). Practical course: say nothing about habitability beyond the Lease's repair and maintenance sections, and give the Sec. 504B.195 disclosure on time.

title: Habitability Cannot Be Waived or Modified in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota does not let a lease waive habitability, and the sentence that does the work is short. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(b): "The parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section." All five covenants in subd. 1(a) stay: the premises and all common areas fit for the use the parties intended; reasonable repair during the term; reasonable energy efficiency where it pays for itself over ten years; compliance with federal, state and local health and safety laws, including rental licensing ordinances; and heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit in every place meant for habitation, kitchens and bathrooms included, from October 1 through April 30 unless a utility company requires it lowered. Two covenants carry a tenant-fault exception and three do not. The exception for the tenant's willful, malicious or irresponsible conduct sits in clause (2), reasonable repair, and clause (4), health and safety compliance. It is not in clause (1) fitness, clause (3) energy efficiency or clause (5) heat, so you owe heat even where the tenant broke the heater. Minnesota has no rule letting a tenant accept named defects in return for a stated rent reduction, and no separate-document rule for agreeing a lower heat level; some states have both and Minnesota has neither, so do not borrow that language. Signing after a look round changes nothing: subd. 3 says the section is construed liberally and "the opportunity to inspect the premises before concluding a lease or license shall not defeat the covenants established in this section". The Lease's Existing Condition section records what the property was like at delivery; it is not a waiver and cannot work as one. The covenants are also in addition to anything the lease or an ordinance imposes (subd. 4), and they apply to every lease or licence concluded or renewed on or after June 15, 1971, with an estate at will treated as renewed at the start of each rental period, so every live tenancy is covered. The tenant's remedies cannot be waived either, and each bar uses its own words: a lease provision waiving Sec. 504B.381 or Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471 "is contrary to public policy and void" (Sec. 504B.465), and the rent escrow rights "may not be waived or modified" (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 11). Shifting who does specified repair work is a different question, allowed on strict conditions; see Changing Who Does the Repairs in Minnesota and the Tenant Repair and Maintenance Agreement.

title: No Contamination Disclosure in a Minnesota Lease, but Pass On Any Environmental Covenant
bodyText: Nothing in the Minnesota landlord-tenant act, the health chapter, the fire-marshal chapter or the consumer chapters requires you to tell a tenant that a rental property is or was contaminated. There is no brownfield notice, no recorded-cleanup-status statement and no duty to copy an environmental use limitation into a lease. THE ONE NOTIFICATION REGIME THAT EXISTS RUNS TO THE FIRE DEPARTMENT, NOT TO YOUR TENANT. Minn. Stat. Secs. 299F.091 to 299F.099 is the Community Emergency Response Hazardous Substances Protection Act. Under Sec. 299F.094, subd. 1, an EMPLOYER who receives a hazardous substance notification report must send the completed form back to the local fire department within two months, or arrange an inspection instead. Subd. 3 adds a material safety data sheet on request and a 30-day answer to follow-up questions; subd. 4 requires prompt notice of significant changes within 30 days; subd. 5 requires you to permit inspection and help prepare fire and emergency plans. The data is nonpublic (Sec. 299F.095, paragraph (b)). Fines run to $1,000 per violation and a willful or repeated violation is a gross misdemeanor (Sec. 299F.098), but you cannot be convicted without written notice of the violation and a reasonable time to comply (paragraph (f)). Two practical points: the duty is triggered by RECEIVING a report form from the fire department, so most small residential landlords never get one; and under Sec. 299F.093, subd. 1(5) a fire department may require employers in its jurisdiction to post NFPA standard 704 signs showing that hazardous substances are present, with the department supplying the signs or helping you get them. Sec. 299F.099 preempts any local ordinance on the same subject. WHAT STILL REACHES YOU AS A LANDLORD. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) makes you covenant that the premises and common areas are fit for the use intended and that you will maintain them in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state and of local government, including rental licensing ordinances; subd. 1(b) bars waiver. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195 makes you hand a prospective tenant any outstanding inspection citation or condemnation order before they sign or pay, and that section cannot be waived. ENVIRONMENTAL COVENANTS AND CLEANUP AFFIDAVITS. Minnesota's Environmental Covenants Act, Minn. Stat. ch. 114E, and its cleanup chapters, ch. 115B and ch. 115C, were read. None requires contamination information in a residential lease. An environmental covenant runs with the land (Sec. 114E.20(a)). A copy must go to 'each person in possession of the real property subject to the covenant', but 'by the persons and in the manner required by the environmental agency' (Sec. 114E.30(a)(3)). So if your property carries a covenant, the agency may have made you responsible for giving your tenants a copy; read the covenant and the agency's approval. Under Sec. 115B.16, subd. 2, an owner who knew or should have known the property was a hazardous waste disposal site, or is extensively contaminated, must record an affidavit before any transfer of ownership. A lease does not trigger it. Practical course: if your property has a recorded environmental covenant, a no-further-action letter or a known release, disclose what you know in writing before you let it, and attach a copy of any covenant.

title: Minnesota's Community Health Boards: What They Can Do to a Rental
bodyText: Minnesota does not have "health districts" and has no statute making you give health-district rental regulations to a tenant on request. What Minnesota has instead is the COMMUNITY HEALTH BOARD -- a county, city or multicounty body under Minn. Stat. ch. 145A, operating "[u]nder the general supervision of the commissioner" and responsible for recommending "the enforcement of laws, regulations, and ordinances pertaining to the powers and duties within its jurisdictional area" (Sec. 145A.04, subd. 1). Its statutory areas of responsibility include "protecting against environmental health hazards" by, among other things, "identifying and mitigating environmental risks such as food and waterborne diseases, radiation, occupational health hazards, and public health nuisances" (subd. 1a(1)(iv)). FOUR POWERS REACH YOUR RENTAL DIRECTLY. (1) ENTRY. "To enforce public health laws, ordinances or rules, a member or agent of a community health board, county, or city may enter a building, conveyance, or place where contagion, infection, filth, or other source or cause of preventable disease exists or is reasonably suspected" (Sec. 145A.04, subd. 7). The Department of Health has the same power in its own right (Sec. 144.0535). Deliberately hindering either is a MISDEMEANOUR (Sec. 145A.04, subd. 10) -- and so is a board member or agent refusing or neglecting to perform a duty imposed on them (subd. 11). (2) A TEN-DAY ABATEMENT ORDER. This is the one to know. "If a threat to the public health such as a public health nuisance, source of filth, or cause of sickness is found on any property, the community health board, county, city, or its agent shall order the owner or occupant of the property to remove or abate the threat within a time specified in the notice but not longer than ten days" (Sec. 145A.04, subd. 8(a)). Notice is served on the owner, occupant or agent by registered or certified mail, by an officer authorised to serve a warrant, or by a person aged 18 or older who is not reasonably believed to be a party (subd. 8(b)); if the owner is unknown or absent with no known representative, the notice is POSTED on the property (subd. 8(c)). If you fail or neglect to comply, the board, county or city "shall remove or abate the nuisance, source of filth, or cause of sickness described in the notice from the property" (subd. 8(d)) -- and the cost comes back to you. Note the order runs to "the owner or occupant": your tenant can be the person served, and so can you. (3) AN INJUNCTION. "In addition to any other remedy provided by law", the board, county or city may sue "to enjoin a violation of statute, rule, or ordinance that the board has power to enforce, or to enjoin as a public health nuisance any activity or failure to act that adversely affects the public health" (subd. 9). (4) LEAD ORDERS. A state lead order under Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9504 is enforced by the community health board "under a local ordinance or as a public health nuisance under chapter 145A" (Sec. 144.9509, subd. 1), and where a child has an elevated blood lead level the assessing agency must assess the unit and "inspect all common areas accessible to a child" (Sec. 144.9504). See "Minnesota Lead Notices: None at Signing, One That Overrides Your Lease". TWO DEFINITIONS IN THE LEAD CHAPTER ARE WORTH YOUR ATTENTION, because they decide whether an order lands on you. "Lead order" means "a legal instrument to compel a property owner to engage in lead hazard reduction according to the specifications given by the assessing agency" (Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9501, subd. 20) -- the property owner, which is you. And "compensation" is defined to include "rental payments, rental income, or salaries derived from rental payments" (subd. 33), while "renovation" means modification of a pre-1978 affected property "for compensation" that disturbs known or presumed lead-containing painted surfaces (subd. 26b). Read together, work you do on your own pre-1978 rental can be "renovation" and therefore "regulated lead work" (subd. 26a), because the rental income is the compensation. The minor repair and maintenance carve-out is narrow: under 20 square feet outside or under six square feet in an interior room, with activities within 30 days in the same room counted as one project, and it never applies to window replacement or to demolition of a painted surface or building component. WHERE THE RULES THEMSELVES COME FROM. Not from the board. The commissioner of health may adopt rules for the preservation of the public health under Sec. 144.12, subd. 1, but that power covers lodging houses and public sleeping places kept for gain, camps, tourist camps, summer hotels and resorts -- not ordinary rental dwellings -- and the commissioner's rules "shall not conflict with the charter or ordinance of a city of the first class upon the same subject". A community health board's own role on rental housing standards is to enforce, to recommend local ordinances to a county board or city council (subd. 13), and to advise the commissioner. So the substantive rental rules are the city's, and Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(4) is the state hook that makes them your covenant: you must maintain the premises and all common areas in compliance with health and safety laws "of the local units of government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing". THE STATE HAS ITS OWN PARALLEL ROUTE, which is not the board's. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.99, subd. 1 lets the commissioner of health enforce a long list of statutes, and the list it prints includes "144.12, subdivision 1, clauses (1), (2), (5), (6), (10), (12), (13), (14), and (15)", "144.1222", "144.71 to 144.74" and "144.9501 to 144.9512". The commissioner may act by entering property, issuing correction orders, issuing administrative penalty orders up to $10,000 per violator per inspection, suing for an injunction, and issuing a 72-hour cease and desist order where continuing would be an immediate risk to public health. A penalty must be forgiven, except for repeated or serious violations, if you show in writing before the 31st day after receiving the order that you have corrected the violation or developed an acceptable corrective plan. WHAT TO DO. Find your county or city community health board, keep the contact in your files, and treat any notice it sends as having a deadline of ten days or less. There is no state requirement to hand a tenant a copy of the board's regulations, but there is nothing wrong with telling a tenant who to call, and a tenant can require a code inspection anyway under Sec. 504B.185.

title: The September 30 Energy Assistance Notice You Probably Do Not Know About
bodyText:
If you bill tenants for gas or electricity separately from rent in a shared-metered residential building, Minnesota gives you an annual written notice duty with a hard date. Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 15: 'By September 30 of each year, a landlord of a shared-metered residential building who bills for gas, electric utility charges, or both separate from rent must inform tenants in writing of the possible availability of energy assistance from the low-income home energy assistance program. The information must contain the toll-free telephone number of the administering agency.'

Three things to note. It is annual and dated, so it is not satisfied once at move-in — it recurs every year by September 30, just before the cold weather period starts on October 1. It must be in writing. And it must carry the administering agency's current toll-free number, so a template with a stale number does not comply.

This is not a lease clause. It is a recurring notice, so it belongs in your annual compliance calendar rather than in the lease, and putting it only in the lease would not discharge it in later years. A violation of subd. 15 is not listed among the subdivisions that § 504B.216, subd. 16 converts into a violation of § 504B.161 or § 504B.221, but the attorney general may investigate and prosecute violations of the section under subd. 17.

title: The Heat Duty You Cannot Shift, and What Changed in 2025
bodyText:
Minnesota's heat covenant is in every residential lease by operation of law, and it is not waivable. Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(5) requires you 'to equip or furnish heat at a minimum temperature of 68 degrees Fahrenheit in all places intended for habitation including kitchens and bathrooms from October 1 through April 30, unless a utility company requires and instructs the heat to be reduced'. Subdivision 1(b) then says the parties 'may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section'.

Two changes in 2025 matter, and they pull in the same direction. One act added the words 'in all places intended for habitation including kitchens and bathrooms', so a building that hits 68 degrees in the living room but not the bathroom no longer complies. The same act also inserted 'capable of maintaining', which would have softened the duty to a question about the equipment. A special session later the same year deleted those words again, with effect from July 1, 2025. The duty is therefore to actually furnish heat at 68 degrees, not merely to install a system that could.

Paying is not the same as furnishing. You may allocate the cost of gas, electricity or fuel to the tenant, and the lease can put the account in the tenant's name. What you cannot do is make the tenant responsible for whether the property is heated. If the tenant's gas is shut off and the unit drops below 68 degrees in the heating season, the covenant is still yours. The only delegation Minnesota allows is narrow: under subd. 2 you may agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance, but only with adequate consideration and in a conspicuous writing, and no such agreement may waive subd. 1 or relieve you of maintaining common areas.

What happens if heat fails. Loss of heat is an express emergency under § 504B.381, subd. 1(2)(iv), which lets a tenant petition a judge after trying to give you 24 hours' notice, and get an order on an ex parte showing that you must begin remedying it immediately. A tenant may also deposit rent with the court administrator and ask for abatement under § 504B.385. If you interrupt heat yourself, § 504B.221 gives treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees.

Two more heating-season points. The utility side is governed by the cold weather rule in § 216B.096, which runs October 1 through April 30 and limits when a utility may disconnect a customer's heating service. And a tenant who leaves the property between November 15 and April 15 without giving you three days' notice commits a misdemeanour under § 504B.155, because of the freezing risk — the lease section on that is a separate item in this library. The section has applied to every lease concluded or renewed on or after June 15, 1971, so it applies to all of your tenancies without qualification.

title: Your HOA and Your Minnesota Tenant: Chapter 515B Acts Through You, Not the Lease
bodyText:
If your rental is a unit in a condominium or a planned community, the association's rules come from the development's own declaration and bylaws, not from Minnesota's landlord-tenant act. Minn. Stat. ch. 504B has nothing in it about homeowners', unit owners' or community associations at all -- the only associations it knows are TENANT associations, which are a different thing entirely (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.212 and the definitions in Sec. 504B.001 subds. 13a and 13b; see "Tenants Have a Statutory Right to Organize"). So nothing in the landlord-tenant act caps an association's lease-approval fee, regulates a deposit the association takes from your tenant, lets the association collect rent from your tenant when you fall behind, or limits what the association may ask about your tenant. The optional Association Approval of Lease clause is therefore a pure term of the bargain in Minnesota, and it is lawful.

ONE MINNESOTA POINT THAT DOES BITE ON THAT CLAUSE. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.120 subd. 1 requires you to disclose ALL nonoptional fees in the lease, and to describe the sum of rent and all nonoptional fees as the Total Monthly Payment on the first page; subd. 2 makes a violation cost you treble damages and possibly the tenant's attorney fees. If the association's application or approval fee is charged to your tenant, it is a fee your tenant must pay to get the tenancy, so name it in the lease. The cautious course is to fill the blank with Landlord unless the association bills your tenant directly.

WHAT CHAPTER 515B ADDS. Minnesota's common interest community law, Minn. Stat. ch. 515B, was read whole, with the older condominium acts in ch. 515 and ch. 515A. It does not cap a lease-approval fee, regulate a deposit taken from your tenant, or let the association collect rent from your tenant. Its tenant rules run through the association's rule power and through you. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 515B.3-102(a)(1), the association may adopt reasonable rules regulating the use of units and the 'conduct of unit occupants', and regulating or prohibiting animals. If an occupant or the occupant's invitee damages the common elements or another unit, the association may assess the repair cost not covered by insurance against your unit (Secs. 515B.3-115(g) and 515B.3-1151(g)). So your lease should make the tenant answer to you for that cost.

In an older condominium under ch. 515, tenants are themselves 'subject to' the act, the declaration and the bylaws (Minn. Stat. Sec. 515.28(a)).

From January 1, 2027, Minn. Stat. Sec. 515B.3-107(f) says an association 'has no authority to regulate the parking of a unit owner or a guest, tenant, or invitee of the unit owner within an improved public right-of-way that a unit of government maintains and repairs', except to require compliance with applicable statutes, laws and ordinances. The same subsection says a 'unit owner or resident' must be permitted to park a personal or work vehicle in the parking area designed for the unit, subject to three provisos.

Chapter 515B's limits on association fines, late fees and attorney fees run from the association to the UNIT OWNER and never mention a tenant. Any leasing restriction comes from your own declaration, bylaws and rules, so read them before you let the unit.

title: What a Minnesota Holdover Actually Costs the Tenant
bodyText:
Minnesota gives you no holdover number, for any kind of holdover. There is no double or treble rent, no statutory liquidated-damages figure, no 150 percent per diem cap, and - unlike several states - no separate, higher measure for a tenant who stays on deliberately. A deliberate holdover and a good faith one are treated the same, which means neither has a figure.

What Minnesota gives you instead is three things. Holding over after the term ends, or after rent becomes due contrary to the lease, is a ground to recover possession by eviction (Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subdivision 1). Every person in possession of land out of which rent is due is liable for the amount or proportion of rent due from the land they hold, recoverable in a civil action, and the lease itself may be used in evidence to prove the amount - and that section expressly does not deprive you of any other remedy, including one secured by your lease (Minn. Stat. section 504B.125). And if a tenant holds over on urban real estate without your express agreement, no tenancy longer than the shortest interval between rent payments under the expired lease is implied (Minn. Stat. section 504B.141) - so a holdover does not hand the tenant another year, and the expired lease's rent interval is the yardstick.

Put together: your recovery is the rent at the expired lease's rate plus your actual documented loss, unless your lease sets a daily figure. Because Minnesota sets no ceiling, a daily holdover charge in the lease is lawful, and the library offers one.

Two cautions if you use it. Keep the daily figure at the daily equivalent of monthly rent rather than a multiple of it: Minnesota has no multiplier to point to, and its late fee statute goes out of its way to say a late fee is neither interest nor liquidated damages, which is the kind of reasoning a court may apply to a charge that looks like a penalty. And do not accept rent for a continued tenancy if you want possession - accepting rent with knowledge of a breach can waive your right to evict for it.

Ignore any generic lease language about double rent capped at what applicable law allows; in Minnesota that cap is ordinary rent, so the doubling language gives you nothing and misleads you. This covers Minnesota's statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws.

title: Minnesota Does Not Make a Home Business a Protected Use
bodyText:
Minnesota's landlord-tenant statutes do not make a home-based business a permitted use of a rented dwelling, bar a lease from restricting one, or set conditions on a landlord who allows one. There is no Minnesota equivalent of the West Virginia home-based business act. So the lease governs, and the library's standard residential-use-only clause, which already applies in Minnesota, is enforceable on its own terms.

Three Minnesota-specific points are worth holding in mind before you either permit or refuse a business use.

First, if you do permit one, you widen your own habitability covenant. Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subd. 1(a) writes into every residential lease a covenant that the premises and all common areas are 'fit for the use intended by the parties'. The intended use is whatever the lease says it is. A lease that permits a tenant to see clients, store stock, or run equipment at the property has made that part of the intended use, and the parties may not waive or modify the covenants this section imposes. If you mean to permit a business use, describe it narrowly.

Second, your own compliance duty runs to local law. The same subdivision, at clause (4), makes you covenant to maintain the premises in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state, and of the local units of government, 'including ordinances regulating rental licensing'. A home occupation that needs a zoning permit or a licence the property does not hold is a local-law problem that lands partly on you. Whether a particular home occupation is allowed at all is a zoning question under Minnesota's enabling acts and the city's own ordinance.

Third, licensed family child care in a rented home is a separate question with its own answer. See the family-child-care topic rather than treating it as an ordinary home business.

title: No Homestead Waiver in a Minnesota Lease: the Word Does Not Appear
bodyText:
A homestead-waiver clause has nothing to do in a Minnesota residential lease, and the reason is worth understanding rather than just taking on trust.

The word is not there. "Homestead" does not appear in Minnesota Statutes chapters 504B, 363A, 325D, 325F, 299F, 144, 484 and 327C, and it does not appear in the Minnesota Constitution at all.

The constitution does protect exempt property, but not under that name and not in a way a lease can reach. Minn. Const. art. I, § 12, headed "Imprisonment for debt; property exemption", provides: "No person shall be imprisoned for debt in this state... A reasonable amount of property shall be exempt from seizure or sale for the payment of any debt or liability. The amount of such exemption shall be determined by law." It then carves out debts for work done or materials furnished in constructing, repairing or improving the same property, and extends seizure to all real property for a debt to a laborer or servant for labor performed. Note what that structure does: the constitution guarantees that some exemption exists and leaves its size to the legislature. It says nothing about whether a debtor may agree in advance to give it up.

Why the clause is empty in a lease anyway. A homestead exemption protects a debtor's own home from seizure for a debt. A residential tenant does not own the home they rent, so there is no homestead interest in the leased premises for the tenant to waive. The exemption your tenant might have attaches to property they own elsewhere, and your lease is not the instrument that reaches it. A clause asking a tenant to waive a homestead exemption as a condition of renting is asking for something the tenancy does not involve.

The personal-property side, which is the part that could matter. If you obtain a money judgment against a former tenant for rent or damages, collection runs into the statutory exemptions for a judgment debtor's personal property — household goods and the like. Those exemptions are in Minn. Stat. § 550.37. Clothing, utensils, food, and household furniture, appliances and electronics up to a value cap are exempt (subd. 4). That exemption "may not be waived except with regard to purchase money security interests." Others, such as tools of a trade or a motor vehicle, may be waived only by a boldface statement in a form the statute prints, signed and dated when the contract is signed, next to a list of the property (subd. 19). A general waiver in a lease does neither. Minnesota's homestead law, Minn. Stat. ch. 510, protects "the house owned and occupied by a debtor as the debtor's dwelling place" (§ 510.01), which confirms that a tenant has no homestead in the rented premises.

So: do not include a homestead-waiver clause. It addresses an interest the tenant does not have in the premises, Minnesota's own exemption law is not in Chapter 504B, and the personal-property exemptions either cannot be waived at all or only by a separate, itemised boldface statement that a lease form is the wrong place for.

title: Your Rental Application Must Offer the ITIN Option
bodyText: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.117 is a required application-content rule, and it is the one Minnesota provision that speaks to immigration status at the point of application. A landlord must provide on a rental application the option for a prospective tenant to submit an individual taxpayer identification number or a Social Security number, and the statute prints the form of words to use: SSN or ITIN, followed by a blank. A landlord must not deny a rental application solely because the prospective tenant provided an individual taxpayer identification number. The limit is in the section too, and it is a real one: nothing in the section prevents a landlord from denying an application if the consumer credit report attached to an individual taxpayer identification number is insufficient. So an ITIN cannot be the reason for a denial, but a thin or absent credit file behind it can be - provided that is genuinely your reason and you apply the same standard to everyone. This one bites on the application form, not the lease, so it is a product obligation rather than lease text. If your application has a single field labelled Social Security Number, it does not comply. Two neighbouring provisions to keep straight. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.111 says that notwithstanding any other state law or city ordinance to the contrary, a landlord may ask for the tenant full name and date of birth on the lease and application - so those two items are expressly permitted. And Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.212, subd. 2(a) makes contacting federal or state law enforcement related to a tenant immigration status one of the acts you may not take in retaliation after a tenant does one of six protected things. That is a retaliation rule, not a general ban on asking: Minnesota has no statewide immigration-status inquiry prohibition. Some Minnesota cities do, and a municipal ordinance is outside this library - check your city separately.

title: Minnesota Already Has Three Dispute-Resolution Regimes, and One Is Your Duty
bodyText:
Minnesota's landlord-tenant act says nothing about mediation, arbitration or informal dispute resolution, and no Minnesota statute authorises an informal-resolution clause in a residential lease the way Oregon's does. A non-binding clause rests on freedom of contract and is lawful here because it gives nothing up.

Three dispute-resolution regimes already apply to you, though, and one of them is your own duty.

Court-annexed resolution is the big one. The supreme court must run a statewide alternative dispute resolution programme for civil cases filed with the courts, and its rules must require the use of non-binding alternative dispute resolution in all civil cases except for good cause shown by the presiding judge (Minn. Stat. Sec. 484.76). The methods include arbitration, mediation, neutral expert fact-finding, minitrials, private trials and consensual special magistrates, and they are non-binding unless the parties validly agree otherwise. Alternative dispute resolution may not be required in civil commitment matters or in matters arising under the patient and resident rights sections, the domestic abuse act or the vulnerable-adult act. In Ramsey and Hennepin counties a judge may also order non-binding resolution where more than $7,500 is in controversy, with a neutral each party may remove once as of right (Sec. 484.74), and a judicial district may run its own mandatory non-binding arbitration system (Sec. 484.73). The rules that carry all this are the General Rules of Practice.

Utility bills come with a compulsory ladder, and part of it is a duty on you. A tenant disputing a bill or claiming a violation of the shared-metered billing rules must first try to resolve it with you. If the tenant disagrees with your proposed resolution, you must tell the tenant of the right to file a complaint with the Public Utilities Commission's consumer affairs office and give the tenant that office's current telephone number and email address (Sec. 216B.024). You must also offer a payment plan for an overdue utility bill and make the same referral if you cannot agree (Sec. 216B.023). Those duties are covered under the utility topics.

A fair housing charge has resolution built in. Charging parties and respondents must be offered, and may request, an opportunity to resolve a charge through mediation or another alternative process, and the limitation period is suspended while the parties are voluntarily engaged in one (Sec. 363A.28).

Small money has a cheap forum. A tenant may bring an action to recover a deposit in conciliation court, and several filing fees and routing decisions in the landlord-tenant act are pegged to conciliation court's limits (Sec. Sec. 504B.178, 504B.375, 504B.381 and 504B.385).

The limit on what your lease can do is the important part. The tenant's rights in a rent escrow action may not be waived or modified, and a lease provision waiving the emergency tenant remedies action or the tenant remedies action is contrary to public policy and void. A clause making informal resolution a precondition to any of those remedies would therefore be void. Keep any such clause non-binding, charge nothing for it, and say expressly that it does not delay or limit any statutory notice, deadline or remedy, or any action for possession or emergency relief.

Binding arbitration is a different question. The library does not offer an arbitration clause, and you should take advice before adding one.

title: No Jury Unless Someone Demands One; No Statute on Waiving It
bodyText:
Start with the default, because it is the opposite of what landlords often assume. In a Minnesota eviction there is no jury unless somebody asks for one. Minn. Stat. § 504B.335, paragraph (b) is the whole of it: "Either party may demand a trial by jury." Paragraph (c) adds that "the proceedings in the action are the same as in other civil actions, except as provided in sections 504B.281 to 504B.371". So the court tries the case unless a party demands a jury, and the practical effect of a lease jury-waiver clause is only to stop the tenant demanding one.

The constitution allows a jury waiver, and says how. Minn. Const. art. I, § 4 provides: "The right of trial by jury shall remain inviolate, and shall extend to all cases at law without regard to the amount in controversy. A jury trial may be waived by the parties in all cases in the manner prescribed by law." So waiver is constitutionally contemplated — but only "in the manner prescribed by law", which points at the rules of court rather than at the lease.

There is no Minnesota statute on a lease jury-waiver clause, in either direction. Nothing permits it; nothing voids it. Minnesota has no standard-form contract statute making a jury or class-action waiver presumptively unconscionable, and no statute of frauds provision requiring a signed writing for an agreement waiving a constitutional right. Chapter 504B says nothing about a lease waiving the § 504B.335(b) demand, and § 504B.335 carries no non-waiver sentence of its own — note that Minn. Stat. § 504B.465, despite its "WAIVER NOT ALLOWED" headnote, reaches only § 504B.381 and §§ 504B.395 to 504B.471, so it does not protect § 504B.335.

What the rest of the jury machinery says. Minn. Stat. § 504B.351 lets the court discharge a jury that cannot agree and impanel a new one. Minn. Stat. § 504B.355 prescribes the form of verdict and expressly contemplates the action being "tried without a jury", with the court making the finding. Minn. Stat. § 504B.345, subd. 1(a) speaks of "the court or jury". None of them touches waiver by agreement.

In one proceeding there is no jury for anyone to waive. Minn. Stat. § 504B.421, the hearing section of the tenant remedies action, provides: "If issues of fact are raised, they must be tried by the court without a jury." So in a tenant remedies action under Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.395 to 504B.471 the question does not arise — and a lease clause purporting to waive a jury there would be waiving nothing, while Minn. Stat. § 504B.465 makes any waiver of those sections "contrary to public policy and void" in any event.

In one proceeding a jury is the default and a lease clause cannot touch it. Minn. Stat. § 363A.33, subd. 1 provides that a person bringing a civil action for an unfair discriminatory practice, or a respondent, "is entitled to a jury trial". Read with Minn. Stat. § 363A.31, subd. 1, which voids a prospective lease waiver of any Human Rights Act right or remedy, a lease jury-waiver clause cannot reach a discrimination claim. Draft the clause, if you use one, so it does not purport to.

One nearby rule is worth more to you than the jury question, and it is easy to miss. Minn. Stat. § 504B.335, paragraph (e) bars the court from requiring a tenant to put up money before the case ends: "The court may not require the defendant to pay any amount of money into court, post a bond, make a payment directly to a landlord, or by any other means post security for any purpose prior to final disposition of an action". The one exception is where final disposition may be delayed more than ten days, when the court may order security it approves "based on the totality of the circumstances", and even then the amount "may not include any amounts allegedly owed prior to the date of filing of the action and may not exceed the amount of the monthly or periodic rent that accrues during the pendency of the action". An appeal bond under Minn. Stat. § 504B.371, subd. 3 is unaffected. A lease clause requiring the tenant to pay rent into court, or to post security, as a condition of defending an eviction is asking the court to do what paragraph (e) forbids it to do.

Where that leaves a clause. A jury-waiver clause is not statutorily void in Minnesota, and it is also doing less than it appears to, because the jury is not the default. Whether a pre-dispute contractual waiver satisfies "the manner prescribed by law" under Minn. Const. art. I, § 4 is a question of court rules and case law. Take advice before including one, and do not pair it with any requirement that the tenant pay money or post security to defend.

title: No Key-Control or Staff-Screening Mandate - with One Narrow Exception
bodyText:
Minnesota has no key-control mandate for ordinary rental housing. Nothing requires you to issue keys against a receipt, keep a master-key log, limit who holds a passkey, change keys between tenancies, or screen or background-check the staff and contractors who hold keys, and nothing imposes extra duties on a larger complex.

Run a key policy anyway, because the absence of a statute is not the absence of exposure. Issue keys against a signed receipt, keep a list of who holds a master key, collect keys when staff leave, and screen anyone who will hold one. An incident involving a staff member with a key is a negligence problem for you whatever chapter 504B says, and Minn. Stat. section 504B.211 makes an unannounced entry by 'the landlord's agent or other person acting under the landlord's direction and control' your violation, at up to $500 a time.

There is one real key-control rule in Minnesota, and it is narrow. If you operate housing with services that is exempt from assisted living facility licensure, Minn. Stat. section 325F.722, subd. 2(c)(5) requires your written contract to state that the resident has a right to have and use a lockable door, that you provide the locks, that 'Only a staff member with a specific need to enter the unit shall have keys', and that advance notice must be given before a staff member enters when possible. That is a genuine need-to-hold rule, it has to be in the contract, and those settings must comply with chapter 504B as well.

Two things to watch on the money side. First, if you charge for keys, fobs or re-keying, Minn. Stat. section 504B.120 requires every nonoptional fee to be disclosed in the lease and shown in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, and gets you treble damages if you skip it; a key charge that a tenant cannot avoid is nonoptional. Second, Minnesota imposes no duty to re-key at turnover, so a turnover re-key is your own cost and not something to pass to the outgoing tenant unless the lease says so and the keys actually went missing - which is what the Keys clause in the lease does.

On staff screening, Minnesota's background-study machinery is real but it is not yours. The statutes that require criminal background studies run to licensed health and care settings and to fire departments, not to residential landlords. The one screening rule Minnesota does impose on a landlord is about screening tenants, not staff: Minn. Stat. section 504B.173 governs the applicant screening fee - no fee where the landlord knows no unit is or will be available, a written receipt on request, the criteria disclosed in writing before the fee is taken, the fee returned in the listed cases, and a $100 civil penalty on top of the fee for getting it wrong.

title: What a Minnesota Tenant Can Recover When You Breach, Section by Section
bodyText:
Start with what Minnesota does not have, because it shapes everything else. There is no single 'landlord noncompliance' section, and there is no general right for a tenant to walk away from the lease because you breached it. The statutory termination rights are all situational: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.153 (a new-construction unit not ready on the move-in date), Sec. 504B.206 (victims of violence), Sec. 504B.265 (death of the tenant) and Sec. 504B.266 (infirmity of the tenant). Habitability is conspicuously not on that list. A tenant whose unit you fail to maintain gets a court process, not an exit.

The gateway is a definition, and it is wider than landlords expect. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.001, subd. 14 defines 'violation' to include a violation of a health, safety, housing, building, fire prevention or housing maintenance code; 'a violation of this chapter'; a violation of any law protecting tenants from discrimination; a violation of tenant rights and landlord obligations for public and subsidised tenancies; and 'a violation of an oral or written agreement, lease, or contract for the rental of a dwelling in a building'. So an ordinary breach of your own lease is a statutory 'violation'. That is what opens rent escrow and the tenant remedies action, which are covered in their own notes and not repeated here.

Then the money, and the point is that there is no single figure. Each breach carries its own measure, and several of them are multipliers rather than damages:
- Unlawful removal, exclusion or forcible keeping out, in bad faith: treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees (Sec. 504B.231).
- Interrupting electricity, heat, gas or water: treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus fees, cut back to actual damages only in the three situations the section lists (Sec. 504B.221).
- Barring or penalising a call for police or emergency assistance: $250 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees (Sec. 504B.205, subd. 5).
- Disclosing a violence victim's information: $2,000 in statutory damages, plus reasonable attorney fees and costs, whether or not the tenant lost anything (Sec. 504B.206, subd. 2(d)).
- A tenant-screening-report violation: 'the greater of $1,000 or actual damages', costs including costs of investigation, and fees -- and the action runs 'against a residential tenant screening service or landlord' (Sec. 504B.245).
- A new-construction unit not ready: the tenant elects either recovery under Sec. 504B.231 or 'the greater of one month's rent, $1,000, or actual damages', plus fees and costs (Sec. 504B.153, subd. 4).
- Willful and malicious destruction of the property: actual damages, costs, fees and equitable relief -- and this one runs in both directions, landlord against tenant as well (Sec. 504B.165).
- In a tenant remedies action: attorney fees against you capped at $500, a cap that 'does not apply to awards made under section 549.211 or other specific statutory authority' (Sec. 504B.425(g)).
- Getting locked out: the tenant's fastest route is not damages at all but Sec. 504B.375, a summary petition that can put the sheriff at your door the same day with an order restoring possession.

Two structural points worth more than any of those figures. First, every one of those sections says the same thing about itself: the remedies are 'in addition to and shall not limit other rights or remedies', and a lease provision waiving the section is 'contrary to public policy and void'. The multipliers are a floor, not a ceiling, and you cannot buy them down. Second, and this is the one most people get backwards: Minn. Stat. Sec. 8.31's private damages action does not reach a breach of chapter 504B. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.501 says 'the attorney general has authority under section 8.31 to investigate and prosecute violations of this chapter', which is enforcement authority and nothing more. The private remedy in Sec. 8.31, subd. 3a only reaches 'the laws referred to in subdivision 1', and chapter 504B is not one of them. Manufactured home parks are the exception and the contrast: Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.15 says 'Any violation of sections 327C.015 to 327C.14 is a violation of a law referred to in section 8.31, subdivision 1', which does open the Sec. 8.31 private action. So the same conduct carries a consumer-protection claim in a park and does not in an apartment building. Read the section you actually breached.

We offer no lease clause here. Everything above is a tenant's remedy against you, which is not something a lease can create, limit or usefully restate -- and the non-waiver sentences mean a clause that tried would be void. Minnesota law does let you keep your own side of the ledger: Sec. 504B.165 gives you an action for willful and malicious destruction, and Sec. 504B.471 confirms that none of the tenant-remedies machinery 'alters the ultimate financial liability of the landlord or residential tenant for repairs or maintenance of the building'. If you want a clause recording your own remedies, you may add one; have a Minnesota lawyer check it first, because the line between recording your rights and waiving the tenant's is where these sections bite.

title: No Minnesota Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Minnesota does not require a residential landlord to carry liability insurance. There is no mandate, no minimum limit, no certificate to file and nothing to disclose to a tenant about your own cover. Four things are worth knowing anyway. Your liability to third parties is untouched by the habitability covenants. The covenants statute says in terms that nothing in it alters the liability of a landlord for injury to third parties (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 5). So the covenants are not a ceiling on your exposure and insurance is not a substitute for them. You cannot contract out of the covenants, and insurance does not change that. Neither party may waive or modify them, and no agreement may relieve you of maintaining common areas (Sec. 504B.161, subds. 1 and 2).
