Minnesota also has no statute voiding a landlord's liability-limiting lease language, so such clauses are judged by common-law standards instead - the library's clause on the tenant's own property insurance already carves out gross negligence and wilful misconduct for that reason. Showing the unit to your insurer is a lawful reason to enter. A reasonable business purpose expressly includes showing the unit to a prospective buyer or to an insurance representative, which still needs a good-faith effort at not less than 24 hours' notice, a stated time or window, and entry between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. (Sec. 504B.211, subds. 2 and 3). And if a court ever appoints an administrator for your building, the administrator spends the rents on debt service, taxes, insurance and the services you were obliged to provide (Sec. 504B.425). Insurance is on that list, so a lapsed policy becomes someone else's problem solved with your rent. If a Minneapolis or St. Paul licence requires cover, that is a municipal matter to check locally. Carry adequate cover because it is sensible, not because Minnesota makes you.

title: No Lien for Rent in Minnesota, but One Real Lien for Storage Costs After a Writ
bodyText: Minnesota gives you NO lien and no right of seizure over a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.101 is one sentence: 'The remedy of distress for rent is abolished.' And Sec. 504B.001 subd. 3 defines what was abolished: 'the act of a landlord seizing personal property of the tenant or other person to enforce payment of rent'. There is no agricultural exception, no exception for a written lease, and no exception for a lease that says otherwise. A lease clause giving you a lien, a security interest or a right to hold the tenant's goods for rent therefore buys you nothing, and acting on it is dangerous: taking or holding a tenant's property, or shutting the tenant out, exposes you to the ouster remedies in Sec. 504B.231 and the criminal penalty in Sec. 504B.225, and Sec. 504B.375 (unlawful exclusion or removal, actual or constructive) cannot be waived by a lease. THERE IS ONE REAL LIEN AND IT IS NOT FOR RENT. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.365 subd. 3, when a sheriff executes a writ of recovery and the tenant's property goes to storage somewhere other than the premises, 'the plaintiff has a lien on all the personal property for the reasonable costs and expenses incurred in removing, caring for, storing, and transporting it to a suitable storage place'. You may 'enforce the lien by detaining the personal property until paid', and if nothing has been paid for 60 days after the order to vacate was executed you may hold a public sale under Minn. Stat. Secs. 514.18 to 514.22. That lien is for your COSTS, not your rent; it arises only after a writ has been executed and only on the off-premises storage track; and Sec. 504B.365 'may not be waived or modified by lease or other agreement'. The on-premises track is different and leads to Sec. 504B.271's 28-day hold instead -- see "After an Eviction Writ, Where You Store the Property Changes the Law That Applies" and "Property Abandoned After Termination" clause, which set out both tracks and the inventory, notice and care duties that come with them. What Secs. 514.18 to 514.22 actually are, since they are easy to misread: Sec. 514.18 subd. 1 gives a lien to 'whoever, at the request of the owner or legal possessor of any personal property, shall store or care for or contribute ... to its preservation, care, or to the enhancement of its value', with a right to retain possession, and Sec. 514.22 sets out how the sale is conducted -- by the sheriff or a deputy, with the property in view, and only enough sold to satisfy what is due. They are a storage-and-care lien on goods, borrowed by Sec. 504B.365 for its sale machinery. They are not a landlord's lien and they are not a crop lien.

title: Minnesota Has No State Landlord Registry, But Your City Almost Certainly Does
bodyText: There is no Minnesota landlord registry and no state rental licence. No statute requires you to register as a landlord, register a rental property with a state agency or a county assessor, hold a state rental licence, or employ an in-state agent because you live out of state. Two general business filings can still reach you. If you rent under a name that does not set out the true name of every owner, you must file an assumed-name certificate with the Secretary of State before you start, and an eviction you bring before filing can be stayed until you do, with $250 costs against you (Minn. Stat. Secs. 333.01, 333.02 and 333.06). And an out-of-state limited liability company that owns income-producing real property here must obtain a certificate of authority naming a Minnesota registered agent, and cannot maintain an eviction until it does (Minn. Stat. Secs. 322C.0802, 322C.0803, subd. 2, and 322C.0808; see "Minnesota Asks Every Landlord for an Agent, Not Just Out-of-State Ones"). RENTAL LICENSING IN MINNESOTA IS MUNICIPAL, AND STATE LAW SAYS SO THREE TIMES. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(4) is the hinge: you covenant to maintain the premises and all common areas in compliance with the health and safety laws "of the local units of government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing". So a city rental licence is not merely a city matter -- failing to comply with it breaches the statutory habitability covenant, which cannot be waived or modified (subd. 1(b)) and which routes a tenant into rent escrow and the tenant remedies action. The other two references confirm the same architecture. Sec. 504B.204 bars you from accepting rent or a deposit once the premises have been "ordered to be vacated due to violations of a housing, health, or fire code or rental licensing ordinance", on pain of actual damages plus three times everything collected, plus costs and attorney fees. And Sec. 504B.381, subd. 1(1) lets a tenant petition for emergency relief "when a unit of government has revoked a rental license". Losing a city licence therefore has two immediate state-law consequences: you must stop collecting rent if a vacate order follows, and your tenant gets a fast-track court route. Find out whether your city licenses or registers rentals, what it costs, what inspection it requires and what happens on renewal -- and do it before you let a unit. ONE STATE RULE DOES ATTACH TO A CITY LICENCE, and it is easy to miss. Minn. Stat. Sec. 471.9995 provides that "[a]ny license or registration or certificate of occupancy or a similar document that is issued by a home rule charter or statutory city or by a town and that is required to be posted in a building containing multiple rental dwelling units shall contain a statement that tenants of the dwelling units may contact the attorney general for information regarding the rights and obligations of owners and tenants under state law", and "[t]he statement shall include the telephone number and address of the attorney general." Read it carefully: the duty to include the statement falls on the CITY that issues the document, not on you. Your part is to post what the city gives you, where the city requires it to be posted. HOW THIS INTERACTS WITH YOUR OWN DISCLOSURE DUTY. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.181 makes you disclose the manager's and the landlord's or agent's name and address, and post that information conspicuously on the premises; subd. 2(a) says the posting duty "is complied with if notices posted in compliance with other statutes or ordinances contain the information required by this section", so a city-issued posted licence carrying the right information can do double duty. And subd. 2(b) only requires the separate attorney general notice "[u]nless the landlord is required to post a notice by section 471.9995" -- so where the city document is required to be posted, that second notice falls away. One relief worth knowing: subd. 4's bar on maintaining an action to recover rent or possession does NOT bite for a failure to post the subd. 2(b) notice or a Sec. 471.9995 notice. See "Disclosure of Landlord and Manager" clause and "Skipping the Landlord Disclosure Can Block Your Eviction". NOT A LANDLORD LICENCE, BUT CHECK IT ANYWAY: if someone manages or leases property for you for a fee, real estate licensing under Minn. Stat. ch. 82 may reach them. Take advice on it rather than assuming.

title: Possession and Money Are Two Separate Cases in Minnesota
bodyText:
A Minnesota eviction action gets you the premises, not the rent. Minn. Stat. section 504B.345, subd. 1(a) says that if the court or jury finds for the landlord, the court immediately enters judgment that the landlord shall have recovery of the premises, taxes the costs against the defendant, issues execution for the costs, and immediately issues the writ. Costs, not rent. There is no provision anywhere in the eviction sections for a money judgment for unpaid rent or for damage to the premises.

So the money is a separate civil action, and Minn. Stat. section 504B.125 is the provision to work from. Every person in possession of land out of which rent is due is liable for the amount or proportion of rent due, "Such rent may be recovered in a civil action", the lease instrument may be used in evidence by either party to prove the amount due, and "Nothing herein contained shall deprive landlords of any other legal remedy for the recovery of rent, whether secured to them by their leases or provided by law." Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1(a) adds that a nonpayment eviction "is equivalent to a demand for the rent" - it satisfies the demand, it does not collect it.

Termination does not wipe out the money either. Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, subd. 2 is explicit for the unlawful-activities covenant: a breach voids the tenant's right to possession, but "All other provisions of the lease or license, including but not limited to the obligation to pay rent, remain in effect until the lease is terminated by the terms of the lease or operation of law." And Minn. Stat. section 504B.206(c) preserves a tenant's liability for delinquent unpaid rent or other amounts owed before a violence-victim termination, while Minn. Stat. section 504B.265, subd. 2 preserves the estate's liability for rent and restoration costs after a termination on the tenant's death.

Where abandonment ends the tenancy, the rent stops sooner than a landlord expects and there is a duty to mitigate. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.154, subd. 1(a), if a tenant abandons during the lease term the landlord must make reasonable efforts to rent the unit at a fair rental value; the agreement terminates when a new tenancy begins, or on the date the landlord has notice of the abandonment if the landlord fails to use reasonable efforts to re-let at a fair rental value or accepts the abandonment as a surrender, and "The tenant shall not be liable for rent after the termination of the tenancy." For a periodic tenancy or tenancy at will, subd. 1(b) caps liability at the notice period required to end the lease, running from the date the landlord has notice. Subd. 2: "Any waiver of the rights provided by this section shall be void and unenforceable."

Two more limits on what a remedies clause can buy you. Minn. Stat. section 504B.172 makes an attorney fees clause reciprocal: if a residential lease specifies an action, circumstances, or an extent to which the landlord may recover attorney fees, directly or through additional rent, the tenant is entitled to attorney fees on winning the same type of action in the same circumstances and to the same extent, or is entitled to costs under Minn. Stat. section 549.02. And redemption is cheap for the tenant whatever the lease says: Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1(a) caps the attorney's fee payable on redemption at $5.

title: Minnesota Has No Rent Acceleration Statute - and That Is Not Permission
bodyText:
No Minnesota statute authorises, regulates or caps a residential rent acceleration clause, and none provides for liquidated damages on an early termination. The only statutory mention of liquidated damages in landlord-tenant law is a disclaimer about something else: Minn. Stat. section 504B.177(a) says of a late fee that "Any late fee charged or collected is not considered to be either interest or liquidated damages."

Silence here is not permission, for three reasons that each come from a statute you can read.

First, mitigation. Minn. Stat. section 504B.154 requires reasonable efforts to re-let at a fair rental value where a tenant abandons, terminates the agreement when a new tenancy begins, and says the tenant is not liable for rent after termination; for a periodic tenancy the cap is the notice period. A clause accelerating the balance of the term runs straight into that, and subd. 2 makes any waiver of the section's rights void and unenforceable.

Second, fee disclosure. If an accelerated sum operates as a charge on the tenant rather than rent as it falls due, Minn. Stat. section 504B.120 is in play: a landlord must disclose all nonoptional fees in the lease, the sum of rent and all nonoptional fees must be described as the Total Monthly Payment and listed on the first page of the lease, and a landlord who violates the section is liable for treble damages with discretionary attorney fees.

Third, the late fee cap shows the legislature's approach to charges for late rent: Minn. Stat. section 504B.177 requires a written agreement, requires it to specify when the fee will be imposed, and caps it at eight percent of the overdue rent payment. A lease that cannot charge more than eight percent for a late payment, but claims the whole remaining term on a default, is not a coherent document.

This library does not offer an acceleration clause. A landlord who wants one may add their own and should take legal advice first, because whether it is enforceable in Minnesota turns on case law on penalties and mitigation.

title: Asking a Minnesota Tenant to Waive the Right to Call Police Is Itself the Breach
bodyText: Minnesota regulates the landlord's side of police involvement harder than most states, and the sharpest point is one landlords miss: under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.205 subd. 2(b), 'A residential tenant may not waive and a landlord may not require the residential tenant to waive the residential tenant's right to call for police or emergency assistance.' That is a BIDIRECTIONAL non-waiver. It bars your CONDUCT IN ASKING, not just the effect of the term -- so you breach the section by asking for the waiver even if the tenant refuses, and even if nothing is ever signed. Only three sections of chapter 504B are written this way: Sec. 504B.205, Sec. 504B.206 (victims of violence terminating a lease) and Sec. 504B.211 (notice before entry). WHAT ELSE SUBD. 2 FORBIDS: you may not bar or limit a tenant's right to call for police or emergency assistance 'in response to domestic abuse or any other conduct, including but not limited to mental health or health crises', and you may not impose a penalty on a tenant for calling. The conduct list is deliberately open -- it is not limited to domestic abuse, and it expressly covers a mental-health or health crisis. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: subdivision 4 says the section is not to be construed to condone or permit any breach of a lease or of law by the tenant, and it names disturbing the peace and quiet of other tenants, damage to property and disorderly conduct. So the call is protected; the underlying conduct is not immunised. Act on the conduct, never on the call, and make sure your file shows which one you acted on. THE REMEDY: subdivision 5 lets the tenant sue you and recover $250 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. Subdivision 6 gives the attorney general authority under Sec. 8.31 to investigate and prosecute violations -- that is investigate-and-prosecute authority only, and it is NOT a Sec. 8.31 private right of action. The tenant's private action is subdivision 5's own. YOUR OWN DEALINGS WITH LAW ENFORCEMENT, where Minnesota does say something. Sec. 504B.171 subd. 2 lets you assign to the county or city attorney the right to bring an eviction action for a breach of the unlawful-activities covenant; the assignment must be in writing on a form the attorney provides, the attorney decides whether to accept it, the court filing fee is waived if they do, and you keep all the rights and duties after the writ issues, including removing the tenant's personal property. Sec. 504B.211 subd. 4 lets you enter without the usual notice where you reasonably suspect immediate entry is necessary because of conditions relating to building security or law enforcement, or to comply with a local ordinance about unlawful activity in the unit. And Sec. 504B.212 subd. 2 makes it retaliation to contact federal or state law enforcement about a tenant's immigration status after the tenant does any of the protected things that subdivision lists. Minnesota's child and vulnerable-adult maltreatment reporting duties bind listed professionals, not landlords as such, and anyone else may report voluntarily (Minn. Stat. Secs. 260E.06 and 626.557, subd. 3). But two general rules bind you and your staff. Anyone who discovers a deceased person must promptly report the death to the coroner or medical examiner if it was sudden or unexpected or may be due to anything other than natural disease, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, and violating a coroner's or medical examiner's order not to disturb the body or the scene is a gross misdemeanor (Minn. Stat. Sec. 390.11, subds. 1, 7 and 8). And a person at the scene of an emergency who knows that someone is exposed to or has suffered grave physical harm must give reasonable assistance, which may mean calling police or medical help, if that can be done without danger; failing to is a petty misdemeanor (Minn. Stat. Sec. 604A.01, subd. 1). WHY THERE IS NO CLAUSE HERE: a lease term about the tenant's right to call is not offered, in any form, including a term that only 'acknowledges' the right. Subdivision 2(b) bars you from requiring a waiver, and a term that conditions, qualifies or even restates the right invites an argument that you required one. The right exists without the lease saying so. If you want something in writing, put it in your staff and management instructions, not in the lease.

title: A City Cannot Make You Evict for Police Calls -- or Fine You for Them
bodyText: If your property is in a city with a crime-free or 'excessive call' ordinance, read Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.205 subd. 3 before you comply with it. That subdivision says the section 'preempts any inconsistent local ordinance or rule including, without limitation, any ordinance or rule that: (1) requires an eviction after a specified number of calls by a residential tenant for police or emergency assistance in response to domestic abuse or any other conduct, including but not limited to mental health or health crises; or (2) provides that calls by a residential tenant for police or emergency assistance in response to domestic abuse or any other conduct, including but not limited to mental health or health crises, may be used to penalize or charge a fee to a landlord.' Both halves matter to you. The first means a city cannot make you evict a tenant for calling, so an ordinance that says it does is no defence to the tenant's claim against you under subdivision 5. The second means a city cannot charge you a fee or penalise you because your tenants called -- which removes the usual commercial reason a landlord gives for leaning on a tenant to stop calling. But the preemption is not total. The same subdivision ends: 'This subdivision shall not otherwise preempt any local ordinance or rule that penalizes a landlord for, or requires a landlord to abate, conduct on the premises that constitutes a nuisance or other disorderly conduct as defined by local ordinance or rule.' So a nuisance-abatement ordinance aimed at CONDUCT on the premises survives; what does not survive is an ordinance that counts CALLS. The practical test is the one the statute draws: is the city counting the conduct, or counting the calls? Check the ordinance where the property sits, and get advice if it appears to count calls.

title: Minnesota Lead Certificates Go on the Worksite, Not on the Lease
bodyText: Minnesota issues lead certificates, but none of them is a lease exhibit. There is no lead-safe certificate to attach to a Minnesota lease and no certificate to give a tenant. What Minnesota has is a licensing and certification regime for the PEOPLE AND FIRMS who do lead work, and as a landlord you sit inside it. YOU DO NOT GET THE HOMEOWNER EXEMPTION. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9505, subd. 1(d) exempts an individual residential property owner, or a related adult, who performs regulated lead work on the residence. The same paragraph then takes the exemption away in three situations, and a rental hits at least two of them: when the work is a renovation performed for compensation; when a child with an elevated blood level has been identified in the residence or the building it is in; and when the residence is occupied by one or more individuals who are not related to the property owner. A tenant is normally unrelated to you, so the exemption does not reach your rental. AND RENT COUNTS AS COMPENSATION. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9501, subd. 33 defines compensation as 'money or other mutually agreed upon form of payment given or received for regulated lead work, including rental payments, rental income, or salaries derived from rental payments.' Subd. 26b then defines renovation as the modification of any pre-1978 affected property for compensation that disturbs known or presumed lead-containing painted surfaces, unless it is done as lead hazard reduction. So work you do on a pre-1978 rental is renovation for compensation because you collect rent. WHAT FALLS BELOW THE LINE. Renovation does not include minor repair and maintenance. Subd. 26b(b) defines that as work disturbing painted surfaces totalling less than 20 square feet outside, or less than six square feet in an interior room. Two riders cut it down. Window replacement and demolition of a painted surface, building component or portion of a structure are never minor. And all work disturbing painted surfaces in the same room within 30 days of other such work counts as ONE project against those limits. Total demolition of a freestanding structure is also outside renovation (subd. 26b(c)). For LEAD HAZARD REDUCTION the thresholds are lower still: subd. 17(c) excludes work totalling less than 20 square feet on exterior surfaces or less than two square feet in an interior room. THE CERTIFICATES, AND WHERE THEY HAVE TO BE. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9505, subd. 1h a person who performs, or employs individuals to perform, renovation for compensation must be certified as a RENOVATION FIRM: written, signed by the commissioner, naming the holder, valid two years, 00. Subd. 1g does the same for a CERTIFIED LEAD FIRM, for regulated lead work other than renovation, valid one year, 00. Each certificate, or a copy, 'must be readily available at the worksite for review by the contracting entity, the commissioner, and other public health officials'. That is a worksite posting duty, not a lease attachment. Individual licences for lead workers, supervisors, inspectors, risk assessors, project designers and renovators are in subds. 1a to 1e, each carried by the individual. Under subd. 1(b) nobody may even advertise or present themselves in those roles without the licence or certificate. IF YOU HIRE SOMEONE, YOU HAVE YOUR OWN DUTY. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9505, subd. 6 makes a contracting entity who wants regulated lead work done for its benefit include in the specifications and contracts a requirement that the work be done by licensed contractors and subcontractors, and it says no contracting entity shall allow the work to be performed for its benefit 'unless the contracting entity has seen that the person has a valid license or certificate.' Your failure to comply does not relieve the contractor of anything. THE TEETH. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.99, subd. 4(c) lets the commissioner issue a certified lead firm, or a person performing regulated lead work, an administrative penalty of at least $5,000 per violation per day, up to $10,000 for each violation. Subd. 11 makes a conviction for violating these sections a misdemeanour. Subds. 8 and 9 let the commissioner refuse, condition, suspend or revoke a certificate for serious or repeated violations, false information, letting someone else use your certificate, or a conviction in the previous five years. PRACTICAL POINTS. Do not let a tenant-repair agreement become a lead problem: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 2 lets you agree that the tenant performs specified repairs if the agreement is supported by adequate consideration and set out in a conspicuous writing, but no such agreement waives subd. 1 - and it cannot make an unlicensed person lawful to use on regulated lead work. And Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9509, subd. 2 makes it a petty misdemeanour to discriminate against or otherwise sanction an employee who complains to or cooperates with the assessing agency.

title: Minnesota Lead Notices: None at Signing, One That Overrides Your Lease
bodyText:
Minnesota has a full Lead Poisoning Prevention Act, but it asks you for NO lead notice at lease signing. There is no state lead disclosure form, no lead certificate and no information packet to hand a new tenant. For a pre-1978 rental the notice you give at signing is the federal lead-based-paint disclosure and pamphlet, which the library carries in its own lead disclosure clause. Minnesota adds four things, and none of them is a lease document.

ONE: A WORK-START NOTICE, AND IT GOES TO THE STATE, NOT THE TENANT. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9505, subd. 4(a), at least five working days before starting work at each regulated lead worksite, the person performing the regulated lead work must give written notice to the commissioner of health and the appropriate community health board. Subd. 4(b) takes a lead hazard screen, lead inspection, lead risk assessment, lead sampling technician work, renovation and lead project design out of that requirement.

TWO: A 30-DAY NOTICE IF YOU DO LEAD-ORDER WORK YOURSELF. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9504, subd. 8, if you do not hire a person licensed under Sec. 144.9505 to comply with lead orders, you must tell the assessing agency when regulated lead work will begin, in the Sec. 144.9505, subd. 4 form, within 30 days after you receive the orders.

THREE: THE STATE DOES THE TENANT NOTIFYING. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9504, subd. 3, at the time of a lead risk assessment or after a lead order the assessing agency arranges a home visit and informs the property owner, the landlord and the tenant about lead exposure, nutrition, safety measures, the steps before, during and after lead hazard reduction, and community, legal and housing resources. Under subd. 2(e) the agency also notifies owners, landlords and tenants at a child's or pregnant tenant's addresses for the previous 12 months that an elevated blood lead level was found at the property, without identifying the person. Those are the agency's notices, not yours.

FOUR, AND THIS IS THE ONE THAT OVERRIDES YOUR LEASE. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9504, subd. 7(b) says that a resident of rental property who is notified by an assessing agency to vacate during lead hazard reduction, 'notwithstanding any rental agreement or lease provisions', (1) is not required to pay rent for the time they are out, (2) may elect to terminate the tenancy immediately, effective the day they vacate, and (3) if they terminate, is not liable for any further rent or other charges. Subd. 7(c) then puts two duties on you: let the tenant back in after lead hazard reduction and the clearance inspection are finished, unless they terminated; and if they terminated, RETURN ANY SECURITY DEPOSIT DUE UNDER MINN. STAT. SEC. 504B.178 WITHIN FIVE DAYS of the date the tenant vacates. Five days is far shorter than the ordinary deposit deadline, so treat a lead-hazard-reduction vacate as a five-day deposit clock. Nothing in your lease can change any of this.

ONE MORE THING ABOUT THE PAMPHLET. Minnesota defines a 'disclosure pamphlet' in Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.9501, subd. 8a as the EPA pamphlet 'Renovate Right: Important Lead Hazard Information for Families, Child Care Providers and Schools', and Sec. 144.9508, subd. 2(l) directs the commissioner to adopt rules consistent with sections 406(a) and 406(b) of the Toxic Substances Control Act. The duty to hand that pamphlet out therefore sits in the health department's rules rather than in the statute. If you renovate a pre-1978 rental, assume the pamphlet is required and check the current rule.

title: What a Minnesota Lease and Application Must Contain
bodyText: Minnesota has no single list of required lease contents. Instead, nine separate rules each put something in the lease or in the rental application, and a missing item is a missing disclosure rather than untidy drafting. Four apply to every written residential lease. The lease must identify the lease start date and the lease end date, and that information must appear on the first page (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.146). If move-in or move-out falls on a day other than the first or last day of the month and the rent is prorated, the lease must also state the prorated amount for those months. All nonoptional fees must be disclosed in the lease, and rent plus all nonoptional fees must be described as the Total Monthly Payment and listed on the first page (Sec. 504B.120, subd. 1). Getting that wrong exposes you to treble damages and possibly attorney fees. The name and address of the person who manages the premises, and of the landlord or an agent authorised to accept service of process, must be disclosed either in the rental agreement or otherwise in writing before the tenancy starts (Sec. 504B.181, subd. 1). Until that is done, or the tenant has known it for 30 days, you cannot maintain an action to recover rent or possession. And in a residential building with 12 or more units a written lease is mandatory and must identify the specific unit before the tenant signs (Sec. 504B.111); failing to provide a lease is a petty misdemeanor. Four more depend on what you charge and how you bill. If you charge any pet fee, charge or deposit, the lease must disclose that no additional fee, charge or deposit may be required for a service or support animal (Sec. 504B.113, subd. 3(b)); omitting it lets the tenant sue to recover the pet fees paid. If you apportion natural gas or water and sewer, a lease entered into or renewed on or after January 1, 2025 must carry an attachment in the statute's own words explaining how the bill is calculated (Sec. 504B.216, subd. 10). You must also give the tenant, in the lease or in a separate written notice, a list of the tenant's rights to copies of the apportioned utility bills (Sec. 504B.216, subd. 5(d)). And if you submeter any utility, or apportion natural gas, the lease must say when utility bills will be issued, unless you give the tenant a written statement at the outset of the term instead (Sec. 216B.023, subd. 1(b)). The ninth rule is about the application rather than the lease. A rental application must offer the option to give an individual taxpayer identification number instead of a Social Security number, in the form "SSN or ITIN: . .", and you must not deny an application solely because the applicant gave an ITIN (Sec. 504B.117). One further item is permitted rather than required, and is worth taking. A signed, dated acknowledgment that the tenant received a copy of the lease may sit in the lease itself, and it is prima facie evidence that you met the copy duty (Sec. 504B.115, subd. 1). Minnesota has no blank-space or completeness statute, but fill or strike every placeholder before anyone signs: an unfilled start date or Total Monthly Payment is a missing required item, not a typo. Manufactured home park lot agreements have a separate contents list of their own in Sec. 327C.02, subd. 1, and are not covered here.

title: No Initials Requirement - but Two Things Must Be on the First Page
bodyText: Minnesota never requires a tenant to initial a lease provision, or to sign any clause separately from the lease itself. Nothing in Minn. Stat. ch. 504B makes a term unenforceable for want of initials, and no term becomes enforceable because the tenant initialled it. What Minnesota does require is a mix of conspicuousness, placement and delivery, and those are the rules to get right. Two things must appear on the FIRST page of the lease. The Total Monthly Payment, meaning rent plus every nonoptional fee added together under that name, must be listed there, and every nonoptional fee must be disclosed in the lease; getting this wrong costs treble damages and possibly the tenant's attorney fees. The lease start date and lease end date must also be on the first page, together with the prorated rent amount if a move-in or move-out falls other than on the first or last of the month. Two things must be in a conspicuous writing. An agreement that the tenant will do specified repairs or maintenance works only if it is supported by adequate consideration and set out conspicuously, and it can never waive your habitability covenants or your duty to maintain common areas. A prelease deposit may only be taken under a conspicuous written agreement stating when it comes back and that you must return it within seven days. Finally, give the tenant a copy. Where there is a written lease you must give a copy to each tenant whose signature appears on it. You may take a signed, dated receipt, either as a separate document or as an acknowledgment inside the lease, and that receipt is prima facie evidence the tenant got their copy. Skipping it hands the tenant a defence in most actions to enforce the lease. Use that receipt instead of initials: it is the one signature-gathering step Minnesota actually rewards.

title: Minnesota Does Not Require You to Record a Residential Lease
bodyText: No Minnesota statute requires a residential lease to be recorded or registered with the county recorder, the registrar of titles or any state body, and no statutory right turns on whether you record one. A residential lease is fully enforceable between you and your tenant unrecorded. There is no recording fee to budget for, no deadline, and no penalty for not recording. This is the opposite of the American Samoa pattern, where no instrument passes an interest in land until it is registered. MINNESOTA MENTIONS A RECORDED LEASE EXACTLY ONCE, AND ONLY TO SAY WHAT HAPPENS IF THERE IS ONE. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.251 is headed RECORDING OF NOTICE OF CANCELLATION OF LEASES and opens "[w]here a lease has been duly recorded" -- an if, not a must. In that case the county recorder "must record a copy of the notice of cancellation or termination of the lease that has been presented for recording by the landlord, landlord's agent, or attorney", the notice must come with proof of service and an affidavit of the landlord or the landlord's agent or attorney stating that the tenant has not complied with its terms, and the recorded notice "is prima facie evidence of the facts stated in it". So recording is a precondition of that clean-up procedure, not an obligation. If you have recorded a long lease, remember Sec. 504B.251 exists when you terminate it, because an unrecorded cancellation leaves the recorded lease sitting on the title. SHOULD YOU RECORD ANYWAY? For an ordinary residential tenancy, no. The benefit of recording -- notice to anyone later dealing with the land -- matters for a long-term or commercial lease, not a 12-month apartment letting, and it comes with a cost: a recorded lease is public, it stays on the title until a cancellation is recorded, and Sec. 504B.251 then requires you to produce proof of service and a sworn affidavit before the recorder will clear it. Take advice before recording a residential lease longer than a few years, and if you do record, record the cancellation when the tenancy ends. WHAT MINNESOTA REQUIRES INSTEAD OF REGISTRATION IS DISCLOSURE AND POSTING. Sec. 504B.181 makes you disclose the manager's and the landlord's or agent's name and address in the rental agreement or otherwise in writing before the tenancy starts, and post that information conspicuously on the premises -- see "Disclosure of Landlord and Manager" clause and "Skipping the Landlord Disclosure Can Block Your Eviction". And where a city requires a licence, registration or certificate of occupancy to be posted in a building of multiple rental dwelling units, Sec. 471.9995 makes the city put the attorney general's contact details on it. Neither is lease registration. There is also no state landlord registry -- see "Minnesota Has No State Landlord Registry, But Your City Almost Certainly Does". ONE PLACE RECORDING DOES MATTER, and it is not the lease: a redemption under Sec. 504B.291 can be recorded, and the county recorder and registrar of titles appear there. That is about an eviction judgment, not about registering a tenancy.

title: No Maximum Lease Length - but Two Things Go on the First Page, and One Cap Bites in Foreclosure
bodyText:
Minnesota sets no maximum or minimum length for a residential lease. What it does set are rules about stating the length, putting it in writing, and one cap that applies only when the building is in financial trouble.

Start with the statement of length: a written residential lease must identify the lease start date and the lease end date, and that information must be on the FIRST page. If a move-in or move-out falls on a day other than the first or last of the month and rent is prorated, the prorated amount must be on the first page too. Minnesota has a second, separate first-page duty: rent plus every nonoptional fee, added together and described as the Total Monthly Payment, also belongs on the first page, with treble damages for getting it wrong. Plan the first page around both.

Writing: a lease for more than one year has to be in writing to be enforceable, and separately, a landlord of a building with 12 or more residential units must have a written lease for each unit, identifying the specific unit before the tenant signs, on pain of a petty misdemeanor.

The one real cap on length: once you have received notice of a contract for deed cancellation or a mortgage foreclosure sale, you may only grant a periodic lease of no more than two months, or the time left in the cancellation or redemption period if that is shorter, or a fixed term ending no later than that period. That lasts until the contract is reinstated or paid, the default cured, the mortgage satisfied, the property redeemed, or a receiver appointed. It does not apply to a manufactured home park, and it does not apply at all if the holder or mortgagee agrees not to terminate the lease except for lease violations for at least a year, and the lease does not make the tenant prepay rent for a month beginning after that period. Breaking the cap costs a $500 civil penalty.

One last point about the end of a term: if the tenant holds over without your express agreement, no tenancy longer than the shortest interval between rent payments under the expired lease is implied. A month-to-month rent cycle produces a month-to-month holdover, not a new year.

title: No Parity Rule Between Lease Types, But One Inside Each Lease
bodyText:
Minnesota has no lease-type parity rule. Minnesota's landlord-tenant statutes contain nothing that bars terms more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant or the reverse, caps the rent difference between a month-to-month tenancy and a fixed term, or requires that the same rules, deposits or fees apply across lease types. There is no Minnesota counterpart to the Washington provision. You may price and term a month-to-month tenancy differently from a one-year lease.

What Minnesota does have is a parity rule inside each lease, and it is the one landlords break by accident. Minn. Stat. section 504B.147 applies wherever a residential lease gives the landlord a notice period for notice to quit or notice of a rent increase that differs from the period the tenant must give to quit. Where it applies, the tenant may give notice using either period, whichever suits them, and the landlord may not give a notice to quit or a notice of a rent increase shorter than the period the lease requires of the tenant. 'Notice to quit' expressly includes a notice of nonrenewal. The requirements may not be waived or modified by the parties, and any lease provision waiving them is contrary to public policy and void. So the asymmetry to avoid is not between your lease types - it is between your own notice period and your tenant's in the same lease.

Two other symmetry rules are worth a glance when you draft. Minn. Stat. section 504B.135 lets either party end a tenancy at will by written notice at least as long as the rent interval or three months, whichever is less, which is a rule stated for both sides alike. And if any part of your portfolio is a manufactured home park, Minn. Stat. section 327C.03, subd. 3 requires that all periodic rental payments charged to residents be uniform throughout the park, with only three permitted reasons for charging one resident more: the larger size or location of the lot, or the special services or facilities furnished by the park. That is uniformity between residents rather than between lease types, and it has no counterpart for an ordinary tenancy.

title: No Type-Size Rule for the Lease, But Three for Particular Notices
bodyText:
Minnesota sets no minimum type size for a residential lease. Minnesota's statutes contain no point size, typeface or line spacing for the lease as a whole, and nothing making an undersized lease inadmissible or unenforceable. There is no Minnesota counterpart to the New York evidentiary rule. So the formatting of your lease document is a drafting decision, not a compliance one.

Three specific documents do carry a stated type size, and two of them will cross your desk. If any part of your portfolio is a manufactured home park, Minn. Stat. section 327C.02, subd. 5 requires that a prospective resident, before being asked to sign a rental agreement, be given the statutory IMPORTANT NOTICE 'printed verbatim in boldface type of a minimum size of ten points'; the notice must be provided with the park residency application and posted in a conspicuous and public location in the park. In an eviction of a public housing tenant, Minn. Stat. section 504B.268, subd. 1 requires the complaint to carry, on its first page in bold 12-point type, the statement 'If financially unable to obtain counsel, the defendant has the right to a court-appointed attorney.' A third sits outside the tenancy: a contract for deed cancellation notice carries its own type-size rule, which matters only if you sell on contract.

Where Minnesota does regulate the look of lease text, it does it with a word rather than a number, and the word is 'conspicuous', and it is worth separating its two uses. Applied to a document, it governs the writing: Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subd. 2 allows a tenant-maintenance agreement only if it is supported by adequate consideration and 'set forth in a conspicuous writing', and Minn. Stat. section 504B.175, subd. 2(a) allows a prelease deposit only on 'a conspicuous written agreement'. Applied to a place, it governs posting rather than type: Minn. Stat. sections 504B.181, subd. 2, 504B.195, subd. 1(b), 504B.211, subd. 5 and 504B.271, subd. 1 each require a notice in 'a conspicuous place'. One nearby rule is a number, and it is about placement rather than size: Minn. Stat. section 504B.120, subd. 1 requires the sum of rent and all nonoptional fees to be described as the Total Monthly Payment and 'listed on the first page of the lease'. Design your lease so that anything the law calls conspicuous actually reads as conspicuous, and keep the Total Monthly Payment on page one.

title: No Limitation Period in the Landlord-Tenant Act; Chapter 541's Six Years Governs
bodyText:
Chapter 504B sets no deadline for anything. Minnesota's landlord-tenant act contains no limitation period at all — not for your suit for unpaid rent, not for damages to the premises, not for a tenant's deposit claim. The phrase "statute of limitations" does not appear in the chapter, nor does the word "barred", and the only time limit expressed in years or months anywhere in it is an unrelated condition in Minn. Stat. § 504B.266 about an accessible unit becoming available within two months.

That means the general limitation chapter, Minn. Stat. ch. 541, governs. Your suit for unpaid rent or other money due under the lease is an action "upon a contract or other obligation", which must be brought within six years (Minn. Stat. § 541.05, subd. 1(1)). A claim for damage to the premises is also six years, whether brought on the lease or as "a trespass upon real estate" (subd. 1(3)). A tenant's claim under a landlord-tenant statute, such as the deposit statute, is "a liability created by statute", also six years (subd. 1(2)). But an action "upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture" has two years (§ 541.07(2)). Whether a statutory penalty, such as punitive damages for a bad-faith deposit withholding, falls in that two-year class only case law could settle, so treat two years as the safe deadline for a penalty claim. A debt "primarily for personal, family, or household purposes" also has six years under § 541.053. Once that period runs, a later payment or a written or oral reaffirmation does not revive the claim. Before it runs, a written, signed acknowledgment or promise can extend it, and § 541.17 says it "shall not alter the effect of a payment of principal or interest". Whether a partial payment restarts the clock is left to case law, so do not count on it. Once you have a judgment, an action on it must be begun within ten years of its entry (§ 541.04).

Three narrower limitation periods.

A Human Rights Act claim must be brought quickly. Under Minn. Stat. § 363A.28, subd. 3(a) a discrimination claim must be brought as a civil action, filed with a local commission, or filed in a charge with the commissioner "within one year after the occurrence of the practice". Paragraph (b) suspends that one-year period while the parties are voluntarily in a dispute resolution process — arbitration, conciliation, mediation or a grievance procedure — and a respondent who takes part without notifying the department and the charging party in writing "is barred from raising the defense that the statute of limitations has run unless one year plus a period of time equal to the suspension period has passed". If a tenant proposes mediation of a discrimination complaint, taking part without that written notification costs you the limitation defence.

A Plain Language Contract Act claim runs six years from signature. The library's "Minnesota's Plain-Language Lease Requirement" records, from Minn. Stat. § 325G.34, subd. 5, a six-year limitation running from the date the consumer executes the contract.

The antitrust period, for completeness, is four years: Minn. Stat. § 325D.64, subd. 1 bars an action under Minn. Stat. §§ 325D.49 to 325D.66 "unless commenced within four years of the date upon which the cause of action arose", with a continuing violation deemed to arise at any time during the period of the violation. It has nothing to do with a lease and is not the one that governs your rent claim.

A warning about shortening a period by contract. Because Chapter 504B says nothing about limitation, there is no Minnesota landlord-tenant non-waiver sentence pointed at a lease clause that shortens the time for a tenant to sue. That is not a green light. Chapter 541 is silent on shortening its periods by contract, which leaves it to case law; several specific Chapter 504B remedies carry their own non-waiver sentences that a general time-bar clause would collide with, and a prospective waiver of a Human Rights Act remedy is void outright under Minn. Stat. § 363A.31, subd. 1. Do not add a clause shortening the time to bring a claim without advice.

title: Minnesota Sets No Liquidated-Damages Measure
bodyText: Minnesota sets no liquidated-damages figure for a residential lease breach and has no statute authorising an agreed-damages term. Minnesota's late-fee statute says a late fee is neither interest nor liquidated damages. Where Minnesota does supply a measure, it is actual loss. An action for willful and malicious destruction of leased residential rental property gives the prevailing party actual damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees, and that section cannot be waived by the lease. The deposit statute is the same shape, and it is the main reason to avoid preset sums: you may hold back only amounts reasonably necessary to remedy a default in paying rent or other funds due under an agreement, or to restore the premises to their move-in condition apart from ordinary wear and tear, you carry the burden of proving why you withheld, and any waiver of that section is void. A flat sum written into the lease and taken from the deposit is therefore very hard to defend, whatever the lease calls it. A late fee is the one preset charge Minnesota clearly allows, and only if you agreed it in writing, the agreement says when it applies, and it stays within 8% of the overdue rent payment. So the library offers no general liquidated-damages clause for Minnesota. Whether a particular agreed sum would be enforced or struck down as a penalty is a common-law question that only a court can settle, so if you want such a term, get advice first and tie the figure to a loss you can actually show.

title: Abandonment Is the Only Route to the Premises Without a Writ
bodyText:
There is one situation in which a Minnesota landlord may take the premises back without a writ, and it is not unpaid rent. It is abandonment, and the statutes treat it carefully.

Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.271, subd. 1(a), if a tenant abandons rented premises the landlord may take possession of the tenant's personal property remaining there, and must store and care for it, with a claim against the tenant for the reasonable costs of removing, storing and caring for it. The landlord may sell or dispose of the property 28 days after receiving actual notice of the abandonment, or 28 days after it reasonably appears the tenant has abandoned, whichever is later, and must make reasonable efforts to notify the tenant of the sale at least 14 days beforehand by personal service in writing or by first class and certified mail to the tenant's last known address or usual place of abode if known, and must post notice of the sale conspicuously on the premises at least two weeks beforehand.

Get it wrong and the penalties are severe. Under subd. 2, if the landlord fails to let the tenant retake possession within 24 hours of written demand, or within 48 hours excluding weekends and holidays where the property was stored off the premises, the tenant recovers punitive damages up to twice the actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, in addition to actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. In setting them the court considers the nature and value of the property, the effect of the deprivation on the tenant, whether the landlord unlawfully took possession of it, and whether the landlord acted in bad faith. Under subd. 3, a landlord who unlawfully took possession pays the removal, storage and care costs. Subd. 4 adds that any lease or other agreement provision by which the section is waived by a tenant "is contrary to public policy and void."

Abandonment also ends the rent clock, which cuts against a landlord. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.154, subd. 1(a), if a tenant abandons during the lease term the landlord must make reasonable efforts to re-let at a fair rental value; the agreement is terminated on the date a new tenancy begins, or on the date the landlord has notice of the abandonment if the landlord fails to use reasonable efforts to re-let at a fair rental value or accepts the abandonment as a surrender, and the tenant is not liable for rent after termination. For a periodic tenancy or tenancy at will, subd. 1(b) caps the tenant's rent liability at the notice period required to end the lease, running from the date the landlord has notice of the abandonment. Subd. 2: "Any waiver of the rights provided by this section shall be void and unenforceable."

So do not treat unpaid rent as abandonment. An empty-looking unit with rent owing is still the tenant's unless it has actually been abandoned, and the penalty for guessing wrong is the ouster and lockout exposure in "What a Lockout Costs You in Minnesota".

title: What a Lockout Costs You in Minnesota
bodyText:
Four separate provisions attach to a Minnesota lockout, and they stack. Each carries its own non-waiver sentence, so no lease term reduces any of them.

Loss of possession. Minn. Stat. section 504B.375 gives the tenant the summary action described in "Never Lock a Minnesota Tenant Out for Unpaid Rent", and the court puts the tenant back in. Subd. 4: a lease provision waiving the section "is contrary to public policy and void."

Damages for ouster. Minn. Stat. section 504B.231(a): if a landlord, an agent, or other person acting under the landlord's direction or control unlawfully and in bad faith removes, excludes or forcibly keeps out a tenant from residential premises, the tenant may recover treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees. Paragraph (b) adds that any lease or other agreement provision by which the section is waived by a tenant "is contrary to public policy and void."

Cutting utilities. Minn. Stat. section 504B.221(a): if the landlord or someone under the landlord's direction or control interrupts or causes the interruption of electricity, heat, gas or water services to the tenant, the tenant may recover treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees. It is a defence that the interruption resulted from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant or someone under the tenant's direction or control, and the tenant recovers only actual damages where the tenant gave no notice of the interruption, or where the landlord reinstated the service or made a good faith effort to reinstate it or took other remedial action within a reasonable time after notice, or where the interruption was to repair faulty equipment or protect occupants' health and safety and service was restored or a good faith effort made within a reasonable time. Paragraph (b) carries the same non-waiver sentence.

A criminal offence. Minn. Stat. section 504B.225 makes a landlord, agent or person acting under the landlord's direction or control who unlawfully and intentionally removes or excludes a tenant, or intentionally interrupts electrical, heat, gas or water services with intent to unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant, guilty of a misdemeanour. The burden is on the landlord: the statute presumes the interruption was made with intent to unlawfully remove or exclude once it is established that the landlord intentionally interrupted the service, and "The burden is upon the landlord to rebut the presumption." It too carries the same non-waiver sentence.

Each of sections 504B.221, 504B.225 and 504B.231 also extends to occupants and owners of residential real property subject to a mortgage foreclosure or contract for deed cancellation where the redemption or reinstatement period has expired. And removing a tenant's property in breach of the writ procedure is itself an unlawful ouster: Minn. Stat. section 504B.365, subd. 5 makes a landlord who enters and removes the tenant's personal property in violation of that section guilty of an unlawful ouster under section 504B.231 and subject to penalty under section 504B.225, unless the premises has been abandoned, and says "This section may not be waived or modified by lease or other agreement."

title: Never Lock a Minnesota Tenant Out for Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
Minnesota has no self-help lockout. There is no opt-in scheme letting a lease authorise changing the locks for delinquent rent, no advance-notice-plus-key-access procedure, and no version of it available to any kind of residential landlord. Unpaid rent is collected by an eviction action under Minn. Stat. section 504B.291 and possession is taken only on the writ under Minn. Stat. section 504B.365. Minn. Stat. section 504B.281 says no person may occupy or take possession of real property except where allowed by law, and then only peaceably.

The core prohibition is Minn. Stat. section 504B.375, and its reach is wider than most landlords assume. Subd. 1(a) applies to "actual or constructive removal or exclusion of a residential tenant which may include the termination of utilities or the removal of doors, windows, or locks." So shutting off the heat, taking a door off, or pulling a lock counts as a lockout even though you never changed a key, and a tenant to whom the section applies may recover possession.

The remedy is fast. The tenant presents a verified petition to the district court describing the premises and the landlord, stating the facts showing the exclusion or removal was unlawful including a statement that no writ has been issued and executed against the tenant, and asking for possession. If it clearly appears from the petition or a separate affidavit that the exclusion or removal was unlawful, subd. 1(c) says the court "shall immediately order that the residential tenant have possession of the premises." The sheriff executes the order immediately by demanding possession from the landlord or the landlord's agent, and if the landlord does not comply the officer takes whatever assistance is necessary and immediately puts the tenant back in. If nobody is in charge, the officer enters and puts the tenant back in. Under subd. 1(d) the tenant furnishes such security, if any, as the court finds appropriate, and the court must consider the tenant's ability to afford it.

You get a motion, not a defence. Under subd. 2 the landlord may move to dissolve or modify the order on at least two days' notice, but unless the tenant fails to prove the facts and grounds the order stands, and "A landlord bringing a motion under this subdivision may recover possession of the premises only by an eviction action or otherwise provided by law." On dissolution the court assesses costs against the tenant, subject to Minn. Stat. section 563.01, and may allow damages and reasonable attorney fees for the wrongful order. If the order is affirmed, costs are taxed against the landlord and the tenant may be allowed reasonable attorney's fees. The order is final for appeal under subd. 3, with ten days to appeal.

A lease clause cannot touch any of this. Subd. 4 says: "A provision of an oral or written lease or other agreement in which a residential tenant waives this section is contrary to public policy and void." The section also applies, under subd. 6, to occupants and owners of residential real property subject to a mortgage foreclosure or contract for deed cancellation where the redemption or reinstatement period has expired, and to mortgagees and contract for deed vendors. Under subd. 5 the section is an additional summary remedy, and except where it expressly provides otherwise, Minn. Stat. sections 504B.285 to 504B.371 do not apply to proceedings under it - so the protections a landlord has in an ordinary eviction are not available here.

title: Changing Who Does the Repairs in Minnesota
bodyText:
Minnesota lets you move repair and maintenance work to the tenant in one way, and the whole subject is in a single sentence. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 2: you "may agree with the tenant or licensee that the tenant or licensee is to perform specified repairs or maintenance, but only if the agreement is supported by adequate consideration and set forth in a conspicuous writing". Both conditions must hold. Adequate consideration means the tenant gets something real in return, so a rent reduction stated as a figure, not a thank-you. A conspicuous writing means the agreement stands out where a reader will see it. And the work must be specified: you list the tasks, you do not hand over maintenance in general.

Two limits sit in the same sentence. No such agreement "may waive the provisions of subdivision 1", which is the five habitability covenants, and no such agreement may "relieve the landlord or licensor of the duty to maintain common areas of the premises". So the answer to the question some states answer the other way is no: you cannot make the tenant responsible for a common-area condition, garbage removal from common areas included, in a way that lifts the duty off you. You can ask a tenant to carry waste to the collection point as a task, and you remain the one who must maintain the common areas.

Minnesota sets no precondition you must satisfy first, no good-faith recital, no limit to single-family homes or small buildings, and no requirement that the agreement be a document separate from the lease. A conspicuous section inside the lease, with the consideration stated, satisfies the statute for any residential property. That is unusual, so do not copy another state's separate-document wording into a Minnesota lease.

Two more points about where financial responsibility ends up. The covenants are in addition to any covenant or condition imposed by law, ordinance or the lease (subd. 4), so an agreement under subd. 2 adds a tenant task; it does not subtract a landlord duty. And where a tenant uses the rent escrow or tenant remedies machinery, Sec. 504B.471 says the purpose of those sections "is to provide additional remedies and nothing contained in those sections alters the ultimate financial liability of the landlord or residential tenant for repairs or maintenance of the building" -- the court's orders move who does the work and who holds the money, not who ultimately owes. The optional clause is the Tenant Repair and Maintenance Agreement.

title: Meter Charges: No Conservation Surcharge, and No Charge for the Meter Itself
bodyText: Minnesota has no meter conservation charge of the kind some states let a utility put on a bill to repay an energy-efficiency or on-bill financing agreement, so there is no notice to give a new tenant about one and no rent deduction for one. What Minnesota does regulate, and strictly, is what you may charge around a meter. If you submeter or separately bill a utility in a shared-metered residential building, you may not charge or collect from tenants any administrative, capital or other expense associated with installing, maintaining, repairing, replacing or reading a submeter, unless the expense is caused by the tenant's willful, malicious or negligent conduct. The only two extras allowed are one administrative billing charge of up to $8 per billing period and one late payment charge of up to $5 a month, which may not compound. You must bill at the rate the utility charges you and show both the present and the last preceding submeter readings, the reading date, your rate and the utility's rate to you, the tenant's share of taxes and surcharges, any credit passed through, any administrative billing charge, the total, and the due date with the late-fee date and amount. If a tenant tells you in writing that a submeter is misreading and explains why, you must investigate promptly, refund any overcharge, and if you do not check the meter and give the tenant the test results within a reasonable time you lose the right to collect any undercharge for that period. Submetering also puts you under the Public Utilities Commission's authority. If a bill your tenant pays carries a special charge, say so in the lease.

title: No Military Air Zone Disclosure Duty in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota requires no military air zone disclosure in a residential lease. There is no Minnesota counterpart to the Virginia military air installation noise and accident-potential-zone disclosure with its 30-day termination right, and nothing like the Indiana military installation notice. WHERE SUCH A RULE WOULD LIVE IF MINNESOTA HAD ONE. Minnesota regulates airport zoning and avigation easements in Minn. Stat. ch. 360. Airport zoning boards also act by ORDINANCE. So a Minnesota landlord near an airfield should check the local airport zoning ordinance. WHAT STILL APPLIES. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) makes you covenant that the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended by the parties and that you will keep them in reasonable repair; subd. 1(b) bars waiver of those covenants. Aircraft noise is not a disrepair, but a tenant who would not have signed had they known is a tenant with a grievance. WHAT TO DO. Nothing is required. If the property is under a flight path, on or near a military airfield, or inside an airport zoning district, say so in writing before signing and say it plainly. It costs a sentence, and it converts a later complaint into a signed acknowledgment. If an avigation easement is recorded against the property, say that too and describe what it allows. Do not promise quiet you cannot deliver: see the quiet-possession rows for what Minnesota does imply into every lease.

title: Unpaid Municipal Water and Sewer Charges Can Land on Your Property Tax Bill
bodyText: Minnesota lets a city or town go after the property, not just the person who used the water. Minn. Stat. § 444.075, subd. 3e says the governing body 'may make the charges a charge against the owner, lessee, occupant or all of them'. It may also 'provide and covenant for certifying unpaid charges to the county auditor with taxes against the property served for collection as other taxes are collected'. Two things follow. The municipality may bill the tenant, the owner, or both — your tenant being the named customer does not take you off the hook. And if the charges go unpaid, they can be certified to the county auditor and collected with your property taxes, which in practice behaves like a lien on the property. You cannot contract out of this, and Minnesota says so expressly in the middle of the shared-metered utility statute. Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 13(g) provides that the section does not restrict or prohibit a municipal utility provider from exercising its authority under § 444.075, subds. 3 and 3e. That authority is, in the statute's words, the authority 'to make contracts with and impose utility charges against property owners and to certify unpaid charges to the county auditor with taxes against the property served for collection as a tax'. So the tenant protections elsewhere in § 504B.216 do not displace the municipality's power over the property. A lease clause making the tenant responsible for water and sewer is still worth having, because it gives you a contract claim against the tenant. What it cannot do is stop the municipality certifying the charge against your property. Price and manage that risk rather than drafting around it. For water and sewer in a building you own, assume you are the ultimate payer. Minnesota also gives the tenant a route that protects you from a service cut when you are the one in default. Under § 504B.216, subd. 13(c), where you have not paid the municipal water and sewer bill, the municipality must give a tenant a copy of each unpaid bill on request. The tenant then has a continuing right to pay the current charges and keep service, with no deposit requirement and with reasonable notice of any disconnection. 'Current charges' expressly excludes your own arrears and late fees (subd. 13(d)). Whether your particular city actually certifies unpaid utility charges to the county, and on what timetable, is set by that city's ordinance, policy or practice. Section 504B.216, subd. 13(c) itself defers to 'the period of time provided by the governing ordinance, policy, or practice'. That is a municipal question. Check your city's utility billing ordinance, or ask counsel, before relying on any assumption about timing.

title: Minnesota Has No Nonrefundable Deposit, So There Is Nothing to Notify
bodyText: Some states let you keep part of a deposit if you say in the lease that it is nonrefundable, and require a particular notice when you do. Minnesota has no such notice rule, because it does not allow the thing the notice would describe. The deposit section governs any deposit of money whose function is to secure performance of the lease or any part of it, other than money that is exclusively an advance payment of rent. The test is what the money does, not what you call it. So a move-in deposit, a cleaning deposit, a redecorating charge taken at signing, a key or fob deposit, a pet deposit: if its function is to secure the tenant's performance, it is a security deposit, the whole section applies, and the word nonrefundable in your lease is void, because any attempted waiver of the section is void and unenforceable. Three lawful routes remain for money you genuinely want to keep. Charge it as rent, which is the payment for occupancy and is not a deposit. Charge an applicant screening fee before the tenancy, which has its own rules about receipts, disclosure and return. Or charge for a real optional service the tenant actually chooses and receives. And if a charge is nonoptional, it has to be disclosed in the lease and included in the Total Monthly Payment on the first page of the lease, with treble damages and possibly the tenant's attorney fees if it is not. Practical consequences: do not use the words nonrefundable deposit anywhere in a Minnesota lease, keep every refundable sum in one clearly labelled security deposit, and remember that money taken before the lease is signed is a prelease deposit, which must be applied to the deposit or rent once the lease is signed and can never be kept as a fee.

title: No Separate Document for a Nonrefundable Charge
bodyText: No Minnesota statute requires a nonrefundable charge to be set out in a document separate from the lease, or signed or initialled on its own, the way Wisconsin requires a NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document for deductions beyond its statutory list. There is nothing to put in such a document, because Minnesota has no nonrefundable deposit at all: money whose function is to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit however it is labelled. Minnesota pushes in the opposite direction on fees. A nonoptional fee has to be in the lease agreement itself, and the sum of rent and all nonoptional fees has to be described as the Total Monthly Payment and listed on the first page of the lease, with treble damages and possibly the tenant's attorney fees for a breach, so putting a charge in a side document is the opposite of compliance. Minnesota does require two separate writings, and neither is a nonrefundable-charge notice: a conspicuous written agreement before you take any money from a prospective tenant to hold a unit, stating the circumstances in which it comes back and that it will be returned within seven days of one of them; and, where natural gas or water and sewer is apportioned, a prescribed lease attachment explaining how the utility bill is worked out. Keep both as what they are, and keep every charge in the lease.

title: Minnesota Asks Every Landlord for an Agent, Not Just Out-of-State Ones
bodyText: Minnesota has no rule requiring an out-of-state individual owner to name an in-state agent. An out-of-state entity is different. A foreign limited liability company that owns income-producing real property in Minnesota is transacting business here, so it must first obtain a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State naming a registered office and agent for service of process in Minnesota, and until it has one it may not maintain an eviction or any other action in a Minnesota court; its leases stay valid, and while it is unregistered it is treated as having appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process (Minn. Stat. Secs. 322C.0802, 322C.0803, subd. 2, and 322C.0808). A foreign corporation transacting business here without a certificate of authority may not maintain an action until it gets one, and faces a penalty of up to $1,000 plus $100 a month; whether renting out property is transacting business for a corporation is a case-law question (Minn. Stat. Secs. 303.03 and 303.20). And whoever you are, owning property in Minnesota lets a Minnesota court hear a claim arising from it, with the summons served on you personally outside the state (Minn. Stat. Sec. 543.19). What Minnesota does instead is require EVERY landlord to name an agent who can be served, and it backs that up with teeth. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.181 subd. 1 you must disclose, in the lease or otherwise in writing before the tenancy starts, the name and address of the person authorised to manage the premises and of the landlord or 'an agent authorized by the landlord to accept service of process and receive and give receipt for notices and demands'. If you do not, two things happen. Subd. 3 deems your caretaker, your manager, or whoever receives the rent to be your agent for service of process, notices and demands, and obliges that person to pass what they receive to you personally or by certified mail, return receipt requested. And subd. 4 bars you from maintaining any action to recover rent or possession unless you have complied, or the tenant knew or was told at least 30 days before you started the action. So the practical risk for an owner living out of state is not a registration you have missed -- it is that the person collecting your rent becomes your agent for service by default, and that your eviction fails if the disclosure was never made. See "Disclosure of Landlord and Manager" clause and "Skipping the Landlord Disclosure Can Block Your Eviction", which cover that section and the pleading rule that goes with it. Whether Minnesota requires income-tax withholding on rent paid to a nonresident owner is a question for Minnesota's tax chapters. If you own Minnesota rental property from out of state, ask your accountant about withholding, and if you own through an out-of-state entity, get its certificate of authority before you need to file an eviction; neither belongs in the lease. If you rent under a name that does not show your true name, see "Squatters and Other Questions Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law" on the assumed-name certificate.

title: Charging a Tenant for Serving a Notice
bodyText: No Minnesota statute lets you charge a tenant a fee for preparing, delivering or serving a notice, and none forbids it, so a notice fee would be a pure contract term. Minnesota keeps the work cheap: you or your agent deliver the 14-day notice before a nonpayment eviction personally or by first class mail, and you or your agent serve the summons and complaint - no officer is required. Four rules shape any charge of this kind. First, redemption. In a nonpayment eviction the tenant may be restored to possession at any time before possession is delivered by paying the rent in arrears with interest, the costs of the action, and an attorney's fee of no more than $5, so a notice fee is not something you can demand as the price of letting the tenant stay. Second, court costs. If you win, the court taxes the costs against the tenant and issues execution for them, so a lease fee covering the same filing or service cost is double recovery; in Hennepin County District Court, library and filing fees are not required of the defendant in an eviction action at all. Third, attorney fees. If your lease lets you recover attorney fees, directly or through additional rent, the tenant becomes entitled to attorney fees on winning the same type of action, so a notice fee that is really a lawyer's charge cuts both ways. Fourth, disclosure. A fee the tenant cannot avoid must be disclosed in the lease and included in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, with treble damages and possible attorney fees for getting it wrong. And in a rent escrow case consolidated with a nonpayment eviction, the court may not make the tenant pay your filing fee as the price of keeping possession once the tenant has deposited everything the court finds is owed. For those reasons the library offers no notice-fee clause for Minnesota. Nothing in the statutes bans one: if you want it, write your own, take advice first, keep it to your actual cost, and never charge for the same cost the court taxes. Some cities require a longer pre-eviction notice period than 14 days. See the companion row on eviction penalty clauses, "Penalty and Fee Clauses Tied to an Eviction"; the two answer one question from opposite ends.

title: Minnesota's Notice-to-Quit Rules Cannot Be Waived, and the Lease Sets the Period
bodyText:
Minnesota's answer to "may a lease shorten or waive the notice to quit" has two halves, and landlords usually get the first one wrong.

For most leases there is no statutory notice-to-quit period to waive. Chapter 504B sets a termination notice period only for a tenancy at will, under Minn. Stat. section 504B.135: the notice must be in writing and the time of the notice must be at least as long as the interval between the times rent is due, or three months, whichever is less. A fixed-term lease that simply expires needs no notice to quit at all, because Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subd. 1(a)(2) makes holding over after the term a ground in itself. So where a lease sets a notice period for a fixed-term tenancy, that period is the lease's own choice and not a statutory minimum the lease is shortening. A waiver of a rule Minnesota does not have is empty rather than lawful.

The second half is a real and non-waivable constraint, and it bites on the period the lease chooses. Minn. Stat. section 504B.147 applies wherever a residential lease gives the landlord a different notice period for a notice to quit or a rent increase than it requires of the tenant for a notice of intention to quit, and "notice to quit" there includes a notice of nonrenewal. Subd. 2 lets the tenant give notice using either the tenant's own lease period or the landlord's. Subd. 3 says the landlord may not give a notice to quit or a notice of rent increase shorter than the period the lease requires of the tenant. Subd. 4 is headed "No waiver" and says: "The requirements of this section may not be waived or modified by the parties to a residential lease. Any provision, whether oral or written, of a lease or other agreement by which any provision of this section is waived by a tenant is contrary to public policy and void."

The practical rule for drafting: make the landlord's notice period and the tenant's the same. An asymmetric lease gives the tenant the choice of either period and caps the landlord at the longer of the two, so the asymmetry only ever works against you.

Two termination-notice sections also forbid a LONGER period, which is the reverse of what landlords expect. Minn. Stat. section 504B.265, subd. 3 makes void and unenforceable any attempted waiver of the two-month termination right on the death of a tenant "and any lease provision or agreement requiring a longer notice period than that provided by this section", though the parties may otherwise modify the section's specific provisions. Minn.
