Stat. section 504B.266 does the same for termination on the infirmity of a tenant, making void and unenforceable any waiver "including lease provisions or other agreements that require a longer notice period than those provided for in this section". Do not lengthen either one.

title: No Content Rule for a Quit Notice - but Two Notices Have Mandatory Contents
bodyText: Minnesota does not regulate the general form or content of a notice to quit or a notice to vacate, and it does not forbid you putting extra material in one. But extra material rarely does what a landlord hopes. A notice is a one-sided document: it cannot change the lease, and a term that appears only in a notice or on a move-out form is not agreed unless the tenant agrees to it. Worse, several Minnesota rights cannot be waived at all, so a move-out form that asks the tenant to give up a deposit claim, to accept a charge, or to shorten a notice period is void as to that term however it is signed. Two specific notices DO have mandatory contents, and these are the ones to get right. The 14-day notice before a nonpayment eviction must state the total amount due, give a specific accounting of unpaid rent, late fees and other charges, name and give the address of the person authorized to receive rent and fees, and carry three prescribed statements word for word: one about the right to seek legal help and Legal Aid, one about applying for financial help, and one warning that an eviction case may be filed if the total is not paid or the tenant does not move out within 14 days. It must be delivered personally or by first class mail. If it is missing or defective the court dismisses the case without prejudice and expunges the file, so this is the costliest notice in Minnesota to get wrong. The second is tied to the end of the tenancy. Once either side has given notice of an intention to end the tenancy, or before the term ends, you must notify the tenant in writing of their option to request a move-out inspection and of their right to be present at it. Practical rule: keep notices short and limited to what the statute asks for, send anything you want agreed as a separate document the tenant signs, and do not use a move-out form to add terms the lease never had.

title: Where Minnesota Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText:
Minnesota leaves very little to the lease. Most of Chapter 504B operates whether your lease mentions it or not, and 30 of its sections carry a sentence saying a lease cannot waive them. The list of places where Minnesota law genuinely lets your lease decide something is short, and this entry is that list. Every item on it has a clause in this library already, which is the point of writing it down.

Where the lease decides, and the clause that covers it.

A late fee exists only if you agreed one in writing. Minn. Stat. § 504B.177, paragraph (a): "A landlord of a residential building may not charge a late fee if the rent is paid after the due date, unless the tenant and landlord have agreed in writing that a late fee may be imposed." This is the clearest optional term in the chapter — no writing, no late fee, however late the rent. Covered by "Late Fee" clause and "Late Fee Limit" clause.

You can reserve your right to evict after taking part of the rent. Minn. Stat. § 504B.291, subd. 1 provides that a rental payment applied to the balance due "does not waive the landlord's action to recover possession of the premises for nonpayment of rent", and paragraph (d) contemplates the court finding a claim for earlier periods "waived" on the circumstances. Covered by "Partial Payment of Rent in Arrears" clause, with "Reserve Your Rights Every Time You Accept Late Rent" explaining it.

You can agree that the tenant performs specified repairs, on three conditions. Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 2 lets you agree the tenant will "perform specified repairs or maintenance, but only if the agreement is supported by adequate consideration and set forth in a conspicuous writing" — and then: "No such agreement, however, may waive the provisions of subdivision 1 or relieve the landlord or licensor of the duty to maintain common areas of the premises." So: specified, paid for, conspicuous, and never the common areas. Covered by "Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness" clause.

You can agree an entry time outside the statutory window. Minn. Stat. § 504B.211, subd. 2 limits entry to between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. "unless the landlord and tenant agree to an earlier or later time". Covered by "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause. Be careful here: the same subdivision carries the bidirectional non-waiver, so you may agree a time but you may not require the tenant to give up the notice right as a condition of the tenancy.

You can agree alternative arrangements if new construction is delayed. Minn. Stat. § 504B.153 requires you to offer the tenant choices including reasonably equivalent alternative housing, "unless otherwise agreed upon by" the parties. Covered by "New Construction Not Ready by the Start Date".

You can set your own holdover and tenant-damage figures, because Minnesota sets none. There is no statutory holdover multiplier and no statutory damage formula, so these are your numbers, stated as your figure rather than as a statutory limit. Covered by `holdover` and "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause, with "Minnesota Has No Holdover Damages Multiplier" and "When the Tenant Causes the Damage: What Minnesota Gives You, and What It Doesn't".

One option exists and is deliberately not offered. Minn. Stat. § 504B.291, subd. 1(b) provides that "If the lease provides that the landlord must give more than the 30 days' notice provided in paragraph (a), then notice must be the same as that provided in the lease" — in an action on a lease for a term of more than 20 years. The option is real and lawful, but it runs the wrong way: it lets the lease give the tenant more notice than the statute requires, not less, and it only bites on leases over 20 years. No clause is offered. If you are letting on a term that long, have a lawyer draft the notice provisions.

A caution about reading this list as permission. Where Minnesota law is silent, your lease can usually speak — but silence in Chapter 504B often means a general statute governs instead, not that nothing does. The limitation period for suing a former tenant is the clearest example: Chapter 504B sets none, and the answer is Minnesota Statutes chapter 541, not your lease. See "No Limitation Period in the Landlord-Tenant Act; Chapter 541's Six Years Governs".

title: Ordnance and Demolition: Nothing Required. Shared Meters: Plenty, and Already Covered
bodyText: This topic bundles three California disclosures. Minnesota has none of the first two and a strong version of the third. ORDNANCE: ABSENT. California tells a tenant when the property is within a mile of a former federal or state ordnance location. Minnesota has no such rule. The explosives-handling and dangerous-weapons sections that mention munitions regulate conduct, not disclosure. DEMOLITION: ABSENT. California makes a landlord who has applied for a demolition permit tell applicants and tenants before accepting a deposit or rent. Minnesota has nothing equivalent. Minnesota's demolition references are a redevelopment definition (Minn. Stat. Sec. 469.002), the lead act's carve-outs for window replacement and total demolition (Sec. 144.9501, subd. 26b), and a manufactured home park closure provision (Sec. 327C.095). What a Minnesota landlord actually owes on the way to a demolition comes from elsewhere in the lease: the termination-notice rules, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195 if a condemnation order or an inspection citation is outstanding, and Sec. 504B.204 if the premises are condemned. See the termination-notice, inspection-condemnation-disclosure and condemned-premises rows. SHARED METER: PRESENT. Minnesota is stronger than California here. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.216 governs utility service in shared-metered residential buildings, and Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 216B.022, 216B.023 and 216B.024 add submetering rules, billing and consumer protections, and dispute resolution. Parts of Sec. 504B.216 may not be waived by contract or otherwise. Laws 2026, ch. 81 adds a final submetered utility bill rule at Sec. 504B.216, subd. 7a and Sec. 216B.023, subd. 3a. Those duties are not restated here, because they already have their own rows: see utility-apportionment, utility-submetering-disclosure and utility-disclosure-attachment. If your building has a shared or master meter, read those rows before you draft anything. WHAT TO DO. Nothing is required on ordnance or demolition. If you know the property sits on or near a former military or ordnance site, or you intend to demolish, say so in writing before signing - a planned demolition is exactly the kind of fact a tenant will say they would have acted on, and Minnesota gives them a non-waivable fitness and repair covenant under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) and (b) to argue from.

title: Facilities Minnesota Names, and Facilities the Lease Turns Into Obligations
bodyText:
Minnesota does not hand you a list of facilities you must install. The duty works the other way: a short list of named items, plus everything you chose to provide.

The named items are in Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subd. 1(a), which puts five covenants in every residential lease. Three of them are specific enough to be a checklist. You must equip or furnish heat at a minimum temperature of 68 degrees Fahrenheit in all places intended for habitation including kitchens and bathrooms from October 1 through April 30, unless a utility company requires and instructs the heat to be reduced. You must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair, including extermination of insects, rodents, vermin or other pests. And you must make the premises and all common areas reasonably energy efficient by installing weatherstripping, caulking, storm windows and storm doors where the measure will pay for itself in energy savings over ten years, interest included. Subd. 1(b): 'The parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section.' That is already set out in Your Basic Habitability Duties; what follows is the part that is not.

What you choose to provide can become an emergency obligation, and the statute says so by name. Minn. Stat. section 504B.381, subd. 1(2) lets a tenant petition for emergency relief over 'the following services and facilities when the landlord is responsible for providing them': a serious infestation, loss of running water, loss of hot water, loss of heat, loss of electricity, loss of sanitary facilities, a nonfunctioning refrigerator, 'if included in the lease, a nonfunctioning air conditioner', 'if included in the lease, no functioning elevator', any conditions, services or facilities posing a serious and negative impact on health or safety, and 'other essential services or facilities'. Read the two 'if included in the lease' items carefully: an air conditioner and an elevator become emergency items because the lease mentions them. A refrigerator is on the list unconditionally. So list what comes with the unit accurately - the Appliances and Equipment Included clause is the place - and understand that listing an air conditioner is a choice with a consequence, not just a selling point.

Shifting maintenance to the tenant is possible and narrow. Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subd. 2 lets you agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance, 'but only if the agreement is supported by adequate consideration and set forth in a conspicuous writing', and 'No such agreement, however, may waive the provisions of subdivision 1 or relieve the landlord or licensor of the duty to maintain common areas of the premises.' Three limits there: real consideration, conspicuous writing, and nothing that touches the common areas.

One supplied facility has its own statute, and it is not in chapter 504B. If the property has a garage with an automatic opener, Minn. Stat. section 325F.83 requires the system to meet an automatic reversing requirement, bars anyone from installing, servicing or repairing one that does not, requires a red DANGER label and written notice to the occupant when one fails the on-site test, and - this is the part for your lease - makes the occupant of a rented home tell the owner about a nonfunctioning or malfunctioning reversing device within 24 hours of discovery. A violation carries the remedies of Minn. Stat. section 8.31, including a private right of action. Minn. Stat. section 325F.82, subd. 4 defines residential building to include an apartment building with an attached or unattached garage, so this is not a single-family rule.

Alarms are separate and already covered: Minnesota splits the smoke alarm and carbon monoxide alarm duties, and the library carries both. Finally, the items Minnesota does not make you supply are worth knowing too - there is no statutory duty to provide window screens, laundry, air conditioning, a mailbox beyond the postal rules, off-street parking, a fire sprinkler system in ordinary private rental housing, or an electric vehicle charger.

title: No Owner Move-In Statute - but Your Notice Period Is Not Yours Alone to Set
bodyText:
Minnesota has no owner move-in law in either direction. No statute gives you a right to end a lease because you or a relative want to live in the property, and none limits such a right either: no holding period, no relocation payment, no duty to re-offer the unit. Because Minnesota is also not a just-cause state, you may simply reserve the right in the lease, and the library offers that as an optional clause.

Three Minnesota points decide how it has to be written. First, the notice period. Minn. Stat. 504B.147 says the notice you give to quit or not renew can never be shorter than the notice your lease asks the tenant to give you, and that cannot be waived. Never write a flat number into an owner-occupancy clause without also saying it is at least as long as the tenant's own notice period, or raising the tenant's figure elsewhere will quietly make your clause unlawful. The tenant may also choose either period when they give notice.

Second, timing and retaliation. A termination notice served within 90 days of the tenant's good-faith attempt to enforce a right, or their good-faith code complaint, puts the burden on you to prove the notice was not retaliatory. If you have had a repair dispute, document when you decided to move in.

Third, possession. A reserved termination right does not let you take the property back yourself. You recover possession only through an eviction, and shutting off utilities or removing doors, windows or locks is an unlawful exclusion the tenant can sue over.

There is one real Minnesota owner-occupancy rule, and it only applies after a foreclosure. Where a tenant holds a bona fide lease that runs past the redemption period, the successor in interest normally has to let that lease run out. But if the successor, or an immediate later bona fide purchaser, will occupy the unit as their primary residence, the successor may instead give at least 90 days' written notice to vacate, no sooner than the end of the redemption period. The same 90-day rule applies to a Section 8 tenancy. That is a buyer's right, not a sitting landlord's.

title: No Parking-Rules Notice Statute - Posting Is What Matters, and One Rule Changes in 2027
bodyText:
Minnesota has no parking-rules notice statute. Nothing requires you to hand a tenant the parking rules before signing, nothing prescribes a heading or a format for them, nothing stops you changing them during the term, nothing limits the vehicle information you may ask for, and nothing makes a parking permit expire with the lease. Parking rules bind a tenant in Minnesota because the lease makes them part of the lease - so attach them, and get a receipt.

The place the law does bite is towing, and it bites on posting rather than on notice to the tenant. Minnesota's towing rules sit in chapter 168B, not in the landlord-tenant chapter, and as the library's towing row records, an unposted multi-unit residential lot has no timeframe available to it at all. If you manage anything larger than a duplex, post the lot. A parking rule in the lease does not substitute for the sign.

Two neighbouring regimes do have rules-notice requirements, and knowing them stops you importing the wrong figure. A manufactured home park is tightly regulated: Minn. Stat. section 327C.02, subd. 1 requires every lot rental agreement to be in writing and to include 'the rights, duties and obligations of the parties, and all rules applicable to the resident'; subd. 2 requires at least 60 days' written notice in writing of any rule change, and a rule adopted or amended after the resident entered the agreement 'may be enforced against that resident only if the new or amended rule is reasonable and is not a substantial modification of the original agreement'; subd. 4 says 'Any attempt to waive or circumscribe any privilege or right guaranteed by law to a resident or a park owner is void'; and subd. 5 prescribes a verbatim notice in boldface type of a minimum size of ten points, which includes the line that all park rules and policies must be reasonable. Minn. Stat. section 327C.05 adds that no park owner shall adopt or enforce unreasonable rules and lists four presumptively unreasonable ones. None of that applies to an apartment or a house, and 60 days is not a figure to copy into an ordinary lease.

The second regime is new. If the unit you rent out is in a common interest community, Laws 2026, chapter 82, section 6 adds Minn. Stat. section 515B.3-107, paragraph (f), effective January 1, 2027: the association 'has no authority to regulate the parking of a unit owner or a guest, tenant, or invitee of the unit owner within an improved public right of way that a unit of government maintains and repairs', except to require compliance with applicable statutes, laws and ordinances, and the paragraph goes on to say a unit owner or resident must be permitted to park a personal or work vehicle on the part of the owner's property or of the limited common element allocated to the unit that was designed or later modified for parking - subject to not encroaching on another owner's property, not blocking a pedestrian walkway and not interfering with the association's maintenance. So an association parking rule you pass on to your tenant may be unenforceable from that date, and a lease that promises the tenant will obey the association's street-parking rules will be promising something the association cannot require.

Practical version: attach the rules, have the tenant acknowledge receipt, give written notice of any change, post the lot for towing, and check any association rule you are passing on against the January 2027 change.

title: Minnesota Has No Single Non-Waiver Section: Six Different Formulas, Section by Section
bodyText:
Minnesota has no single non-waiver section. It has a non-waiver sentence attached to individual sections, scattered across Chapter 504B, and they are not written the same way. As in force today there are 36 operative sentences across 30 sections, in six distinct formula families, and the family you are looking at changes what the sentence does. Quote the section you care about; do not assume a house phrase.

The families, with the statute's own words:

1. "Contrary to public policy and void" — 14 sentences. The standard form reads: "Any provision, whether oral or written, of any lease or other agreement, whereby any provision of this section is waived by a tenant, is contrary to public policy and void." It appears at Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.144, 504B.147, subd. 4, 504B.153, subd. 3, 504B.165, 504B.182, subd. 4, 504B.195, subd. 5, 504B.204, 504B.221, 504B.225, 504B.231, 504B.271, subd. 4, 504B.315, 504B.375, subd. 4 and 504B.465.

2. "Void and unenforceable" — 8 sentences, at Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.114, subd. 2, 504B.116, 504B.154, subd. 2, 504B.178, subd. 10, 504B.265, subd. 3, 504B.266, subd. 4 and 504B.435 (twice). Several of these do not use the word "waiver" at all. Minn. Stat. § 504B.114, subd. 2 voids the term directly: "Any requirement or lease provision that violates this subdivision is void and unenforceable."

3. Passive "may not be waived" — 5 sentences, at Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.147, subd. 4, 504B.216, subd. 2(c) and subd. 14(2), 504B.365, subd. 5 and 504B.385, subd. 11.

4. Active "the parties may not waive or modify" — 3 sentences, at Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.161, subd. 1(b), 504B.161, subd. 2 and 504B.171, subd. 3. These are the two that should change how you draft, because they bar modification and not merely waiver. Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 1(b) reads: "The parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section." A clause that softens the habitability covenants, rather than waiving them outright, is caught just the same.

5. Bidirectional: "a residential tenant may not waive and a landlord may not require the residential tenant to waive" — 3 sentences, at Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.205, subd. 2(b), 504B.206, subd. 5 and 504B.211, subd. 2. This family does something the others do not. It bars your conduct in asking, not only the term's effect. Ask a tenant to give up the right to call for police or emergency assistance, or the right to prior notice of entry, and you have breached the section even if the tenant refuses and nothing goes in the lease. Minn. Stat. § 504B.211, subd. 2 limits its instance to a waiver sought "as a condition of entering into or maintaining the lease".

6. A 2026 addition carries two sentences of its own. Minn. Stat. § 504B.2136, added by Laws 2026, ch. 81, sec. 3 and effective August 1, 2026 by its own terms for eviction actions filed on or after that date, bars naming a tenant's minor child as a defendant and then says, in paragraph (b): "The requirements of this section may not be waived or modified by the parties to a residential lease. Any provision, whether oral or written, of a lease or other agreement by which any provision of this section is waived by a tenant is contrary to public policy and void."

Two traps worth knowing. First, Minn. Stat. § 504B.465 is headed "WAIVER NOT ALLOWED" and reads as though it covers the tenant-remedies part, but it reaches only "section 504B.381 or sections 504B.395 to 504B.471". Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.385 and 504B.391 fall outside it; the rent-escrow non-waiver is Minn. Stat. § 504B.385, subd. 11 in its own terms. Second, one non-waiver rule that expressly names a lease lives outside Chapter 504B altogether: Minn. Stat. § 363A.31, subd. 1 makes any provision "of a lease, contract, or other agreement or instrument" purporting to waive a Human Rights Act right or remedy "contrary to public policy and void" where it reaches claims arising after the waiver was signed.

Two old applicability limits are now spent. Minn. Stat. § 504B.161 applies only to leases concluded or renewed on or after June 15, 1971, and Minn. Stat. § 504B.178 only to tenancies commencing or renewed on or after July 1, 1973. Both catch every live tenancy.

title: No No-Notice Entry for Scheduled Services - and Asking for It Is Itself the Violation
bodyText:
Minnesota does not let you write a standing no-notice entry right for routine service visits, and this is one of the places where a clause borrowed from another state will put you in breach.

Service work is a lawful reason to enter. Minn. Stat. section 504B.211, subd. 3 lists nine reasonable business purposes and says the list 'includes, but is not limited to' them. Clause (3) is performing maintenance work. Clause (7) is 'prearranged housekeeping work in senior housing where 80 percent or more of the residential tenants are age 55 or older' - the only scheduled-service purpose the statute names, and it is narrow. But a lawful purpose is only half of what subd. 2 requires. You must also make a good faith effort to give notice of not less than 24 hours, the notice must specify a time or anticipated window of time, and you may enter only between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless you and the tenant agree otherwise. Filter changes, pest treatment, smoke-alarm checks and quarterly inspections all sit inside that rule. There is no exception for work on a published schedule, and no exception for work the lease lists.

You cannot contract out of it. The last sentence of subd. 2 is: 'A residential tenant may not waive and the landlord may not require the residential tenant to waive the residential tenant's right to prior notice of entry under this section as a condition of entering into or maintaining the lease.' Two separate things are prohibited there, and the second one is your conduct: asking a tenant to sign a clause giving up notice for scheduled visits is itself the thing the statute bars, whether or not you ever rely on it. What is allowed is real-time agreement - 'A residential tenant may permit a landlord to enter the rented premises with less than 24 hours notice if desired' - so a text message on the day, answered yes, is fine. A signature at lease signing is not.

The price of getting it wrong is in subd. 6: a rent reduction up to full rescission of the lease, recovery of the damage deposit less anything retained under Minn. Stat. section 504B.178, up to a $500 civil penalty for each violation, and reasonable attorney fees. A violation is also a violation of Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, the habitability covenant, which opens the tenant-remedies machinery. A quarterly service round through 40 units with no notice is 40 violations, not one.

Two scope points. Manufactured home parks are outside the section entirely under subd. 7, and run on chapter 327C instead. And if you operate housing with services that is exempt from assisted living licensure, Minn. Stat. section 325F.722, subd. 2(c)(5) adds a tighter rule for your own staff: the resident has a right to a lockable door, you must provide the locks, and 'Only a staff member with a specific need to enter the unit shall have keys, and advance notice must be given to the resident before entrance by the staff member, when possible.' Housekeeping and service staff are staff members for that purpose, and that setting must comply with chapter 504B as well (subd. 8).

Practical version: list the services and the frequency in the lease so the tenant expects them, then give 24 hours' notice with a time window for each actual visit. Scheduling and notice are different obligations, and the lease can only do the first one.

title: No Minnesota Pre-Treatment Pesticide Notice for Rentals
bodyText: Minnesota imposes no duty on a landlord to notify tenants before a pest treatment. There is no advance notice period, no posted warning, no form, no re-entry interval you must tell tenants about, no duty to tell a tenant what was applied or to keep and produce a record of applications, and no special notice for a pregnant tenant, a child, an allergy or a neighbouring unit. Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.245, on pesticides, is about landscape application contracts. WHAT GOVERNS INSTEAD IS THE ORDINARY ENTRY RULE, and in practice it does most of the work. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.211, subd. 2 lets you enter only for a reasonable business purpose and after a good faith effort to give the tenant reasonable notice under the circumstances "of not less than 24 hours in advance of the intent to enter"; the notice "must specify a time or anticipated window of time of entry"; and entry must be between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless you and the tenant agree otherwise. "Performing maintenance work" is a listed reasonable business purpose (subd. 3(3)), and a pest treatment is maintenance work. So you do owe a tenant 24 hours' notice of the ENTRY, even though you owe no notice about the TREATMENT. Two more points from the same section: the tenant cannot waive the notice right and you cannot require a waiver as a condition of signing or keeping the lease (subd. 2); and if you enter when the tenant is not present without having given prior notice, you must leave a written disclosure of the entry in a conspicuous place in the premises (subd. 5). The penalty under subd. 6 runs to a rent reduction up to full rescission of the lease, return of the deposit less lawful retentions, up to a $500 civil penalty for each violation and reasonable attorney fees, and a violation of the section is also a violation of Sec. 504B.161. Emergency entry without notice is available under subd. 4, but it is for immediate danger, tenant safety and local unlawful-activity ordinances -- a scheduled spray is not an emergency. WHAT WE RECOMMEND ANYWAY, because the absence of a statute is not the absence of risk. Give written notice of a pest treatment that says the date and time window, what will be applied, how to prepare the unit, how long to stay out and when it is safe to return, and keep a copy. Four reasons. The entry notice is compulsory anyway, so the marginal cost is one paragraph. The pest control operator's own licence conditions and label requirements may require occupant notification. A tenant who was not told how to prepare has a ready answer to any later attempt to charge them, which matters because Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(2) makes extermination your duty unless the problem was caused by the tenant's "willful, malicious, or irresponsible" conduct. And a tenant who is harmed by an unannounced application will not be arguing about notice statutes. A LEASE CLAUSE IS OFFERED UNDER A DIFFERENT TOPIC, not here: "Pest Reporting and Treatment" clause carries the tenant's cooperation and preparation duties and the cost allocation, and "Pests Are Your Problem in Minnesota, and the Escape Hatch Is Narrow" explains the unwaivable duty behind them. There is also no bed bug disclosure duty in Minnesota -- see "No Bed Bug Disclosure Statute in Minnesota". AND CHECK YOUR CITY. Pesticide application in cities is a subject Minnesota regulates, and a city may have its own notice or posting rule for multifamily buildings.

title: No Minnesota Pet Fact Sheet -- But Subsidized Accessible Units Have a Pet Right You Cannot Evict Around
bodyText: Minnesota has no state fact sheet about pets and eviction, and no duty to give one with the lease. Some states require exactly that -- a state-prepared sheet handed over when the landlord knows the tenant has a dog or cat. Minnesota has nothing of the kind: no fact sheet, no brochure, no pamphlet, no information sheet, and no pet-specific pre-eviction notice. BUT THERE IS A MINNESOTA PET RULE YOU ALMOST CERTAINLY DO NOT KNOW ABOUT, and it limits what you can do about an animal rather than what you must hand out. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.261 says that in a multiunit residential building, a tenant of a DISABILITY ACCESSIBLE UNIT, where the tenant or the unit receives a subsidy that directly reduces or eliminates the tenant's rent responsibility, MUST BE ALLOWED to have two birds, or one spayed or neutered dog, or one spayed or neutered cat. That is a right, not something you grant. The limits on it are specific: the renter may not keep or have visits from an animal that is a threat to the health or safety of other individuals, or that causes a noise nuisance or noise disturbance to other renters. You may require an additional damage deposit in an amount reasonable to cover damage the animal is likely to cause, and that deposit is refundable when the renter leaves to the extent it exceeds the damage the animal actually caused. Note what that is NOT: it is not pet rent, and it is not a non-refundable fee. If you have subsidised disability accessible units, a general 'no pets' or 'pets only with approval' policy does not apply to a qualifying tenant's two birds or one dog or cat, and an eviction on that ground would be built on a clause the statute overrides. Two other Minnesota pet rules sit nearby and are covered elsewhere in this library: you may not require declawing or devocalization, and you must disclose in the lease the bar on extra fees for service and support animals if you charge anything under a pet policy.

title: What You May Charge for a Pet in Minnesota
bodyText:
Minnesota does not use the words pet rent, pet fee or pet deposit anywhere in its statutes, and it sets no cap on a security deposit, so what you may charge for a pet is mostly your own choice inside four rules.

First, a pet deposit is deposit money. Any money whose function is to secure performance of the lease, other than an advance payment of rent, falls under the deposit statute, so a refundable pet deposit carries 1 percent simple noncompounded interest, must be returned or accounted for in writing within three weeks of the end of the tenancy, and may be held back only in amounts reasonably necessary to cover a default in paying rent or other funds due under an agreement or to restore the premises to their move-in condition. That statute cannot be waived.

Second, pet rent and any nonrefundable pet fee are fees, not deposits, so they must be disclosed in the lease, and treble damages plus possible attorney fees follow a disclosure failure. Where the lease approves a pet from the start, treat the pet rent as a nonoptional fee for that tenant and include it in the first-page Total Monthly Payment; where a pet may be added later, list it as an optional fee.

Third, charge nothing for a service animal or support animal needed as a reasonable accommodation - and if you charge any pet fee, charge or deposit at all, your lease must itself disclose that prohibition, or the tenant can sue to recover the pet fees paid.

Fourth, in a multiunit building, a tenant of a disability accessible unit whose rent responsibility is reduced or eliminated by a subsidy must be allowed two birds, or one spayed or neutered dog, or one spayed or neutered cat; for that animal you may charge an additional damage deposit in an amount reasonable to cover likely damage, refundable when the tenant leaves to the extent it exceeds the damage actually caused.

You may never require a tenant to declaw or devocalize an animal you allow, and a lease provision that does is void and unenforceable.

Manufactured home parks are a different regime with a $4 per pet per month cap.

title: No Readability Test and No Statement of Consumer Restrictions
bodyText:
Minnesota's plain-language rule is about how your lease is written. It is not the apparatus this topic is usually about — there is no readability score to hit, no statement of consumer restrictions to attach listing every waiver the tenant is making, no optional attorney general preapproval of your form, and no dollar threshold above which the rule stops applying.

The obligation that does exist is recorded in this library at "Minnesota's Plain-Language Lease Requirement". Minnesota's Plain Language Contract Act reaches a residential lease of a term not exceeding three years, which is most leases, and requires the lease to be written in clear and coherent language using words with common, everyday meanings, appropriately divided and captioned. That row also carries the remedies, the good-faith safe harbour, the six-year limitation period, and the important landlord-favourable limit that a violation is not a defence to a claim arising from the tenant's own breach and not a defence to an eviction. Read it rather than this entry for the rule itself.

The Plain Language Contract Act is Minnesota Statutes chapter 325G.

One nearby requirement, because it uses the same words and is not about your lease. Minn. Stat. § 504B.275 directs that the attorney general's published statement of landlord and tenant rights be "written using words with common, everyday meanings" — the same standard, applied to the attorney general's document rather than to yours. Do not read it as a lease obligation.

What this means for drafting. The practical effect of all of this is a constraint, not a citation: keep sentences short, use ordinary words, caption your sections, and do not write a 90-word sentence. That is the whole of what the plain-language regime asks of a Minnesota lease.

title: Your Apartment Pool Is a Public Pool Under Minnesota Law
bodyText:
This is the single fact most Minnesota landlords get wrong. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.1222, subd. 4(d) defines "public pool" to mean any pool other than a private residential pool that is, among other things, "open to residents of a multiunit apartment building, apartment complex, residential real estate development, or other multifamily residential area", or that is operated by a person in a "motel, camp, resort, club, condominium, manufactured home park, or political subdivision".

Your residents-only apartment pool is therefore a PUBLIC pool, regulated by the commissioner of health, even though no member of the public can use it. Subdivision 1 puts the commissioner in charge of adopting rules and enforcing the laws and rules on the operation, maintenance, design, installation and construction of public pools. The detailed rules are Minnesota Rules, chapter 4717 -- read them or ask the Department of Health.

FOUR DUTIES ARE IN THE STATUTE ITSELF, so you can rely on these without the rules. (1) Construction. For a public pool built after January 1, 2009 without a gravity outlet or drain, each pump must be connected to at least two suction outlets in parallel with suction outlet covers meeting ASME/ANSI standards (subd. 1b).

(2) Equipment. Since January 1, 2011 every existing public pool must have an unblockable suction outlet or drain, or at least two parallel suction outlets with ASME/ANSI covers, or a gravity outlet or drain, or another system the commissioner determines is equally effective or better at preventing the risk of injury or death from pool drainage systems; the earlier January 1, 2009 deadline applied to pools less than four feet at their deepest (subd. 1c(a) and (b)). All drain covers and grates must be installed with screws meeting the manufacturer's specifications (subd. 1c(c)).

(3) An ANNUAL CERTIFICATION. Under subd. 1c(d), "all public pool owners" must certify to the commissioner each year, on the commissioner's form, that all outlets except unblockable drains have manufacturer-stamped ASME/ANSI-compliant covers, and that all covers and grates including mounting rings have been inspected to confirm they are properly installed and not broken or loose. That is a recurring filing with your name on it.

(4) A DAILY INSPECTION AND AN IMMEDIATE CLOSURE RULE. Subd. 1d(a): "The pool operator is required to conduct a physical inspection of the drain covers and grates on a daily basis", and the record required by Minnesota Rules, part 4717.0750 must show the inspection was done every day the pool is open. Subd. 1d(b): if at any time an outlet cover or grate is missing, broken or loose, "the pool must be closed immediately", and it may not reopen until the missing or broken cover or grate is replaced to the manufacturer's specifications, or the loose one is reattached to them.

PLANS, FEES AND VARIANCES. Plans and specifications for construction, installation or alteration, and requests for a variance, go to the commissioner with the fees set by subd. 1a: $1,600 per pool, $900 per spa pool, $650 per slide, $700 for alterations that do not change the pool's size or configuration, $200 for removal or replacement of disinfection equipment only, and $550 for a request for a variance from the public pool and spa rules. For projects valued at $250,000 or more the fee is the greater of the itemised sum or 0.5 percent of the documented estimated project cost, capped at $15,000. Plans submitted less than 30 days before construction carry a late fee of 50 percent of the original plan review fee, and since January 1, 2009 plans must be certified by a professional engineer registered in Minnesota.

PORTABLE WADING POOLS -- READ THE CONDITION, NOT JUST THE DEPTH. Subd. 2a says a portable wading pool "shall be defined as a private residential pool and not as a public pool for purposes of public swimming pool regulations under Minnesota Rules, chapter 4717", provided it has a maximum depth of 24 inches and is capable of being manually emptied and moved. But that carve-out only reaches a pool "located at a family day care or group family day care home licensed under Minnesota Rules, chapter 9502, or at a home at which child care services are provided under section 142B.05, subdivision 2, paragraph (a), clause (2)".

The licensed-child-care location is the trigger; the 24-inch depth and the manual-emptying test are extra conditions on top of it. So subd. 2a does NOT say that any shallow portable pool is exempt. Put a portable wading pool out for residents at an apartment complex and subd. 2a gives you nothing -- you are back in subd. 4(d), which asks only whether the pool is "open to residents of a multiunit apartment building, apartment complex, residential real estate development, or other multifamily residential area". Subd. 2b does the same job for a full swimming pool at a licensed family day care home, again only because of where it is. If you want to put a kiddie pool in a shared courtyard, treat the public-pool regime as engaged until the Department of Health tells you otherwise.

THE SPA CARVE-OUT, PLAINLY. Subd. 2d is written in short-term-rental language: it speaks of renting "through a resort" and of testing the water "prior to check-in by each new rental party". Its centre of gravity appears to be resorts and short-term lettings, NOT a 12-month residential tenancy. We nevertheless offer "Hot Tub or Spa Notice (Single-Unit Rental)" clause for a long-term lease of a stand-alone single-unit house with a hot tub, because the paragraph's own criteria are met by one and because the downside of guessing wrong runs one way only: if the exemption does not apply, the spa was never exempt, and it is then an unpermitted public pool with no plan review, no annual certification and no daily drain inspection. Complying with subd. 2d costs a notice and a water test. Being wrong about it costs the whole public-pool regime.

ONE RELAXATION YOU MAY BE ABLE TO USE, and it is narrow: subd. 2c says a pool with a zero-depth area may be used without a lifeguard present if access to the pool area is prohibited to people under 18 during the time no lifeguard is present. Everything else about lifeguards, barriers, fencing, signage and water chemistry is in chapter 4717, not in the statute.

HOW IT IS ENFORCED, which Sec. 144.1222 does not tell you. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.99, subd. 1 lists Sec. 144.1222 among the statutes enforceable under that section. The commissioner may examine and copy your records and "enter upon any property, public or private" to act (subd. 2). The commissioner may issue a CORRECTION ORDER stating the deficiencies, the specific statute and the time by which the violation must be corrected. You may ask the commissioner to reconsider that order in writing by certified mail within 15 calendar days, but a request does not stay it (subd. 3). The commissioner may issue an ADMINISTRATIVE PENALTY ORDER up to $10,000 for each violator for all violations found in one inspection. Except for repeated or serious violations, that penalty must be forgiven if you show in writing before the 31st day after receiving the order that you have corrected the violation or developed an acceptable corrective plan (subd. 4(a)). The commissioner may also seek an injunction (subd. 5). And the commissioner may issue a CEASE AND DESIST order, effective for a maximum of 72 hours and backed by a posted sign, if continuing the activity would be an immediate risk to public health (subd. 6). The commissioner may also deny or refuse to renew a permit, licence, registration or certificate where you have unresolved violations or a persistent pattern of them (subd. 8).

The 31-day forgiveness window is the practical point: fix it and document it. Nothing in Sec. 144.1222 requires any pool text in your lease, so a pool clause in a Minnesota lease is a house-rules term rather than a statutory disclosure.

title: Putting Air Conditioning in the Lease Turns a Breakdown Into an Emergency
bodyText: This is the cooling rule most Minnesota landlords do not know, and it is an opt-in risk you create yourself. Minn. Stat. § 504B.381 lets a tenant petition a judge for emergency relief, after attempting to give you 24 hours' notice, and the court can order you to begin remedying the problem immediately on an ex parte showing. Subdivision 1(2) lists what counts as an emergency. Alongside the loss of running water, hot water, heat, electricity and sanitary facilities, the list includes, at clause (viii), 'if included in the lease, a nonfunctioning air conditioner'. The words 'if included in the lease' are doing all the work. Minnesota does not make air conditioning a habitability requirement. But the moment your lease includes it, a broken unit stops being an ordinary repair item and becomes a statutory emergency with an ex parte route to a judge, a filing fee set at the conciliation court rate, and the relief available under § 504B.425 — which includes rent abatement and, in a serious case, an administrator appointed over the building. Clause (ix) does the same for a non-functioning elevator. So decide deliberately whether air conditioning is part of what you are letting. If you do include it, resource it: you are committing to a repair timetable measured in hours rather than days during a Minnesota heat wave. If you do not include it, say so clearly, and do not describe air conditioning in the lease or in advertising as something you provide. Note also that § 504B.120, subd. 1 requires your advertising and your lease to be straight about what comes with the unit. The emergency route does not reach an emergency 'that is the result of the deliberate or negligent act or omission of a residential tenant or anyone acting under the direction or control of the residential tenant' (§ 504B.381, subd. 6), so a unit the tenant broke is not your emergency.

title: No Minnesota Right to Install a Window or Portable Cooling Device
bodyText: Minnesota gives tenants no right to install a portable or window air conditioner, and it imposes no duty on a landlord to allow one. It also sets no maximum indoor temperature. The habitability covenant in Minn. Stat. § 504B.161 requires heat at a minimum temperature in winter; it says nothing about cooling. Some states require a lease that restricts window units to say so expressly. Minnesota has no such requirement, so a reasonable restriction on window and portable units is an ordinary lease term here, governed by your lease rather than by statute. Keep it reasonable anyway: § 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(1) requires the premises to be 'fit for the use intended by the parties' and subd. 1(a)(4) requires compliance with health and safety laws including local ordinances, and neither covenant can be waived or modified (subd. 1(b)). A blanket ban enforced through a Minnesota heat wave against a tenant with a medical need would also be a reasonable-accommodation question under the Human Rights Act, not a cooling question. Two Minnesota rules do touch cooling, and both are worth knowing. The first is a trap, and it has its own note in this library. The second is in § 504B.216, subd. 12: an eviction for unpaid electric utility charges may not be filed, and one already filed must be stayed, during a heat emergency — defined as 'any period when an excessive heat watch, heat advisory, or excessive heat warning issued by the National Weather Service is in effect' (subd. 12(g)(3)). So Minnesota protects a tenant's electricity when it is dangerously hot, even though it gives no right to the air conditioner that electricity would run. A city may regulate cooling by ordinance. That is a municipal question, and § 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(4) already obliges you to comply with local health and safety laws.

title: No Minnesota Tenant Right to a Plug-In Solar Device
bodyText: Several states now give tenants a right to install a plug-in solar panel or a small battery, sometimes with a notice procedure and a limit on what restrictions a landlord may impose. Minnesota has nothing of that kind. The word 'solar' does not appear anywhere in Minnesota's landlord-tenant act, its public safety and fire chapter, its human rights act, or its consumer-protection chapters. Nor is there a Minnesota provision voiding lease restrictions on solar energy systems. Every solar, photovoltaic and plug-in provision in the Public Utilities chapter (Minn. Stat. ch. 216B), the energy chapter including the property-assessed clean energy provisions (ch. 216C) and the real property chapter with its solar provisions (ch. 500) is a utility standard, a community solar garden, a financing programme or an easement. None gives a tenant a right to install a device or voids a lease restriction. The solar provisions in the 2025 and 2026 session laws are utility-side renewable-generation standards or public construction appropriations, not tenant rights. What this means for your lease today. A tenant installing anything on the exterior of the building, or wiring anything into it, is making an alteration, and your general alterations and consent provisions govern it — Minnesota supplies no statutory override. So you may require written consent and reasonable conditions. Still, keep the restriction generic rather than writing a clause that recites 'Minnesota law gives Tenant no right to install solar'; a city or a later statute could change that. The only energy provision in Minnesota's landlord-tenant act runs the other way and binds you, not the tenant. Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(3) requires you 'to make the premises and all common areas reasonably energy efficient by installing weatherstripping, caulking, storm windows, and storm doors when any such measure will result in energy procurement cost savings ... that will exceed the cost of implementing that measure, including interest, amortized over the ten-year period following the incurring of the cost'. That covenant cannot be waived or modified (subd. 1(b)). It is a cost-effectiveness-gated duty about the building envelope, not about generation. If a tenant asks, get advice before refusing flatly, and check whether a city ordinance or an incentive programme condition applies. For a property in a homeowners or common interest community, Minn. Stat. § 500.216 limits the association's power to bar a roof-mounted solar energy system. It protects an owner who solely owns and maintains the entire building, not a tenant.

title: Minnesota Counts Units in the Building, Not Doors in Your Portfolio
bodyText:
Start with the headline, because it is the opposite of what landlords in many states are used to. Minnesota has no small-landlord exemption from its landlord-tenant act. Chapter 504B does not exempt an owner of one house, or four units, or any other number, from the habitability covenants, the deposit rules, the entry rules, the fee-disclosure rules or the eviction procedure. If you own a single rental in Minnesota, you are subject to essentially the whole chapter.

Minnesota does use count-based thresholds, but almost all of them count units in one building rather than doors across your portfolio, and they add duties rather than lifting them. The ones to know:

Twelve or more. Minn. Stat. section 504B.111 requires a landlord of a residential building with 12 or more residential units to have a written lease for each unit, identifying the specific unit before the tenant signs. Failure is a petty misdemeanour. Below 12 units an oral lease is lawful, which is a trap in the other direction.

Four or more. Minn. Stat. section 363A.10, subd. 2 defines 'covered multifamily dwellings' as a building of four or more units with one or more elevators, and the ground floor units of other buildings of four or more units; subd. 1(3) attaches accessible-design duties to those, for first occupancy after March 13, 1991.

More than one unit. Several duties turn simply on the building having multiple units: the shared-metered billing regime in Minn. Stat. section 504B.216, which applies to a building with multiple separate residential dwelling units served by fewer meters than there are units; the subsidised accessible-unit pet right in Minn. Stat. section 504B.261, which applies 'in a multiunit residential building'; the eviction posting rule in Minn. Stat. section 504B.332, subd. 4; and the city-document notice in Minn. Stat. section 471.9995, which reaches a document 'required to be posted in a building containing multiple rental dwelling units'.

Eighty percent aged 55 or over. Minn. Stat. section 504B.211, subd. 3(7) makes prearranged housekeeping work a reasonable business purpose for entry in senior housing where 80 percent or more of the residential tenants are 55 or older, and Minn. Stat. section 363A.21, subd. 2(b)(3) uses an 80 percent test for housing for elderly persons.

Two threshold rules deserve separate attention. The first is the only genuinely portfolio-keyed threshold Minnesota has: Minn. Stat. section 504B.001, subd. 13a defines a tenant association as a group of tenants from two or more rental units 'that are owned or operated by the same landlord'. That counts across your holdings, not within one building, so two separate single-family rentals of yours can produce a tenant association with the organising and access rights that go with it. The second is the familial-status exemption at Minn. Stat. section 363A.21, subd. 2(a), which does not apply to familial status in 'any owner-occupied building containing four or fewer dwelling units'. Read the two limbs together, not separately. A five-unit building you live in is outside the exemption. A four-unit building you do not live in is outside it too. You need both limbs at once, and losing either one puts you back inside the prohibition.

title: A Lease Cannot Require the Tenant to Bond or Post Security to Defend
bodyText:
Do not write a lease term requiring the tenant to post a bond, pay rent into court, or give security as a condition of answering, defending, counterclaiming or appealing an eviction. The bars in Minn. Stat. sections 504B.335(e), 504B.371, subd. 3 and 504B.285, subd. 4 are addressed to the court - the court "may not require" it - so they are not tenant rights a lease can ask the tenant to give up, and a lease term cannot give the court a power the statute withholds.

Section 504B.285, subd. 4 is the strictest. Where the landlord files an eviction for failure to pay for utility service in a shared-metered building and the tenant has filed a natural gas or electricity complaint with the Public Utilities Commission under Minn. Stat. section 216B.024, the court must stay the action and must not require the tenant to pay any money into court, post a bond, pay the landlord directly, or post security for any purpose before the complaint is finally disposed of; and if the action then proceeds, the court must not require any posting for utility charges. Where the tenant has not filed such a complaint, or the action is for unpaid water and sewer charges, and the tenant qualifies for a court fee waiver under Minn. Stat. section 563.01, the court again must not require any posting. Only where the tenant neither filed a Commission complaint nor qualifies for a fee waiver may the court, in its discretion, require money or security, and then for prospective utility charges only. Paragraph (c) adds that a court "must not require a tenant to post rent as a condition of a tenant asserting an affirmative claim or defense, or a counterclaim related to landlord utility billings or practices."

Read paragraph (b) for what it is. It is scoped to an eviction action "for failure to pay for utility service in a shared-metered building", not to rent generally. The provision that bars a deposit in an ordinary rent eviction is Minn. Stat. section 504B.335(e), and it has the ten-day exception described in "Bonds in a Minnesota Possession Action: Who Posts What". Do not cite subd. 4(b) for the general rule.

title: Bonds in a Minnesota Possession Action: Who Posts What
bodyText:
Minnesota has no possession bond of the kind some states use, where a landlord posts security and takes possession before trial, or where a tenant must bond to defend. There is no pre-trial bond route to possession at all. Possession comes from judgment and the writ under Minn. Stat. sections 504B.345 and 504B.365.

Before final disposition, the default is that the tenant posts nothing. Minn. Stat. section 504B.335(e) says the court "may not require the defendant to pay any amount of money into court, post a bond, make a payment directly to a landlord, or by any other means post security for any purpose prior to final disposition of an action". There is one exception: if final disposition may be delayed more than ten days, the court may order security in a form and amount it approves based on the totality of the circumstances, and that amount may not include any amount allegedly owed before the filing date and may not exceed the monthly or periodic rent accruing during the pendency of the action.

On appeal, the tenant bonds only for going rent. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.371, subd. 3, a party appealing who remains in possession must give a bond to pay all costs of the appeal, comply with the court's order, and pay the regular rent due to the party excluded from possession as it accrues. The statute then limits it: "The court may not require a bond including back rent, late fees, disputed charges, or any other amount in excess of the regular rent as it accrues each month." The same bond is required under subd. 5(b) where the appealing party gets a stay of a writ already issued.

There is exactly one landlord-side bond, and it is worth knowing. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.371, subd. 7, where the landlord prevailed on a claim under Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, subd. 2 - a breach of the covenant against unlawful activities - subds. 1, 4 and 5 do not apply if the landlord gives a bond conditioned to pay all costs and damages if the judgment of restitution is reversed on appeal and a new trial ordered. The court then issues the writ notwithstanding the notice of appeal, as if no appeal had been taken. That is the only circumstance in which a Minnesota landlord bonds to get or keep possession.

One more security appears if you lock a tenant out. In the tenant's summary action under Minn. Stat. section 504B.375, subd. 1(d), the tenant furnishes such security, if any, as the court finds appropriate for the costs and damages the landlord may sustain if the order was wrongly obtained, and in setting it the court must consider the tenant's ability to afford monetary security. Under subd. 3, a party to that action who appeals and remains in possession must bond for the appeal costs, obedience to the order, and the rent and damages accruing to the party excluded during the appeal.

title: Private Wells: No Results for the Tenant, Unless Your Well Is a Public Water System
bodyText: Minnesota does not make a landlord hand well test results to a tenant - unless the well is big enough to be a public water system, in which case a different and real duty switches on. THE ORDINARY CASE: NO DUTY TO THE TENANT. Nothing in the Minnesota landlord-tenant act, the health chapter, the fire-marshal chapter or the consumer chapters requires you to test a private well, to give a tenant the results, or to disclose anything about the water before signing. The state treats private well testing as VOLUNTARY and funds it that way: Laws 2025, ch. 36 appropriates money 'for ensuring safe drinking water for private well users in southeast Minnesota and statewide by designing and implementing voluntary interventions to reduce health risks to private well users, including identifying private well locations, studying the occurrence and magnitude of contaminants in private wells, developing guidance and conducting outreach and education about well testing and mitigation, awarding grants to local governments, and offering well testing.' THE CASE THAT CATCHES SOME LANDLORDS: YOU MIGHT BE A SUPPLIER. Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 144.381 to 144.387 is the Safe Drinking Water Act of 1977. Sec. 144.382, subd. 5 defines a supplier as 'a person who owns, manages or operates a public water supply', and subd. 4 gives public water supply the meaning of public water system in the federal Safe Drinking Water Act, United States Code, title 42, section 300f, clause (4). If your well serves enough units or people to be a public water system, you are a supplier, and Sec. 144.385 then says that if the system has violated a rule of the commissioner, has a variance or exemption granted, or fails to comply with the terms of the variance or exemption, 'the supplier shall provide public notice of the fact pursuant to the rules of the commissioner.' Sec. 144.384 is the step before: on discovering a violation of a maximum contaminant level or treatment technique the commissioner notifies the supplier, states the rule violated, and sets a date to correct it or to ask for a variance. The penalty is serious. Under Sec. 144.386, subd. 3 a supplier who fails to comply with Sec. 144.385, or who disseminates false or misleading information about that notice, is punished under subd. 2: a gross misdemeanour, a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment of up to 364 days, or both. Subd. 1 adds a civil fine of up to $1,000 for each day a violation continues. And under Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.99, subd. 4(b) a large public water supply serving more than 10,000 people faces an administrative penalty of at least $1,000 per day per violation for breaching Sec. Sec. 144.381 to 144.385. Whether a particular well crosses the public-water-system line turns on the federal definition, so check it with the Department of Health rather than guessing. WHAT STILL APPLIES WHATEVER YOUR WELL IS. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) makes you covenant that the premises are fit for the use intended by the parties, that you will keep them in reasonable repair, and that you will maintain them in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state and of local government including rental licensing ordinances; subd. 1(b) bars waiver. Water you cannot drink is a fitness problem. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.35 also puts the commissioner in general charge of all springs, wells, ponds and streams used as a source of water supply for domestic use, with power to order a person to stop polluting. WHERE THE WELL RULES ACTUALLY LIVE. Minnesota regulates well construction, sealing and licensing in Minn. Stat. ch. 103I and the health department rules under it. Sec. 144.99, subd. 1 confirms chapter 103I is enforced through the health commissioner. WHAT TO DO. Test the well, keep the results, and give a tenant a copy. Minnesota does not require it, no law stops you, and it is the cheapest answer to a later complaint that the water made someone ill.

title: Three Reasons Minnesota's Prohibited-Acts Clause Cannot Be the Shared One
bodyText:
Minnesota's version of a prohibited-acts clause has to be built differently from the shared one other states use, for three reasons, and each of them is a trap worth knowing.

FIRST, THE COVENANT IS ALREADY THERE AND CANNOT BE MODIFIED. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.171 subd. 1 puts the unlawful-activities covenant into every lease, oral or written, and subd. 3 says 'The parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenant imposed by this section.' So a clause that restates the covenant in your own words risks being read as a modification, and the extra reach is the part that fails. The Minnesota clause therefore names the covenant and expressly says it does not repeat, narrow or widen it.

SECOND, THE ENTRY LIMB IS DIFFERENT HERE. The shared clause used in other states bars a tenant from refusing entry, and in those states that is safe because they have no entry-notice statute. Minnesota does. Sec. 504B.211 subd. 2 lets you enter only for a reasonable business purpose and after a good faith effort to give reasonable notice of not less than 24 hours, with a stated time or window, between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless you agree otherwise. The same subdivision says 'A residential tenant may not waive and the landlord may not require the residential tenant to waive the residential tenant's right to prior notice of entry under this section as a condition of entering into or maintaining the lease.' That is bidirectional: your ASKING for the waiver is the breach. A bare 'Tenant will not refuse entry' clause is exactly the term a tenant would characterize as a required waiver, so the Minnesota clause puts your notice duty first and then bars only UNREASONABLE refusal after notice.

THIRD, FOUR FAULT WORDS, NOT ONE. The shared clause says 'intentionally or negligently'. Minnesota's destruction action, Sec. 504B.165, requires 'willful AND malicious' conduct. Three other Minnesota sections use three further phrasings. A lease may lawfully set a wider contract standard than a statute, but do not write 'negligently' and then cite Sec. 504B.165 as the authority for it, because the section does not say that.

TWO THINGS THE CLAUSE MUST NEVER REACH. A tenant's right to call for police or emergency assistance is protected by Sec. 504B.205, and that section is bidirectional too, so you may not even require a waiver of it; subdivision 4 confirms that the call is protected but the underlying conduct is not, which is why you act on the conduct and never on the call. And Sec. 504B.212 subd. 1(f) says 'No landlord shall prohibit or adopt any rule prohibiting residential tenants or nonresident tenant organizers from peacefully organizing, assembling, canvassing, leafleting, or otherwise exercising within the building their right of free expression for tenant organizing purposes', and you may not require prior permission or set unreasonable time, place and manner limits. A broadly drafted 'no soliciting' or 'no distributing materials' house rule collides with that, so the Minnesota clause carves it out on its face.

title: The Attorney General Can Investigate Any Chapter 504B Violation
bodyText:
Since 2024 the attorney general has had express enforcement authority over the whole of the landlord-tenant act. Minn. Stat. § 504B.501, added by Laws 2024, ch. 118, sec. 30, reads in full: "The attorney general has authority under section 8.31 to investigate and prosecute violations of this chapter."

What that imports is substantial. Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 2 lets the attorney general obtain discovery before any civil action is commenced and without leave of court — written interrogatories answerable in 20 days, document production on 15 days' notice, and depositions. Subdivision 2a backs that with a court order compelling compliance. Subdivision 2b lets the attorney general accept a written assurance of discontinuance, filed with and approved by the district court, which is not an admission but is punishable as contempt if broken. Subdivision 3 gives the courts jurisdiction to enjoin violations and to award the state a civil penalty "in an amount to be determined by the court, not in excess of $25,000", and subdivision 3c lets a court appoint an administrator to monitor, maintain or wind up the affairs of a business.

One limit is worth getting right, because it is easy to overstate. Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 3a — the private action for "any person injured", with damages, costs of investigation and reasonable attorney fees — is keyed to "a violation of any of the laws referred to in subdivision 1". Chapter 504B is not in subdivision 1's list. Where the legislature wanted a tenant to have the subdivision 3a remedy it said so expressly: Minn. Stat. § 504B.195, subd. 2 entitles the tenant to "remedies provided by section 8.31, subdivision 3a". Where it wanted attorney general enforcement it used the investigate-and-prosecute formula instead, at Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.205, subd. 6, 504B.216, subd. 17 and 504B.501. On that reading Minn. Stat. § 504B.501 gives the attorney general chapter-wide powers and does not give tenants a new private right of action. No Minnesota case deciding the point was available here, so treat it as the better reading rather than a settled one, and do not rely on it as a shield.

The practical consequence is about records, not drafting. An attorney general inquiry under this section reaches you before any lawsuit, with interrogatories and document demands, over any Chapter 504B violation — fee disclosure, deposits, entry notice, the lot. Keep your lease versions, fee schedules, entry notices and deposit accounting in a state you could produce on 15 days' notice.

title: You May Not Require Declawing or Devocalization, and the Clause Is Void
bodyText:
Minnesota bars you from making declawing or devocalization a condition of a tenancy, and the bar is wider than it first looks. Minn. Stat. § 504B.114, subd. 2 applies to "a landlord who allows an animal on the premises" and says that landlord shall not:

(1) advertise a property for occupancy "in a manner designed to discourage application for occupancy of that real property because an applicant's animal has not been declawed or devocalized";
(2) refuse to allow or negotiate occupancy, "or otherwise make unavailable or deny to another person the occupancy of a real property because of that person's refusal to declaw or devocalize an animal"; or
(3) "require a tenant or occupant of real property to declaw or devocalize an animal allowed on the premises".

Then: "Any requirement or lease provision that violates this subdivision is void and unenforceable." That is one of very few Minnesota provisions that voids a lease term outright rather than voiding a waiver.

Four points of reach that matter in practice.

The section bites before there is a lease. Minn. Stat. § 504B.114, subd. 1(c) defines "application for occupancy" as "all phases of the process of applying for the right to occupy a real property, including but not limited to filling out applications, interviewing, and submitting references". A question asked at a showing or on the phone is inside the section.

"Animal" is as broad as it gets. Minn. Stat. § 504B.114, subd. 1(b) takes the meaning from Minn. Stat. § 343.20, subd. 2: "every living creature except members of the human race." This is not a cats-and-dogs rule.

"Declawing" and "devocalizing" each cover "performing, procuring, or arranging for" the procedure, so requiring the tenant to arrange it is as much a violation as doing it.

The section is keyed to a landlord "who allows an animal on the premises". A genuine no-pets property is outside subdivision 2 by its own terms — though a service or support animal is not a pet, and Minn. Stat. § 504B.113 and Chapter 363A govern there.

Enforcement is public, not private. Under Minn. Stat. § 504B.114, subd. 3 a city attorney, a county attorney or the attorney general may sue for injunctive relief and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per advertisement for clause (1) and up to $1,000 per animal for clause (2) or (3), paid to the entity that brought the action. The section gives the tenant no damages of their own.

Check any pet clause, pet addendum, pet-screening form and advertisement against this section. The ban is on the requirement, so a clause saying a declawed cat is preferred, or charging less for one, is the kind of thing clause (1) is aimed at.

title: Minnesota Has No List of Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText:
Minnesota has no enumerated prohibited-lease-terms statute. There is no section anywhere in the landlord-tenant act, or in the consumer statutes, that lists the clauses a residential lease may not contain. If you are used to working from a single banned-terms list, there is nothing here to work from, and the absence is not permission.

What Minnesota has instead is three things.

First, a non-waiver sentence attached to individual sections, 36 of them across 30 sections of Chapter 504B, written in six different formulas. A clause that waives or softens one of those sections fails. See "Minnesota Has No Single Non-Waiver Section: Six Different Formulas, Section by Section" for the formulas and the section list, because they are not interchangeable and one family bars you from even asking.

Second, a handful of provisions that void a term outright, without any waiver analysis. Minn. Stat. § 504B.114, subd. 2 is the clearest: "Any requirement or lease provision that violates this subdivision is void and unenforceable." Minn. Stat. § 504B.265, subd. 3 and § 504B.266, subd. 4 each void not only a waiver but "any lease provision or agreement requiring a longer notice period than that provided by this section" — so a lease that lengthens the notice to terminate on a tenant's death or infirmity is void in that respect even though it waives nothing.

Third, the one lease-term bar that sits outside Chapter 504B. Minn. Stat. § 363A.31, subd. 1 provides that any provision "of a lease, contract, or other agreement or instrument which purports to be a waiver by an individual of any right or remedy provided in this chapter is contrary to public policy and void if the waiver or release purports to waive claims arising out of acts or practices which occur after the execution of the waiver or release." That is the Human Rights Act, and it is the only Minnesota non-waiver provision that names a lease in its own text.

Three things a careful reader will look for and not find. There is no statutory ban on an exculpatory, indemnity or hold-harmless clause in a residential lease; see "No Statute Bans an Exculpatory Clause, but the Habitability Covenants Cannot Be Modified". There is no confession-of-judgment ban reaching a residential lease: the only Minnesota confession-of-judgment prohibition, Minn. Stat. § 325F.91, sits inside the rental-purchase regime, which Minn. Stat. § 325F.84, subd. 7 confines to "property that is not real property under the laws of this state". And there is no money penalty for knowingly using a prohibited term.

Two sections worth knowing because their headnotes mislead. Minn. Stat. § 504B.120 is headed "PROHIBITED FEES" but prohibits no clause: it requires every nonoptional fee to be disclosed in the lease and the sum of rent and nonoptional fees to be shown as the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, with treble damages and attorney fees for a violation. Minn. Stat. § 504B.151 is headed "RESTRICTION ON RESIDENTIAL LEASE TERMS FOR BUILDINGS IN FINANCIAL DISTRESS" and restricts the lease's permitted length once you have had notice of a contract-for-deed cancellation or a foreclosure sale, not its contents.

Because there is no list, the discipline has to be the other way round: for each clause you want, find the section it touches and read that section's own non-waiver sentence.

title: Promises to Repair: No Form Rules, but They Bind You
bodyText: Minnesota has no rule about the form of a promise to repair. No statute requires your promise to clean, repair or improve the unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. Some states require all three. Minnesota requires none of them. That is not good news, because Minnesota makes the promise bite in a different way. Once a promise is in the lease, breaking it is a statutory "violation". Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.001, subd. 14(5) defines a violation to include "a violation of an oral or written agreement, lease, or contract for the rental of a dwelling in a building", and since 2025 that clause is inside the tenant's two main procedures. In a rent escrow action the tenant gives you written notice specifying the violation, delivered personally or sent to the person or place where rent is normally paid, and if it is not corrected within 14 days the tenant may deposit the rent with the court administrator (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 1(c)). In a tenant remedies action the tenant must inform you in writing at least 14 days before bringing the action (Sec. 504B.395, subd. 4). Both of those used to cover only code violations and violations of chapter 504B; Laws 2025, ch. 32, art. 4, secs. 6 and 7 added clause (5), so a broken lease promise now reaches rent escrow, retroactive rent abatement, a court order to remedy, a court-appointed administrator, and the fines in Sec. 504B.391. On top of that, Sec. 504B.161, subd. 4 makes the statutory covenants additional to "any covenants or conditions imposed by law or ordinance or by the terms of the lease or license". So a lease sentence promising more than the statute holds you to the larger promise; it does not replace the covenant with a softer one. A false promise carries a further, less settled risk. Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.69, subd. 1 makes a "false promise" enjoinable where it is used with intent that others rely on it in connection with the sale of merchandise, and Sec. 325F.68, subd. 2 defines merchandise to include real estate. Whether that reaches a residential lease is unsettled, because the same statute writes "sale or lease" elsewhere when it means both. Treat it as a live risk, not a safe harbour, and see Minnesota's unconscionability row for the full reasoning. Practical course: promise only what you will do, put it in the lease or an addendum with a date you can meet, and do it. An oral promise is as binding as a written one and much harder to prove you kept.

title: No Proposition 65 in Minnesota, and the One Warning That Does Reach a Tenant
bodyText:
Minnesota has no Proposition 65. No Minnesota law makes a landlord post or deliver a general warning about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm.

Minnesota's chemical laws are PRODUCT BANS aimed at manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers, not occupancy warnings aimed at tenants: organohalogenated flame retardants in children's products, upholstered residential furniture, residential textiles and mattresses (Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.071), bisphenol-A (Sec. 325F.175), and formaldehyde in children's products (Sec. 325F.177), each with a companion section barring substitution of a chemical known or suspected to cause cancer, genetic damage or reproductive harm. None of them reaches a lease.

THERE ARE EXACTLY THREE PRESCRIBED WARNING TEXTS IN MINNESOTA LAW THAT COULD TOUCH A DWELLING, AND ONLY ONE REACHES A TENANT. (1) The urea formaldehyde IMPORTANT HEALTH NOTICE in Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.18, subd. 1(a). This one does reach a lessee, but only where a BUILDER leases a newly built housing unit containing urea formaldehyde to its INITIAL OCCUPANT, and never for manufactured housing. It is the clause offered under this topic.

(2) The Radon Warning Statement in Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.496, subd. 4. That runs to a BUYER, not a tenant, and the Act reaches a lease only where the lease carries an option to purchase. See the radon-disclosure rows.

(3) NFPA standard 704 hazardous-substance signs. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.093, subd. 1(5) a fire department may require EMPLOYERS in its jurisdiction to post signs showing that hazardous substances are present, and must supply the signs or help the employer obtain them. That is a fire-department requirement on an employer, not a lease disclosure, and Sec. 299F.099 preempts any local ordinance on the subject.

WHAT TO DO. If you do not build the unit you let, Minnesota asks you for no chemical warning at all. If a California landlord's Proposition 65 sign has made you wonder whether Minnesota needs one, it does not.
