Give your tenant the federal lead-based-paint disclosure for a pre-1978 unit, the Sec. 504B.195 copy of any outstanding inspection citation or condemnation order, and - if you built the unit - the formaldehyde notice. Beyond that, disclose what you actually know: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) makes you covenant that the premises are fit for the use intended and that you will keep them in reasonable repair, and those covenants cannot be waived.

title: No Property-Tax Statement to Tenants — but You Do Owe a Certificate of Rent Paid
bodyText: Minnesota does not require you to tell a residential tenant what share of their rent goes to property taxes. There is no annual property-tax-portion statement, no July deadline, no duty to re-issue anything when rent changes, and no rule requiring it in the lease - nothing like the statements some states require. Minnesota's landlord-tenant chapter requires only the disclosures it names: the landlord and manager's name and address, nonoptional fees and the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, outstanding inspection and condemnation orders, a pending foreclosure, and the utility and submetering disclosures. Property tax is not among them. BUT MINNESOTA DOES PUT A DIFFERENT ANNUAL DUTY ON YOU, and it is easy to miss because it sits in tax law rather than landlord-tenant law. Minnesota's renter's credit works from a Certificate of Rent Paid that the LANDLORD issues to the renter. Under Minn. Stat. § 290.0693, subd. 4, the owner or managing agent of property rented as a homestead must give a certificate of rent paid, on the commissioner of revenue's form, to each person who is a renter on December 31. It must be made available before February 1 of the following year. A renter who moves out earlier may be given it at move-out, or it may be mailed to a forwarding address the renter provides. You must also file a copy of each certificate with the commissioner by January 31, and keep a duplicate or equivalent record for four years. Each failure to give or to file a certificate carries a $50 penalty (Minn. Stat. § 289A.60, subd. 12(b)-(c)). Knowingly overstating the rent constituting property taxes on a certificate carries a larger penalty (subd. 12(d)). You do not work out a tax share yourself: the statute fixes 'rent constituting property taxes' at 17 percent of the gross rent actually paid (§ 290.0693, subd. 1(j)). 'Gross rent' means rent paid at arm's length for the right of occupancy (subd. 1(e)). Minn. Stat. § 290A.19 now applies the same duty to manufactured home park owners. So: do not expect a property-tax disclosure obligation in your lease, and do expect to issue a Certificate of Rent Paid to each renter every year. Get the current form from the Minnesota Department of Revenue. One practical step helps the tenant and costs you nothing: keep base rent separate in your ledger from utility, parking, pet and other charges, so the figure you certify is defensible.

title: Unlawful Use Voids the Right to Possession, Not the Lease
bodyText:
Minnesota has no general unlawful-purpose statute that voids or annuls a residential lease. There is no provision making a lease void because the premises were used for a prohibited purpose, and no Minnesota nuisance or criminal section is known to annul the tenancy. What Minnesota has is narrower and more useful: a covenant implied into every lease about specific unlawful activities, with a specific and partial consequence.

The covenant, and what it covers. Minn. Stat. § 504B.171, subd. 1(a) provides that "In every lease or license of residential premises, whether in writing or parol, the landlord or licensor and the tenant or licensee covenant" that neither will allow, on the premises or in the common area and curtilage: controlled substances in violation of any criminal provision of chapter 152; prostitution or prostitution-related activity as defined in Minn. Stat. § 617.80, subd. 4; the unlawful use or possession of a firearm in violation of Minn. Stat. § 609.66, subd. 1a, § 609.67 or § 624.713; or stolen property or property obtained by robbery. Subdivision 1(a)(2) adds that the common area and curtilage will not be used by either party, or others under their control, to manufacture, sell, give away, barter, deliver, exchange, distribute, purchase or possess a controlled substance.

Note that the covenant binds you too. It is a covenant of "the landlord or licensor and the tenant or licensee", not a tenant promise. And it has a knowledge limit that protects both of you: "The covenant is not violated when a person other than the landlord or licensor or the tenant or licensee possesses or allows controlled substances in the premises, common area, or curtilage, unless the landlord or licensor or the tenant or licensee knew or had reason to know of that activity."

The consequence is possession only, and the rent survives. Minn. Stat. § 504B.171, subd. 2 is precise about this: "A breach of the covenant created by subdivision 1 voids the tenant's or licensee's right to possession of the residential premises. All other provisions of the lease or license, including but not limited to the obligation to pay rent, remain in effect until the lease is terminated by the terms of the lease or operation of law." So the lease is not void. The tenant's right to possess is. You still have to terminate the lease, and the rent obligation continues until you do. A clause drafted on the assumption that unlawful use makes the whole lease void would be wrong about Minnesota law and would give away the rent.

You may also hand the eviction to a prosecutor. Under subdivision 2 you may assign the right to bring the eviction action to the county or city attorney, in writing on that office's form, and that office decides whether to accept. If it does, the court filing fee is waived and you keep all other rights and duties, including removal of the tenant's personal property after the writ issues.

Cannabis is carved out, expressly and non-waivably. Minn. Stat. § 504B.171, subd. 1(c): "A landlord cannot prohibit a tenant from legally possessing, and a tenant cannot waive the right to legally possess, any cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products, or using any cannabinoid product or hemp-derived consumer product, other than consumption by combustion or vaporization of the product and inhalation of smoke, aerosol, or vapor from the product." You may ban smoking and vaping it. You may not ban possessing it, and you may not ask the tenant to waive that.

The whole section is non-waivable in both directions. Minn. Stat. § 504B.171, subd. 3: "The parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenant imposed by this section." Modification is barred, not just waiver — so a lease clause that widens the covenant, or narrows the knowledge limit, is as vulnerable as one that waives it.

Two cross-references rather than repetition. Minn. Stat. § 504B.171, subd. 2a limits what a crime-free lease provision may do about conduct away from the premises, and the library answers that at "The Unlawful-Activities Covenant Is in Every Minnesota Lease Whether You Write It or Not". A separate exception for sober housing programmes sits at Minn. Stat. § 504B.1715. Neither is restated here.

Drafting conclusion. A purpose-limitation clause in a Minnesota lease should state the permitted residential use and the tenant's own duties, and should not claim that unlawful use voids the lease — because Minn. Stat. § 504B.171, subd. 2 says it voids the right to possession and leaves everything else, including the rent, standing.

title: Minnesota Has No Statutory Recycling Notice for Tenants — but Your City May
bodyText: Some states require a landlord to tell tenants where and how to recycle on the premises, sometimes at move-in and sometimes annually. Minnesota imposes no such duty by statute. The word 'recycling' does not appear anywhere in Minnesota's landlord-tenant act, its human rights act, its public safety and fire chapter, its consumer-protection chapters or its manufactured-home-park chapter. There is no required recycling disclosure, no notice form and no annual reminder. On recycling, that statutory answer understates the picture, for two reasons. First, Minnesota's recycling and solid-waste law lives in a separate chapter, and a tenant-notice duty could sit there. Second, and much more likely to affect you in practice, recycling in Minnesota is largely a county and city matter. Several Minnesota cities require recycling service at multi-unit buildings and require the owner to inform residents how to use it. Whether your building is covered, and what you have to tell tenants, depends on the ordinance where the property sits. That is a municipal question — check the ordinance or ask counsel. The route by which a local recycling ordinance binds you is worth knowing, because it is not optional. Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(4) makes it a covenant in every residential lease 'to maintain the premises and all common areas in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state, and of the local units of government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing, where the premises are located during the term of the lease or license'. Under subd. 1(b) the parties 'may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section'. So if your city's ordinance requires recycling service and resident information, complying with it is already a non-waivable lease covenant, whether or not the lease mentions recycling. Practical position. You may put recycling instructions in the lease or in house rules, and it is sensible to do so, but in Minnesota that is a management choice rather than a statutory disclosure. If you charge separately for refuse or recycling collection, remember that § 504B.120, subd. 1 requires every nonoptional fee to be disclosed in the lease and included in the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, with treble damages for getting it wrong.

title: The Tenant's Right to Redeem a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText:
In a Minnesota nonpayment eviction the tenant can stop the eviction by paying, right up to the last moment. Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1(a) says the tenant may, at any time before possession has been delivered, redeem the tenancy and be restored to possession by paying to the landlord or bringing to court the rent in arrears, with interest, the costs of the action, and an attorney's fee not to exceed $5, and by performing any other covenants of the lease.

Read the $5 literally. It is the statute's figure and it has not been changed: whatever a lease says about recovering attorney fees, redemption costs the tenant an attorney's fee of no more than $5. Do not budget for your legal costs out of a redemption.

Redemption may also be made with a written guarantee rather than cash, from a federal, state or local government agency, or from any other organisation that qualifies for tax-exempt status under United States Code, title 26, section 501(c)(3) and that administers a government rental assistance programme, has sufficient funds available, and guarantees that funds will be provided to the landlord. A landlord cannot insist on cash where a qualifying guarantee is tendered.

There is a partial route too. Under subd. 1(b), where the tenant has paid the rent in arrears but cannot pay the interest, costs and attorney's fee, the court may permit the tenant to pay those into court and be restored to possession within the same period, if any, for which the court stays the order to vacate under Minn. Stat. section 504B.345.

Two things follow for how you apply money you receive. Under subd. 1(d), once a complaint is pending, rental payments must first be applied to rent claimed as due in the complaint from prior rental periods before any part of a payment goes to rent claimed for the current period, unless the court finds the claim for the prior periods has been waived. And redemption is lost if you combine grounds: subd. 1(a) makes the right available "unless the landlord has also sought to evict the tenant by alleging a material violation of the lease under section 504B.285, subdivision 5".

Finally, keep your rent records. Subd. 1(a) creates a rebuttable presumption that the rent has been paid if the tenant produces copies of one or more money orders, or original receipt stubs evidencing the purchase of a money order, where the documents total the amount of the rent, include a date or dates approximately corresponding with the date rent was due, and, for money order copies, are made payable to the landlord. The presumption is rebutted if the landlord produces a business record showing the rent was not paid, and the landlord may also put in other evidence. A landlord without a contemporaneous rent ledger can lose a nonpayment case to a photocopy.

title: No Minnesota Right to Display a Religious or Cultural Object
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute giving a tenant a right to affix or display a religious or cultural object on a dwelling, a door, a doorpost, or a common area. There is no mezuzah statute and no religious-display statute of any kind in the landlord-tenant code or in the Human Rights Act. The Minnesota Constitution does not supply one either, and it is worth being clear why. Minn. Const. art. I, Sec. 16 protects freedom of conscience - the right of every person to worship according to the dictates of his own conscience shall never be infringed, no one may be compelled to attend, erect or support any place of worship, no control of or interference with the rights of conscience is permitted, and no preference may be given BY LAW to any religious establishment or mode of worship. Those words bind the state. They do not make a private landlord house rule unconstitutional, and the same is true of art. I, Sec. 3, the liberty-of-the-press clause. What does constrain you is the discrimination law, and it constrains you twice. Creed and religion are both enumerated grounds in Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.09, so a display rule written or enforced so as to hit one faith is a protected-class problem, and subd. 1(2) catches discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental and in the furnishing of facilities or services. And Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.15 makes it an unfair discriminatory practice for a lessor, sublessee, assignee or managing agent of real property to engage in any reprisal against a person because that person opposed a practice forbidden under the chapter, or because that person ASSOCIATED with people of a different creed or religion. Reprisal there includes any form of intimidation, retaliation or harassment. So the practical position is that a neutral, uniformly applied and uniformly enforced rule about what may be attached to doors, walls and windows is lawful, because nothing grants a display right - but the rule has to survive both of those sections in operation, not just on paper, and a request to keep a religious item up may well arrive as a request for an accommodation. One exemption is worth knowing, because it is the single place where the constitutional conscience clause does operative work in the Act. Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.26 provides that nothing in the chapter prohibits a religious association, corporation or society not organized for private profit, or an educational institution it controls, consistent with the protections or privileges of the First Amendment and article I, section 16, of the Minnesota Constitution, including ministerial exceptions, from limiting admission to or giving preference to persons of the same religion or denomination, or from taking any action with respect to housing and real property. The limit on the exemption matters as much: it does not apply to secular business activities whose conduct is unrelated to the religious and educational purposes for which the body is organized. So faith-based housing has real latitude here; a commercially operated portfolio does not get it by having a religious owner. This library does not offer a display-restriction clause. Nothing in Minnesota law requires one, the protected-class downside of a badly drafted or unevenly enforced one is treble compensatory damages under Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.33, subd. 8(a) plus a mandatory civil penalty, and the upside is small. A landlord who wants one may add it and should take advice on it first.

title: Rent Concessions: No Minnesota Rule, Two Minnesota Traps
bodyText:
Minnesota has no statute that regulates rent concessions as such. No section of chapter 504B, and no 2025 or 2026 session law, tells you how to give free rent, a rent credit, a rebate or a move-in special, or requires you to disclose one in any particular form. Two Minnesota rules still shape how you write one.

The first is a trap in the late fee statute. Minn. Stat. section 504B.177, paragraph (a) says that for late fee purposes the "due date" does not include a date, earlier than the date in the written or oral lease, by which the tenant earns a discount if the rent is paid. So if your lease sets rent due on the 5th but offers a discount for paying by the 1st, the 1st is not the due date. A late fee may only run from the 5th, and it may not exceed 8% of the overdue rent payment. An early-payment discount is lawful in Minnesota; using its date as the late fee trigger is not.

The second is the fee disclosure statute. Minn. Stat. section 504B.120, subdivision 1 makes you disclose all nonoptional fees in the lease, state the sum of rent plus all nonoptional fees as the Total Monthly Payment on the first page of the lease, and disclose nonoptional fees and whether utilities are included in any advertisement or posting for the unit. A violation costs treble damages and the court may award the tenant attorney fees.

That matters for a concession in two ways. If you advertise a unit at a concession price, the advertisement must still disclose the nonoptional fees. And if the concession changes what the tenant actually pays each month, the first-page Total Monthly Payment figure has to be true to the lease you are signing.

Put every concession in the lease itself, with its amount or value and the exact rental periods it applies to, so there is no argument later about what was given.

If you want the concession back when the tenant breaches or leaves early, get advice before writing a clawback: Minnesota has no statute permitting one, and section 504B.177 is a reminder that Minnesota courts and the legislature look closely at charges that behave like penalties. Minneapolis or St. Paul ordinances may add their own advertising or disclosure rules.

title: Five Times Minnesota Stops You Collecting the Rent
bodyText: Minnesota does not have a general rule stopping you collecting rent just because the unit has code violations. It has something more targeted: five situations where your right to the rent, or your right to sue for it, is cut off or reduced. Learn them, because three of them bar you before you ever get to court. FIRST, CONDEMNATION. Once the premises have been condemned, declared unfit for human habitation, ordered vacated for a housing, health or fire code or rental licensing violation, or ordered vacated for a government taking, you - or your agent, or anyone acting under your direction or control - may not accept rent or a security deposit at all. You become liable for actual damages plus three times everything you collected after the date of condemnation, plus costs and attorney fees, the violation also violates your statutory covenants, and the section is to be liberally construed for tenants. A lease term waiving it is contrary to public policy and void (Minn. Stat. section 504B.204). SECOND, DISCLOSURE. No action to recover rent or possession may be maintained unless you have disclosed the name and address of the person managing the premises and of the landlord or an agent authorised to accept service, in the lease or otherwise in writing before the tenancy, and posted the same information conspicuously - or unless the tenant already knew or was told at least 30 days before you filed (Minn. Stat. section 504B.181). The duty follows the money: it is enforceable against any successor landlord and against any individual to whom rent is paid. THIRD, THE PRE-FILING NOTICE. For nonpayment, the 14-day written notice under Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subdivision 1a comes first, with its mandatory contents, and the court must dismiss and expunge if you did not give it. FOURTH, AN ADMINISTRATOR. If the court appoints an administrator in a tenant remedies action, your right to collect rent becomes void and unenforceable - from the petitioning tenant from the time the court signs the order for judgment, and from the other tenants from service of the judgment - until the administration ends (Minn. Stat. section 504B.435). FIFTH, ABATEMENT. In a rent escrow action the court may order rent abated, including abating future rent until you fix the violation, and in a tenant remedies action it may find how far uncorrected violations impair the tenant's use and enjoyment and abate the rent accordingly (Minn. Stat. sections 504B.385 and 504B.425). While an escrow case is pending the tenant must keep paying rent to you or as the court directs and may not simply withhold it. Two more points worth knowing. You must give a prospective tenant copies of outstanding inspection citations that threaten health or safety, and of any condemnation order, before they sign a lease or pay rent or a deposit (Minn. Stat. section 504B.195). And a tenant whose building is destroyed or becomes uninhabitable through no fault of their own may vacate and surrender it; you can only contract out of that so far as your statutory covenants allow (Minn. Stat. section 504B.131). On the other side, you do not need a separate demand for rent before suing: an eviction action for nonpayment is itself equivalent to a demand for the rent (Minn. Stat. section 504B.291). A city's own rental licensing rules may add to this.

title: Raising Rent in Minnesota: Your Own Lease Sets the Notice Floor
bodyText:
Minnesota sets no statewide limit on how much or how often you may raise rent, and no statute ties an increase to an index. What it does regulate is the notice, and the rule catches landlords out.

Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.147, if your lease gives you a notice period for a rent increase (or for a notice to quit) that differs from the period the lease requires of the tenant for a notice of intention to move out, two things follow. Your notice of a rent increase may not be shorter than the period the lease requires of the tenant. And the tenant may use either period for their own notice to move out, choosing whichever suits them.

So the figure you write into the lease for the tenant becomes the floor on your own rent-increase notice: ask the tenant for 60 days and you owe at least 60 days yourself. The section says plainly that its requirements may not be waived or modified by the parties, and that a lease provision waiving any part of it is contrary to public policy and void, so you cannot draft around it. A notice of nonrenewal counts as a notice to quit for this purpose.

Separately, for an ordinary month-to-month tenancy there is no rent-increase statute at all. A tenancy at will ends on written notice at least as long as the interval between rent payments, or three months, whichever is less (Minn. Stat. section 504B.135), so in practice a month-to-month rent change happens either by the tenant's agreement or by ending the tenancy with proper notice and offering new terms.

Three more limits. You may not increase rent or decrease services as a penalty for a tenant's good faith complaint or report of a code violation; the burden is on you to show otherwise for 90 days after the complaint (Minn. Stat. section 504B.441), and a retaliatory increase is a defence to a nonpayment eviction if the tenant tenders the rent due under the original obligation (Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subdivision 3). Minnesota has no market-rate safe harbour here, and nothing makes a lease clause the condition of a lawful increase.

You may not require a tenant to renew a lease sooner than six months before the current lease expires, if the lease runs longer than ten months, and a waiver of that is void (Minn. Stat. section 504B.144) - so a renewal rent figure cannot be locked in earlier than that.

And to enforce an automatic renewal clause in a lease with an original term of two months or more, you must serve or mail by certified mail a written notice that points the tenant to the automatic renewal provision, at least 15 but not more than 30 days before the tenant's own notice deadline (Minn. Stat. section 504B.145).

Finally, rent control: Minnesota allows a city ordinance approved at a general election, and St. Paul has one. Check the local ordinance before setting any increase. This covers Minnesota's statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws.

title: Rent-Increase Notice: The 60-Day Figure Is the Manufactured Home Park Rule
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute that fixes a number of days' notice before a rent increase on an ordinary residential lease. If you have heard that Minnesota requires 60 days, that figure is real but it is not yours: Minn. Stat. section 327C.06 requires a manufactured home park owner to give a lot resident 60 days' written notice of a rent increase, bars an increase whose purpose is to pay a civil or criminal penalty imposed on the park owner, and allows only two rent increases in any 12-month period. Chapter 327C governs manufactured home park lots, not apartments or houses, so none of that applies to an ordinary residential tenancy. What does apply is relative, not absolute. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.147, where your lease gives you a notice period for a rent increase, or for a notice to quit, that differs from the period the lease requires of the tenant for a notice of intention to move out, your rent-increase notice may not be shorter than the tenant's period, and the tenant may choose either period for their own notice to move out. A notice of nonrenewal counts as a notice to quit. None of that may be waived or modified, and a lease provision waiving any of it is contrary to public policy and void. The practical effect is that you set your own figure and your own lease sets the floor under it. For a month-to-month tenancy there is no rent-increase notice statute at all. A tenancy at will ends on written notice at least as long as the interval between rent payments, or three months, whichever is less (Minn. Stat. section 504B.135), and that notice must run a full rental period and take effect at the end of one. So a month-to-month increase happens either because the tenant agrees to it or because you properly end the tenancy and offer new terms. Where the lease has an automatic renewal clause and an original term of two months or more, you must also serve personally or mail by certified mail a written notice drawing the tenant's attention to the renewal clause, at least 15 but not more than 30 days before the tenant's own notice deadline (Minn. Stat. section 504B.145). Write a generous notice period into your lease, give the notice in writing, and check whether the city has a voter-approved rent-stabilization ordinance, because St. Paul does and a local ordinance can add its own notice and cap rules. This covers Minnesota's statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws.

title: Splitting Rent Into Installments: Late Fees, Partial Payments and Proration
bodyText:
Minnesota has no statute that lets or stops you taking rent in sub-monthly installments, so a payment schedule is simply a matter for the lease.

Three Minnesota rules decide how to write one. First, the late fee. Minn. Stat. section 504B.177, paragraph (a) caps a late fee at 8% of the overdue rent payment, and only if the tenant and you have agreed in writing that a late fee may be imposed and the agreement says when. With an installment schedule the overdue rent payment is the overdue installment, so 8% is measured against that installment, not against a whole month's rent. Do not let an installment schedule turn into several late fees for the same month's rent.

Second, partial payments. Minnesota will not let you declare by lease that an installment is not a partial payment of rent; no statute says that. What Minnesota does give you is narrower and more useful: under Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subdivision 1(c) the parties may agree, but only in writing, that a partial payment of rent in arrears accepted before the order for restitution is issued goes against the balance and does not waive your action for possession. The lease can be that writing, and the library offers it. Subdivision 1(d) separately requires that rental payments be applied to rent claimed in the complaint from earlier rental periods before the current one, unless the court finds that earlier claim waived.

Third, proration. The final month's rent must be prorated at the average daily rate when the term ends before the last day of the month, using the actual number of calendar days in that month, and that applies to every lease including one requiring last month's rent in advance. Any attempted waiver of it, by contract or otherwise, is void and unenforceable (Minn. Stat. section 504B.116). An installment schedule cannot get around it.

Remember too that every cash payment needs a written receipt, immediately if the tenant pays in person and within three business days otherwise (Minn. Stat. section 504B.118, subdivision 2), so more payment dates means more receipts. This covers Minnesota's statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws.

title: Your Counterclaim for Possession in a Tenant's Rent Escrow Action
bodyText:
The one express counterclaim in Minnesota's landlord-tenant act is the landlord's, not the tenant's, and a landlord facing a rent escrow action should know it exists.

Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.385 a tenant who says a violation exists in the building may deposit the rent due with the court administrator instead of paying it to the landlord, after giving the notice that subd. 1(b) or 1(c) requires. Minn. Stat. section 504B.385, subd. 2 then lets the landlord file a counterclaim for possession of the property, in cases where the landlord alleges that the tenant did not deposit the full amount of rent with the court administrator. That is the ground - a short deposit, not the merits of the violation.

Four mechanics matter. The court must set the hearing on the counterclaim not less than seven nor more than 14 days from the day of filing it. If the escrow hearing and the counterclaim hearing cannot be heard the same day, the matters must be consolidated and heard on the date set for the counterclaim. The contents of the counterclaim must meet the requirements for a complaint under Minn. Stat. section 504B.321 - so the attachments, the itemised accounting and the subsidy statement all apply. And it must be served as provided in Minn. Stat. section 504B.332, except that the affidavit of service or mailing may be brought to the hearing rather than filed with the court beforehand. The court must provide a simplified form.

Expect the defences in Minn. Stat. section 504B.415, which subd. 3 makes available: that the alleged violations do not exist or have been removed or remedied; that they were caused by the wilful, malicious, negligent or irresponsible conduct of a complaining tenant or someone under that tenant's direction or control; or that a tenant unreasonably refused the landlord or the landlord's agent entry to part of the property to correct the violation, where the effort to correct was made in good faith.

Two things a lease cannot do about any of this. Minn. Stat. section 504B.385, subd. 11 says the tenant's rights under that section "may not be waived or modified and are in addition to and do not limit other rights or remedies which may be available to the residential tenant and landlord, except as provided in subdivision 1." And Minn. Stat. section 504B.441 applies to these proceedings, so a retaliation claim is available.

title: Minnesota Does Not Make a Tenant Pay Rent In to Defend an Eviction
bodyText:
Several states make a tenant deposit the rent with the court before the tenant may raise a defence or a counterclaim in a possession action. Minnesota does the opposite. Minn. Stat. section 504B.335(e) says the court "may not require the defendant to pay any amount of money into court, post a bond, make a payment directly to a landlord, or by any other means post security for any purpose prior to final disposition of an action". The one exception, and the cap on it, are set out in "Bonds in a Minnesota Possession Action: Who Posts What". Do not expect the tenant's defence to be conditioned on money.

There is no statutory tenant counterclaim provision in the eviction action, and none is needed. Minn. Stat. section 504B.335(c) provides that the proceedings are the same as in other civil actions except as Minn. Stat. sections 504B.281 to 504B.371 provide, so the ordinary civil rules on pleading supply the answer. Minn. Stat. section 504B.335(a) also requires the court, in setting a trial date, to allow for the opportunity for the defendant to seek legal counsel and raise affirmative defences. The statutory defences a landlord should expect are the retaliation defence in Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subd. 2, with the burden shifting to the landlord where the notice to quit was served within 90 days of the tenant's protected act, and the penalty rent increase defence in subd. 3, which requires the tenant to tender the rent due under the original obligation.

Where utility billing is involved the bar is absolute and expressly extends to counterclaims. Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subd. 4(c) says a court "must not require a tenant to post rent as a condition of a tenant asserting an affirmative claim or defense, or a counterclaim related to landlord utility billings or practices." Subd. 4(b) deals with the eviction for failure to pay for utility service in a shared-metered building and is described in "A Lease Cannot Require the Tenant to Bond or Post Security to Defend".

Money does come into court in two places, but neither is a condition of defending. The first is redemption: under Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1(a) the tenant may bring the rent in arrears to court to redeem, and under subd. 1(b) may be permitted to pay the interest, costs and attorney's fee into court. The second is the tenant's own rent escrow action under Minn. Stat. section 504B.385, which the tenant starts, not the landlord. While that action is pending, subd. 1(d) requires the tenant to keep paying rent to the landlord or as the court directs and says the tenant "may not withhold rent to remedy a violation".

title: No Splitting Rent Collection From the Repair Duty — the Definition Does the Work
bodyText: Some states say outright that no lease, assignment, deed, trust deed or security instrument can let someone collect the rent free of the duty to keep the unit fit. Minnesota has no sentence like that. It reaches the same place by two other routes, and the result for you is the same: whoever is in control of the property and taking the rent carries the landlord's duties. The first route is the definition. For the whole of Minnesota's landlord-tenant chapter, a 'landlord' is an owner of real property, a contract for deed vendee, a receiver, an executor, a trustee, a lessee, an agent, or any other person directly or indirectly in control of rental property (Minn. Stat. section 504B.001, subdivision 7). A lender taking an assignment of rents, a trustee under a trust deed, a receiver and a management company are each inside that list or inside the words 'directly or indirectly in control', so handing over rent collection does not hand off the chapter. The second route is the non-waiver rule on the covenants themselves. In every residential lease or licence you covenant that the premises and common areas are fit for the use intended, that you will keep them in reasonable repair, that you will meet applicable federal, state and local health and safety laws including rental licensing ordinances, that you will make them reasonably energy efficient, and that you will supply heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit in every place intended for habitation from October 1 to April 30. The statute says the parties 'may not waive or modify' those covenants (Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subdivision 1). You may agree with the tenant that the tenant will do specified repairs or maintenance, but only for adequate consideration and in a conspicuous writing, and even then the agreement cannot waive the covenants or relieve you of maintaining common areas. The section is to be liberally construed, and letting the tenant inspect before signing does not defeat it. It applies to every lease or licence concluded or renewed on or after June 15, 1971, and estates at will are treated as renewed at the start of each rental period, so it covers every live tenancy. The disclosure statute makes the same point about money: it is enforceable against any successor landlord and against any individual to whom rent is paid, and if the required disclosure was not made, whoever collects the rent is treated as the agent authorised to accept notices and service of process (Minn. Stat. section 504B.181). The practical steps. If you assign rents to a lender, hire a management company, put the property in a trust or sell it, say in that agreement who performs the repair, heat, code and disclosure duties - because the statute will not split them for you, and the tenant can pursue whoever is in control. If a court appoints an administrator in a tenant remedies action, the administrator collects the rents and spends them on making the building habitable first, and your right to collect rent is void and unenforceable until the administration ends. One last point on receipts, which is a different sense of the same words: when a tenant pays rent or any other payment in cash you must give a written receipt, immediately if they pay in person and within three business days if not. That duty carries no express non-waiver sentence, but waiving it would be worthless to you, because since August 1, 2026 a violation of that section gives the tenant an affirmative defence to a nonpayment eviction, and on a showing of violation the eviction must be dismissed with the tenant's attorney fees (Minn. Stat. section 504B.118). This covers Minnesota's statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws.

title: No Minnesota Rent-Reporting Law
bodyText: Minnesota has no rent-reporting law. Nothing in Minnesota's landlord-tenant chapter, and nothing in the 2025 or 2026 session laws, requires you to offer positive rent reporting to a credit bureau, lets a tenant elect into or out of it, sets a signature block for that election, or requires you to notify a tenant before you report a late payment to a credit bureau. So reporting is a business decision you make with your reporting vendor, not something Minnesota regulates. Three cautions. First, federal law does regulate it. If you furnish payment information about a tenant to a consumer reporting agency you become a furnisher under the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, with accuracy and dispute-investigation duties. Get advice before you start reporting, and never report an amount you are still in dispute with the tenant about. Second, Minnesota regulates the other direction tightly - reports about tenants that you obtain or that screening services hold. Minnesota's tenant screening report regime in Minn. Stat. sections 504B.235 to 504B.245 gives a tenant rights to disclosure, correction and a written explanation, and the remedy in section 504B.245 runs against the landlord as well as the screening service: the greater of $1,000 or actual damages, costs of investigation and reasonable attorney fees, with attorney general enforcement. That is covered in the library's screening rows. Third, do not treat a rent-reporting programme as a fee. If you charge the tenant anything for it, it is a fee that has to be disclosed under Minn. Stat. section 504B.120, subdivision 1, and if the tenant cannot avoid it, it is a nonoptional fee that has to be inside the Total Monthly Payment on the first page of the lease. A nonoptional rent-reporting charge left off the first page carries treble damages. Keep rent reporting voluntary and free, or price it inside the Total Monthly Payment.

title: No Tax to Add to Rent — but a Tax Charge Is a Nonoptional Fee
bodyText: Nothing in Minnesota's landlord-tenant law puts a tax on residential rent, and nothing in it lets you add a tax, a tax reimbursement or a tax surcharge to the rent as a separate line. There is also no Minnesota statute in that chapter banning a landlord from passing a repealed local tax through to a tenant, and no burden-of-proof rule about it - questions other states answer and Minnesota does not. Whether residential rent is taxable is a question for Minnesota's sales and use tax chapter, so do not take this as advice that residential rent is or is not taxable; ask your accountant, and if the answer is that some charge in your lease is taxable, treat the tax as part of that charge rather than as a separate add-on the lease authorises. The Minnesota rule that does bite is the fee disclosure rule. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.120, subdivision 1 you must disclose all nonoptional fees in the lease, state the sum of rent plus all nonoptional fees as the Total Monthly Payment on the first page of the lease, and disclose nonoptional fees in any advertisement or posting for the unit. A tax, surcharge or tax reimbursement the tenant cannot avoid is a nonoptional fee. If you bill it, it belongs inside the first-page Total Monthly Payment, in a figure the tenant can read before signing. Leaving it out exposes you to treble damages and the tenant's attorney fees under subdivision 2. And do not relabel it as rent: Minnesota does not let you redefine fees as rent, and a late fee is expressly neither interest nor liquidated damages under Minn. Stat. section 504B.177. So the practical answer is that there is no tax clause to write. Charge a single rent figure, keep every nonoptional charge inside the Total Monthly Payment, and leave tax questions to your accountant.

title: Who Can Inspect a Minnesota Rental, and Why Your Lease Cannot Let Them In
bodyText:
Minnesota has no statewide rental inspection programme. No state statute requires a periodic inspection of a rental dwelling, sets an inspection cycle, or issues a state inspection certificate. Periodic rental inspection in Minnesota is a city programme, usually tied to a city rental licence, and Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(4) is the state hook that makes a city programme your problem: you covenant to maintain the premises and all common areas in compliance with the health and safety laws "of the local units of government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing". That express reference to rental licensing is as far as state law goes. We do not resolve city ordinances here, so find out whether your city licenses and inspects rentals, and on what cycle.

FIVE INSPECTION ROUTES DO COME FROM STATE LAW. (1) A TENANT CAN ORDER AN INSPECTION, and this is the one landlords most often do not know. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.185, subd. 1, if a residential tenant requests it -- or a housing-related neighbourhood organisation with a tenant's written permission, or such an organisation alone if the building is unoccupied -- "an inspection shall be made by the local authority charged with enforcing a code claimed to be violated". The inspector must then tell you and the tenant in writing about any code violations found, and "[a] reasonable period of time must be allowed in which to correct the violations" (subd. 2). Miss that period and the tenant can escrow rent under Sec. 504B.385 or bring the tenant remedies action under Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471.

(2) Health. Officers and employees of the Department of Health "shall have the right to enter any building, conveyance, or place where contagion, infection, filth, or other source or cause of preventable disease exists or is reasonably suspected" (Sec. 144.0535), and a member or agent of a community health board, county or city has the same right to enforce public health laws, ordinances or rules (Sec. 145A.04, subd. 7). Deliberately hindering them is a misdemeanour (Sec. 145A.04, subd. 10).

(3) Fire. Fire officials "at all reasonable hours may enter into all buildings and upon all premises within their jurisdiction for the purpose of examination, after proper consent from the occupant or owner or pursuant to an administrative search warrant" (Sec. 299F.09). After a fire, Sec. 299F.08 governs instead: immediate entry during and within a reasonable time after the fire, then consent or an administrative search warrant, with the judge weighing the scope of the search, prior entries, time of day, lapse of time, continued use of the building and the owner's efforts to secure it.

(4) Lead. Where a child has an elevated blood lead level, "[i]n a building with two or more dwelling units, an assessing agency shall assess the individual unit in which the conditions of this section are met and shall inspect all common areas accessible to a child" (Sec. 144.9504), and a lead order is enforced by the community health board "under a local ordinance or as a public health nuisance under chapter 145A" (Sec. 144.9509, subd. 1). See "Minnesota Lead Notices: None at Signing, One That Overrides Your Lease".

(5) Pools. If you have a pool, the annual owner certification and the daily drain inspection in Sec. 144.1222 apply -- see "Your Apartment Pool Is a Public Pool Under Minnesota Law".

NOW THE POINT THAT MATTERS MOST, AND IT IS A TRAP. Your lease cannot give an inspector advance permission to enter. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.211, subd. 3(4) does make "allowing inspections by state, county, or city officials charged in the enforcement of health, housing, building, fire prevention, or housing maintenance codes" a reasonable business purpose -- but that is a purpose for YOUR entry, on YOUR 24 hours' notice, not a right handed to the inspector. And subd. 2 closes the door on drafting round it: "A residential tenant may not waive and the landlord may not require the residential tenant to waive the residential tenant's right to prior notice of entry under this section as a condition of entering into or maintaining the lease." Separately, where a fire official needs consent, Sec. 299F.09 asks for consent "from the occupant or owner" -- the occupant at the door, not a signature you collected months earlier.

So a lease paragraph saying the tenant consents in advance to inspections at any time is worse than useless: asking for the signature is itself the conduct Sec. 504B.211 prohibits, and the penalty under subd. 6 runs to a rent reduction up to full rescission of the lease, return of the deposit less lawful retentions, up to a $500 civil penalty for EACH violation and reasonable attorney fees, with a violation of the section also being a violation of Sec. 504B.161.

What works instead is a cooperation clause that routes entry through the lease's own entry section -- see "Government Inspections" clause -- plus asking the tenant to let the inspector in and letting the inspector deal with any refusal through its own authority.

ONE MORE DUTY ONCE AN INSPECTION HAPPENS. If a citation issues on an inspection order that the inspector marks as threatening health or safety, or a condemnation order lands, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195 makes you hand copies out -- to the tenant within 72 hours, to anyone before they sign a lease or pay rent or a deposit, and to a new owner -- and that duty cannot be waived; see "You Must Hand Over Outstanding Inspection and Condemnation Orders". Do not confuse any of this with Sec. 504B.182, which is headed INITIAL AND FINAL INSPECTION REQUIRED but is about your move-in and move-out condition inspections with the tenant, for deposit purposes only.

title: Repair Costs Are Not a Way Out of a Minnesota Lease
bodyText: No Minnesota statute lets you end a lease, or refuse a repair, because the repair would cost too much. There is no threshold measured against the rent, against the property's value or against a percentage of anything, for you or for the tenant. The covenants in Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161 are stated without a cost limit and cannot be waived or modified, so expense is not a defence to them. One covenant has a cost test built in, and it runs the other way: the energy-efficiency duty in subd. 1(a)(3) is owed only where weatherstripping, caulking, storm windows or storm doors will save more in energy procurement cost than the measure costs, with interest, over the ten years after the cost is incurred. That is a limit on one duty, not a route out of a lease. What does end a tenancy over condition is the tenant's right, not yours. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.131 a tenant or occupant of a building that is destroyed, or becomes uninhabitable or unfit for occupancy, through no fault or neglect of the tenant or occupant, may vacate and surrender it. Cost is irrelevant to that right; fault is what matters, and a tenant who caused the damage has no statutory walk-away. The library covers that at Fire or Casualty: The Tenant May Leave. Two cost-related rules exist nearby and neither is a termination right. A court in a tenant remedies action may order the tenant to remedy a violation and deduct the cost from the rent on terms the court decides is just (Sec. 504B.425(c)), and before giving a court-appointed administrator funds the court must weigh the property's long-term economic viability, including the repairs needed to bring it into code compliance, the market value and whether present and future rents will cover the cost of repairs or rehabilitation (Sec. 504B.445, subd. 8). Those are the court's calls once a case is running. Neither gives you a cost-based exit. Practical effect: if a repair is uneconomic, your options are to do it, to sell, or to end the tenancy on ordinary grounds with the ordinary notice -- not to treat the cost as a reason the duty stops. A lease term letting you terminate because repairs are expensive would be an attempt to modify the covenants, which subd. 1(b) forbids.

title: No Small-Landlord Escrow Exemption, and No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states let a landlord with only a few units, or an owner living on site, opt out of the tenant's rent escrow or repair remedies by giving a notice. Minnesota has no such exemption and no such notice. Do not put one in a Minnesota lease. Minnesota's rent escrow action, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.385, applies wherever "a violation exists in a residential building", and "residential building" is defined broadly enough to cover a single-family home, an apartment building, a mixed-use building and a manufactured home park (Sec. 504B.001, subd. 11). There is no unit-count threshold, no owner-occupier carve-out and no registration or disclosure that switches the section off. The same is true of the tenant remedies action at Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471 and the emergency action at Sec. 504B.381. A lease term purporting to opt out would be void twice over, and each bar uses its own words. Sec. 504B.385, subd. 11: "The residential tenant rights under this section may not be waived or modified and are in addition to and do not limit other rights or remedies which may be available to the residential tenant and landlord, except as provided in subdivision 1." Sec. 504B.465: "Any provision of a lease or other agreement in which a provision of section 504B.381 or sections 504B.395 to 504B.471 is waived by a residential tenant is contrary to public policy and void." The words "except as provided in subdivision 1" do not create an exemption for you; subdivision 1 is the set of steps the tenant must take before depositing rent. Two fee points, because they are the nearest thing to a cost barrier and both run against you. The court administrator may charge the tenant a filing fee at the conciliation-court rate, but that is subject to an inability-to-pay affidavit (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 4), so a tenant without money still gets in. And where the escrow case is consolidated with your counterclaim for possession or a nonpayment eviction and you win, the court "may not require the residential tenant to pay the landlord's filing fee as a condition of retaining possession of the property when the residential tenant has deposited with the court the full amount of money found by the court to be owed" (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 9(c)). What you can do instead of opting out is make the escrow route unnecessary: answer repair requests promptly, and remember the tenant must keep paying rent to you or as the court directs while an escrow case runs and "may not withhold rent to remedy a violation" (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 1(d)). See Minnesota's Tenant Repair Remedies for the whole menu.

title: Repair Notice: Your Duty Does Not Wait for a Letter
bodyText:
Start with the point most landlords get wrong: your duties under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161 do not wait for notice. The five covenants are stated flatly, with no notice condition attached, so you owe reasonable repair, fitness, code compliance and winter heat whether or not anyone has written to you. Notice matters to the tenant's remedies, not to your duty.

The remedies each carry their own notice step, and the timings differ. For a code violation found on a municipal inspection, the tenant must wait until the time the inspector allowed to make repairs has run out without satisfactory repairs, unless the tenant claims the time allowed is excessive (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 1(b); Sec. 504B.395, subd. 3). For any other violation -- a breach of chapter 504B, of a discrimination law, of public or subsidised tenancy rights, or of the lease itself -- the tenant must give you written notice specifying the violation, delivered personally or sent to the person or place where rent is normally paid, and you have 14 days to correct it before rent can be deposited with the court administrator (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 1(c)). A tenant remedies action needs written notice to you at least 14 days before it is brought, which a court can excuse only if you cannot be located despite diligent efforts (Sec. 504B.395, subd. 4). Emergencies are different: for a revoked licence, a condemnation order or a loss of water, heat, electricity or sanitary facilities, the tenant need only attempt to notify you 24 hours before going to court, and a court may act with no notice to you at all if reasonable efforts to reach you failed (Sec. 504B.381, subd. 4). A tenant may also simply ask the local authority to inspect, and the inspector then tells you both in writing what was found and allows a reasonable period to correct it (Sec. 504B.185).

Your lease may ask for repair requests in writing, and the library's Repair Requests section does. Treat it as a record-keeping tool, not a condition. It cannot shorten or replace the statutory steps: the covenants may not be waived or modified (Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(b)), rent escrow rights "may not be waived or modified" (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 11), and a lease provision waiving Sec. 504B.381 or Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471 "is contrary to public policy and void" (Sec. 504B.465). So a clause requiring written requests does not stop a tenant relying on what you actually knew, and it does not limit any statutory defence.

Do not write a clause saying verbal notice is enough. No Minnesota statute lets a lease designate verbal notice for these procedures, and Sec. 504B.385, subd. 1(c) says the tenant "must give written notice". The only place chapter 504B accepts oral notice is Sec. 504B.216, where a tenant in a shared-metered building may give oral or written notice of an intention to pay for continued utility service, with written notice to follow within 24 hours -- a different subject.

What actually protects you are the cure windows above and the defences in Sec. 504B.415: that the violation does not exist or has been remedied; that it was caused by the willful, malicious, negligent or irresponsible conduct of a complaining tenant or someone under that tenant's direction or control; or that a tenant unreasonably refused you entry to fix it while you were trying in good faith. Each of those depends on your records. Log every request however it arrives -- call, text, e-mail or letter -- with the date, and log what you did.

title: Every Minnesota Disclosure, by When It Is Due and What Carries It
bodyText:
Minnesota has no single disclosure statute and no state disclosure form. What it has is about a dozen separate duties, and the thing that trips landlords up is not the content but the TIMING and the VEHICLE -- some go in the lease, some are handed over before anyone signs, some get posted on the wall, and one is annual. This note lists them all. Each item points to the note that explains it.

WHAT GOES IN THE LEASE OR THE APPLICATION. Nine rules put something in the document itself. Four apply to every written lease: the start and end dates and any prorated amount on the first page; all nonoptional fees plus a first-page Total Monthly Payment; the landlord's and manager's name and address; and, in a building of twelve or more units, a written lease identifying the unit. Four depend on what you charge. They are the service-and-support-animal fee notice if you charge any pet fee, the apportionment attachment if you apportion gas or water, the list of bill-copy rights that goes with it, and the billing schedule if you submeter. The ninth is on the application: the 'SSN or ITIN' option. That list and its consequences are in the lease-contents note.

WHAT YOU HAND OVER BEFORE ANYONE SIGNS. Four, and none of them lives in the lease. (1) Outstanding inspection and condemnation orders, to any person 'before signing a lease or paying rent or a security deposit to begin a new tenancy' (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195, subd. 1(a)(2)) -- see the inspection-and-condemnation note. (2) If you have had notice of a contract for deed cancellation or a mortgage foreclosure sale, written notice of that and of the date the cancellation or redemption period ends, 'before entering into a lease under this section and accepting any rent or security deposit' (Sec. 504B.151, subd. 1(b)), carrying a $500 civil penalty -- see the foreclosure-disclosure rows. (3) If you take a screening fee, a written disclosure of the screening service's name, address and telephone number and 'the criteria on which the decision to rent to the prospective tenant will be based', given before you accept the fee (Sec. 504B.173, subd. 3(1)), plus notice within 14 days of a rejection identifying the criteria the applicant failed to meet -- see the screening-fee note. (4) If your building contains accessible units, 'the landlord must inform nondisabled persons and families that do not include a disabled family member of the possibility of being offered a non-disability-equipped unit as provided under this section before a rental agreement to rent an accessible unit is entered' (Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.40, subd. 2(a)). That is a pre-signing disclosure in the Human Rights Act, not in chapter 504B, which is why it has been missed. If you rent an accessible unit to a household without a disabled member, tell them in writing first that they may later be asked to move to an equivalent unit at the same rent.

WHAT GOES ON THE WALL. Two postings, both under Sec. 504B.181, subd. 2. A printed or typewritten notice with the landlord and manager information 'in a conspicuous place on the premises' -- and the subdivision is satisfied if a notice you already post under another statute or ordinance carries the same information. And, 'unless the landlord is required to post a notice by section 471.9995', a second notice saying that a copy of the Attorney General's statement of landlord and tenant rights is available from the attorney general on request. Section 471.9995 is the alternative: it makes a city or town put that attorney-general referral on the rental licence, registration or certificate of occupancy itself, so where your city does that you do not post the second notice. Note the asymmetry in Sec. 504B.181, subd. 4: failure to make the subd. 1 disclosure blocks any action to recover rent or possession, but 'failure by the landlord to post a notice required by subdivision 2, paragraph (b), or section 471.9995 shall not prevent any action to recover rent or possession'. The posting is the one disclosure failure in the chapter whose rent-and-possession consequence the statute expressly takes away. Also non-health-and-safety inspection orders get a posted summary rather than a copy (Sec. 504B.195, subd. 1(b)).

TWO VERBATIM TEXTS THAT ARE NOT YOURS TO PARAPHRASE, each shown in full in its own note. The urea formaldehyde IMPORTANT HEALTH NOTICE under Sec. 325F.18, subd. 1(a), whose scope is narrow: it binds a BUILDER who sells or leases to the INITIAL OCCUPANT a housing unit containing urea formaldehyde, and it does not apply to manufactured housing. And the spa pool NOTICE under Sec. 144.1222, subd. 2d(e), which must be conspicuously posted at the spa and 'provided to renters upon check in'. Both exist as their own rows with the text reproduced exactly; use those, not a retyped version.

MANUFACTURED HOME PARKS ARE A SEPARATE AND LONGER LIST. Four duties, plus one that is annual. Before a prospective resident is asked to sign, they must be given the IMPORTANT NOTICE set out word for word in Sec. 327C.02, subd. 5, 'printed verbatim in boldface type of a minimum size of ten points', provided with the park residency application AND posted 'in a conspicuous and public location in the park'. The park owner must give each resident a copy of the signed rental agreement 'with a copy of the evacuation or shelter plan attached' (Sec. 327C.025). Before water and sewer billing starts, 'in each of the three months prior to commencement of utility billing, a park owner must provide the resident with a sample bill' (Sec. 327C.04, subd. 6). And the park's written procedures and criteria for evaluating a buyer in an in-park sale must be 'included with the rental application and... available at no charge to residents, prospective buyers, and their agents' (Sec. 327C.07, subd. 2(1) and (2)). The annual one is in the Sec. 327C.02, subd. 5 notice itself: 'By February 1 of each year, the park must give you a certificate of rent paid as required by Minnesota Statutes, sections 290.0693, subdivision 4, and 290A.19.'

AND TWO THINGS MINNESOTA DOES NOT ASK YOU FOR, which matter because landlords arriving from other states expect them. There is no state lead disclosure at signing -- the pre-1978 notice you give is the federal one -- and the Radon Awareness Act's warning statement runs to a buyer, not a tenant, reaching a lease only where the lease carries an option to purchase. Both have their own notes. There is no Minnesota mold disclosure at all. And the one piece of paper most landlords assume is theirs to produce is not: the Attorney General writes and revises the statement of landlord and tenant rights under Sec. 504B.275, holds a public meeting on it each year, and makes it available. Your duty is the posted notice that it exists, not the document.

title: What Minnesota Does and Does Not Limit About Your Fees
bodyText:
Minnesota has no list of fees you may or may not charge a residential tenant, no cap on a markup when you rebill a service a third party bills you for, and no notice period for adding a fee during the term. What it does have is a disclosure rule with teeth: every nonoptional fee must be in the lease, and rent plus all nonoptional fees must appear on the first page as the Total Monthly Payment, with treble damages and possible attorney fees for getting it wrong.

The specific limits come from separate statutes, so check each fee against them. Before the tenancy you may take an applicant screening fee (with its own receipt, disclosure and return rules) and a prelease deposit under a conspicuous written agreement. A late fee needs a written agreement and cannot exceed 8% of the overdue rent payment.

If you bill any utility separately from rent, your only permitted extras are one administrative billing charge of up to $8 per billing period and one late payment charge of up to $5 a month, which may not be compounded; no other fee or charge for utility service is allowed, including the cost of installing, maintaining, repairing, replacing or reading a submeter, and you may not bill a tenant for utilities used in common areas, in your own spaces or in vacant units. You may not charge any fee for using an alternative when your digital payment platform is not working.

Your advertising must disclose nonoptional fees and whether utilities are included. Minnesota also treats it as a deceptive trade practice to advertise, display or offer a price that leaves out a mandatory fee or surcharge; that law is written for goods and services generally, so the safe course is to advertise the Total Monthly Payment.

To add a nonoptional fee in the middle of a term, get the tenant's written agreement, because the lease must disclose it. Minnesota sets no fixed notice period for a rent increase, but if your lease gives the tenant a notice period for quitting, your notice of a rent increase may not be shorter than that, and that rule cannot be waived. This covers Minnesota's statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws.

title: No Duty to Give a Tenant the State Rights Guide
bodyText:
No. There is no Minnesota statute requiring a landlord to give a tenant a state-published rights and responsibilities guide, before signing, at renewal or at any other time, and no acknowledgment for the tenant to sign.

Minnesota does publish such a document. Minn. Stat. § 504B.275 makes it the attorney general's duty to "prepare and make available to the public a statement which summarizes the significant legal rights and obligations of landlords and residential tenants of rental dwelling units", revised annually. But the section's duties fall on the attorney general, not on you: prepare, revise, hold a public meeting, publish. Nothing in it, and nothing elsewhere in the landlord-tenant act, requires a landlord to deliver it, attach it, offer it or obtain a receipt for it. Manufactured home park residents are excluded from the section.

So there is nothing to put in the lease on this topic and no acknowledgment clause to draft. If a lease form you are adapting from another state carries a rights-guide receipt or acknowledgment, delete it rather than leaving it in — a signed acknowledgment that the tenant received a document you had no duty to give, and may not have given, is a liability with no upside.

Two things not to confuse with this. The attorney general's statement is not the same as the pre-eviction notice under Minn. Stat. § 504B.321, subd. 1a, which does require you to include prescribed wording telling the tenant about legal aid and financial help — that is a real delivery duty, but it attaches to a notice before filing an eviction, not to the lease. And the plain-language obligation recorded at "Minnesota's Plain-Language Lease Requirement" is about how your own lease is written, not about handing over a government document.

If you want to give new tenants the attorney general's statement anyway, do. It costs nothing and a tenant who knows the rules is easier to deal with. Just do not take a signature for it.

title: House Rules in Minnesota - No Statute, But Eight Limits
bodyText:
Minnesota has no house-rules statute for an ordinary site-built rental. No section sets a test a rule must pass to be enforceable, and none governs changing rules mid-tenancy. Rules in force when the lease is signed are ordinary lease terms, and a later rule binds the tenant only by agreement or at a renewal.

That freedom runs up against eight limits. First, you may not adopt any rule prohibiting tenants or nonresident tenant organizers from peacefully organizing, assembling, canvassing, leafleting or otherwise exercising free expression for tenant organizing in the building. You may not require prior permission, and you may not adopt or enforce rules setting unreasonable limits on the time, place or manner of their meetings or communication (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.212, subd. 1). A bad-faith violation costs up to $1,000 per occurrence plus the tenant's reasonable attorney fees.

Second, a rule change can be retaliation. You may not alter an existing rental agreement, decrease services, increase rent or sue after a tenant reports a code violation, asks for repairs or joins a tenant association, and if you act within 90 days the burden of proof is yours (Sec. 504B.212, subd. 2). Separately, a tenant's lease obligations may not be increased, nor services decreased, as a penalty for complaining of a violation (Sec. 504B.441).

Third, no rule can move your own duties to the tenant. The parties may not waive or modify the landlord's covenants of fitness, repair and compliance with health and safety codes, and no agreement may relieve you of the duty to maintain common areas (Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1).

Fourth, you may not bar or limit a tenant's right to call for police or emergency assistance, or penalise a tenant for calling. The tenant cannot waive that right and you must not ask for a waiver (Sec. 504B.205).

Fifth, you cannot take away the tenant's right to notice before entry as a condition of entering into or keeping the lease (Sec. 504B.211).

Sixth, you cannot prohibit a tenant from legally possessing cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles or hemp-derived consumer products, or from using a cannabinoid or hemp-derived consumer product. A rule against smoking or vaping them is still allowed (Sec. 504B.171, subd. 1).

Seventh, a rule cannot reach conduct away from the property. You may not penalise a tenant or end a tenancy for conduct off the premises and curtilage. There are two exceptions. One is conduct that would be a crime of violence against another tenant, a guest, you or your employees. The other is conduct that results in a conviction for a crime of violence against someone unconnected with the property (Sec. 504B.171, subd. 2a).

Eighth, a rule requiring an animal to be declawed or devocalized is void and unenforceable (Sec. 504B.114).

Two practical points. If a rule carries a charge the tenant cannot avoid, that charge must be disclosed in the lease and counted in the first-page Total Monthly Payment (Sec. 504B.120). And if you run a manufactured home park, none of the above is your regime: chapter 327C gives park lots a full rules code, including a reasonableness test, a 60-day notice requirement for any rule change and a defence to eviction that the rule was unreasonable. This lease is the wrong instrument for a park lot.

title: If the Lease Was Recorded, Ending It Does Not Clear the Title Record
bodyText: This one only bites if the lease was RECORDED, which is unusual for a residential tenancy but does happen with long leases and with ground leases. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.251 says that 'where a lease has been duly recorded, the county recorder must record a copy of the notice of cancellation or termination of the lease that has been presented for recording by the landlord, landlord's agent, or attorney'. Two things must travel with the notice: proof of service, and 'an affidavit of the landlord or the landlord's agent or attorney stating that the tenant has not complied with the terms of the notice'. The recorded notice 'is prima facie evidence of the facts stated in it'. The duty in the section runs on the recorder, not on you -- but the practical point is yours: if a tenant has recorded the lease, ending the tenancy does not by itself clear the record, and a buyer, a lender or a title examiner will still see the lease until you present the notice, the proof of service and the affidavit. Minnesota has three more recording provisions of the same family and they are worth knowing together. Sec. 504B.291 subd. 3: when you recover possession in an eviction action, a certified copy of the judgment is recorded on presentation, and where you recover by the tenant's abandonment or surrender you record your own affidavit instead; either is prima facie evidence. Minn. Stat. Sec. 559.21 does the same twice for a contract for deed cancellation: under subd. 4(e) a copy of the notice with proof of service, plus the seller's affidavit that the purchaser has not complied, may be recorded and is prima facie evidence of the facts stated in it, and subd. 9 adds a further recordable affidavit for an investor seller. Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.095 subd. 11 does it for a manufactured home park sale. None of them creates a duty to record -- each gives you a way to put the end of an interest on the title record and get the benefit of a presumption. A lease term telling the tenant not to record the lease without your consent is lawful in Minnesota, because it waives nothing the statutes give the tenant; the library does not currently offer one, and a landlord who wants one should have it drafted and take advice first.

title: When a Rental Changes Hands, Minnesota Duties Follow Control, Not the Deed
bodyText: Minnesota attaches landlord duties to CONTROL, not to the deed, and that is the single most useful thing to know when a rental changes hands. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.001 subd. 7 defines 'landlord' as 'an owner of real property, a contract for deed vendee, receiver, executor, trustee, lessee, agent, or other person directly or indirectly in control of rental property'. So a buyer, a receiver, a contract-for-deed purchaser, a trustee or a managing agent is the landlord for Chapter 504B purposes from the moment it controls the property, whether or not anyone sends the tenant anything. Three specific carry-overs follow. (1) IDENTITY DISCLOSURE TRANSFERS: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.181 subd. 6 says the section 'extends to and is enforceable against any successor landlord or individual to whom rental payments for the premises are made' -- so the new owner inherits the duty to disclose the manager and the agent for service of process, and inherits subd. 4's bar on maintaining an action to recover rent or possession if it has not been done. See "Disclosure of Landlord and Manager" clause and "Skipping the Landlord Disclosure Can Block Your Eviction". (2) THE DEPOSIT HAS ITS OWN 60-DAY CLOCK under Sec. 504B.178 subds. 5 and 6, including the buyer-side 20-day objection cap -- see "Selling the Property Starts a 60-Day Deposit Clock". (3) YOU MUST DISCLOSE CODE PAPERWORK TO THE BUYER: Sec. 504B.195 subd. 1(a)(3) requires outstanding inspection orders for which a citation has issued, and outstanding condemnation orders, to go to 'a person prior to obtaining new ownership of the property subject to the order or declaration' -- see "You Must Hand Over Outstanding Inspection and Condemnation Orders". WHAT MINNESOTA DOES NOT GIVE YOU: there is no statute requiring you to tell a sitting tenant that you have sold or changed managers, no release-on-sale provision, no statutory right of first refusal for a residential tenant, and no statute on showings during a sale -- the ordinary entry-notice rules apply instead. Put what you need into the lease and the purchase agreement, because the statute will not supply it. One point for a buyer: apart from the deposit, which the new owner takes on under Sec. 504B.178 subd. 6 (above), nothing in Chapter 504B makes the new owner liable for the seller's acts, EXCEPT where the seller's lease was signed under the financial-distress rules, where Sec. 504B.151 subds. 3 and 4 set out exactly what a holder does and does not take on.

title: Minnesota Has No Sanitary Code for Rentals, But It Does Have Two Variances You Can Apply For
bodyText: Start with what does not exist. Minnesota has no state sanitary code for rental dwellings. The commissioner of health's public health rulemaking power under Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.12, subd. 1 reaches "the construction and equipment, in respect to sanitary conditions, of schools, hospitals, almshouses, prisons, and other public institutions, and of lodging houses and other public sleeping places kept for gain" (clause 6), industrial, lumber and migrant labour camps (clause 11), and "the general sanitation of tourist camps, summer hotels, and resorts" (clause 12) -- and it stops there. An ordinary apartment or rented house is not on that list. There is accordingly no state sanitary code variance for a rental dwelling, no procedure for applying for one, and no duty to give a variance to a tenant or attach it to the lease. If you are expecting the Massachusetts pattern -- a state sanitary code for housing, a local board variance, and a duty to hand the variance to tenants and attach it to the rental agreement -- Minnesota has no part of that chain. TWO REAL VARIANCES DO EXIST AND BOTH CAN MATTER TO A LANDLORD. First, the State Fire Code. On application the state fire marshal may grant a variance from the code's minimum requirements "if there is substantial compliance with the provisions of the code, the safety of the public and occupants of such building will not be jeopardized, and undue hardship will result to the applicant unless such variance is granted" (Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.011, subd. 5). Go locally first: no appeal to the fire marshal for a variance from a local fire official's order is accepted "until the applicant has first made application to the local governing body and the local unit has acted on the application", and a local governing body may appoint a board of appeal (subds. 5 and 5a). And subd. 5b is the sentence rental housing owners should know: on a variance appeal the local appeal board or governing body, the state fire marshal, a state administrative law judge and a court "shall take into consideration the benefit to be obtained by complying with the fire marshal's orders and the effect on affordable housing, provided that the spirit of the code is complied with and public safety secured". Second, pools and spas. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.1222, subd. 1a puts "requests for a variance" from the public pool and spa rules on the same footing as construction plans: they are submitted to the commissioner under Minnesota Rules, part 4717.3975 and "shall be accompanied by the appropriate fees", and the fee schedule sets "request for variance from the public pool and spa rules, $550". Since a residents-only apartment pool is a public pool in Minnesota, that variance is available to you -- see "Your Apartment Pool Is a Public Pool Under Minnesota Law". WHAT IS NOT A VARIANCE FOR YOU. Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.6535 is headed VARIANCE OR WAIVER and sets out a full application, criteria, renewal and appeal procedure -- but subd. 1 opens "A hospital may request", and the only requirement it reaches is Sec. 144.55, subd. 3(b). It is a hospital licensing provision and gives a landlord nothing. NO LEASE DUTY ATTACHES TO ANY VARIANCE. Neither Sec. 299F.011 nor Sec. 144.1222 requires you to disclose a variance, deliver it to a tenant or attach it to the lease, and Minnesota's one inspection-paperwork disclosure duty is about something else: Minn. Stat.
