Sec. 504B.195 makes you hand over outstanding inspection orders for which a citation has been issued and outstanding condemnation orders, not variances -- see "You Must Hand Over Outstanding Inspection and Condemnation Orders". WHERE A HOUSING SANITARY CODE WILL ACTUALLY BE. Your city. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.001, subd. 14(1) defines a "violation" by reference to "any state, county or city health, safety, housing, building, fire prevention, or housing maintenance code applicable to the building", and Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(4) requires you to maintain the premises and all common areas in compliance with health and safety laws "of the local units of government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing". Minnesota's housing sanitary standards are municipal, and so is any variance from them, including whether your city makes you give it to tenants. We do not resolve city ordinances in this library.

title: Minnesota Has No Seasonal Tenancy - a Summer Let Is an Ordinary Tenancy
bodyText: Minnesota has no seasonal or vacation tenancy category. Its landlord-tenant act, Minn. Stat. ch. 504B, defines a lease as any oral or written agreement creating a tenancy, with no minimum or maximum length, and defines a residential tenant by occupation of a dwelling for money or services rather than by how long the stay lasts. So a cabin let for the summer, a lake cottage let for a season and a furnished unit let for two months are all ordinary residential tenancies here. Every chapter 504B duty applies to them in full: the habitability covenants, the deposit rules, the written-lease requirement for a building with 12 or more units, the lease start and end date on the first page, and the notice periods for ending a tenancy. Chapter 504B has only a handful of scope exceptions and none of them is seasonal; the two that exclude manufactured home parks are the privacy section and the financial-distress lease section. Two practical consequences. First, do not copy a seasonal or vacation-rental clause from another state's lease: it will usually assume an exemption Minnesota does not give, and a term waiving a chapter 504B right the tenant has is void whatever the lease calls the letting. Second, a short let is still ended by the notice the law and your lease require, and for a tenancy with no fixed end date that notice runs a full rental period. If you genuinely operate a hotel, resort or lodging establishment rather than a rental, a different body of licensing law applies, and you should take advice before treating an occupancy as something other than a tenancy. Local short-term-rental ordinances are a city matter.

title: Where a Minnesota Deposit Sits - and the One Thing the Statute Says About It
bodyText: Minnesota says two things about holding a deposit and then stops. First, the money is held by you for the tenant: it is the tenant's money in your hands, not income. Second, and unusually, the statute says a deposit is not received in a fiduciary capacity within the meaning of the real estate licensing definition of trust funds - a definition that otherwise sweeps in damage deposits - so a licensed broker or property manager who collects a residential security deposit is not holding trust funds under that definition and the deposit does not go into a broker trust account on that basis. What Minnesota does not require is almost everything other states require: no escrow account, no trust account, no separate or dedicated account, no federally insured institution, no bar on mixing the deposit with your own money, no surety or guarantee bond you may post instead, no duty to tell the tenant which bank holds it, and no unit-count threshold that switches any of that on. You may keep it in your operating account. That freedom costs you nothing only if you keep the money traceable, because four duties run whether or not you set it aside: one percent simple noncompounded interest accrues from the first day of the month after it is paid in full; you must return it with interest, or send a written statement of the specific reasons for withholding, within three weeks of the tenancy ending, or within five days where the tenant left because the building was legally condemned through no fault of the tenant; in any dispute you carry the burden of proving the reason for any withholding; and if your interest in the property ends you have 60 days to transfer it with interest to your successor and tell the tenant, or to return it. A lease term waiving any of that is void. Minneapolis and Saint Paul regulate deposits by ordinance, so check the city rule where your property is.

title: One Percent Interest on the Deposit, and How to Work It Out
bodyText: You owe the tenant interest on the security deposit, and Minnesota states the rate and the method exactly. The rate is simple noncompounded interest at one percent a year. It is not compounded and it does not track any index. It starts on the first day of the month after the month in which the deposit is paid in full, so a deposit paid part-way through March starts earning on April 1. It stops at the earlier of two dates: the last day of the month in which you comply, in good faith, with the duty to return the deposit or send the written statement of reasons for withholding, or the date judgment is entered in a civil action about your liability for the deposit. Any interest amount under one dollar is left out, so a small deposit held a short time may carry none. Work the figure out before you send the refund. Minnesota prescribes no form for showing it, but a one-line calculation on your statement settles most arguments. Three things follow from the interest being the tenant's. It goes back with the deposit, and if you withhold wrongly the penalty is measured on the amount withheld plus the interest on it, so the interest doubles with the rest. When your interest in the property ends, the interest travels with the deposit to your successor or back to the tenant. And a lease term giving up interest is void, as is any other attempted waiver of the deposit section.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Minnesota's security deposit section carries its own non-waiver sentence: any attempted waiver of the section by a landlord and tenant, by contract or otherwise, is void and unenforceable. That covers every part of it - the one percent simple interest, the three-week return and written statement, the five-day return when the tenant leaves because the building is condemned, the limit on what you may withhold, the burden of proving a withholding being on you, the 60-day duty to transfer or return the deposit when your interest in the property ends, the penalty equal to the amount withheld plus interest, and the bad-faith award of up to $500 per deposit. So a lease term that shortens your clock, makes a deposit or part of one nonrefundable, gives up interest, shifts the burden of proof to the tenant, caps your liability, or makes the refund depend on something the statute does not require is simply void; the rest of the lease stands, but you have shown a court you planned to keep money you were not entitled to. This applies to every tenancy commencing or renewed on or after July 1, 1973, and an estate at will is treated as renewed at the start of each rental period, so it applies to every live tenancy. Two neighbouring sections that bear on the deposit are non-waivable in the same terms: the initial and move-out inspection section, and the section requiring disclosure of outstanding inspection and condemnation orders.

title: What a Deposit Mistake Costs You in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota prices deposit mistakes in two layers, and the first one is a doubling. Four failures trigger it: not providing the written statement within three weeks of the tenancy ending; not providing it within five days when the tenant left because the building or dwelling was legally condemned for reasons not due to the tenant's willful, malicious or irresponsible conduct; not transferring or returning the deposit when your interest in the property ends; and not giving the tenant notice of the initial and move-out inspection options, or not completing an inspection the tenant asked for. Any of those, once you have the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, makes you liable for damages equal to the portion of the deposit you withheld plus the interest on it, as a penalty, on top of returning the portion wrongfully withheld and its interest. The same amount leaves your pocket twice. The second layer is bad faith. Retaining a deposit, the interest on it, or any part of either in bad faith adds punitive damages of up to $500 for each deposit, on top of the penalty. Bad faith is presumed if you failed to comply with the return-and-statement duty or the duty on termination of your interest, unless you return the deposit within two weeks after an action for its recovery is started - which is, in practice, your last chance to cap the exposure. Two more points decide real cases. In any action about the deposit, the burden of proving the reason for withholding any part of it, by a fair preponderance of the evidence, is yours; contemporaneous photographs, the move-out inspection and invoices are what discharge it. And the tenant may sue in the county where the property is or, at the tenant's option, in the county where you live, including in conciliation court.

title: No Deposit-Standards Posting Rule in Minnesota
bodyText: Nothing in Minnesota law requires you to post, publish or hand a prospective tenant the standards you use to decide how large a security deposit to ask for, even where you charge different tenants different amounts, and Minnesota has no building-size trigger of the kind South Carolina applies to a landlord of more than four adjoining units. How you set the figure is your decision. Four limits still bite. Minnesota sets no statewide cap on the amount, but Minneapolis and Saint Paul cap deposits by ordinance, so the city rule where the property is may be stricter than the state rule and you have to check it. Whatever you collect, if its function is to secure performance of the lease or any part of it, it is a security deposit and the whole of the deposit section applies to it however the lease labels it. The Minnesota Human Rights Act makes it an unfair discriminatory practice to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of renting a dwelling because of race, colour, creed, religion, national origin, sex, gender identity, marital status, status with regard to public assistance, disability, sexual orientation or familial status, so any difference between applicants needs a written, neutral basis you can show - income, credit, rental history - applied the same way to everyone, and the Act has its own exemptions that are worth checking if you think one applies to you. And the screening fee you charge to run the check is separately regulated, so keep the two apart. The practical advice is to write your deposit standards down for yourself even though you need not publish them: a one-page internal standard, consistently applied, is the cheapest answer to a discrimination complaint. Minnesota's statutes and session laws contain no posting or disclosure rule.

title: No Work Card for Senior Housing Staff, But Two Senior Rules That Do Apply
bodyText: Minnesota has no work card, no permit, no licence and no mandatory background check for maintenance, housekeeping or management staff in housing for older persons, or in any other private rental housing. The phrase work card does not appear in Minnesota law at all. Staff screening in ordinary rental housing, including 55-plus housing, is your own policy. Licensed settings are different: assisted living and health-care facilities carry their own staff requirements, and those are not rental-housing rules. Two senior-specific rules do apply to you, and both are easy to get wrong. First, entry. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.211, subd. 3(7) lists prearranged housekeeping work in senior housing where 80 percent or more of the residential tenants are age 55 or older as a reasonable business purpose for entering a unit. Read what that does and does not do. Subd. 3 only defines what counts as a reasonable business purpose; the duty in subd. 2 still stands, so you must still make a good faith effort to give at least 24 hours notice, still specify a time or window, and still enter between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless the tenant agrees otherwise. Prearranged housekeeping is a permitted REASON to enter, not an exception to notice. The tenant may agree to less than 24 hours notice if they wish, but you may not require that agreement as a condition of entering into or maintaining the lease. Getting this wrong is expensive: subd. 6 allows a rent reduction up to full rescission of the lease, return of the damage deposit, up to a $500 civil penalty for each violation and attorney fees, and makes the breach a breach of Sec. 504B.161 as well. Second, the two 80-percent tests are not the same test. Sec. 504B.211, subd. 3(7) measures 80 percent or more of the RESIDENTIAL TENANTS being age 55 or older. The fair housing elderly-housing exemption at Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.21, subd. 2(b)(3) measures something different: housing intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person 55 or older per unit, where at least 80 percent of the UNITS are occupied by at least one person 55 or older per unit, with published policies demonstrating that intent. A building can satisfy one and fail the other. Do not use a 55-plus designation you rely on for one purpose as evidence for the other. Also note what the elderly-housing exemption actually buys you. Sec. 363A.21, subd. 2 exempts housing for elderly persons from the FAMILIAL STATUS prohibition only - not from the rest of Sec. 363A.09. Race, creed, religion, disability, status with regard to public assistance and the other grounds still apply in full. And one more exposure worth knowing if your residents are older: Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.71 adds a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation, on top of the ordinary consumer-fraud and deceptive-trade-practices penalties, where the prohibited conduct is perpetrated against a senior citizen (defined there as 62 or older) or a disabled person, and subd. 4 gives an injured person their own civil action for damages, costs of investigation and attorney fees.

title: No Minnesota Duty to Disclose a Registered Offender
bodyText: Minnesota does not require a landlord to disclose to applicants or tenants that a registered predatory offender lives at or near the property. The landlord-tenant act contains nothing on it. Neither does the Human Rights Act, the fire and safety chapter, the health chapter or the consumer-protection chapters. THE NOTIFICATION REGIME RUNS THROUGH THE POLICE. Minnesota's predatory-offender community-notification statute, Minn. Stat. Sec. 244.052, was read. It makes the local law enforcement agency, not a landlord, disclose information about an offender, scaled to the offender's risk level (subd. 4). For risk level III offenders, the Department of Corrections must post the information on a public website (subd. 4b). The section's immunity from liability covers agencies, officials and those acting on their behalf, not a landlord who passes information on (subd. 7). It also says it imposes no duty on a real estate licensee under chapter 82 to disclose information about a registered offender (subd. 8). WHAT YOU CAN RELY ON. There is no Minnesota statute requiring the disclosure to be in the lease, so no clause is offered. Two things cut the other way and are worth knowing. You may not deny a rental application based on a court file that is not public, has been expunged, or has been destroyed (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.173 subd. 3a), so a record you cannot lawfully act on is not a record you should be circulating. And if you do volunteer information about a resident, you are making a statement about an identified person with no statutory protection for doing so. The safe answer to an applicant who asks is to tell them where the public registry information comes from and let them look, rather than to answer the question yourself.

title: No Minnesota Offender Occupancy Rule for Most Landlords -- Enforce Conduct, Not Status
bodyText: Minnesota does not restrict where a registered predatory offender may live in rental housing, impose a proximity rule on a landlord, or make it an offence to lease a dwelling to two registered offenders who will live together. There is one narrow exception, below. Several states have one or more of those; nothing of the kind appears in the landlord-tenant act. WHAT MINN. STAT. SEC. 244.052 DOES. The proximity rules in Minnesota's community-notification statute bind the agency supervising a risk level III offender, not you. When such an offender is released or moves while on supervised release, the agency must consider proximity to other level III offenders and to schools, child care, parks and similar places, and mitigate concentration where it presents a risk of reoffending (subd. 4a(a)). THE ONE LANDLORD RULE. Suppose you own or manage an apartment building, hotel, motel or lodging establishment and have an agreement with an agency that shelters domestic abuse victims. Then you may not knowingly rent to both level III offenders and domestic abuse victims at the same time (subd. 4a(b)). If you learn after renting that a tenant is a level III offender, the statute says you may evict the offender; it sets no separate procedure, so use the ordinary eviction process. Local ordinances are a further question this library never resolves, and residency-restriction ordinances are exactly the kind of thing cities adopt. Check the city where the property sits and take advice. WHAT A LEASE MAY SAY. No clause is offered, and the reason is not that Minnesota forbids one. It is that an occupancy restriction aimed at a class of person, resting on no Minnesota statute, is a term you should not adopt from a form. Three Minnesota rules do bear on it and are worth knowing. You may not deny a rental application based on a pending eviction action, a court file that is not public, has been expunged, or has been destroyed, or an eviction that did not end in a writ of recovery (Sec. 504B.173 subd. 3a). Every lease already contains the Sec. 504B.171 covenant against controlled substances, prostitution-related activity, unlawful firearm use or possession and stolen property on the premises, in the common area and in the curtilage, and neither party may waive or modify it -- so conduct on the property is already covered without an occupancy clause. And Sec. 504B.171 subd. 2a caps what you may do about any off-premises conduct of a tenant, a household member or a guest. Enforce conduct, not status.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Disclosure, But Two First-Page Duties and One Posting Trap
bodyText:
Minnesota has no occupancy disclosure that applies because the property is a single-family home, and no rule requiring a lease disclosure to be in type larger than the rest of the lease. If you rent out a house rather than an apartment, the state's disclosure duties are the same ones as for any other rental.

Two placement duties do exist, and both are about the first page rather than the type size. Minn. Stat. section 504B.146 requires a written residential lease to identify the lease start date and the lease end date, and to indicate the prorated rent where move-in or move-out falls on a day other than the first or last of the month; it then says the information 'must be provided on the first page of the lease'. Minn. Stat. section 504B.120, subd. 1 requires the sum of rent and all nonoptional fees to be described as the Total Monthly Payment and listed on the first page of the lease, with treble damages under subd. 2 for a violation. Plan page one around both of them.

The one place Minnesota's disclosure duties really do turn on how many units the building has is worth knowing precisely, because it works the opposite way from what a landlord would guess. Minn. Stat. section 504B.181, subd. 2(b) requires you to post a notice on the property stating that a copy of the attorney general's statement of tenant rights and responsibilities is available - 'unless the landlord is required to post a notice by section 471.9995'. And Minn. Stat. section 471.9995 reaches only a city or town licence, registration or certificate of occupancy 'required to be posted in a building containing multiple rental dwelling units'. A single-family rental is therefore outside section 471.9995, so the subd. 2(b) posting duty is never lifted for it: at a house you must do the posting yourself, whereas at a multiunit building the city-issued posted document can carry it for you. That is one more duty for the single-family landlord, not one fewer.

title: No Shoreline or Lake-Access Disclosure Duty in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota requires no shoreline or lake-access disclosure to a residential tenant. There is nothing like the Rhode Island shoreline-access notice: no statement of where the public shore right begins, no notice that a tenant may or may not use a dock or a beach, and no rule about advertising lake access. WHY THAT IS UNSURPRISING. Minnesota regulates shoreland through Minn. Stat. ch. 103F and the shoreland and floodplain ordinances that counties and cities adopt under it. Shoreland management is a land-use regime aimed at development, setbacks and water quality, not at what a lease must say. The shoreland, shoreline and riparian provisions of the 2025 and 2026 session laws are conservation easements, habitat restoration appropriations, riparian buffer programmes or land conveyances. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR A LAKE-PROPERTY LEASE. Nothing is required, so what the tenant gets is what your lease gives them. That makes the lease the only place the question is answered, and silence invites an argument. If the property has shore frontage, a dock, a boat slip, a mooring, a swimming area or a shared association access, say in the lease whether the tenant may use it, who maintains it, who stores and launches what, and whether guests are included. If access is through a neighbour's land, an easement or a homeowners association, say so and say what the tenant must comply with. If the shore is NOT included, say that too. Two Minnesota points to keep in view. A common interest community or association rule is a separate layer, under chapter 515B. And a local shoreland ordinance may limit what can be built, stored or launched; that is a municipal matter, so check it with the county or city rather than relying on this row. FINALLY, THE HABITABILITY FLOOR STILL APPLIES. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) makes you covenant that the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended by the parties and that you will keep them in reasonable repair, and subd. 1(b) says the parties may not waive or modify those covenants. If you let a lake property and the dock is part of what the tenant is paying for, a rotten dock is a repair question, not merely a disappointment.

title: You Cannot Shorten the Showing Notice in the Lease, Even in a Separate Addendum
bodyText:
There is nothing to waive here, and trying to waive it is the violation. Minnesota is the opposite of the states where a lease can set its own showing notice.

Start with what you are allowed to do. Minn. Stat. section 504B.211, subd. 3 names showings twice: showing the unit to prospective residential tenants during the notice period before the lease terminates, or after the tenant has given notice to move; and showing the unit to a prospective buyer or to an insurance representative. So end-of-lease showings and sale viewings are squarely lawful purposes. What the statute does not do is give them a different notice. Subd. 2's notice - a good faith effort, not less than 24 hours, a specified time or anticipated window of time, entry only between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. - applies to a showing exactly as it applies to a repair.

The waiver route is closed, and closed in two directions. Subd. 2 ends: 'A residential tenant may not waive and the landlord may not require the residential tenant to waive the residential tenant's right to prior notice of entry under this section as a condition of entering into or maintaining the lease.' A clause saying the tenant agrees to same-day notice for showings during the last 60 days is the waiver the first limb forbids, and presenting it for signature is the conduct the second limb forbids. Nor can you move it to a separate signed addendum: Minnesota has no provision like Delaware's permitting a shortened showing notice in a separate document, and putting the same waiver on its own page does not change what it is.

What does work is agreement at the time. Subd. 2 says in terms that 'A residential tenant may permit a landlord to enter the rented premises with less than 24 hours notice if desired.' A text message asking whether 2 p.m. today suits, answered yes, is a lawful showing on two hours' notice. So ask for flexibility; do not draft for it. In practice, tell the tenant early that showings are coming, offer a standing window the tenant finds convenient and confirm each visit, and give the full 24 hours' notice whenever the tenant has not said yes to less.

If you get it wrong, subd. 6 gives the tenant a penalty that may include a rent reduction up to full rescission of the lease, recovery of the damage deposit less anything retained under Minn. Stat. section 504B.178, up to $500 for each violation, and reasonable attorney fees - and a round of unannounced showings is one violation per entry. A violation is also a violation of Minn. Stat. section 504B.161. Showings are also the moment when a landlord is most tempted to enter while the tenant is out; if you do enter without the tenant present and without prior notice, subd. 5 requires you to leave a written disclosure of the entry in a conspicuous place in the unit.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection — but the 14-Day Notice Unlocks Emergency Assistance
bodyText: Minnesota has no shutdown rent protection. Nothing in Minnesota's landlord-tenant law, and nothing in the 2025 or 2026 session laws, gives a federal or state employee extra time to pay rent during a government shutdown, suspends late fees for a furloughed tenant, pauses evictions during a lapse in appropriations, or requires you to offer a payment plan. There is no Minnesota rent moratorium of any kind on the books, for a shutdown or for any other emergency. Rent stays due on the day the lease says. What Minnesota gives instead is a route to assistance, built into the eviction process, and it is worth knowing because it can get you paid. Before you can file for nonpayment you must serve a 14-day written notice, and the statute makes you put two specific sentences in it: one telling the tenant they have a right to seek legal help and where to find it, and one telling them how to apply for financial help - their local county or Tribal social services office, MNBenefits.mn.gov, or the United Way information line. Minnesota then goes further than most states: receiving that notice is by statute sufficient demonstration of an emergency situation to qualify the tenant for county emergency assistance, and the county must not require the tenant to provide additional verification of the emergency, or additional verification that you will accept the funds. So a furloughed tenant who gets your 14-day notice is already holding the document the county needs. If a government or Tribal agency, or a tax-exempt organisation running a government rental assistance programme, will cover the arrears, the tenant may also redeem the tenancy with that body's written guarantee of funds rather than cash. Practical approach during a shutdown: serve the 14-day notice promptly and correctly, because it is what unlocks the assistance, and keep any payment arrangement you agree in writing. If you agree to take part of the arrears, use the written partial-payment clause the library offers so accepting it does not cost you your case. And remember the one timing rule that does exist: if your online rent portal is down and the alternative you offered is not working either, you may not charge a late fee or file an eviction over the unpaid rent. A city may have its own eviction notice or assistance rules.

title: Minnesota Does Not Restrict Renting Out a House in a Single-Family Zone
bodyText:
No Minnesota statute limits renting out a home in a single-family zone, requires the owner to live on the lot in order to rent it, caps how many houses on a block or in a zone may be rented, or imposes any owner-occupancy condition on a residential lease. There is no Minnesota counterpart to the Kentucky provision. If a limit of that kind applies to one of your properties, it comes from the city's or county's own zoning or rental licensing ordinance.

The one thing the legislature has done recently pushes the other way, which is useful context. Laws 2025, ch. 32, sec. 13, headed LOCAL ACTIONS TO SUPPORT HOUSING, directs the commissioner of the Housing Finance Agency, where practicable, to award up to five percent of the total available points in a competitive capital development program to proposals in a jurisdiction that meets any of eight listed criteria. Two of them are about single-family zones: the jurisdiction 'allows for duplexes, accessory dwelling units, or townhomes within 50 percent of the area within the jurisdiction zoned for single-family housing, excluding areas covered by state or local shoreland regulations', and the jurisdiction 'does not mandate lot sizes larger than one-eighth of an acre for new single-family home construction'. So Minnesota is paying cities to loosen single-family zoning rather than tightening what may be rented in it. The section binds the agency's scoring and not any city, it is effective the day following final enactment of that act, and it expires on December 31, 2029.

Where Minnesota law does distinguish a one-family or owner-occupied property, it is for other purposes entirely, and the two that matter are both narrower than landlords expect. Minn. Stat. section 363A.21, subd. 1(2) exempts a resident owner or occupier of a one-family accommodation who rents out a room or rooms from the housing discrimination section, but only as to discrimination 'by sex, gender identity, marital status, status with regard to public assistance, sexual orientation, or disability' - not as to race, colour, creed, religion, national origin or familial status. And Minn. Stat. section 363A.21, subd. 2(a) takes the familial-status prohibition off 'any owner-occupied building containing four or fewer dwelling units'. Neither says anything about whether you may rent the house out.

title: No Minnesota Smart-Lock Statute - but Four Rules Govern What You Install
bodyText:
Minnesota has no smart-lock law. Nothing tells you whether you may fit a keypad or app-based lock, whether you must offer a physical key as well, what you may collect from an entry log or how long you may keep it, or what notice you owe a tenant before switching the building over. Washington's smart-access statute has no Minnesota counterpart. That leaves four rules that do apply, and they decide most of the practical questions.

First, the lock is a habitability item. Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subd. 1(a) puts in every residential lease a covenant that the premises and all common areas 'are fit for the use intended by the parties' and a covenant 'to keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair during the term'. Subd. 1(b): 'The parties to a lease or license of residential premises may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section.' A smart lock that is dead when the batteries run out, or that only works through the tenant's own phone and your own network, is still your problem, and you cannot write that away. Keep a mechanical override or a managed key, and restore a failed credential as a repair.

Second, disabling a tenant's credential is a lockout. Minn. Stat. section 504B.375, subd. 1(a) reaches 'actual or constructive removal or exclusion of a residential tenant which may include the termination of utilities or the removal of doors, windows, or locks', and the tenant gets a same-day order restoring possession. Switching off an app credential over unpaid rent is the modern version of changing the barrel, and a lease provision waiving that section is 'contrary to public policy and void' in its own words. Minn. Stat. sections 504B.225 and 504B.231 add a misdemeanour and treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees.

Third, entering through the system is entering. Minn. Stat. section 504B.211 does not care how the door opens: a reasonable business purpose, a good faith effort at not less than 24 hours' notice, a stated time or window, and 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. A remote unlock for a contractor is an entry and needs the notice. And if a system gives you a record of the tenant's own comings and goings, remember what the section is called - RESIDENTIAL TENANT'S RIGHT TO PRIVACY - and that subd. 6 prices a violation at up to $500 each.

Fourth, charging for access hardware is a fee. If a tenant cannot get in without the fob, the card or the app, the charge for it is not optional, and Minn. Stat. section 504B.120 requires every nonoptional fee to be disclosed in the lease and included in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, with treble damages for getting it wrong.

Two more things worth knowing. Minnesota does regulate one powered entry device, and it is not a lock: Minn. Stat. section 325F.83 requires residential automatic garage door opening systems to meet the automatic reversing requirement, and makes the occupant of a rented home tell the owner about a malfunctioning reversing device within 24 hours. And if you operate housing with services exempt from assisted living licensure, Minn. Stat. section 325F.722, subd. 2(c)(5) gives the resident a right to 'have and use a lockable door to the resident's unit', requires you to provide the locks, and limits keys to 'a staff member with a specific need to enter the unit' - which constrains how freely you may hand out credentials.

The building code is where installation standards would live, so have an electrician or your code official confirm anything you hard-wire.

title: Minnesota Bans Smoking in Your Common Areas, and a Drift Waiver Will Not Help You
bodyText:
Minnesota has no smoke-drift statute, and it does have a smoking ban that most landlords do not realise applies to them. Both halves need stating, because the ban is yours to enforce and the drift is yours to disclose.

The ban first. The Minnesota Clean Indoor Air Act, Minn. Stat. sections 144.411 to 144.417, prohibits smoking in a 'public place', and section 144.413, subd. 2 defines public place to include, in terms, 'common areas of rental apartment buildings'. So your hallways, stairways, lobbies, laundry rooms, elevators and shared restrooms are already smoke-free by statute, and you do not need a tenant to complain for you to be in breach. The definition of smoking in subd. 4 is wide: any lighted or heated product containing or derived from nicotine, tobacco, marijuana or other plant intended for inhalation, and it includes carrying or using an activated electronic delivery device, so vaping counts.

Your duty is active, not passive. Minn. Stat. section 144.416(a) puts it on 'the proprietor or other person, firm, limited liability company, corporation, or other entity that owns, leases, manages, operates, or otherwise controls the use of a public place' to 'make reasonable efforts to prevent smoking' by posting appropriate signs and by asking a person smoking where it is prohibited to stop and, if they do not, to leave - and if they refuse to leave, to handle it as you would any disorderly person or trespasser. Paragraph (b) bars you from providing ashtrays or matches where smoking is prohibited, and expressly allows you to be stricter than the Act. The sanction is in section 144.417, subd. 2(a): a proprietor or entity controlling the area who 'knowingly fails to comply' is guilty of a petty misdemeanour, and under subd. 2(b) the person smoking commits one too. Under subd. 3, the commissioner of health, a community health board or 'any affected party' - which includes a tenant - may sue to enjoin repeated violations.

Inside the unit, the Act leaves it to you. Minn. Stat. section 144.4167, subd. 3 says nothing in the Act prohibits smoking in 'private homes, private residences, or private automobiles when they are not in use as a place of employment'. So whether a tenant may smoke in the apartment is a lease question, and the library's Smoking Policy clause answers it. Watch one edge: section 144.413, subd. 1b makes an indoor area a 'place of employment' where two or more people perform services for payment, and it lists hallways among the examples - so a building where staff work is caught twice over, and a home office with on-site employees is caught too.

On drift between units there is nothing. No Minnesota statute addresses tobacco or cannabis smoke moving from one apartment into another, and none says whether a tenant can agree in advance to put up with it. That is not a licence to draft a waiver. Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subd. 1(a) puts a covenant in every lease that the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended and will be kept in reasonable repair, and subd. 1(b) says the parties 'may not waive or modify' it - so a clause by which the tenant accepts whatever drifts in is at best worthless against a serious case. Worse, section 144.417, subd. 2(d) prohibits penalising, discriminating against or in any manner retaliating against a customer 'because the... customer exercises any right to a smoke-free environment provided by sections 144.414 to 144.417 or other law', and subd. 2(c) separately prohibits retaliation against anyone who in good faith reports a violation. Threatening a tenant who complains about a neighbour's smoke is the conduct those paragraphs describe.

So: post the signs, enforce the common areas, decide the inside of the unit in the lease, disclose plainly that the building is not smoke-tight if smoking is permitted anywhere in it, and treat a drift complaint as a maintenance complaint rather than as a nuisance you can disclaim. Cities may also be stricter than the Act - section 144.417, subd. 4(a) preserves that - and a Minneapolis or St. Paul ordinance is a municipal matter.

title: A Late Benefit Payment Is Not a Defence in Minnesota - But Three Things Still Help the Tenant
bodyText:
Minnesota gives a tenant no defence, continuance or reinstatement right on the ground that a Social Security payment, a housing voucher payment or any other government benefit arrived late. There is no provision suspending a nonpayment eviction while a benefit is pending and no reinstatement on late receipt. Rent that is not paid is unpaid whatever the reason.

Three provisions still change how the case runs, and a landlord should expect all three.

The 14-day notice is itself the tenant's ticket to emergency aid. Under Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 1b(a), receipt of the subd. 1a notice is deemed by a county or other agency requiring verification of an emergency to be sufficient demonstration of an emergency situation under Minn. Stat. section 256D.06, subd. 2 and Minnesota Rules, chapter 9500. Under subd. 1b(b) the county, on receiving a copy of the notice, must not require the tenant to provide additional verification of the emergency, and must not require additional verification that the landlord will accept the funds demanded in the notice. The notice you must send anyway is what unlocks the money, so send it promptly and accurately.

Redemption can be made with a guarantee instead of cash. Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1(a) allows redemption with a written guarantee from a federal, state or local government agency, or from any other organisation that qualifies for tax-exempt status under United States Code, title 26, section 501(c)(3) and that administers a government rental assistance programme, has sufficient funds available, and guarantees that funds will be provided to the landlord. You cannot insist on cash where a qualifying guarantee is tendered.

Late fees on a subsidised tenancy are calculated differently. Minn. Stat. section 504B.177(c) requires a late fee charged by a landlord who has entered into a housing assistance payments contract with the federal, state or local government to be calculated and assessed only on the portion of rent payable by the tenant. Under paragraph (a) a late fee needs a written agreement specifying when it will be imposed and may not exceed eight per cent of the overdue rent payment; under paragraph (b) a conflicting federal statute, regulation or handbook for a federally subsidised tenancy lets the landlord publish and implement a complying schedule instead.

There may also be federal protections for benefit income that no Minnesota statute supplies. FEDERAL: this library's Minnesota sources do not include the United States Code or the Code of Federal Regulations, so no statement is made here about any federal anti-attachment, anti-garnishment or subsidised-housing grievance protection that may apply to a tenant's Social Security or voucher income. Take advice before treating benefit income as an ordinary debt collection target.

title: Public Assistance Status Is a Protected Class in Minnesota Housing
bodyText:
Minnesota's Human Rights Act makes status with regard to public assistance a protected class in housing, which is narrower than a benefit-delay defence but more dangerous to get wrong. Minn. Stat. section 363A.03, subd. 47 defines it: "'Status with regard to public assistance' means the condition of being a recipient of federal, state, or local assistance, including medical assistance, or of being a tenant receiving federal, state, or local subsidies, including rental assistance or rent supplements."

Minn. Stat. section 363A.09, subd. 1 makes it an unfair discriminatory practice for an owner, lessee, sublessee, assignee or managing agent, or any of their agents, to refuse to rent or lease to or otherwise deny or withhold real property from any person because of status with regard to public assistance, and to discriminate against any person because of it "in the terms, conditions or privileges of the sale, rental or lease of any real property or in the furnishing of facilities or services in connection therewith". Clause (3) also reaches advertisements, signs, application forms, and any record or inquiry made in connection with a prospective rental that expresses directly or indirectly any such limitation, specification or discrimination. Subd. 6 makes it an unfair discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with a person in the exercise or enjoyment of a right that section grants, or because that person exercised it or helped someone else to.

So bringing or threatening an eviction because a tenant is on assistance or holds a voucher, or treating a voucher tenant worse in the terms of the tenancy, is exposure under chapter 363A and not merely bad practice.

The limit a landlord needs is in the exemption section, and it is clear. Minn. Stat. section 363A.21, subd. 1 says the chapter is not to be construed "to relieve any person or persons of any obligations generally imposed on all persons regardless of any disability in a written lease, rental agreement, or contract of purchase or sale, or to forbid distinctions based on the inability to fulfill the terms and conditions, including financial obligations of the lease, agreement, or contract." Evicting a tenant who has not paid the rent is a distinction based on failure to meet a financial obligation, not on assistance status. Keep the two apart in your records and your correspondence: the ground is the unpaid rent, never the benefit.

Section 363A.21, subd. 1(2) also exempts a resident owner or occupier of a one-family accommodation renting a room or rooms in it, where the discrimination is by sex, gender identity, marital status, status with regard to public assistance, sexual orientation or disability. The other exemptions to section 363A.09 are in Minn. Stat. sections 363A.22 and 363A.26 and are not described here.

title: What Minnesota Source-of-Income Protection Does and Does Not Cover
bodyText: Minnesota protects source of income in housing, but only one source of it, and the boundary is where landlords go wrong in both directions. The protected ground is status with regard to public assistance, and Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.03, subd. 47 defines it exactly: the condition of being a recipient of federal, state, or local assistance, including medical assistance, or of being a tenant receiving federal, state, or local subsidies, including rental assistance or rent supplements. It is an enumerated ground in the housing section, Sec. 363A.09, so refusing to rent, or varying the terms, because an applicant pays with a voucher or receives medical assistance is a protected-class problem, not a business judgement. What it does not cover is every other lawful source of money. Wages from a particular employer, self-employment income, child support, alimony, a private pension, savings, or help from family are not protected sources under Minnesota law. So a uniformly applied income test, or an income-to-rent ratio, is not a source-of-income problem in itself - but it becomes one the moment it is applied so as to exclude subsidy recipients, for example by measuring the whole rent against the tenant own share of it rather than against the tenant income plus the subsidy. There is a second provision most landlords never see. Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.16, subd. 2 makes it an unfair discriminatory practice to discriminate in the extension of personal or commercial credit against any person who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rent supplements, because the person is a recipient of those subsidies or assistance. If you offer payment plans, deferred rent, or any other credit to tenants, that is a separate duty from the Sec. 363A.09 one and it is framed around credit rather than around renting. Minnesota has no standalone voucher-acceptance statute with its own exemption set. Acceptance and everything else flow from the same enumerated ground, so they carry the same exemptions, at Secs. 363A.21, 363A.22 and 363A.26.

title: No Special-District Statement Required in a Minnesota Lease
bodyText: Minnesota requires no special-district disclosure or representation in a residential lease. There is no duty to tell a tenant that the property sits in a special taxing district, an improvement district or an assessment district, no prescribed statement to that effect, and no rule about who represents the tenant interests in such a district. Special districts certainly exist in Minnesota - fire and emergency medical service districts, tourism improvement districts and others. Where a district charge does fall on someone, in the district laws described here it falls on the property owner or on a business, not on a residential tenant. Two practical points. If you intend to pass any district assessment or service charge through to a tenant, the obligation that bites is not a district-disclosure rule but Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.120: every nonoptional fee must be disclosed in the lease and included in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, and failure carries treble damages. And a special assessment certified against the property with the taxes is an owner liability; do not assume you may recover it from a tenant without a clear lease term that itself complies with Sec. 504B.120.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty in Minnesota, and a Grant If You Need One
bodyText: Minnesota requires no sprinkler disclosure in a residential lease. There is no Minnesota counterpart to the New York rule that a lease must state whether the unit has a sprinkler system, or to the Connecticut and Maryland sprinkler notices. Two Minnesota sprinkler statutes are worth knowing: Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.48, the retrofit requirement for existing PUBLIC HOUSING buildings, which does not reach a private landlord and is covered in its own row ("No Fire-Sprinkler Duty for Private Rental Housing"), and Minn. Stat. Sec. 144.50, which requires a state-fire-marshal-approved sprinkler system in a facility running a treatment programme where children live with a parent. Neither requires anyone to tell a tenant anything. NO DISCLOSURE DOES NOT MEAN NO DUTY TO MAINTAIN. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a) makes you covenant that the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended, that you will keep them in reasonable repair, and that you will maintain them in compliance with the applicable health and safety laws of the United States, of the state and of local government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing. Subd. 1(b) bars waiver. If your building has a sprinkler system, keeping it working is squarely inside that covenant and inside the State Fire Code. AND THERE IS MONEY. If you own an existing residential building that is seven stories or more in height, or 75 feet or more above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access, and at least two-thirds of its units are affordable to households at or below 60 percent of area median income, the Minnesota Housing Finance Agency runs a High-Rise Sprinkler System Grant and Loan Program. It funds installation and, if necessary, relocation of residents during installation. The maximum grant is $2,000,000 per eligible building. A grant to a for-profit owner needs a 50 percent match; a nonprofit needs 25 percent, and nonprofit applicants get priority. The seven-storey route into eligibility was added in 2025. WHAT TO DO. You do not have to say anything, but a one-line statement of whether the unit has a sprinkler system is cheap and heads off a dispute - and if you say it, make it true and keep it true. New construction and remodelling are governed by the State Building Code and State Fire Code, which Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.48, subd. 4 expressly says it does not supersede.

title: Minnesota's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Minnesota caps very few of the amounts you charge, but it attaches hard numbers to a lot of the amounts you can be made to pay. Here is the money map, with the section to read. WHAT YOU MAY CHARGE. A late fee may not exceed 8% of the overdue rent payment, and only if you and the tenant agreed in writing that a late fee may be imposed and the agreement says when (section 504B.177). There is no statewide cap on the security deposit, though a city may set one. You must pay the tenant simple noncompounded interest on a deposit at 1% per year, and any interest amount under $1 is excluded (section 504B.178). In a shared-metered building your administrative billing charge may not exceed $8 and the late payment charge for all utilities billed may not exceed $5 a month, not compounded (section 504B.216). An applicant screening fee is limited by section 504B.173. A service charge on a bounced check is capped by Minnesota's bad-check statute, which the library covers separately. There is no cap on rent itself, and no holdover multiplier. WHAT YOU CAN BE MADE TO PAY. Failing to disclose nonoptional fees or the first-page Total Monthly Payment: treble damages plus possible attorney fees (section 504B.120). Accepting rent or a deposit after a condemnation or vacate order: actual damages plus three times everything you collected, plus costs and attorney fees (section 504B.204). Bad faith retention of a deposit: punitive damages up to $500 for each deposit, on top of other damages (section 504B.178). Shutting off utilities or locking a tenant out: treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees (sections 504B.221 and 504B.231). Interfering with a tenant's right to call police or emergency help: $250 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees (section 504B.205). Breaching a victim's lease-termination rights: statutory damages of $2,000 plus attorney fees and costs (section 504B.206). Entering without proper notice: a civil penalty up to $500 for each violation, plus lease termination, deposit recovery and attorney fees (section 504B.211). Interfering with a tenant association in bad faith: up to $1,000 per occurrence plus attorney fees (section 504B.212). Mishandling a tenant's property left behind: punitive damages up to twice actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, on top of actual damages and attorney fees (section 504B.271). A tenant screening report violation: the greater of $1,000 or actual damages, plus investigation costs and attorney fees, and the remedy runs against you as well as the screening service (section 504B.245). A violation of the pet declawing and devocalization ban: a civil penalty up to $1,000 per advertisement or per animal (section 504B.114). Restricted lease terms in a building in financial distress: a $500 civil penalty (section 504B.151). New construction not ready: the greater of one month's rent, $1,000, or actual damages, plus attorney fees and costs (section 504B.153). A screening-fee violation: the fee back plus a civil penalty up to $100, filing costs and attorney fees - and if a prospective tenant misstates material information, up to $500 the other way (section 504B.173). Willfully ignoring a repair order: $250 for the first failure, $500 for the second on the same violation, $750 for the third and each one after (section 504B.391). Abusing the expedited eviction hearing: a civil penalty up to $500, which rose to $750 on August 1, 2026 (section 504B.321, subdivision 2). TWO SMALL FIGURES THAT CUT YOUR WAY. On redemption in a nonpayment eviction the tenant pays the arrears, interest, costs and an attorney's fee of no more than $5 - so do not expect your fees back through redemption (section 504B.291). And in a tenant remedies action the court's attorney fee award against you is capped at $500, except under section 549.211 or other specific statutory authority (section 504B.425). Watch two things. Attorney fees are reciprocal: if your lease lets you recover them in a situation, the tenant gets them in the same situation (section 504B.172). And the attorney general can investigate and prosecute violations of the whole chapter. A city may cap amounts this list does not.

title: The Six Ways a Minnesota Tenant Can End a Lease Early - One Without Lifting a Finger
bodyText:
Minnesota gives a tenant six statutory ways out of a lease before it ends, and one of them happens without the tenant doing anything. Each is already drafted in this library, so this is the map rather than the detail.

First, a victim of violence. A tenant who fears imminent violence after domestic abuse, criminal sexual conduct, sexual extortion or harassment may end the lease without penalty or liability on signed, dated advance written notice with a qualifying document, and that right cannot be waived.

Second, death. On the death of the tenant, or of all tenants, either you or the personal representative of the estate may end the lease on at least two months' written notice effective on the last day of a calendar month. This one does not apply to a tenancy at will, and a lease term demanding a longer notice is void.

Third, infirmity. A tenant found by a medical professional to need to move into a care facility may end the lease on at least two months' written notice with the medical documentation and proof of acceptance or a pending application. You can defeat this one by offering an available accessible unit in the same complex within two months, where that is what the tenant needs.

Fourth, the property becoming unusable. A tenant may vacate and surrender a building destroyed or made uninhabitable or unfit for occupancy through no fault or neglect of the tenant or occupant.

Fifth, new construction not ready. Where new construction will not be available by the move-in date in the lease, you must notify every affected tenant within seven days and before the move-in date, and offer a choice of equivalent alternative housing, a payment equal to the rent, or ending the lease and getting everything back.

Sixth, and this is the one that operates by itself. If a tenant abandons the unit and you fail to make reasonable efforts to re-rent at fair rental value, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the rental agreement is terminated on the date you had notice of the abandonment and the tenant owes no rent after that.

Two things Minnesota does not give. There is no state military-service termination right: the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act is the route, and it is federal law. And no Minnesota statute makes you set these rights out in the lease, unlike some states. You may still want to, because a tenant who knows the rule is less likely to simply disappear.

title: Minnesota Has No Steam Radiator Cover Rule for Rental Housing
bodyText: Some states require a landlord to fit a cover or guard on a steam radiator on request, and some make a lease rider about it mandatory. Minnesota has neither. There is no radiator-cover duty, no request procedure, and no required lease rider anywhere in Minnesota's landlord-tenant act, its public safety and fire chapter, or its consumer-protection chapters. There is one place Minnesota does regulate hot radiators, and it is worth knowing about because it can reach a rental unit. Licensed child care programmes must guard them. The 2026 session requires that, when in use, fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, solid-fuel-burning appliances, space heaters, steam radiators, outdoor fire pits and other potentially hot surfaces such as steam pipes 'must be protected by guards or protective covering to keep hands and bodies away, prevent burns, and prevent fires', and that radiators and other hot surfaces in areas used by children must be shielded or insulated. Those are child care licensing requirements, not tenancy requirements. If your tenant runs a licensed family child care from the unit, the rule binds the programme, and your tenant may need to guard the radiators to keep their licence — which is a good reason to be reasonable about a request rather than a legal duty to grant it. What does bind you is the general covenant. Under Minn. Stat. § 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(1) the premises and common areas must be 'fit for the use intended by the parties', subd. 1(a)(2) requires reasonable repair, and subd. 1(a)(4) requires compliance with the health and safety laws of the United States, the state and local units of government, including ordinances regulating rental licensing. Those covenants cannot be waived or modified (subd. 1(b)). So an exposed, leaking or dangerously hot radiator can still be a repair obligation, a fitness problem, or a local-code violation even though no statute says the word 'cover'. A city ordinance could also impose a guarding requirement; that is a municipal question. Practical position: you may offer radiator covers as an amenity, and you may agree to fit one, but do not write a clause that purports to make covers the tenant's responsibility or to disclaim radiator safety. That would run at subd. 1(b).

title: No Stigmatized-Property Disclosure Duty in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota has no stigmatized-property disclosure rule for landlords, and no Minnesota statute is known to require you to tell a tenant that someone died, was killed or took their own life in the unit, that an occupant had HIV or AIDS, that the property is said to be haunted, or that a registered offender lives nearby. Minnesota's real-property disclosure statutes are in Minn. Stat. ch. 513. Minn. Stat. Sec. 513.61 is a single-sentence duty placed on a SELLER of residential real property, which is consistent with chapter 513 being a sale statute rather than a lease statute, so treat chapter 513 as an open question rather than a settled absence. The sex-offender registry question is in the same position, because it turns on Minnesota's registration and community notification statutes. DO NOT CONFUSE THIS WITH DISCRIMINATION LAW. For HIV and AIDS, the sections that matter to a landlord are in the Minnesota Human Rights Act, Minn. Stat. ch. 363A. Refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because of a person's disability is unlawful, and the fair-housing and protected-class rows cover that ground. A landlord who volunteers a former occupant's HIV status is far more likely to create a problem than to solve one. THREE RELATED MINNESOTA RULES THAT DO EXIST, EACH WITH ITS OWN ROW. (1) Death of a tenant: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.265 lets either the landlord or the personal representative of the tenant's estate terminate a residential lease on at least two months' written notice effective the last day of a calendar month, and subd. 3 makes any attempted waiver, or any longer notice period, void and unenforceable. See the tenant-death rows. (2) Methamphetamine contamination: Minnesota has no disclosure duty but does have an occupancy ban and a recorded affidavit. See the meth-disclosure rows. (3) Inspection and condemnation orders: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195, subd. 1 makes you give a person a copy of an outstanding citation or condemnation order before they sign a lease or pay rent or a deposit, and subd. 5 makes any lease waiver of that section contrary to public policy and void. WHAT TO DO. Minnesota requires no stigma disclosure, so answer an applicant's direct question honestly rather than evasively, and do not volunteer a former occupant's health information. If a prospective tenant asks something you would rather not answer, say you are not able to comment rather than saying something untrue: Minn. Stat. Sec. 325F.69, subd. 1 makes a misrepresentation or misleading statement made with the intent that others rely on it unlawful in connection with the sale of merchandise, and Sec. 325F.68, subd. 2 defines merchandise to include real estate and services.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove - But a Refrigerator Is on Minnesota's Emergency List
bodyText:
Minnesota does not require you to supply a stove or a refrigerator. It does not say so in terms; there is simply no section that imposes the duty. But the refrigerator is a trap, because of where Minnesota keeps the rest of its habitability list. Your repair covenant is to keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair, and it expressly takes in the services and conditions listed in Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.381, subd. 1 (Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1). Neither you nor the tenant may waive or modify that covenant. The incorporated list is the emergency list, and it includes a serious infestation, loss of running water, loss of hot water, loss of heat, loss of electricity, loss of sanitary facilities and - named in its own right - a nonfunctioning refrigerator.

Read the list closely, because the drafting is deliberate. A nonfunctioning air conditioner counts only "if included in the lease", and so does a non-working elevator. The refrigerator carries no such qualifier. What it does carry is the list's opening words, which reach these services and facilities "when the landlord is responsible for providing them".

So a refrigerator you provide sits inside your unwaivable repair covenant, and a broken one is also express grounds for the tenant to petition the court for emergency relief. A refrigerator the tenant brings is a different thing, and the safe way to record that is in writing at move-in.

A stove is not on the list at all, and neither is an oven, a dishwasher, a microwave, a washer or a dryer. That is not a free pass. The same list closes with any conditions, services or facilities that pose a serious and negative impact on health or safety, and with other essential services or facilities, and a home with no way to cook may well arrive there. A gas appliance you provide also runs into your duty to comply with health and safety laws.

Two things are not optional whatever you do about appliances. You must equip or furnish heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit in every place intended for habitation, kitchens and bathrooms included, from October 1 through April 30, unless a utility company requires it reduced. And hot water is on the emergency list in its own right.

The practical course: decide deliberately whether you supply a stove and a refrigerator, write down what is at the property at move-in and who owns each item, and do not leave an old appliance behind with a disclaimer attached to it.

title: No Student Tenancy Rules, and Student Status Is Not Protected in Minnesota Housing
bodyText:
Minnesota has no student-tenancy regime. Minnesota's landlord-tenant statutes set no special lease terms, notice periods, deposit rules, joint-and-several rules, academic-year term limits or subletting rules for student renters, and do not treat off-campus student housing differently from any other rental. Chapter 504B applies to a student tenancy exactly as it applies to any other residential tenancy in Minnesota.

Student status is also not a protected class. The Minnesota Human Rights Act's housing provision, Minn. Stat. section 363A.09, lists race, color, creed, religion, national origin, sex, gender identity, marital status, status with regard to public assistance, disability, sexual orientation and familial status. Student status is not on that list, and neither is age - the Act protects age in employment and education but not in housing and real property, which Minn. Stat. section 363A.02, subd. 1 sets out class by class. The Act's educational-institution provision, Minn. Stat. section 363A.13, reaches admission and the services an institution renders; it is not a landlord rule.

That does not make a no-students policy safe, and it is worth being careful rather than clever about it. Three of the protected classes sit close to the ones landlords reach for when they mean 'student'. Marital status is protected, so a rule aimed at unmarried people sharing a unit is a problem. Status with regard to public assistance is protected, and it is the class Minnesota landlords most often fall foul of. And familial status is protected, which catches a rule aimed at a young household with a child. Any occupancy standard you use should be neutral, applied to everyone, and tied to a code limit rather than to who the applicant is. If your property is near a campus and you want to manage turnover, do it with the lease term, the notice provisions and your screening criteria, which is where Minnesota lets you work.

title: Refusing a Subsidy Inspection Is a Discrimination Problem, Not an Entry Problem
bodyText: No Minnesota statute says anything about a subsidy programme's inspection in terms. Four Minnesota rules decide the question anyway, and the first one is the important one. You cannot refuse the tenancy because of the subsidy. Status with regard to public assistance is a protected class in Minnesota real property law, and the definition reaches a voucher holder expressly: it means the condition of being a recipient of federal, state or local assistance, or of being a tenant receiving federal, state or local subsidies, including rental assistance or rent supplements (Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.03, subd. 47). It is an unfair discriminatory practice to refuse to rent on that basis, to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental on that basis, or to use any application form, record or inquiry that expresses such a limitation directly or indirectly (Sec. 363A.09, subd. 1). So refusing the programme's inspection in order to avoid taking a voucher tenant is discrimination in the terms and conditions of the rental, however it is dressed up. The exemptions are narrow: the main one is a resident owner-occupier letting a room in a one-family accommodation (Sec. 363A.21, subd. 1). Second, the inspection is an entry, and Minnesota's entry rule governs it. You may enter only for a reasonable business purpose and after a good-faith effort to give reasonable notice of not less than 24 hours, the notice must specify a time or a window, and entry must be between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless you and the tenant agree otherwise (Sec. 504B.211, subd. 2). The list of reasonable business purposes expressly includes allowing inspections by state, county or city officials enforcing health, housing, building, fire prevention or housing maintenance codes, and the list is not exhaustive (subd. 3). The tenant may not waive, and you may not require the tenant to waive, the right to prior notice as a condition of entering into or keeping the lease. Third, breaking the subsidy programme's own rules is a chapter 504B problem, not just a programme problem. The definition of "violation" that opens rent escrow and the tenant remedies action includes a violation of any applicable tenant rights and landlord obligations for public and subsidised tenancies under local, state or federal law (Sec. 504B.001, subd. 14). So a refusal that breaches your obligations under the programme can put the rent in the hands of the court administrator. Fourth, if an inspection has already produced an order, you have a separate disclosure duty. Outstanding inspection orders for which a citation has been issued, and outstanding condemnation orders, must be given to the tenant and to anyone about to sign a lease or pay a deposit. That duty cannot be waived and is covered under the inspection and condemnation disclosure topic. What Minnesota does not give you is a rule about a tenant who will not let the inspector in. There is no statute making that a breach, so it is a matter for your entry clause and the programme's own contract. The terms of a housing assistance payments contract and the federal inspection standards are federal, and are outside this research. Minneapolis and St. Paul may add their own rules, which is a municipal matter.

title: No Subsidy Split for an Abatement — but Proration of the Final Month Is Mandatory
bodyText: Minnesota sets no formula for splitting a rent reduction between a subsidised tenant's share and the agency's share when part of a unit becomes unfit. Nothing tells you how much of an abatement comes off the tenant's portion, and nothing tells you what happens to the housing assistance payment. But Minnesota is not silent on rent and habitability, and three of its rules decide most of what you need to do. First, Minnesota does have a mandatory rent proration rule, and it is about days, not condition. When a lease term ends before the last day of the final month, the final month's rent must be prorated at the average daily rate for that month, using the actual number of calendar days in the month the lease expires, so the tenant pays only for the days occupancy is allowed. That applies to every lease, including one requiring the last month's rent in advance, and any attempted waiver of it by you and the tenant, by contract or otherwise, is void and unenforceable (Minn. Stat. section 504B.116). So if a unit becomes unfit and the tenancy ends early, the proration is not optional. Second, abatement is the court's job and it is measured by impairment, not by a percentage. In a rent escrow action the court may order retroactive rent abatement, release part of the escrowed rent to pay for repairs, or abate future rent until you remedy the violation; in a tenant remedies action it may find the extent to which uncorrected violations impair the tenant's use and enjoyment of what they contracted for and abate the rent accordingly (Minn. Stat. sections 504B.385 and 504B.425). The tenant and you may also agree in writing apportioning escrowed rent between you, and the court administrator must release it on those terms. Note what the statute does not say: it does not say whose share of a subsidised rent the abatement comes off. Third, Minnesota does know how to protect the tenant's portion, and it did so for late fees only. If you have a housing assistance payments contract with a federal, state or local government, a late fee must be calculated and assessed only on the portion of rent payable by the tenant - never on the government's share (Minn. Stat. section 504B.177). Treat that as the pattern to follow by analogy, not as a rule about abatement. Two absolutes to remember. After a condemnation, a declaration that the premises are unfit, or an order to vacate, you may not accept rent or a deposit at all - no proration, nothing (Minn. Stat. section 504B.204). And a tenant of a building that is destroyed or becomes uninhabitable through no fault of theirs may vacate and surrender it (Minn. Stat. section 504B.131). Practical approach for a voucher or project-based tenancy: follow the programme's own abatement rules and your contract with the agency; put any reduction of the tenant's share in writing; tell the agency; and never bill the tenant for a share the agency has abated or recaptured. This covers Minnesota's statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws.

title: Late Fees When the Tenancy Is Subsidized
bodyText:
Minnesota's late fee statute has two separate subsidy rules, and they do different work. Keep them apart.

The first is about the schedule. If a federal statute, regulation or handbook permitting late fees for a tenancy subsidized under a federal program conflicts with Minnesota's general late fee rule - the one requiring a written agreement and capping the fee at 8% of the overdue rent payment - then you may publish and implement a late payment fee schedule that complies with the federal rule instead. That is an override you operate outside the lease, by publishing a schedule; it is not something the lease grants you, and it applies only where there is an actual conflict with a federal rule that permits late fees.

The second is about the base, and it is not limited to federal programs. If you have entered into a housing assistance payments contract with the federal, state or local government, any late fee must be calculated and assessed only on the portion of rent payable by the tenant - never on the government's share. For this rule a housing assistance payments contract means the programs described in sections 1437f and 1485 of title 42 of the United States Code, as well as any other program under which you contract to receive rent from the tenant and also to receive payment from the government. So a project-based or voucher tenancy where you collect part of the rent from an agency is covered even if it is not one of the two named programs.

Both rules can apply to the same tenancy: a federal schedule can set the amount while the tenant-portion rule still sets what the fee is calculated on.

Two more things. A late fee is never interest and never liquidated damages. And since August 1, 2026, if your digital payment platform and the alternative you offered are both not working for the tenant, you may not take adverse action over the unpaid rent, including assessing late fees. Check your program documents before relying on a federal schedule.

title: A Court Can Hand Your Building to an Administrator and Switch Off Your Right to Rent
bodyText: Minnesota's tenant remedies action can take your building out of your hands. If the court finds the complaint proved, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.425, paragraph (d) lets it appoint an administrator with the powers in Sec. 504B.445, and direct that rents be deposited with that administrator -- from the day judgment is entered for petitioning tenants or neighbourhood organisations, and from the day the judgment is served on all the building's other residential AND commercial tenants. The administrator then uses the rents to remedy the violations by paying debt service, taxes and insurance and providing the services necessary to ordinary operation and maintenance that you are obligated to provide but fail or refuse to provide. WHAT THE ADMINISTRATOR MAY DO (Sec. 504B.445, subd. 4) is wide: collect rents from residential and commercial tenants, evict them for nonpayment or other cause, enter into leases for vacant dwelling units, rent vacant commercial units with your consent, contract for materials, labour and services including third-party utility service, provide services you refuse or fail to provide, and petition the court for an order letting it encumber the property or receive federal, state or municipal money. Where a municipality advances that money it recovers it by special assessment on the real estate, bearing interest at a rate it sets but capped at the open-end credit sales rate under Minn. Stat. Sec. 334.16, subd. 1(b), collected like any other special assessment. Subd. 6 sets the order of payment: necessary repairs and services to keep the building habitable come first, and if nothing is left for tax and mortgage payments, those remain YOUR responsibility. Subd. 3 lets the court enter judgment against you for the administrator's reasonable services and expenses when the administration ends. The administrator cannot be you, your inspector, the complaining tenant, or anyone living in that tenant's unit (subd. 1), and is personally liable only for misfeasance, malfeasance or nonfeasance of office (subd. 7). THEN THE PART THAT HURTS MOST. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.435 suspends your right to be paid at all. Once an administrator is appointed under Sec. 504B.425, paragraph (d), "any right of the landlord to collect rent from the petitioner is void and unenforceable from the time the court signs the order for judgment until the administration is terminated", and "[a]ny right of the landlord to collect rent from other tenants is void and unenforceable from the time of service of judgment as set forth in section 504B.431 until the administration is terminated". Note the two different start dates and note that the second sentence reaches tenants who never sued you. Service of the judgment is personal on every residential and commercial tenant whose obligations it affects, or by posting on the door plus certified mail if personal service fails with due diligence (Sec. 504B.431). HOW IT ENDS (Sec. 504B.461): either the appropriate governmental agency certifies that the violations found at judgment have been remedied, or the court orders termination under Sec. 504B.445, subd. 5 because the available funds are insufficient to remedy them promptly -- in which case the court proceeds to judgment under Sec. 504B.425, paragraph (e), rent abatement. The administrator then accounts to the court with the bills and receipts and is discharged. Under Sec. 504B.425, paragraph (f) the court may keep jurisdiction over the building for a further YEAR after the administration ends and order you to maintain it in compliance with all applicable state, county and city health, safety, housing, building, fire prevention and housing maintenance codes. Two more things. The Minnesota Housing Finance Agency may run a revolving loan fund to pay administrators' administrative expenses for properties occupied by low- and moderate-income people, and "[l]andlords must repay administrative expense payments made from the fund" (Sec. 504B.451) -- so public money spent on the administration comes back to you as a debt. And none of this can be contracted out of: Sec. 504B.465 says any lease provision in which a tenant waives Sec. 504B.381 or Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471 "is contrary to public policy and void".
