On top of the administration, willfully ignoring a repair order carries the escalating fines and the gross misdemeanour described in "Fines and a Gross Misdemeanour for Ignoring a Repair Order".

title: How a Minnesota Building Gets to Receivership, and Where You Can Stop It
bodyText: An administrator is the end of a road with several exits. The road starts with a "violation" as Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.001, subd. 14 defines it -- a violation of any state, county or city health, safety, housing, building, fire prevention or housing maintenance code applicable to the building; a violation of chapter 504B itself; a violation of any federal, state, county or city law protecting tenants from discrimination; a violation of applicable tenant rights and landlord obligations for public and subsidised tenancies; or a violation of an oral or written agreement, lease or contract for the rental of a dwelling. So a plain lease breach is a "violation" that can start this. WHO CAN BRING IT (Sec. 504B.395, subd. 1): a residential tenant of the building; a housing-related neighbourhood organisation with a tenant's written permission; such an organisation on its own for an UNOCCUPIED building in its geographical area; or a state, county or local department or authority charged with enforcing health, housing or building maintenance codes. Three of those four are not your tenant. THE EXITS. First, where a code inspection has been made under Sec. 504B.185, no action may be brought until the time the inspector allowed to make repairs has expired without satisfactory repairs -- unless the tenant alleges that the time allowed is excessive (subd. 3). Repair inside the inspector's deadline and the action cannot start. Second, for a violation other than an inspector's code violation, you must be informed in writing of the alleged violation at least 14 days before the action is brought, and that notice can only be waived if the court finds you cannot be located despite diligent efforts (subd. 4). Answer in those 14 days and you have the best exit there is. Third, the action must be started by a verified complaint and a summons issued by a judge or court administrator, and for an inspector's code violation the complaint must carry a certified copy of the official inspection report, or else a statement that an inspection was requested, demand was made on you, and a reasonable period has elapsed (subds. 5 and 6). Fourth, at judgment the court has a menu, and appointing an administrator is only one item on it: it may order you to remedy the violations if it is satisfied corrective action will be taken promptly; it may order the tenant to do the work and deduct the cost from rent; it may abate the rent; or it may grant any other just relief including attorney fees against you capped at $500, a cap that does not apply to awards under Minn. Stat. Sec. 549.211 or other specific statutory authority (Sec. 504B.425). PROMPT CORRECTIVE ACTION IS THE ARGUMENT THAT KEEPS YOUR BUILDING. Two neighbouring routes reach the same relief faster. Rent escrow under Sec. 504B.385 lets a tenant deposit rent with the court administrator and the court may then order relief under Sec. 504B.425, release the escrowed rent to pay for the repairs, order future rent deposited or abated, and impose the Sec. 504B.391 fines. The emergency action under Sec. 504B.381 reaches you on 24 hours' attempted notice, or none at all if the court finds reasonable efforts failed -- and its subd. 1(1) trigger is squarely a code matter: a unit of government revoking a rental licence, issuing a condemnation order or a notice of intent to condemn, or otherwise deeming the property uninhabitable. Its subd. 1(2) list is a serious infestation, loss of running water, hot water, heat, electricity or sanitary facilities, a nonfunctioning refrigerator, a nonfunctioning air conditioner or elevator if included in the lease, any condition posing a serious and negative impact on health or safety, and other essential services or facilities. Sec. 504B.381, subd. 6 is your defence there: it does not extend to emergencies resulting from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of a tenant or anyone under the tenant's direction or control.

title: Passing Tax and Insurance Increases to the Tenant: Lawful, but the First-Page Rule Gets in the Way
bodyText: No Minnesota statute lets a residential lease pass a property tax increase or an insurance premium increase through to the tenant, and no Minnesota statute forbids it either. There is no rule here requiring the clause to state the tenant's exact share, and none requiring you to refund the tenant's share of a later tax abatement - both things other states require. Because Minnesota is silent, a tax-and-insurance escalation clause is lawful as a matter of contract, and you may write one. The library does not offer one for Minnesota, for a specific reason you should weigh before you do. Minn. Stat. section 504B.120, subdivision 1 requires you to disclose all nonoptional fees in the lease and to state the sum of rent plus all nonoptional fees as the Total Monthly Payment on the first page of the lease. A share of a future tax or premium increase is a charge the tenant cannot avoid, so it is a nonoptional fee - and its amount is unknown when the lease is signed, so it cannot honestly be included in a first-page total. Subdivision 2 makes a violation expensive: the tenant recovers treble damages and the court may award reasonable attorney fees. Relabelling the pass-through as rent does not help, because Minnesota does not let you redefine fees as rent. Two safer routes. Build your expected tax and insurance costs into the rent figure itself, so the Total Monthly Payment on page one is true. Or, for a lease longer than a year, use a scheduled or indexed rent change - rent is rent, not a fee, and the library offers a clause for it. If you still want a tax escalation clause, take advice from a Minnesota lawyer first and work out how the charge will appear on the first page of the lease. One more thing to remember: you may not charge the tenant any part of a penalty or interest for your own late payment of taxes or premiums, because that is your cost, not a cost of the tenancy. A common interest community may have its own association rules.

title: Cable, Satellite and Internet Access in Minnesota Rentals
bodyText:
Minnesota does have a building-access rule for cable, and it is in the cable statute, not the landlord-tenant act.

Chapter 504B itself is silent. No provision there gives a communications provider a right to enter or wire a rental building, gives a tenant a right to take service from the provider of the tenant's choice, requires you to allow an antenna or a satellite dish, or bars you from charging subscribers and non-subscribers different rent. The nearest thing is a rule about providers rather than landlords: Minn. Stat. section 325F.6945 prohibits an internet service provider from blocking lawful content, degrading lawful traffic, paid prioritization and the listed zero-rating practices for its Minnesota customers, enforceable by the commissioner of commerce. That binds the provider's conduct and says nothing about your building.

CABLE ACCESS TO BUILDINGS OF FIVE OR MORE UNITS. Under Minn. Stat. section 238.23, subd. 1, a property owner "shall provide a cable communications system access to the property owner's multiple dwelling complex." A "multiple dwelling complex" is a site with more than four dwelling units, other than a common interest community or a manufactured home park (section 238.02, subd. 28a). The access is perpetual and transferable. Subdivision 2 says its purpose is to let residents choose among competing services, and that no resident has to subscribe. You may set reasonable conditions for safety, function and appearance, and approve installation plans, though approval may not be unreasonably withheld (section 238.24, subds. 1 and 2). You may require a bond, and relocation when you rehabilitate or maintain the premises. The cable system bears the cost and indemnifies you for damage (subds. 3 to 5 and 7). It must compensate you for any loss in market value, and reimburse up to $100 (under ten units) or $200 of your plan-review costs (subd. 8). If you refuse, it may obtain a court order granting access (section 238.25), and no person may interfere with its facilities (section 238.27).

TELEPHONE IN SHARED-SERVICE BUILDINGS. Where private shared telephone, video or broadband services operate in your building, a tenant may connect directly to the local telephone company. At the tenant's request you must make facilities or conduit space available (section 237.681, subd. 3).

THE FEDERAL ANTENNA RULE. Under 47 C.F.R. section 1.4000(a), a lease provision may not impair a tenant's installation, maintenance or use of a satellite dish or similar antenna one meter or less across, or a broadcast antenna, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a private balcony or patio. A restriction needed for a clearly defined safety objective or for historic preservation is allowed if it is no more burdensome than necessary (paragraph (b)). The rule covers only property in the tenant's exclusive use or control, not common areas.

One more multi-unit access right, and it is not a telecom one. Minn. Stat. section 211B.20 makes it unlawful to deny access to an apartment house or other multiple unit residence to a qualifying candidate campaigning in the district, with campaign volunteers; a violation is a petty misdemeanor. You may still deny entry to a particular unit, require identification or an appointment, limit numbers and hours (access must be allowed at least 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.), and deny entry for good cause (subd. 2). See "You May Not Keep a Political Candidate Out of a Multi-Unit Building".

Two more things to get right. First, if you bulk-bill internet or television and the tenant cannot avoid the charge, it is a nonoptional fee, and Minn. Stat. section 504B.120 requires every nonoptional fee to be disclosed in the lease and included in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, with treble damages for getting it wrong. Second, letting an installer into the unit is an entry: if you do it, Minn. Stat. section 504B.211 applies, because the section's definition of landlord in subd. 1 includes 'the landlord's agent or other person acting under the landlord's direction and control'. Make the appointment the tenant's and be present only if the tenant is.

title: Minnesota Has No Tenant Bankruptcy Rule; Federal Law Controls - Stop and Take Advice
bodyText:
No Minnesota statute says anything about what happens to a residential tenancy when the tenant files for bankruptcy. There is no state provision on the automatic stay, on whether a lease is assumed or rejected, on a pending eviction, or on rent that accrued before the filing. Minnesota's landlord-tenant act is silent.

FEDERAL: bankruptcy is federal law. A bankruptcy petition stays the commencement or continuation of a court action against the debtor, any act to obtain possession of property of the estate, and any act to collect a claim that arose before the filing (11 U.S.C. section 362(a)(1), (3) and (6)). Two exceptions reach residential evictions. If you obtained a judgment for possession before the petition was filed, the stay does not stop you continuing the eviction (section 362(b)(22)). But that exception waits 30 days if the tenant certifies that nonbankruptcy law would let the tenant cure the whole monetary default after judgment, and deposits the next 30 days' rent with the clerk. If the tenant then certifies a full cure, the exception does not apply unless the court so orders on your objection (section 362(l)). Whether Minnesota's right to redeem by paying the arrears (Minn. Stat. section 504B.291) counts as that kind of post-judgment cure only case law could settle, so assume the tenant can use it. An eviction based on endangering the property or illegal use of controlled substances may proceed 15 days after you file and serve a certification under penalty of perjury (section 362(b)(23) and (m)). It is held up if the tenant objects in time and shows the situation did not exist or has been remedied. In a chapter 7 case, a residential lease the trustee does not assume or reject within 60 days after the order for relief is deemed rejected (section 365(d)(1)). And once the case begins, a lease may not be terminated or modified solely because of a clause conditioned on the filing or on the tenant's insolvency or financial condition (section 365(e)(1)).

What to do instead. If a tenant tells you they have filed, or you receive a notice from a bankruptcy court, stop the eviction where it is and get advice from a lawyer who practises bankruptcy before you take another step - including before you file, before you ask the court for a writ, and before you send a demand for rent. Continuing an eviction or a collection effort against a tenant in bankruptcy can expose you to consequences no Minnesota statute will protect you from.

Two Minnesota points that do survive and are worth knowing. Minn. Stat. section 504B.291, subd. 1(a) makes an eviction action for nonpayment "equivalent to a demand for the rent", so the filing of your eviction is itself a demand - relevant to what you have already done before you learn of a bankruptcy. And Minn. Stat. section 504B.171, subd. 2 keeps the rest of the lease alive after a tenant loses the right to possession, including the obligation to pay rent, so a claim for rent is not extinguished by the loss of possession under Minnesota law whatever a bankruptcy filing does to it.

A lease clause will not help. Do not write a term making a bankruptcy filing a default or an automatic termination. Once the case begins, 11 U.S.C. section 365(e)(1) stops a lease being terminated or modified solely because of such a clause, and this library offers no clause for it.

title: Minnesota Has No General Tenant-Confidentiality Duty, and One Very Sharp Specific One
bodyText: Minnesota imposes no general duty on a landlord to keep tenant information confidential. There is no statute saying what you may and may not do with an applicant file, a tenant payment history, or a complaint, and no general consent regime. Data practices law governs government bodies, not private landlords. So in the ordinary case your limits come from contract, from the fair housing record-and-inquiry ban, and from the one specific statute below - not from a confidentiality code. The fair housing limb is easy to miss because it is not framed as confidentiality. Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.09, subd. 1(3) and subd. 2(3) make it unlawful to make any record or inquiry in connection with a prospective rental that expresses, directly or indirectly, any limitation or discrimination as to a protected class. That reaches what you write down and store, not only what you decide, so a field recording an applicant religion or public-assistance status is a problem in itself. The specific duty is Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.206, subd. 2, and it is the strictest information rule in Minnesota landlord-tenant law. Where a tenant gives notice terminating as a victim of violence, four things become undisclosable and none of them may be entered into any shared database or provided to any person or entity. There are two features worth understanding as a matter of system design rather than lease drafting. First, subd. 2(c) makes those requirements paramount and provides that they supersede any other document or form previously signed by the tenant, including any release of information form. A blanket release in your application or lease is simply void against this, so collecting one buys you nothing. Second, subd. 5 is one of chapter 504B bidirectional non-waiver provisions: a residential tenant may not waive, AND A LANDLORD MAY NOT REQUIRE the residential tenant to waive, the rights under the section. That bars your conduct in asking, not merely the effect of the term - so presenting a tenant with a waiver or a broad information-release form touching this material is itself a breach, whether or not the tenant signs it. The companion entry for this library, "Victim Information Is Confidential and Overrides Anything They Signed", sets out the four categories, the exceptions and the $2,000 statutory damages. Two points of detail to read there carefully: the exceptions include use with the tenant consent, so the bar is on a PREVIOUSLY SIGNED blanket release rather than on contemporaneous agreement; and subd. 2(d) attaches the $2,000 to a violation of THIS SECTION, not merely of the subdivision. Practical upshot for your forms: do not run a general release-of-information clause, do not design screening fields that capture protected-class data, and keep victim-of-violence material out of any shared system, including anything your management software shares with other operators.

title: The Only Tenant Display Right Minnesota Has Is About Organizing
bodyText: Minnesota gives tenants no general right to display a flag, a political sign, a banner or a poster, and puts no lease-content restriction on a landlord about displays. There is one real exception, it is narrow, and it is easy to break by accident with an ordinary house rule. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.212, subd. 1(f) provides that no landlord shall prohibit or adopt any rule prohibiting residential tenants or nonresident tenant organizers from peacefully organizing, assembling, canvassing, leafleting, or otherwise exercising within the building their right of free expression for tenant organizing purposes. It adds two things that catch people out. You may not require tenants and tenant organizers to obtain prior permission to engage in protected activities. And you may not adopt and enforce rules that set unreasonable limits as to time, place, and manner of the meetings or communication with tenants in the building. Subd. 1(a) then names the activities you must allow, and two of them are display in substance: distributing information or leaflets in the common areas of the residential building, INCLUDING BULLETIN OR COMMUNITY BOARDS, and distributing information or leaflets to individual units. So a rule reserving the lobby notice board to management, a blanket no-leaflets rule, or a no-posting rule applied to a tenant association notice, is a problem. The limits of the exception matter as much. It runs to expression FOR TENANT ORGANIZING PURPOSES, so it is not a political-sign right and not a general free-speech right in the building. A nonresident organizer must be accompanied in the building by a tenant who lives there (subd. 1(e)). You are not required to give a tenant association any information about a tenant, including mailing address, telephone number or electronic contact information (subd. 1(b)). Enforcement runs through the retaliation and penalty subdivisions. Under subd. 2(a) you may not increase rent, decrease services, alter the rental agreement, file a legal action, contact law enforcement about a tenant immigration status, or seek possession in retaliation after a tenant joins or attempts to join a tenant association. Under subd. 3 the tenant may recover up to $1,000 per occurrence and reasonable attorney fees - but only where you acted unlawfully AND IN BAD FAITH, which is a real threshold and is often misquoted away. Check your house rules against subd. 1(f) rather than your lease. This is a conduct restriction that exists whatever the lease says.

title: An Employee You House Is a Tenant, Not a Licensee
bodyText:
Minnesota answers this topic in its definitions rather than in an employee-housing statute, and the answer is the one landlords least expect. Minn. Stat. section 504B.001, subd. 12 defines 'residential tenant' as a person occupying a dwelling in a residential building under a lease or contract, oral or written, 'that requires the payment of money or exchange of services', and it adds 'all other regular occupants of that dwelling unit'. A caretaker, resident manager, farm hand or live-in helper who occupies in exchange for work is a residential tenant. There is no licensee or incident-of-employment category that takes them out of chapter 504B.

Four consequences follow, and all four are the ones that cost money when they are missed. The chapter's covenants apply, so Minn. Stat. section 504B.161's habitability covenants attach and may not be waived or modified. Possession comes back only through the court: an eviction under Minn. Stat. section 504B.001, subd. 4 is 'a summary court proceeding to remove a tenant or occupant', and changing the locks or cutting the utilities on a departing employee is an unlawful exclusion under Minn. Stat. section 504B.375, which reaches 'actual or constructive removal or exclusion... which may include the termination of utilities or the removal of doors, windows, or locks' and which a lease may not waive. The notice rules apply as they do to any tenancy. And ending the employment does not of itself end the tenancy - the lease ends the way leases end.

Note also that you may be on both sides of the definition. Minn. Stat. section 504B.001, subd. 7 defines 'landlord' to include an 'agent, or other person directly or indirectly in control of rental property', so a resident caretaker who manages the building is your agent for some purposes and your tenant for others. Minn. Stat. section 504B.181, subd. 1 requires you to disclose to each residential tenant, in the rental agreement or otherwise in writing before the tenancy starts, the name and address of the person authorised to manage the premises - which may be that same caretaker.

What Minnesota does not have is worth stating plainly. There is no signed disclosure of occupancy and vacating conditions for employee housing of the Delaware kind, no requirement to offer a rental agreement when the employment ends, no express caretaker limb in the eviction statute, and no sponsored-guest-worker rent agreement filing of the American Samoa kind. Separate rules may apply to migrant and seasonal farm labour camps.

title: No Minnesota Forwarding Duty and No Attornment Statute, So the Clause Is All You Have
bodyText:
Minnesota imposes no statutory duty on a tenant to tell you about, or hand over, papers served on the tenant in a proceeding against the property -- so the Notice of Proceedings Against the Property clause is doing all the work, and it is enforceable as an ordinary lease requirement. Minnesota also has no attornment statute, and no counterpart to the many states that make a tenant's attornment to a stranger void, and no counterpart to New York's or Mississippi's three-years'-rent forfeiture for failing to notify the landlord.

WHAT MINNESOTA HAS INSTEAD, and it is worth knowing because it cuts both ways. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.121 says a tenant in possession under a lawful lease 'may not deny the landlord's title in an action brought by the landlord to recover possession of the property', unless the tenant held the property under an adverse or hostile claim of title before the lease began. That protects your possession action; it does not make the tenant forward anything.

And Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.181 subd. 3 runs the other way: if you have not made the landlord-and-manager disclosure, your caretaker, your manager or whoever receives the rent becomes your agent for service of process, notices and demands, and must pass them to you personally or by certified mail, return receipt requested -- so the forwarding duty Minnesota does create is on YOUR people, not on the tenant, and it only arises because you did not disclose. Make the disclosure (see "Disclosure of Landlord and Manager" clause) and keep the clause.

ONE PRACTICAL NOTE: in an eviction the summons is served on the tenant, so the clause matters most where someone ELSE is proceeding against the property -- a lender after a foreclosure sale, a competing claimant, a receiver. If a mortgage on your property is foreclosed, do not depend on the tenant forwarding anything: see "After a Foreclosure the New Owner Owes the Tenant 90 Days, and a Good Lease Can Run Out" for what the successor owner must serve and when.

title: No Minnesota Rule on Claims Against a Tenant's Insurance
bodyText: Minnesota has no rule about making a tenant claim on their renter's insurance, and none about you claiming against the tenant's policy. The word "insurance" is scarce in Minnesota landlord-tenant law and nothing in it touches a claim. What does decide the question is the shape of Minnesota's other rules. You cannot use the tenant's policy to carry your own duties. The habitability covenants cannot be waived or modified by either party, and no agreement can relieve you of maintaining common areas. So a lease term requiring the tenant to claim a landlord-responsible repair on their own policy does not shift the duty, which stays with you whatever the lease says and whatever cover the tenant carries. That point, and the lawfulness of requiring renter's insurance in the first place, are covered under the renter's insurance topic and are not repeated here. What you can do is recover from the tenant for damage the tenant caused, and let the tenant decide how to fund it. Minnesota gives you three routes and the tenant's insurer is not one of them. Your repair covenant does not extend to disrepair caused by the wilful, malicious or irresponsible conduct of the tenant or someone under the tenant's direction or control (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1). You may bring an action for wilful and malicious destruction of leased residential rental property and recover actual damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees (Sec. 504B.165). And you may withhold from the security deposit the amounts reasonably necessary to remedy payment defaults or to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted, with the burden of proving the reason for the withholding on you (Sec. 504B.178, subd. 3). Note the vocabularies. Minnesota does not use one phrase for tenant fault: the covenants statute says "willful, malicious, or irresponsible", the destruction statute says "willful and malicious", and the tenant remedies provision says "willful, malicious, negligent, or irresponsible". They are different tests, so do not carry one across to another section. The practical course: treat a claim on the tenant's policy as the tenant's decision, not your remedy. Bill the tenant for what the tenant owes, say so in writing, and get the tenant's written permission before you contact their insurer. Insurance claim handling, unfair claims practices and subrogation live in Minnesota's insurance code, which is outside this research.

title: A Tenant Portal Is Lawful in Minnesota -- and It Adds Two Duties You Did Not Have
bodyText:
Running a tenant portal in Minnesota is lawful, and Minnesota does not stop you from offering one or from encouraging tenants to use it. What Minnesota does is attach consequences to running one, and there are three you need to know.

FIRST, PAYMENTS. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.118, as rewritten with effect from August 1, 2026, defines a 'digital payment platform' as an electronic application or system under your direct control, or run by a vendor under contract with you, that lets a user conduct financial transactions. If you require OR PERMIT tenants to pay through one, you must offer an alternative whenever the platform is not functioning, and you may charge NO FEE for using that alternative. If a tenant fails to pay because both the platform and your alternative are not working for them, you may not take adverse action, and the tenant has an affirmative defence to a nonpayment eviction that results in mandatory dismissal plus attorney fees. The cash-receipt duty survives as subdivision 2. See the digital-payment row in this library for the detail.

SECOND, USING THE PORTAL FOR MESSAGES CREATES AN EVICTION-SERVICE DUTY. Sec. 504B.332 subd. 2(b) says that if you regularly use electronic written communication to communicate with a tenant, then in an eviction action you must make a good faith attempt to tell them electronically that a hearing has been scheduled, at least seven days before the court appearance. That is IN ADDITION to proper service. The message must carry a time and date stamp and state the date, time and place of the hearing from the summons, and it must go by the electronic channel you regularly use or to the last electronic address you have used for them. Your affidavit of service has to say how you complied, or state that you do not use electronic written communication with that tenant and have no electronic address for them. So the portal is not a free convenience: it adds a step you must document.

THIRD, MINNESOTA'S OWN MODEL OF ELECTRONIC DELIVERY IS CONSENT-BASED. Where chapter 504B permits electronic delivery it tends to require the tenant's authorisation -- the clearest example is Sec. 504B.241 subd. 1(c)(4), where a tenant screening file may be disclosed electronically only 'if authorized by the residential tenant'. Several Minnesota duties go the other way: ten sections of chapter 504B require certified or registered mail, and a notice posted conspicuously on the property cannot be posted in a portal instead.

MAKING THE PORTAL MANDATORY. Minnesota's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, Minn. Stat. ch. 325L applies only between parties who have each agreed to transact electronically, judged from the context and their conduct (Sec. 325L.05(b)). Even after agreeing, a party may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically, and that right 'may not be varied by agreement' (Sec. 325L.05(c)). So a portal-only lease term cannot stop a tenant going back to paper for a later transaction. Where a law requires you to give the tenant something in writing, an electronic record satisfies it only if the tenant can print or store it (Sec. 325L.08(a) and (c)). Where a law requires posting, certified or registered mail or another set method, you must still use that method (Sec. 325L.08(b)). Only a first-class or regular mail requirement may be varied by agreement, and only as far as that other law permits (Sec. 325L.08(d)(2)). So offer the portal and get each tenant's agreement to use it, but keep paper available and use the methods chapter 504B names. For payment, Sec. 504B.118 already gives you the answer: you may require the platform, but you must have a working free alternative.

title: No Minnesota Rent-Ledger or Records-on-Request Duty -- but Breach-Notice and SSN Rules Apply
bodyText: Minnesota does not give a tenant a general statutory right to demand your records, and it does not make you produce a rent ledger or an account history on request. There is no tenant-records inspection statute in chapter 504B and no rent-ledger duty anywhere in the eight chapters checked. Minnesota has no general written-information-security-program duty for a landlord, but two data rules do reach you, since you will routinely hold applicants' Social Security or individual taxpayer identification numbers and bank details. First, breach notice. 'Personal information' is a person's name with a Social Security number, a driver's license or Minnesota ID number, or a financial account number with its access code. If such unencrypted computerized data you own is acquired without authorization, you must tell each affected Minnesota resident 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay' (Minn. Stat. Sec. 325E.61, subd. 1). Notice may be written, or electronic if that is how you mainly communicate with the person. Notifying more than 500 people at once also means notifying the national consumer reporting agencies within 48 hours (subd. 2). Second, Social Security numbers. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 325E.59 you must not publicly post one, must not require one to be sent over the internet unless the connection is secure or the number is encrypted, and must limit access to the numbers you hold to the employees, agents or contractors who need it for their duties. Minnesota's Consumer Data Privacy Act, which gives consumers access rights, reaches only businesses handling the personal data of 100,000 or more consumers a year, or of 25,000 or more while deriving over 25 percent of gross revenue from selling it (Minn. Stat. Sec. 325M.12, subd. 1). A small business still must not sell a consumer's sensitive data without prior consent (Sec. 325M.17). What Minnesota does require is a short list of specific documents, each already covered by its own row in this library. You must give a copy of the written lease to every tenant who signed it, and you may take a signed receipt, which is prima facie evidence that they received it (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.115). You must give a written receipt for any rent or other payment made in cash -- immediately if it is paid in person, and within three business days otherwise (Sec. 504B.118 subd. 2). You must give a written receipt for an applicant screening fee if the applicant asks for one (Sec. 504B.173 subd. 1). Before you take a screening fee you must disclose your screening service and your rental criteria in writing, and you must notify a rejected applicant within 14 days identifying the criteria they failed (Sec. 504B.173 subd. 3). And you must give the withholding statement and accounting for a security deposit (Sec. 504B.178). The practical advice is unchanged by the absence of a statute: keep a dated ledger per tenancy, keep screening criteria and decisions in writing, and keep the lease copy receipt, because in Minnesota several of these documents are the evidence that defeats a tenant defence rather than paperwork for its own sake.

title: When an Applicant Asks to See Their Screening File, Minnesota Gives Them a Lot
bodyText: If an applicant or tenant asks to see the screening report you ran on them, Minnesota law tells you where to send them and what they are entitled to -- and it is more than a credit score. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.241 subd. 1, on request and proper identification a residential tenant screening service must disclose to the individual the nature and substance of ALL information in its files on them at the time of the request, AND the sources of that information. 'Proper identification' is defined in Sec. 504B.235 subd. 2 as information generally considered sufficient to identify a person, 'including a Minnesota driver's license, a Minnesota identification card, other forms of identification provided by a unit of government, a notarized statement of identity with a specimen signature of the person, or other reasonable form of identification' -- so the service cannot insist on one particular document. The disclosure is FREE if information in a report was used within the past 30 days to deny the rental or to increase the security deposit or rent; otherwise the service may charge a reasonable amount, must tell the individual the amount before furnishing the information, and may never charge for notifying people that inaccurate information has been deleted. The individual can choose the channel: in person during business hours where the files are kept, by mail within five business days of a written request, a summary by telephone on written request, or electronically where they authorise it and the service offers it. CORRECTIONS: if the individual disputes whether an item is complete or accurate, the service must reinvestigate and record the current status; anything found inaccurate or that can no longer be verified must be deleted from both the file and the report; and on request the service must notify everyone who received the report in the past six months of the deletion. EXPLANATIONS: the service must let the individual explain any eviction report or any disputed item that reinvestigation did not resolve, and that explanation has to be included in the report, though it can be capped at 100 words. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU: these duties sit on the screening service, not on you -- but Sec. 504B.245 lets an injured person sue the service OR THE LANDLORD for the greater of $1,000 or actual damages, plus costs of investigation and attorney fees. So do not stonewall the request. Give the applicant the service's name, address and telephone number, which you already had to disclose in writing before taking a screening fee, and keep a dated note of what you told them and when. If a tenant tells you an item is wrong, wait for the reinvestigation before you act on that item.

title: Snow and Ice Removal by Tenants in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota lets a lease make the tenant clear snow and ice only through a tenant maintenance agreement: the agreement must name the specific work, be supported by adequate consideration (something real in return, such as a stated rent reduction) and be set out conspicuously in writing. A conspicuous section of the lease is enough; it does not have to be a separate document. For that reason the library's general snow-removal clause is not used in Minnesota; use the Tenant Repair and Maintenance Agreement, which has a snow and ice box. No such agreement can waive your duties to keep the premises and all common areas fit and in reasonable repair, or relieve you of the duty to maintain common areas, so the cautious course is to treat snow and ice on shared walks, steps, entrances and parking areas as yours whatever the tenant agrees. Cities may make the owner or the occupant responsible for clearing public sidewalks and may charge unpaid removal costs to the property as a special assessment. Check your city's rule and say in the agreement who clears the public sidewalk.

title: Lawn, Landscaping and Watering by Tenants in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota lets a lease make the tenant mow, care for landscaping or water the yard only through a tenant maintenance agreement: the agreement must name the specific work, be supported by adequate consideration (something real in return, such as a stated rent reduction) and be set out conspicuously in writing. A conspicuous section of the lease is enough; it does not have to be a separate document, and the rule is the same for houses and apartment buildings. For that reason the library's general landscaping clause is not used in Minnesota; use the Tenant Repair and Maintenance Agreement, which has a lawn and landscaping box, and spell out watering, irrigation-system care and who pays for equipment and water. No such agreement can waive your duties to keep the premises and all common areas fit, in reasonable repair and in compliance with health and safety laws, or relieve you of the duty to maintain common areas, so shared grounds stay your responsibility. Cities may make the owner or the occupant responsible for weed elimination and may charge unpaid costs to the property as a special assessment.

title: Fines and a Gross Misdemeanour for Ignoring a Repair Order
bodyText: Ignoring a repair order is the expensive mistake. If a court finds that you have WILLFULLY failed to comply with a court order to remedy a violation, Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.391 makes the fine automatic and escalating: $250 for the first failure to comply; $500 for the second failure to comply with an order regarding the same violation; and $750 for the third and each subsequent failure to comply with an order regarding the same violation. The statute says the court "shall fine", so there is no discretion once willfulness is found. It also turns criminal on repetition. A landlord who willfully fails to comply with a court order to remedy a violation is guilty of a gross misdemeanour if it is the third or subsequent time the landlord has willfully failed to comply with an order to remedy a violation within a three-year period. Note what the three-year count is measured on: willful failures to comply with repair orders, not failures on the same violation, so separate properties and separate problems add up. "Willfully" is doing real work in both subdivisions. A failure you can show was not willful -- parts you could not get, a contractor who did not turn up, entry the tenant refused -- is not what this section punishes. But the burden of looking willful falls on silence, so if you cannot comply in time, go back to the court and say so on the record before the deadline, and keep the evidence of what you tried. These fines sit on top of everything else: they can be imposed in a rent escrow judgment and in a tenant remedies action, alongside rent abatement, an order to remedy and the appointment of an administrator.

title: Minnesota's Tenant Repair Remedies, and What They Cannot Do
bodyText: Minnesota gives a tenant four routes when repairs are not done, and none of them is self-help. First, an inspection. On a tenant's request the local authority charged with enforcing the code must inspect, and the inspector then tells you and the tenant in writing what was found and allows a reasonable period to correct it (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.185). Second, rent escrow (Sec. 504B.385). For an inspector's code violation the tenant waits for the time allowed to run out, then deposits the rent with the court administrator along with a copy of the written notice. For any other violation, including a breach of the lease, the tenant gives you written notice specifying it and you have 14 days. A hearing follows within ten to 14 days. The court may order relief under Sec. 504B.425 including retroactive rent abatement, release escrowed rent to pay for the repairs, order future rent deposited or abated until you remedy the violation, and impose the fines in Sec. 504B.391. Third, a tenant remedies action (Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471). It can be brought by a tenant, by a housing-related neighbourhood organisation with a tenant's written permission, by such an organisation for an unoccupied building in its area, or by a code enforcement authority -- so a complaint can arrive from someone who is not your tenant. The relief in Sec. 504B.425 is wide: an order that you remedy the violation; an order that the TENANT remedy it and deduct the cost from the rent on terms the court thinks just; appointment of an administrator to collect all the rents and do the work; a finding of the extent to which uncorrected violations impair the tenants' use and enjoyment, with rent abated accordingly; continued court supervision of the building for a year after an administration ends; and any other just relief, including attorney fees against you of up to $500, with no cap where Sec. 549.211 or another specific statute applies. Fourth, emergency relief (Sec. 504B.381) for a revoked rental licence, a condemnation order or notice of intent to condemn, or an emergency such as a serious infestation or loss of running water, hot water, heat, electricity or sanitary facilities. The tenant need only attempt to notify you 24 hours ahead, and the court can order you to begin remedying it immediately. That route does not extend to emergencies resulting from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant or anyone under the tenant's direction or control. Three things that are often misunderstood, each in your favour or against you. The tenant may NOT just stop paying: while an escrow case is pending the tenant must pay rent to you or as the court directs and "may not withhold rent to remedy a violation" (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 1(d)), and Minnesota has no self-help repair-and-deduct at all -- for a repair, deduction happens only on a court order under Sec. 504B.425(c). There is one unrelated self-help deduction in chapter 504B and it is worth knowing because it looks similar: in a shared-metered building, where you default on the utility bill and a tenant pays the utility to keep the service on, the tenant may deduct that payment from the next rent and it counts as rent paid (Sec. 504B.216, subd. 13(i)). That is a utility payment, not a repair. An escrow case does not freeze eviction: you may counterclaim for possession if the tenant did not deposit the full rent, and escrow and eviction actions between the same parties are consolidated and heard on the eviction date (Sec. 504B.385, subds. 2 and 8). But you may not use eviction, increased obligations or reduced services as a penalty for the complaint, and for 90 days after it is filed the burden of proving you were not doing that is yours (Sec. 504B.441). None of this can be written out of the lease. A provision waiving Sec. 504B.381 or Sec. Sec. 504B.395 to 504B.471 "is contrary to public policy and void" (Sec. 504B.465), and the escrow rights "may not be waived or modified" (Sec. 504B.385, subd. 11). Nor do these procedures change who ultimately pays: Sec. 504B.471 says they provide additional remedies and nothing in them "alters the ultimate financial liability of the landlord or residential tenant for repairs or maintenance of the building".

title: Two 2025 Acts Now Push the Attorney General's Guide at You -- Use Them
bodyText: Two 2025 acts put the attorney general's landlord-tenant guide in front of landlords without adding anything to your lease, and both are worth knowing because they tell you where to get the current version. FIRST, YOUR CITY NOW HAS TO HAND YOU THE LINK. Laws 2025, ch. 39, sec. 15 created a new section, Minn. Stat. Sec. 471.9994, headed LANDLORD-TENANT GUIDE. It applies when a home rule charter city, a statutory city or a town issues OR RENEWS a rental license, a registration or certificate of occupancy, or a similar document allowing a dwelling unit to be occupied by a residential tenant. In that case the city or town must give the landlord a link to the attorney general's website where the electronic version of the guide is published. It must also give instructions explaining how to request the guide in an alternative format from the attorney general's office. That is a duty on the city, not on you -- but it means every licence renewal is an occasion on which you should receive the current link, and if you do not, ask for it. SECOND, THE HOUSING AGENCY HAS TO PUBLISH IT TOO. Laws 2025, ch. 32, sec. 3 added Minn. Stat. Sec. 462A.07 subd. 21, requiring the commissioner of the Minnesota Housing Finance Agency to publish information on the rights and obligations of landlords and residential tenants, including promotion of the statement required by Sec. 504B.275, and to display that information prominently on the agency website. WHY THIS MATTERS TO YOU. Neither section adds a lease term and neither creates a landlord duty. What they change is practical: the statement is revised annually, so the copy you printed two years ago is out of date, and there are now two official places that must carry or point to the current one. Use the link your city gives you at licence renewal, or the agency website, rather than a stored copy.

title: The Attorney General's Statement: Your Only Duty Is a Posted Notice, and It Is Conditional
bodyText: Minnesota has an attorney general's statement of tenant rights, but almost nothing about it is your duty, and the one duty you do have is CONDITIONAL -- which is the detail most landlords and most lease forms get wrong. WHOSE DUTY IS WHAT. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.275 puts the work on the attorney general: to prepare and make available to the public a statement summarizing the significant legal rights and obligations of landlords and residential tenants, including descriptions of the significant provisions of chapter 504B, to tell tenants in public housing to consult their leases for additional federal-law rights, and to include the attorney general's telephone number and address. The attorney general must revise it annually and hold a public meeting on it. You are not required to prepare it, to obtain it, to hand it to a tenant, or to attach it to the lease. YOUR ACTUAL DUTY, AND THE CONDITION ON IT. Sec. 504B.181 subd. 2(b) reads: 'Unless the landlord is required to post a notice by section 471.9995, the landlord shall also place a notice in a conspicuous place on the property that states that a copy of the statement required by section 504B.275 is available from the attorney general to any residential tenant upon request.' So the duty to post that notice applies only where Sec. 471.9995 does NOT already require a posting. And Sec. 471.9995 is not a duty on you at all -- it is a duty on the CITY OR TOWN. It applies to a rental license, registration, certificate of occupancy or similar document that a home rule charter or statutory city, or a town, issues and that must be posted in a building with multiple rental dwelling units. Such a document has to carry a statement that tenants may contact the attorney general for information about owners' and tenants' rights and obligations, with the attorney general's telephone number and address. Whether your building is in that position depends on the local licensing scheme, which is a municipal question. In practice, posting the Sec. 504B.181 notice anyway is the safe course: over-complying costs you nothing and removes the need to work out whether the condition is met. WHAT FAILING TO POST DOES NOT DO. Sec. 504B.181 subd. 4 says failure to post a notice required by subdivision 2 paragraph (b), or by Sec. 471.9995, 'shall not prevent any action to recover rent or possession of the premises'. That is a real carve-out: the rest of Sec. 504B.181 can bar an action for rent or possession until the landlord and manager identity information is disclosed, but the attorney-general-statement notice is expressly excluded from that consequence. ONE SCOPE EXCEPTION. Sec. 504B.275's own first sentence says that in that section 'residential tenant' does not include residents of manufactured home parks. WHAT MINNESOTA DOES NOT REQUIRE. There is no duty to attach a state-agency statement as the first page of the lease, no duty to have each tenant sign or initial it, and no provision barring you from suing until you have provided it. Several states have one or more of those. Minnesota has none of them.

title: Minnesota Sets No Criminal-Record Look-Back, Conditional-Offer or Income-Test Rule
bodyText: Minnesota does NOT limit how far back you may look at an applicant's criminal record, does not make you defer criminal screening until after a conditional offer, does not cap a minimum-income or rent-to-income test, and gives you no statutory negligence shield for renting to someone with a criminal record. Several states have one or more of those; Minnesota has none of them, and the Minnesota Human Rights Act does not make a criminal record or an eviction record a protected basis in housing. What Minnesota does control is narrower and specific. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.173 subd. 3a says 'No landlord may deny a rental application based on' a pending eviction action, any court file that is not public, has been expunged, or has been destroyed, or any eviction action that did not result in a writ of recovery of premises and order to vacate. Sec. 504B.173 subd. 3 makes you disclose in writing, before you take a screening fee, the name, address and telephone number of the screening service you will use and the criteria your decision will be based on, and makes you notify a rejected applicant within 14 days identifying the criteria they failed to meet -- so your criteria have to be written down before you apply them. Sec. 504B.117 makes you offer an applicant the option of an individual taxpayer identification number instead of a Social Security number. Two boundaries: Minneapolis and Saint Paul have their own tenant-screening ordinances, which are a municipal question -- check the city where the property sits. And the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act is a separate regime. Write your screening criteria down, apply them consistently, keep them inside Sec. 504B.173 subd. 3a, and take advice before adopting a blanket criminal-record rule.

title: Minnesota's Tenant-Screening Report Law Makes YOU Liable Too
bodyText: Minnesota regulates tenant screening reports in Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.235 to Sec. 504B.245, and the money remedy runs against the LANDLORD as well as the screening service -- which is why this is a vendor-selection and vendor-contract matter for you, not just something your screening company worries about. Sec. 504B.245 says that 'any person injured by a violation of section 504B.241 may bring a civil action against a residential tenant screening service or landlord and recover the greater of $1,000 or actual damages, together with costs and disbursements, including costs of investigation and reasonable attorney fees,' plus other equitable relief the court decides. WHAT THE SERVICE MUST DO (Sec. 504B.241): on request and proper identification it must disclose to the individual both the nature and substance of all information in its files on them AND the sources of that information -- free of charge if a report was used in the past 30 days to deny the rental or to increase the rent or security deposit, otherwise for a reasonable charge disclosed in advance. Disclosure is in person at its office, or by mail within five business days of a written request, or as a telephone summary on written request, or electronically if the tenant authorises it. If the tenant disputes an item, the service must reinvestigate, record the current status, and delete anything found inaccurate or no longer verifiable; on request it must notify everyone who received the report in the past six months of the deletion. The service must let the individual explain any eviction report or unresolved disputed item, and that explanation goes into the report (up to 100 words). COURT RECORDS: where a report uses a court file it must give the person's full name and date of birth if the file has them, and must accurately record the outcome including the specific basis of the court's decision when available; and the service has an affirmative duty to verify the current status of court files against Minnesota Court Records Online no more than 24 hours before issuing the report. THE TRAP: Sec. 504B.241 subd. 4(d) gives a safe harbour to the SCREENING SERVICE that reports court information completely and accurately -- the statute gives the landlord no equivalent shield. So choose a service that can show you it runs the 24-hour court check and honours disclosure and correction requests, and say so in your contract with it. Sec. 504B.245 carries its own remedy and does not depend on Sec. 8.31. For the fee side of screening see the applicant-screening-fee rules; for the tenant's own right to see and correct the file, see the tenant-records row.

title: Minnesota's Tenant Duties, All of Them, and Two Are Criminal
bodyText:
Minnesota's tenant duties are not in one list -- they are scattered across chapter 504B and three other chapters, and two of them are criminal offences. Here is the whole roster, built from the statutes rather than from another state's tenant-duty section, because Minnesota has no general 'tenant obligations' statute to copy.

THE COVENANT. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.171 subd. 1 writes into every lease, oral or written, the tenant's covenant not to allow controlled substances in violation of chapter 152, prostitution or prostitution-related activity, the unlawful use or possession of a firearm, or stolen or robbery-obtained property -- on the premises or in the common area and curtilage. Subdivision 1(b) adds the tenant's covenant not to commit a domestic-abuse-type act listed in Sec. 504B.206 subd. 1(a) against another tenant, licensee or authorized occupant. You cannot waive or modify it, and neither can the tenant.

COLD WEATHER. Sec. 504B.155: between November 15 and April 15, a tenant who removes from, abandons or vacates a building with pipes liable to freezing without first giving you three days' notice of intention to do so is GUILTY OF A MISDEMEANOR. It does not apply on termination of the tenancy.

DESTRUCTION. Sec. 504B.165 gives an action for 'willful AND malicious' destruction of leased residential rental property, with actual damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party.

SAFETY DEVICES, three separate reporting duties. A tenant must tell you of a nonfunctioning smoke alarm within 24 hours of discovering it (Sec. 299F.362 subd. 5a), and an occupant who willfully disables a smoke alarm or causes it to be nonfunctioning, resulting in damage or injury, is guilty of a misdemeanor (subd. 6(b)). A tenant must keep a carbon monoxide alarm you installed in good repair and replace one stolen, removed, missing or rendered inoperable during the occupancy (Sec. 299F.51 subd. 3). And a tenant must tell you of a nonfunctioning or malfunctioning reversing device in an automatic garage door opening system within 24 hours of discovering the problem (Sec. 325F.83 subd. 5).

FIRE MARSHAL ORDERS. Under Sec. 299F.18, an occupant served with a fire marshal's written order to remove combustible or explosive material or correct a dangerous condition who fails to comply within 24 hours, or any longer period the order sets, is guilty of a misdemeanor. The material may then be removed, or the condition corrected, at the expense of the building's owner, the person served, or both. So the cost can land on you even when the order was served on your tenant.

REPAIRS THE TENANT AGREES TO DO. Sec. 504B.161 subd. 2 lets you agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance, but ONLY if the agreement is supported by adequate consideration and set out in a conspicuous writing -- and no such agreement may waive subdivision 1 or relieve you of maintaining the common areas.

NOTICE BEFORE LEAVING. Sec. 504B.181 subd. 5: a tenant who moves from or subleases the premises without giving you at least 30 days' written notice voids the owner-identity disclosure provisions of that section as to that tenant.

ONE WARNING THAT MATTERS MORE THAN ANY ITEM ON THE LIST. Minnesota uses FOUR different tenant-fault phrases and they are not interchangeable. Sec. 504B.161 subd. 1(a)(2) and (4) say 'willful, malicious, OR irresponsible'. Sec. 504B.165 says 'willful AND malicious'. Sec. 504B.415(2) says 'willful, malicious, NEGLIGENT, or irresponsible'. Sec. 504B.381 subd. 6 says 'deliberate or negligent'. Never carry one section's phrase into another section's test, and never let a lease clause use a looser phrase and then cite the stricter statute for it.

title: No Notice Rule for Changing Terms - but Your Notice Can Never Undercut the Tenant's
bodyText: Minnesota sets no notice period for changing a lease term mid-tenancy -- not for rules, not for policies, not for fees, and not for rent. During a fixed term you cannot change a term unilaterally at all: the lease is a contract and the tenant has to agree. For a tenancy with no fixed end date, there is no statute letting you impose new terms on notice either, so in practice you have two routes. Get the tenant's agreement to the change, in writing, which is the clean route. Or end the tenancy properly, with written notice at least as long as the interval between rent payments or three months, whichever is shorter, running a full rental period and expiring at the end of one, and offer a new tenancy on the new terms. What Minnesota does have is a relative rule, and it bites on the second route. Where your lease gives you a notice period for a notice to quit or a rent increase that differs from the period it requires of the tenant for a notice of intention to move out, your notice may never be shorter than the tenant's period, and a notice of nonrenewal counts as a notice to quit. The tenant, for their part, may use either period in the lease, whichever they choose. None of that can be waived or modified, and a lease provision waiving any of it is contrary to public policy and void. So never write a flat number for your own notice without also tying it to the tenant's: raise the tenant's figure later and a flat number becomes unlawful. Two things that are not yours. A 60-day rent-increase notice does exist in Minnesota, but it binds manufactured home park owners on lot rent, not ordinary landlords. And an automatic-renewal clause has its own certified-mail notice window. If you want the power to change house rules during a tenancy, say so in the lease, state how much notice you will give, and expect the change to bind only if the lease genuinely reserved it.

title: Federally Subsidized Housing: a One-Year Written Notice on Four Conditions
bodyText:
If you own federally subsidized rental housing, Minnesota makes you give your tenants a full ONE-YEAR written notice in four situations, and this is probably the longest notice duty in Minnesota landlord-tenant law. The four are: a federal Section 8 contract is going to expire; you are going to exercise an option to terminate or not renew a Section 8 contract and mortgage; you are going to prepay a mortgage and the prepayment will end federal use restrictions on the housing; or you are going to terminate a housing subsidy program. If the lease itself begins less than a year before one of those things applies, the notice has to be given at the start of the lease instead.

Two things to watch. The notice is owed to the residential tenants, so it is a building-wide exercise, not a per-unit one, and the trigger is your decision or the contract's expiry, not the tenant's conduct. And the third situation -- prepaying a mortgage -- has been held preempted by a federal court to the extent it creates a longer timeline than federal law allows, so take advice before relying on or ignoring that one.

This duty sits on top of, not instead of, your ordinary termination notices. The notice to end a particular tenancy still follows the usual rules, and a Section 8 tenancy caught by a foreclosure has its own 90-day rule. If your housing is HUD public housing rather than Section 8, note separately that a tenant facing a breach-of-lease eviction there has a right to counsel.

title: No Exemption Notice, Because There Is Nothing to Be Exempt From
bodyText: Some states make you put a statement in the lease telling the tenant that the property is EXEMPT from a statewide rent cap or a just-cause eviction rule. Minnesota has neither law for an ordinary residential tenancy, so there is nothing for a property to be exempt from and no exemption notice belongs in a Minnesota lease. Do not copy one in from another state's form. Minnesota does have its own scope limits, and the point about all of them is that they apply by themselves -- no notice, no statement, nothing in the lease. The ones worth knowing: the financial-distress and pending-foreclosure rules in Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.151 'do not apply to a manufactured home park as defined in section 327C.015, subdivision 8', and do not apply at all where the holder or mortgagee agrees not to terminate the tenant's lease other than for lease violations for at least a year from the start of the tenancy and the lease requires no prepaid rent for a month beginning after the cancellation or redemption period ends; the entry-notice section, Sec. 504B.211, 'does not apply to residential tenants and landlords of manufactured home parks as defined in section 327C.015'; the landlord's habitability covenants in Sec. 504B.161 apply only to leases 'concluded or renewed on or after June 15, 1971'; and the security-deposit section, Sec. 504B.178, applies only to tenancies 'commencing or renewed on or after July 1, 1973'. Those last two dates now catch every live tenancy, so treat both sections as applying to you without qualification. There is one more, and it cuts the other way: the right-to-counsel section, Sec. 504B.268, is limited to public housing, and the one-year notice in Sec. 504B.255 is limited to federally subsidised housing, so a private market landlord is outside both -- again with no notice to give. If you are renting a lot in a manufactured home park, you are in Minn. Stat. ch. 327C and this lease is the wrong instrument -- see "Farm Tenancies and Manufactured Home Parks Are Governed Elsewhere".

title: No Rent Cap, No Just-Cause Rule and No Tenant Right to Buy, So No Notice
bodyText: Some states make you put a notice in the lease telling tenants that a statewide rent cap or a just-cause eviction rule applies, or that they have a right to buy the property before you sell it. Minnesota has none of those laws for an ordinary residential tenancy, so none of those notices belongs in a Minnesota lease. DO NOT copy California-style or Oregon-style tenant-protection language into one. Specifically: there is no statewide rent cap or rent-stabilisation law; there is no just-cause or good-cause requirement for ending an ordinary tenancy, because Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.285 subd. 1(a)(2) and (3) make holding over after the term, and holding over after a notice to quit, grounds in their own right (see "Minnesota Is Not a Just-Cause State, but Six Situations Still Block an Eviction" for the six situations that do block a particular eviction); and there is no right for a residential tenant to buy your property or to be offered it first. TWO THINGS MINNESOTA DOES HAVE, and neither is a lease notice for this lease. (1) MANUFACTURED HOME PARKS GET THE WHOLE PACKAGE, in Minn. Stat. ch. 327C. A park owner may recover a lot only for a listed reason -- Sec. 327C.09 subd. 1 is actually headed 'Cause required'. Rent may not be raised more than twice a year (Sec. 327C.06). And residents get notice of a sale and a chance to buy: when a park is offered to the public through newspaper advertising or a licensed broker, Sec. 327C.096 requires concurrent written notice to each resident household, though it says the notice 'does not grant any property rights in the park and is for informational purposes only'; Sec. 327C.097 requires notice of an unsolicited offer the owner intends to consider, disclosing 'the price range and material terms and conditions upon which the park owner would consider selling'; and Sec. 327C.095 subd. 6 gives residents, through a representative, 45 days to match a purchaser's cash price and material terms where the purchaser intends to close or convert the park. Parks are a different instrument and a different chapter -- see "Farm Tenancies and Manufactured Home Parks Are Governed Elsewhere" and "Closing or Converting a Manufactured Home Park: 12 Months, Fixed 14-Point Words, and a Resident Chance to Buy". (2) FEDERALLY SUBSIDISED HOUSING has a one-year notice. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.255 requires a landlord of federally subsidised rental housing to give tenants one year's written notice where a Section 8 contract will expire, where the landlord exercises an option to terminate or not renew a Section 8 contract and mortgage, where the landlord prepays a mortgage and that ends federal use restrictions, or where the landlord terminates a housing subsidy programme -- and the notice goes in at the start of the lease if the lease begins less than a year before one of those applies. That section is covered in the termination-notice row.

title: No Minnesota Tenant Statute Is Set to Expire, but Five 2026 Dates Are Worth a Diary Note
bodyText: As of October 29, 2026, no Minnesota landlord-tenant statute is on a repeal or expiration clock. Minn. Stat. Secs. 299F.850 to 299F.859, the cigarette fire-safety programme, are repealed only if a federal reduced cigarette ignition propensity standard that preempts them takes effect. Minn. Stat. ch. 504B -- the landlord-tenant act -- and Minn. Stat. ch. 327C -- manufactured home parks -- both run indefinitely. There is also nothing for Minnesota to sunset in the first place, because it has no rent cap, no just-cause regime for ordinary tenancies and no tenant purchase right (see "No Rent Cap, No Just-Cause Rule and No Tenant Right to Buy, So No Notice"). WHAT IS ON A DATE, none of it a sunset of a tenant protection, and all of it worth a diary note. Laws 2026, ch. 81 rewrote Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.118 as PAYMENT OF RENT, added Sec. 504B.2136, added Sec. 504B.216 subd. 7a and amended Sec. 504B.321 subd. 2; its secs. 2, 3 and 5 are effective August 1, 2026 by their own terms and secs. 1 and 4 carry no effective-date clause at all. Laws 2026, ch. 88, the Revisor's corrections act, amended Sec. 504B.361 subd. 1 and REPEALED Sec. 504B.345 subd. 2 -- a repeal, but a technical one, not a sunset. Laws 2026, ch. 82 limits common interest community associations' late fees, fines and attorney fees and adds two new sections; its sec. 1 takes effect the day after final enactment, secs. 2 to 4 and 6 to 14 take effect January 1, 2027, and its sec. 5 carries no effective-date clause. Laws 2026, ch. 80 adds Minn. Stat. Sec. 559.206 and Sec. 559.21 subd. 10 from July 1, 2026, for contracts for deed entered into on or after that date. And one older amendment landed this year: the Revisor's note to Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.095 records that the amendment to subdivision 5 by Laws 2024, ch. 96, art. 2, sec. 9 is effective August 1, 2026. Check each year's new session laws.

title: No Duty to Translate a Minnesota Lease
bodyText: Minnesota imposes no duty to translate a residential lease, no duty to provide it in the language you advertised or negotiated in, and no minimum type size for lease text generally. There is no Spanish-language or Hmong-language lease requirement and no rule about which text prevails if you hand over two versions. If you give a tenant a translation, that is your choice, and the English lease remains the contract unless you say otherwise. One Minnesota statute does carry a translation duty, and it is worth knowing about precisely so you do not reason from it. Minn. Stat. Sec. 327C.095, subd. 6(a) requires that the 45-day notice of a purchaser intent to close or convert a manufactured home park be sent by first class mail and made available in alternative formats or translations if requested by a resident, where the request is a reasonable accommodation due to a disability of an adult resident, or because there is not an adult resident able to speak the language the notice is provided in. The same section, at subd. 1(a), also requires a park closure statement to carry a specified sentence about the Minnesota Manufactured Home Relocation Trust Fund in a font no smaller than 14 point. Both of those live in chapter 327C, which governs manufactured home park lots, and a park lot is outside what this lease is for. They do not reach an ordinary residential tenancy, and nothing like them exists in chapter 504B. What you should still do, even with no duty, is draft plainly. Minnesota Plain Language Contract Act obligations apply to most leases of three years or less and bite on clarity rather than on language choice.

title: Minnesota's Trespass Statute, and Four Limits on Your Side
bodyText: Minnesota's criminal trespass statute, Minn. Stat. Sec. 609.605, has no landlord procedure or prescribed notice form. Three of its clauses do the work. It is a misdemeanor to trespass on another's premises and, 'without claim of right', refuse to leave 'on demand of the lawful possessor' (subd. 1(b)(3)). It is a misdemeanor to return within one year after being told to leave and not to return, without claim of right or 'consent of one with authority to consent' (subd. 1(b)(8)). And it is a misdemeanor to enter the 'locked or posted building of another' without consent. A posting sign must be at least 8-1/2 by 11 inches, placed conspicuously, and carry a general notice warning against trespass (subd. 1(a)(5)(i) and (b)(4)). The statute does not say what form a 'do not return' notice takes, so make it written and dated and keep a copy. Beyond that, there are four lines on your own side. FIRST, YOU CANNOT USE A TRESPASS NOTICE AGAINST A TENANT. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.375 reaches 'actual or constructive removal or exclusion of a residential tenant which may include the termination of utilities or the removal of doors, windows, or locks'. A tenant excluded unlawfully can present a verified petition and, if it clearly appears the exclusion was unlawful, the court 'shall immediately order' that the tenant have possession, directed to the sheriff for immediate execution. A lease provision in which the tenant waives that section is contrary to public policy and void. Barring a tenant from the building is removing them, whatever you call the paperwork. SECOND, A TENANT'S GUESTS ARE A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM STRANGERS. The statute excuses a person who has the 'consent of one with authority to consent'. Whether your tenant has that authority for a guest you have barred, in the unit or the common areas, only case law could settle. So act on a tenant's guest through the lease's guest rules rather than a trespass notice. The lease governs guests; criminal trespass governs strangers; and the overlap is where disputes actually happen. THIRD, TENANT ORGANIZERS ARE PROTECTED AND A BLANKET NO-TRESPASS POLICY WILL CATCH THEM. Under Sec. 504B.212 subd. 1, you must allow tenants and tenant organizers to distribute information and leaflets in common areas and to individual units, to contact tenants, and to convene meetings in a space at the building. Subdivision 1(f) says 'No landlord shall prohibit or adopt any rule prohibiting residential tenants or nonresident tenant organizers from peacefully organizing, assembling, canvassing, leafleting, or otherwise exercising within the building their right of free expression for tenant organizing purposes', and you may not require prior permission. One limit does help you: a tenant organizer who is not your tenant must be accompanied in the building by a tenant who lives there. FOURTH, POLITICAL CANDIDATES HAVE A SEPARATE RIGHT OF ACCESS to multiple-unit residences, with its own conditions and its own exceptions -- see the political-access row in this library. SO WHAT SHOULD YOU DO? Write your guest and common-area rules in the lease, where they bind the tenant. Do not write a trespass procedure into a lease, because the lease cannot bind a non-party and the criminal statute does not depend on it. Before barring anyone from a building, check your city's rules and take Minnesota advice, and carve out tenants, their household, tenant organizers accompanied by a resident, and lawful candidate access.

title: Minnesota Publishes a Tenant Rights Statement and Does Not Make You Deliver It
bodyText:
Minnesota has a statutory tenant-rights statement, and no duty on you to hand it over. Both halves matter, and they are easy to get the wrong way round.

The statement exists, and it is the attorney general's job, not yours. Minn. Stat. § 504B.275 requires that "The attorney general shall prepare and make available to the public a statement which summarizes the significant legal rights and obligations of landlords and residential tenants of rental dwelling units. The statement shall include descriptions of the significant provisions of this chapter." It must tell tenants in public housing to consult their leases for additional federal-law rights, and must carry the attorney general's telephone number and address. The attorney general must revise it annually "as necessary to ensure that it continues accurately to describe the statutory and case law governing the rights and duties of landlords and residential tenants", and must hold a public meeting on it before each issue. The legislature's stated intent is that it "be brief, accurate, and complete in identifying significant legal rights and obligations, and written using words with common, everyday meanings". Residents of manufactured home parks are outside the section by its first sentence.

The section imposes no duty on a landlord at all. It does not say you must give the statement to a tenant, attach it to the lease, offer it, mention it, or get an acknowledgment. Read the section and the duty runs one way only: the attorney general prepares and publishes, the public may obtain. Minnesota has no truth-in-renting act in the sense other states use the term — no required summary of the lease in plain words, no statement of consumer restrictions, no mandatory handbook, no acknowledgment to sign.

What a Minnesota landlord actually has to put in writing. The duties exist, but they are specific disclosures rather than a general rights statement:

Your identity and address, under Minn. Stat. § 504B.181 — covered by "Disclosure of Landlord and Manager" clause.
Every nonoptional fee, in the lease and in the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, under Minn. Stat. § 504B.120 — covered by the fee rows.
Outstanding inspection and condemnation orders, under Minn. Stat. § 504B.195 — covered by "You Must Hand Over Outstanding Inspection and Condemnation Orders".
The prohibition on charging for a service or support animal, if you charge a pet fee, under Minn. Stat. § 504B.113, subd. 3(b).
A copy of the lease, under Minn. Stat. § 504B.115 — covered by "Receipt of Copy of Lease" clause.

And one rights-information duty that does exist, though it comes later than you might expect. Minn. Stat. § 504B.321, subd. 1a requires that before filing an eviction for nonpayment you give the tenant written notice containing, among other things, three prescribed statements in the statute's own words — one telling the tenant "You have the right to seek legal help. If you can't afford a lawyer, free legal help may be available. Contact Legal Aid or visit www.LawHelpMN.org to know your rights and find your local Legal Aid office.", one about applying for financial help, and one explaining that the landlord can file if the total is not paid or the tenant does not move within 14 days. So Minnesota does make you hand a tenant a rights notice — at the pre-eviction stage, not at signing.

Practical point. Do not build a lease around a Minnesota rights-statement requirement, because there is not one. If you want to give tenants the attorney general's statement, you may; it is a sensible thing to do and nothing stops you. Just do not represent it as something the law requires you to deliver, and keep your actual disclosure obligations — identity, fees, inspection orders, lease copy — straight, because those are the ones with consequences.

title: Minnesota Has No Squatter Statute, No Affidavit Removal and No Lock-Change Right
bodyText:
The removal routes other states added over the last few years do not exist in Minnesota. Minnesota's landlord-tenant statutes and its 2025 and 2026 session laws provide no sheriff or constable removal of an unauthorised occupant on the owner's sworn complaint, no police removal of a transient occupant on an affidavit, no ex parte court order against occupants who were never tenants, no 24-hour or expedited squatter hearing, no right to change the locks after an arrest, no treble or three-times-fair-market-rent penalty for wrongful use, and no criminal offence of unlawful squatting with a document-production citation.

One thing does exist. Minnesota's criminal trespass offence is Minn. Stat. section 609.605. The 2026 session confirms the section is live - Laws 2026, ch. 97, sec. 24 amends section 609.605, subd. 2 - but that amendment is a terminology change, replacing 'battered women' with 'domestic abuse victims' in the gross misdemeanour trespass offence about shelter and transitional housing grounds, and it creates nothing for a landlord. Whether and when a police response is available against a person with no colour of right is a section 609.605 question and a question for a Minnesota lawyer, not a lease question.

The practical warning is the one that catches landlords in states like this. Calling the police and having someone removed, where the person has been living in the unit, risks being an unlawful exclusion under Minn.
