Stat. section 504B.375 even though you did not touch the door yourself - that section reaches constructive as well as actual exclusion, the remedy is immediate restoration of possession by the sheriff, and the tenant can also reach Minn. Stat. section 504B.231's ouster damages. If the person has been in the unit, treat them as a tenant and file.

title: In Minnesota the Only Way Out Is an Eviction Action
bodyText:
Minnesota gives you no fast track and no self-help route against an unauthorised occupant. The answer is the eviction action, and it is the eviction action whoever the person is.

Start with two definitions, because they decide most of this. Minn. Stat. section 504B.001, subd. 4 defines 'evict' as 'a summary court proceeding to remove a tenant or occupant from or otherwise recover possession of real property by the process of law set out in this chapter' - so the chapter's own process is how an occupant is removed, not only a tenant. And subd. 12 defines 'residential tenant' to include, after the person occupying under a lease or contract, 'all other regular occupants of that dwelling unit'. A person who has settled in and become a regular occupant is a residential tenant for the whole of chapter 504B, whether or not they ever signed anything and whether or not you approved them.

The ground is there when you need it. Minn. Stat. section 504B.285, subd. 1(a)(2) lets the person entitled to the premises recover possession when 'any person holds over real property after termination of the time for which it is demised or leased to that person or to the persons under whom that person holds possession'. The words 'the persons under whom that person holds possession' are what reach the occupant who came in through your tenant. You do not need a lease with the occupant to name them in the action.

Self-help is barred twice over, and the second bar is the expensive one. Minn. Stat. section 504B.281 says no person may occupy or take possession of real property except where occupancy or possession is allowed by law, and then only in a peaceable manner - and 'no person' includes you. Minn. Stat. section 504B.375 then gives the occupant a summary petition to recover possession, and it applies to 'actual or constructive removal or exclusion ... which may include the termination of utilities or the removal of doors, windows, or locks'. The court can order possession back immediately, the sheriff executes the order immediately, and a lease provision in which a residential tenant waives that section is contrary to public policy and void.

Two further limits are worth knowing before you act. Minn. Stat. section 504B.311 bars an eviction action altogether against an occupant whose lease, or whose ancestor's or predecessor's lease, was terminated more than three years before the action, where the occupant or their predecessor was in quiet possession for three consecutive years immediately before filing. And if you want to go in and look, Minn. Stat. section 504B.211, subd. 3(8) makes 'the landlord has a reasonable belief that the unit is being occupied by an individual without a legal right to occupy it' a reasonable business purpose for entry - but it is still entry under that section, so the 24-hour notice, the time window and the 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. limit apply unless one of the subd. 4 emergencies does.

Practically, your protection is written in advance rather than exercised afterwards. Name every occupant in the lease, keep the guest-stay limit, and act on a long-staying guest before the guest becomes a regular occupant, because once that happens the person has chapter 504B's protections and your only route is the court.

title: Charging Separately for Parking - the Total Monthly Payment Trap
bodyText:
Minnesota has no unbundled-parking rule. Nothing requires you to include parking in the rent, nothing requires you to offer it separately, and nothing caps what you charge for a space. What Minnesota does regulate is how the charge is presented, and that is where the money is.

Start with the only question that matters: can the tenant take the unit without the space? If parking is required, or the unit cannot practically be used without it, the parking charge is a nonoptional fee. Minn. Stat. section 504B.120, subd. 1 then requires you to disclose it in the lease, to add it to the rent and describe the sum as the Total Monthly Payment on the first page of the lease, and to disclose it in any advertisement or posting of the unit along with whether utilities are included. Subd. 2 makes a violation worth treble damages, and the court may award the tenant reasonable attorney fees. That is a formatting duty as much as a drafting one, so an unbundled parking charge buried in the middle of a lease for a unit with no other parking is the classic way to trip it.

If parking is genuinely optional - the tenant could decline it and still take the unit - the charge is outside the Total Monthly Payment, and the optional clause under this topic is the way to document the choice. Keep the paperwork: the thing you will have to show is that the tenant could have said no.

Do not call it rent, and do not assume it is defenceless either. No Minnesota statute lets a lease designate a fee as rent, and Minn. Stat. section 504B.172 recognises fees recovered 'directly, or through additional rent' only to give the tenant reciprocal attorney fees - so the label works against you. But unpaid non-rent charges are not beyond reach: Minn. Stat. section 504B.321, subd. 1a requires the 14-day written notice before an eviction action 'alleging nonpayment of rent or other unpaid financial obligation in violation of the lease', and the notice must give a specific accounting of unpaid rent, late fees and other charges under the lease. So an unpaid parking charge goes in the accounting, not in the rent.

Two situations have their own rules and neither is an ordinary apartment. In a manufactured home park, Minn. Stat. section 327C.03, subd. 1 prohibits any fee other than the periodic rental payment 'for the right to obtain or retain a lot', and subd. 3 requires periodic rental payments to be uniform throughout the park except for lot size or location or special services or facilities, so a park owner's room to charge separately is far narrower than a landlord's - parks are governed by chapter 327C and are outside what this lease is for. And if you rent out a unit in a common interest community, Laws 2026, chapter 82, section 6 adds a new paragraph (f) to Minn. Stat. section 515B.3-107, effective January 1, 2027: the association 'has no authority to regulate the parking of a unit owner or a guest, tenant, or invitee of the unit owner within an improved public right of way that a unit of government maintains and repairs', except to require compliance with applicable statutes, laws and ordinances, and a unit owner or resident must be permitted to park a personal or work vehicle on the part of the owner's property or of the limited common element allocated to the unit that was designed or modified for parking, provided it does not encroach on another owner's property, block a pedestrian walkway, or interfere with the association's maintenance. If you have been telling a tenant that the association controls the street outside, that stops being true on January 1, 2027.

title: Interest on Money a Tenant Owes You
bodyText: Minnesota has no landlord-tenant statute that sets interest on rent, damages or other money a tenant owes you, and none that requires interest to be stated in the lease before you can charge it. Four things in the law bear on it. First, Minnesota law does assume interest can run on rent arrears: in a nonpayment eviction the tenant redeems the tenancy by paying the rent in arrears with interest, the costs of the action, and an attorney's fee of no more than $5. The rate is not stated there. Minnesota's general interest statute fills the gap: interest on 'any legal indebtedness' is 6 percent a year unless a different rate is contracted for in writing (Minn. Stat. § 334.01, subd. 1). The same subdivision bars taking more than 8 percent a year 'for the loan or forbearance of money', and interest may not be compounded. Whether rent arrears are a 'forbearance' under that cap only case law could settle, so if your lease sets a rate, keep it at 8 percent a year or less, simple. Once you sue, prejudgment interest runs from the start of the action or a written notice of claim, except as a contract provides, but it is not awarded on a judgment no larger than the conciliation court limit (Minn. Stat. § 549.09, subd. 1(b)). After judgment, a judgment of $50,000 or less bears simple interest at the rate the state court administrator sets each year from the one-year Treasury yield, at least 4 percent; a larger one bears 10 percent (subd. 1(c)). Second, a late fee is not interest. The statute says so expressly, and caps the late fee at 8% of the overdue rent payment under a written agreement that says when it applies. Treat the late fee and any interest claim as separate things, and do not use interest to get past the 8% cap. Third, the interest Minnesota does fix by statute runs the other way: a security deposit bears simple noncompounded interest at 1% a year, payable to the tenant, and amounts under $1 are excluded. Fourth, where you bill a utility separately and have undercharged the tenant, no interest and no delinquency fee may be charged as part of the payment plan you must offer. Practical course: if you want interest on overdue amounts, say so in the lease with the rate and when it starts, keep it off amounts that are in dispute, and remember that an interest charge is a charge, so a tenant can ask where in the lease it is written.

title: Minnesota Has No Usufruct
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law concept and Minnesota is a common-law state. The word usufruct appears nowhere in Minnesota statutes, session laws or the constitution, and neither do the related civil-law terms. There is no Minnesota rule about a usufructuary letting property, about how long such a lease may run against the owner, or about what happens to the tenancy when the usufruct ends. Minnesota land tenure is allodial - Minn. Const. art. I, Sec. 15 provides that all lands within the state are allodial and feudal tenures of every description with all their incidents are prohibited. If you are dealing with a landlord whose interest is less than full ownership, the questions to ask here are the ordinary common-law ones: what interest does the landlord actually hold, and does the lease outrun it. Minnesota answers those through its own machinery rather than through usufruct, and a lease granted by someone whose interest ends before the term does is a title and authority problem, not a usufruct problem. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.121 is worth knowing in that connection: a tenant in possession under a lawful lease may not deny the landlord title in the landlord possession action, except a tenant who, before entering into the lease, possessed the property under a claim of title adverse or hostile to the landlord.

title: When a Utility Allowance with Tenant-Paid Overage Is Unlawful in Minnesota
bodyText:
A utility allowance with a tenant-paid overage is a normal contract term in many states. In Minnesota it is lawful only outside two settings, and inside them it is flatly barred.

First, a shared-metered residential building — a building with more separate dwelling units than meters. If you bill tenants separately for natural gas, electricity, or water and sewer there, your only permitted charges are an administrative billing charge of up to $8 per billing period and a single late payment charge of up to $5 a month that may not compound. Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 8 then says that apart from that late charge, 'no other fees or charges may be imposed on or collected from tenants for utility service'. Section 216B.023, subds. 4 and 6 say the same thing twice more. An overage charge is a charge for utility service, so there is no room for one. The apportionment formulas are mandatory, and you may not apportion electricity at all.

Second, a lot in a manufactured home park. Section 327C.03, subd. 1 allows 'no fee other than the periodic rental payment' except as §§ 327C.03 and 327C.04 permit, and § 327C.04 caps park utility charges by reference to comparable market and single-family rates. Parks are outside what this lease should be used for in any event.

Where the term is lawful — a single-family house, or a building where the unit has its own meter and you pay the provider from rent — two Minnesota rules still bite. Minn. Stat. § 504B.120, subd. 1 makes you disclose every nonoptional fee in the lease, show rent plus nonoptional fees as the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, and state whether utilities are included in rent; getting that wrong carries treble damages and possible attorney fees. And under § 504B.118, subd. 3, as amended with effect from August 1, 2026, you may not charge a tenant any fee for using an alternative to a digital payment platform.

Practical advice: a variable overage is hard to square with a first-page Total Monthly Payment figure. If you want cost certainty on a property where the allowance is lawful, consider putting the utility in the tenant's own name with the provider instead, or building the expected cost into rent, rather than running an allowance you then have to disclose as a nonoptional fee of unknown size.

title: A Utility Deposit You Hold Is Just Part of the Security Deposit
bodyText: Minnesota has no separate category of landlord-held utility deposit and no separate return rule for one. Two rules fill the gap, and the second is stricter than most landlords expect. First, the definition: the deposit section governs any deposit of money whose function is to secure performance of the rental agreement or any part of it, other than money that is exclusively an advance payment of rent. Money you take to secure the tenant's payment of utilities under the lease secures part of the agreement, so it is a security deposit however the lease labels it - one percent simple noncompounded interest, return with interest or a written statement of the specific reasons for withholding within three weeks of the tenancy ending, withholding limited to what is reasonably necessary, the burden of proof on you, the penalty and the bad-faith award, and no waiver. Unpaid utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease are other funds due to you under an agreement, so you may withhold for them out of the one deposit you hold. Second, if the property is a shared-metered residential building and you bill the tenant for utilities separately from rent, Minnesota closes the door on extra charges entirely. The only charges you may add are one administrative billing charge of up to $8 per billing period and one late payment charge of up to $5 a month, and no other fees or charges may be imposed on or collected from tenants for utility service. A separate utility deposit would be another charge for utility service, and those rules cannot be waived or modified. The same thinking now reaches the end of the tenancy: where you have to estimate a final submetered or apportioned bill because the real one has not arrived, no additional fees or charges may be assessed beyond those two. Deposits the utility itself charges are a different thing and are between the tenant and the utility; a utility may not charge a deposit to a customer who has entered into a payment agreement during the cold weather period, and a tenant who pays current water and sewer charges to keep service on because you did not pay is not subject to any deposit requirements. One point of history worth knowing: the old shared-metered section, Minn. Stat. 504B.215, was repealed in 2024, so do not rely on it; the rules now sit in Minn. Stat. 504B.216 and Minn. Stat. 216B.023.

title: You Can Be Copied on a Tenant Shutoff Notice, but Only if the Tenant Asks
bodyText:
Minnesota's cold weather rule builds in a third-party contact. Under Minn. Stat. § 216B.096, subd. 2(i), a utility must tell customers that it 'will send a copy of any future notice of proposed disconnection of utility heating service to a third party designated by the residential customer'. It must also explain how to request that, and tell the customer to contact the intended third party first. That third party can be you.

The designation belongs to the tenant, not to you. There is no mechanism in Minnesota law by which a landlord authorises the utility to copy them — no owner-side affidavit, no separate document you can file. So ask, do not require. The optional lease section this library offers invites the tenant to name you and says plainly that declining is not a breach.

Why it is worth asking for: a shutoff in a Minnesota winter is a frozen-pipe claim waiting to happen, and the notice gives you days of warning. Customers get this information automatically, because the utility must send every customer a summary of rights and responsibilities between August 15 and October 1 each year, and to every new customer when service starts (§ 216B.096, subds. 2(h) and 3). Once named, you also receive the written notice of the right to appeal a disconnection decision (subd. 8(a)).

Two limits to keep in mind. The regime covers utility heating service — natural gas or electricity used as a primary heating source for the customer's primary residence — and it applies to public utilities and electing cooperatives, with municipal utilities and cooperatives handled differently (§ 216B.096, subds. 1, 2(j), 2(k) and 9). And being copied changes none of your own duties. You still owe heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit from October 1 through April 30 under § 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(5), and that covenant cannot be waived or modified.

title: A Submeter Shutoff Is Still a Shutoff — and Minnesota Treats It as a Crime
bodyText:
If you submeter, the remote shutoff or load limiter is the single most dangerous feature you own. Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 12(a) prohibits 'Disconnection of a tenant's utility service by a landlord for the failure to pay utility service charges'. Subdivision 12(g)(2) then defines disconnection to include 'installation of a service or load limiter or any device that limits or interrupts utility service in any way'. Throttling a tenant's service is disconnecting it. Never use the submeter as a collection tool.

What it costs if you do. A violation of subd. 12 is a violation of § 504B.221 (subd. 12(f)), which gives the tenant treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees. An intentional interruption meant to push a tenant out is a misdemeanour under § 504B.225. That section presumes the unlawful intent once the tenant proves you interrupted service deliberately, and the burden is on you to rebut it. The tenant can also go to court for an immediate order putting them back in possession, because § 504B.375 treats constructive exclusion 'which may include the termination of utilities' as grounds for relief the sheriff then executes. Loss of heat, electricity, running water, hot water or sanitary facilities is separately an emergency under § 504B.381, which a tenant can take to a judge ex parte on 24 hours' notice to you. And § 504B.231 adds treble damages or $500 plus fees for a bad-faith ouster. None of these can be waived by anything in a lease.

What you may lawfully do. You may interrupt service to repair or replace faulty equipment, or to protect occupants' health and safety. Section 504B.221(a)(3) limits the tenant to actual damages where you do that and restore service, or make a good faith effort to, within a reasonable time. The tenant is also limited to actual damages where they never told you about an interruption (§ 504B.221(a)(1)), or where you reinstated or took other remedial action within a reasonable time after being told (§ 504B.221(a)(2)). So document the reason, give notice where you can, and restore quickly — that is what converts a treble-damages claim into an actual-damages one. It is also a defence that the interruption resulted from the tenant's own deliberate or negligent act.

For unpaid utility bills, use the route the statute gives you instead. Offer the payment plan § 216B.023, subd. 7 requires, and if the tenant fails two consecutive payments on it, bring a breach-of-lease claim under § 504B.285, subd. 4 as § 504B.216, subd. 12(c) and (d) allow. Nothing stops the utility itself from disconnecting your building as the law otherwise allows (§ 504B.216, subd. 12(a)).

title: In a Shared-Metered Building You Must Be the Customer of Record
bodyText: Minnesota does not leave this to choice. Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 2(a) provides that the landlord of a shared-metered residential building 'must be the bill payer responsible and must be the customer of record contracting with a utility provider for utility service'. You must also tell the utility provider that the services apply to a shared-metered residential building. A shared-metered residential building is one with more separate dwelling units than meters (subd. 1(e)). Manufactured home parks are expressly excluded. You also may not move a tenant off their own account. Subdivision 2(b): 'A landlord is prohibited from removing a directly metered tenant from the tenant's existing utility account or requesting that a utility remove the tenant from the tenant's existing utility account.' Asking the utility to do it is as much a breach as doing it. Neither rule can be contracted around. Subdivision 2(c) says in terms: 'This subdivision may not be waived by contract or otherwise.' And a violation of subd. 2 is both a violation of § 504B.161 — your non-waivable habitability covenants — and a violation of § 504B.221, which carries treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees (§ 504B.216, subd. 16). The attorney general may investigate and prosecute violations of the section as well (subd. 17). The practical consequence: in a shared-metered building the utility debt is yours, whatever the lease says about who reimburses you. Bill tenants under the rules in § 504B.216 and § 216B.023 if you want to recover the cost, but do not try to put the account itself in a tenant's name, and do not let a third-party billing agent do it for you — 'landlord' includes a third-party billing agent (subd. 1(c)).

title: What Happens if You Fall Behind on the Building Utility Bill
bodyText: Minnesota gives tenants a detailed self-help route when the landlord's own utility bill goes unpaid, and it costs you money and sometimes the account. Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 13 sets it out, and it applies to natural gas, electricity, water and sewer, and also to home heating oil and propane. It starts with a notice you do not control. When the provider issues a final notice proposing to disconnect the building because you have not paid, it must post notice to residents in at least one conspicuous place in or on the building. That posting must give the shutoff date, a number to call, a description of the tenants' rights to continue or restore service, and advice to seek help from legal aid, a private attorney or a housing organisation. A tenant or group of tenants may then pay to keep or restore service. They must first give you oral or written notice of their intention to pay after 48 hours, or a shorter reasonable period; an oral notice must be confirmed in writing within 24 hours. If you still have not paid, three things can follow. For gas or electricity, the tenants may pay the current charges for the most recent billing period and the provider must restore service for at least one billing period. In a building with fewer than five units, one tenant may tell the provider they will become the bill payer responsible and customer of record, and the provider must put the account in that tenant's name going forward. For water and sewer, the municipality must give a tenant a copy of each bill you fail to pay, and the tenant has a continuing right to pay the current charges and keep service, with no deposit and with reasonable notice of any disconnection. For heating oil or propane, the tenants may order and pay for one month's supply. 'Current charges' does not include your arrears or your late fees (subd. 13(d)), so the tenant never has to clear your debt to keep the lights on. Other tenants in the building may chip in on the paying tenant's account (subd. 13(e)). Then the part that hits your rent roll. Under subd. 13(i), after giving you documentation of the payment, the tenant 'may deduct the amount of the tenant's payment to the utility company or municipality from the rental payment next paid to the landlord', and that amount 'is considered payment of rent to the landlord for purposes of section 504B.291'. That is a utility remedy, not a general repair-and-deduct right — Minnesota has no general right for a tenant to do repairs and deduct the cost. But within its own subject it is real: the deduction counts as rent paid, so a nonpayment eviction built on the deducted amount will fail, and the tenant may redeem under § 504B.291 on that footing. You can get the account back. Under subd. 13(f), once you satisfy the provider's requirements for reestablishing service — including paying, or agreeing to pay, all arrears and other lawful charges on the account that went into the tenant's name — you may put service back in your own name. Where it goes if nothing is fixed. Loss of running water, hot water, heat, electricity or sanitary facilities is an emergency a tenant can take to a judge ex parte on 24 hours' notice (§ 504B.381). A tenant may escrow rent with the court administrator and ask for abatement (§ 504B.385). And on a tenant remedies action a court may appoint an administrator to run the building, contract for utility services and pay for them out of rents (§ 504B.425, § 504B.445) — at which point your own right to collect rent is 'void and unenforceable' until the administration ends, and not only against the tenant who petitioned (§ 504B.435). So yes, tenants can effectively get a receiver put over a building where the landlord does not pay the utility. None of these tenant rights can be waived or modified (§ 504B.216, subd. 14(2)), and they do not extend to conditions caused by the tenant's own willful, malicious or negligent conduct (subd. 14(1)). Separately, a municipality keeps its power to charge the owner and certify unpaid water and sewer charges against the property for collection as taxes (§ 504B.216, subd. 13(g); § 444.075, subd. 3e).

title: You Cannot Evict for Unpaid Utilities in Winter, in a Heat Emergency, or on a Medical Emergency
bodyText: These rules apply in a shared-metered building: one where fewer meters measure the building's gas, electricity or water than it has units (Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 1(e); a manufactured home park is excluded). There, utilities you bill separately from rent are enforceable, but only down a narrow channel, and three situations close it entirely. Start with the precondition. Under Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 12(d)(1) you may not bring a breach claim for unpaid utilities 'unless the landlord has offered the tenant a payment plan under section 216B.023, subdivision 7, and the tenant has failed to make two consecutive payments on the plan'. Section 216B.023, subd. 7 requires that plan to be reasonable and to take account of the tenant's financial and any extenuating circumstances they disclose, and requires you to tell the tenant about the Commission's consumer affairs office if you cannot agree. So the payment plan is not optional goodwill; it is the gate. Then the three bars. Under subd. 12(d)(2) an eviction action may not be filed, and any eviction already filed must be stayed, in each of three situations. The first is failure to pay natural gas or electric utility charges during the cold weather period. The second is failure to pay electric charges during a heat emergency. The third is where the tenant tells you or the court that the tenant or a household member has a medical emergency, or that life-sustaining medical equipment needing electricity is in use. For that third one the tenant must supply certification from a licensed medical health care professional within five days of the notice. The cold weather period is October 1 through April 30 (§ 216B.096, subd. 2(b)). A heat emergency is 'any period when an excessive heat watch, heat advisory, or excessive heat warning issued by the National Weather Service is in effect' (subd. 12(g)(3)). Also, rent comes first. Subdivision 12(b): 'If a landlord asserts a tenant owes rent and utilities, sums paid by the tenant to the landlord must first be applied to unpaid rent.' You cannot allocate a payment to the utility balance to manufacture a rent arrears. And in court the tenant does not have to pay to be heard. Under § 504B.285, subd. 4(b), if the tenant has a Public Utilities Commission complaint pending about shared-metered gas or electricity, the court must stay the action and may not require the tenant to pay money into court, post a bond, pay you directly or post security for any purpose before the complaint is finally disposed of — and may not require security for utility charges afterwards either. Where there is no Commission complaint, or the action is for water and sewer, a tenant who qualifies for a court fee waiver also may not be required to post anything (subd. 4(b)(2)); otherwise the court may in its discretion require security for prospective utility charges only (subd. 4(b)(3)). Subdivision 4(c) is broader still: 'A court must not require a tenant to post rent as a condition of a tenant asserting an affirmative claim or defense, or a counterclaim related to landlord utility billings or practices.' The practical upshot: treat separately billed utilities as a slow contract debt, not as leverage. Offer the payment plan early, document it, keep utility balances out of your rent ledger, and expect to wait until May for any eviction that rests on unpaid gas or electricity.

title: Minnesota's Cold Weather Rule, and What It Does and Does Not Do for You
bodyText: Minnesota protects heat in winter through the utility, not through the lease. The cold weather period runs October 1 through April 30 (Minn. Stat. § 216B.096, subd. 2(b)). It is not a blanket moratorium, and it adds no fixed number of days to a notice — it is a conditional protection a customer has to claim. Who it protects and how. A customer whose household income is at or below 50 percent of the state median may not be disconnected, and must be reconnected, if they enter and keep to a mutually acceptable payment agreement based on the household's resources. The utility may not require more than ten percent of household income toward current and past utility heating bills (subd. 5(a)). A customer above 50 percent of state median income also has the right to a payment agreement that takes their circumstances into account, and may not be disconnected while making timely payments under one (subd. 10). The timing rules are strict. The utility must send every customer a summary of rights and responsibilities between August 15 and October 1 each year, and to every new residential customer when service starts (subd. 3). Before disconnecting during the cold weather period it must give a commission-approved notice stating the disconnection date and amount due (subd. 4). It may not disconnect earlier than ten working days after mailing that notice, or seven after personal service, and may not disconnect on a Friday without personal contact and an offer of a payment agreement, nor on a weekend, holiday or the day before one, nor when its own or the Commission's offices are closed (subd. 7(c)). It must investigate whether the dwelling is actually occupied, including at least one visit (subd. 7(d)). Appeals go to the Commission within seven or ten working days depending on how the notice was served (subd. 8). What it does not do. It does not make you the utility's guarantor, and it does not relieve you of anything. If heat is your responsibility, you still owe at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit in all places intended for habitation, kitchens and bathrooms included, from October 1 through April 30 (§ 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(5)), and that covenant cannot be waived or modified. The regime also reaches only 'utility heating service' — natural gas or electricity used as a primary heating source for the customer's primary residence — supplied by a public utility or an electing cooperative; municipal utilities and cooperatives are handled under other sections (subds. 1, 2(j), 2(k) and 9). Minnesota has no statute reachable here barring disconnection during a declared storm or weather emergency as such; what it has instead is the cold weather period and, for electricity, a heat emergency.

title: Never Cut Off a Utility Because the Tenant Did Not Transfer the Account
bodyText:
In some states a lease can give the landlord the right to shut off a utility still in the landlord's name if the tenant has not moved it into their own within a few days. Do not use that clause in Minnesota. It would be unenforceable, and acting on it would expose you to damages, a possession order against you, and a criminal charge.

Minn. Stat. § 504B.221(a) gives a tenant treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees where the landlord 'interrupts or causes the interruption of electricity, heat, gas, or water services to the tenant'. Section 504B.221(b) voids any lease provision waiving the section as contrary to public policy, so the clause itself buys you nothing.

Worse, § 504B.225 makes an intentional interruption carried out with intent to remove or exclude a tenant a misdemeanour, and it presumes that intent once the tenant shows you interrupted service deliberately. The burden is then on you to rebut the presumption. A landlord who cuts off a utility to force a tenant to open their own account is in exactly that position. The tenant can also seek an immediate order restoring possession, because § 504B.375 reaches constructive exclusion 'which may include the termination of utilities'. And § 504B.231 adds treble damages or $500 plus fees for a bad-faith ouster.

In a shared-metered building, § 504B.216, subd. 12(a) prohibits disconnection for unpaid utility charges outright, and subd. 2 bars you from taking a directly metered tenant off their own account or asking the utility to do it — language that 'may not be waived by contract or otherwise'.

What to do instead. Make the transfer a lease obligation with a deadline and a written confirmation, and make the consequence a money claim: if you get billed for a utility that is the tenant's, bill it back as a contract debt, not as rent. Keep it out of the rent ledger, because an unpaid fee is not a nonpayment-of-rent ground on its own. If the tenant still will not comply, the route is a breach-of-lease claim through the eviction process, never the meter.

Once an account has moved into a tenant's name after your own default, § 504B.216, subd. 13(f) lets you put it back in yours once you have paid or agreed to pay the arrears and other lawful charges on it.

title: No Minnesota Veteran Rent Incentive, and Veteran Status Is Not a Protected Class
bodyText: Minnesota offers a private landlord no rent credit, tax credit, subsidy, guarantee or other incentive for renting to a veteran or a servicemember, and imposes no veteran preference on private rental housing. Veteran status is also not an enumerated protected class in housing. The grounds in Minn. Stat. Sec. 363A.09 are race, color, creed, religion, national origin, sex, gender identity, marital status, status with regard to public assistance, disability, sexual orientation, and familial status. Veteran and military status are not among them, and the 2026 amendment to the public-policy section did not add them. Two qualifications. A veteran who receives a federal, state or local subsidy or rental assistance is protected on that basis, because status with regard to public assistance is an enumerated ground and Sec. 363A.03, subd. 47 defines it to include a tenant receiving rental assistance or rent supplements. And a veteran with a service-connected disability is protected on the disability ground, under Minnesota own definition at Sec. 363A.03, subd. 12. So in practice many veteran applicants are protected - just not for being veterans. The word veteran does appear in Minnesota law in places that are not about you. Minn. Stat. Sec. 469.002, subd. 23 defines veterans for the purposes of housing and redevelopment authorities, where a federal contract may provide for veterans preferences; Sec. 484.01 preserves the veterans preference in public employment; and Sec. 82.55 refers to lenders certified by the Veterans Administration. The Minnesota Constitution mentions veterans once, at art. XIII, Sec. 8, which empowers the state to pay adjusted compensation to those who served during the Vietnam conflict or the Persian Gulf War. None of that is a landlord incentive. If you choose to give veterans a discount or a preference, that is your commercial decision. Make sure it is not operated so as to disadvantage an enumerated protected class, and remember that Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.120 requires every nonoptional fee to be disclosed in the lease and in the first-page Total Monthly Payment, so a veteran discount has to be presented as a genuine reduction and not as a fee on everybody else.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule in Minnesota, but Hot Water Is Not Optional
bodyText: Minnesota sets no maximum water heater temperature for a rental, and no duty to adjust one between tenancies. There is no Minnesota counterpart to the Wisconsin rule that a unit-only water heater be set to a maximum before each new tenant moves in, or to the Washington energy-code setting rule. WHAT MINNESOTA DOES REQUIRE: HOT WATER ITSELF, AND A MINIMUM HEAT TEMPERATURE. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(2) makes you covenant to keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair, INCLUDING the services and conditions listed in Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.381, subdivision 1. That list includes the loss of running water, the loss of hot water, the loss of heat, the loss of electricity and the loss of sanitary facilities, each treated as an emergency a tenant can take straight to court under Sec. 504B.381. So hot water is not optional in a Minnesota rental - it is part of a covenant the parties may not waive or modify under subd. 1(b). The one temperature Minnesota does fix is the other direction: Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(5) makes you equip or furnish heat at a minimum of 68 degrees Fahrenheit in all places intended for habitation, including kitchens and bathrooms, from October 1 through April 30, unless a utility company requires and instructs the heat to be reduced. Nothing caps how hot the tap can get. ONE PLACE A 120-DEGREE RULE DOES EXIST, AND IT IS NOT YOURS. Laws 2026, ch. 127 sets child-care centre rules under which the water temperature in sinks accessible to children must not exceed 120 degrees Fahrenheit to prevent scalding, and the furnace, hot water heater and utility rooms must be inaccessible to children. That duty is on the licensed programme, not on the building's owner. If you let to a licensed child-care provider, expect them to need the setting changed, and decide in the lease who may adjust the thermostat on the heater. WHAT TO DO. Nothing is required, but a scald injury to a child or an older tenant is a real exposure and Minnesota gives you a non-waivable fitness covenant to be judged against. Set the heater to a sensible temperature, say in the lease that the tenant must not raise it, and keep the setting documented at move-in alongside the other inspection records. Remember that the State Plumbing Code and the State Building Code may contain their own requirements: those are Minnesota Rules.

title: Waterbeds: No Minnesota Statute, and Four Rules That Shape the Clause
bodyText:
Minnesota says nothing about waterbeds. Nothing requires you to allow one, nothing lets you refuse one as of right, nothing sets a deposit or an insurance requirement, and there is no notice to give. It is a lease question - and it has to be decided in the lease, before the tenant signs.

Four Minnesota rules shape the clause you write.

First, money. Do not invent a waterbed fee or a non-refundable waterbed deposit. Anything you take to secure the tenant's performance or to cover damage is a security deposit under Minn. Stat. section 504B.178, which carries interest, a statutory return procedure and penalties, and whose 'attempted waiver... by a landlord and tenant, by contract or otherwise, shall be void and unenforceable'. And if the charge is one the tenant cannot avoid, Minn. Stat. section 504B.120 requires it to be disclosed in the lease and included in the Total Monthly Payment on the first page, with treble damages for getting it wrong.

Second, insurance is allowed but limited. You may require renter's or liability insurance covering water damage while the item is there, and asking for proof is reasonable. What you may not do is use the insurance requirement to move your own repair duty onto the tenant - the covenants in Minn. Stat. section 504B.161, subd. 1 cannot be waived or modified by the parties under subd. 1(b).

Third, damage. The repair covenant excepts disrepair 'caused by the willful, malicious, or irresponsible conduct of the tenant' or of someone under the tenant's direction or control, so a burst waterbed is recoverable on ordinary principles - but normal wear and tear and pre-existing damage are not, and a clause that says otherwise will not help you when the deposit is deducted.

Fourth, the lease probably already covers it. The library's Use of Property and Common Areas clause says the tenant will not keep a waterbed or other water-filled furniture at the property without the landlord's prior written consent, and that clause applies in Minnesota. So the question for a Minnesota lease is usually not whether to ban waterbeds, but whether to add the conditions on which you will consent - a frame and liner, an approved location and floor, and proof of insurance.

One quirk if you ever operate a manufactured home park, which this lease is not for: Minn. Stat. section 327C.03, subd. 3 prohibits a park owner from charging a resident any fee 'which is based on... the type of personal property used or located in the home'. In a park, a waterbed surcharge is prohibited outright rather than merely ill-advised.

title: No Minnesota Window Guard Requirement or Lease Notice
bodyText: Minnesota has no window guard law. There is no requirement to install window guards or fall-prevention devices, no duty to offer them to a tenant with a young child, no bold-type lease notice, no model notice text set by regulation, and no tenant request procedure. If you are used to the New York City or New Jersey pattern -- a prescribed window guard notice in the lease, a tenant checkbox, and installation on request where a child under a certain age lives in the unit -- Minnesota has none of it. WHERE THE WORD "WINDOW" ACTUALLY APPEARS. Three places matter and none is a guard rule. First, energy efficiency: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(3) covenants that you will make the premises and all common areas reasonably energy efficient "by installing weatherstripping, caulking, storm windows, and storm doors" where the measure will produce energy cost savings exceeding its cost including interest, amortised over the following ten years. That is a storm window duty, not a safety guard duty. Second, unlawful exclusion: Sec. 504B.375 treats constructive removal of a tenant as including "the termination of utilities or the removal of doors, windows, or locks" -- so taking a window out to force a tenant out is an ouster, and a lease provision waiving that section is "contrary to public policy and void". Third, lead. The lead chapter uses windows as a paint component, not as a fall hazard: Sec. 144.9504 speaks of windows and doors "covered with deteriorated lead-based paint" that should be repaired, stripped, planed or covered, and Sec. 144.9501's definitions treat window replacement as taking work outside "minor repair and maintenance". The lead chapter also uses the word "guards" -- "a reasonable effort must be made to protect the child and preserve the intact paint by the use of guards or other protective devices and methods" (Sec. 144.9504) -- but those are paint guards, not window guards. Minnesota's lead notice duties are covered separately by "Minnesota Lead Notices: None at Signing, One That Overrides Your Lease". WHAT YOU STILL OWE. Windows are part of the premises, so Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.161, subd. 1(a)(1) and (2) require them to be fit for the use intended and kept in reasonable repair, and those covenants cannot be waived or modified (subd. 1(b)). A window that will not stay shut, has a broken sash or latch, or has a defective screen is a repair matter and a potential "violation" under Sec. 504B.001, subd. 14(1) if it breaches a city housing code -- which opens the inspection route in Sec. 504B.185, rent escrow and the tenant remedies action. Guard, sill height, opening-limiter and emergency-escape-window requirements for new and altered construction live in the State Building Code, which is rules and not statute. OUR ADVICE, since there is no statute to follow. If a tenant with a young child asks for a window guard, treat it as a request you may grant rather than one you must. Do not promise a guard in the lease unless you intend to install and maintain it, because a promise to repair or install becomes your obligation once made. Check your city's housing code: a few Minnesota cities address window openings and screens in their property maintenance ordinances. And if you do fit guards, make sure they still allow the window to be opened for escape, which the building code requires of bedroom windows.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Minnesota follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Minn. Stat. § 336.3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Minn. Stat. § 336.1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Minnesota's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Minn. Stat. ch. 504B searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Minnesota's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
